entries.title: skill-trigger-bench: listing-budget lint plus a trigger eval with a negative control
entries.why: Two checks for the 'I wrote a skill and the agent never uses it' failure (Python 3.10 or newer, no dependencies, an optional YAML parser; CI for lint and skills; a composite CI action). Its lint runs offline over a folder of skill directories, or one skill: the skill format's spec rules, frontmatter among them, plus a description that 'says what it does, never when to use it', a description budget (all descriptions together against a --budget default of about 15,000 characters), trigger overlap (a TF-IDF cosine of 0.35 or more, listing the shared terms), duplicate names, a body over 500 lines and missing references; output in JSON, SARIF or a code host's CI format, a suggest mode that never edits, and exit 1 on errors. The number that matters is the author's own run over a personal skill folder of the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs: 43 skills whose descriptions total 22,086 characters against the ~15,000 budget, so 'roughly 13 of them may never be shown to the model.' Per the README, descriptions share a listing budget, and once enough skills are installed some are 'silently never offered'; it also prints two real collisions between near-namesake skills, at cosine 0.56 and 0.50. Its eval measures whether a skill is reached for: each prompt is one run of that harness in its headless stream mode, in a fresh temporary project with only the chosen skills and project-only settings, so the user's own skills do not leak in, tools that could change anything turned off and turns capped at 2; only an explicit call of the harness's skill tool naming the skill counts, not reading the skill file by hand. It reports a trigger rate and a false-trigger rate and exits 1 below a minimum trigger rate (default 0.8) or above a maximum false-trigger rate (default 0.2); a dry run prints the prompts with no calls, and a prompt file supplies 10 or more should-trigger and should-not-trigger cases. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, we install the shared skills into six homes with no description budget and no trigger check, and have already paid for the class twice: one seat's copy of the Lab source-collect skill is malformed, with no YAML frontmatter, so it cannot be loaded by name, which the lint's frontmatter rule would flag; and the skill catalog in a live session is large enough that the description budget is plausibly blown. Per the pack, kept deadweight (2026-10-22) audits whether configuration is ignored, kept skillwharf (2026-10-01) counts which skills fired, from logs, after the fact, and kept catstack, driftproof, Harness Wrangler and the blind A/B skill-eval card measure whether a skill improves output; none measures whether a skill is chosen, with a negative control, and the false-trigger side is the part we lack: a skill that fires on everything scores a perfect trigger rate and is useless. We already have: a fleet installer that wires the vault's standing instruction files into the coding CLIs' homes, and the shared skill bundles, canonical in the vault, into the skill homes of two seats and the project mirrors (#skills), marked enforced in the controls inventory on the evidence of seven links that resolve to the fleet contract and one matching checksum, a check run on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory); a byte ceiling on the two files every agent reads before every task, 13,489 B for the fleet contract and 81,155 B for the never-again list (#resident-budget), folded from kept coding-agent-guardrails (2026-09-28), which per the pack caps always-on rules, not the skill listing; the promotion-gate rule that moves a routine or skill up the autonomy ladder only with three clean runs, a rollback tried once and a complete receipt (#promotion-gate), and a replay regression check before a skill or prompt change is promoted, marked proposed in that inventory because its replay set of our own failures is not built yet (#replay-check, #replay-set); and, as policy text only, a new check counted only once it has been seen failing on a deliberately broken input, and a check that examined nothing reporting a gap, never a pass (#check-can-fail). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the offline lint first, with no model, on a copy of each of the six shared skill homes, recording the total description characters and the overlaps; then the eval's dry run; then a 10+10 prompt eval on one shared skill with a negative control; the budget treated as a per-harness measurement, not the tool's 15,000-character constant; and the pack's playbook line: a skill that is never listed cannot be chosen: measure the listing budget and the trigger rate, and ship a negative control so a skill that fires on everything cannot pass. entries.title: lcc: compaction that keeps spans verbatim, stashes what it drops and explains every cut
entries.why: Local context compiler (Python 3.11 or newer; a CLI, a tool server and a plugin for the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs; on the Python package index as local-context-compiler, since the package named lcc there is unrelated) whose compaction does not summarize: kept spans stay byte-identical, removed tool outputs go to a content-addressed stash, and recall re-hashes on read; the placeholder left in a cut's place states lines and size, not tokens, plus the recall id. Every pass writes a relevance-compaction-1.2 JSON report, and its explain command, given the report and the source, gives the reason for every kept or dropped block. Providers are local by default: a rules provider with lossless, recoverable and stashed modes, a local trained ranker and a mechanical provider; an optional remote ranking provider is opt-in only, needs a key and can be switched off by an environment variable, because 'having a key is not consent to send context off-machine.' Its plugin refuses a pass below a 25% gain and keeps the harness's built-in summary, and the report exposes the provider used and whether the pass degraded. The evidence is the author's, not ours: one real session of 193 messages and 75 tool calls went from 57,083 to 28,807 tokens (−49.5%), 43 of 43 messages byte for byte and 33 tool outputs removed, each one recallable; across 266 long sessions the median cut was 22.7% (middle half 15–32%, best 65%), with 0 messages lost; a pre-registered 172-request test found an agent answering from the stashed context plus recall did as well as full context on file recall (+0.006, 95% CI −0.023 to +0.034) with 36.6% fewer tokens, calling recall for 90% of questions about removed content; and a summary of the same sessions in the style of a built-in compact command got 73% of exact values right, against 98% for full or verbatim context. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our long runs, packs and stream transcripts are lossy at the boundary: kept compaction-stress-lab (2026-10-11) measured how lossy, one compaction keeping about 1 in 5 exact tool-printed details, but it is a study, not a mechanism; kept context-guard (2026-09-30) caps growth and forces a handoff; kept agent-memory (2026-10-22) lints memory rot; kept ai-coding-gateway trims noisy tool output; and none makes a cut inspectable and reversible. Per the pack, the transferable rule is one we keep asserting in prose, that a lossy step must leave a receipt, what was dropped and why, and a hash-checked way back, with 'structural PASS is not answer quality' as the honest boundary the README itself draws; and none of it is applied here: no per-drop receipt, no recall id, no re-hash on read and no rule that keeps the summary when the gain is under 25%. We already have: streaming output required on every long Mac CLI run, one seat having no stream-json mode and a compressed session file (#launch), a convention that nothing blocks (#controls-inventory); the vault as the team's long-term memory, a context repo rather than a chat log (#vault); done receipts whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted, a manual control in that inventory (#done-receipt), and, as policy text only, a check that examined nothing reporting a gap, never a pass, while a passing check says what it examined (#check-can-fail); the promotion-gate rule that a routine or skill moves up the autonomy ladder only with a complete receipt, each run's record of what it did, its inputs, outputs and side effects, beside three clean runs and a rollback tried once (#promotion-gate); the 10-11 run-log lesson, not a Decision lock, in which a tracing plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hung 1.5–6+ minutes per tool call and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons); and an ai-coding-gateway-style trim of noisy tool output listed among the Lab follow-ups as new practice, not installed (playbook §11, Lab follow-ups). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pattern plus a measure-only trial: its measure-session command run offline on one stored transcript, counts only, and its explain command on a compacted copy; the receipt fields, dropped span ids, hash, recall id and the degraded flag, adopted for pack truncation; no install of its compaction plugin until the seat's harness version supports function hooks and we have a rollback; and the pack's playbook line: a cut you cannot inspect is a guess: keep spans verbatim, stash what you remove, and make every drop explain itself with a hash-checked way back. The pack's stop condition: if the transcripts are unreadable or the 25% floor is not met, keep only the receipt pattern, with no blocking compaction and no remote provider. Installing its plugin or tool server in a live seat, setting the early-access function-hooks flag, compacting or blocking a live session, turning on the remote ranking provider, or changing how packs are truncated would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and any hook change is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the evidence numbers all come from the author's own sessions; its local trained ranker was trained on transcripts of the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs, so two of our other seats are out of distribution, and plain text uses the mechanical provider; the plugin needs version 2.1.274 or later of that harness and an early-access function-hooks flag; its protection rules 'reduce, but do not rule out, lost evidence'; the optional remote ranking provider sends context off-machine and, per the pack, must stay off; an Apache-2.0 notice covers one optional integration; MIT, 15 stars, created 2026-06-19, pushed 2026-10-23 08:54 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: skillrouter: a small resident skill core, the rest of the library searched on demand
entries.why: Skill router for an agent host (Node 20 or newer; a CLI, a local tool server and a routing skill; version 0.2.0-beta.1) that splits an agent's skill library into two tiers to prevent context bloat: the core, a minimal set of frequently used skills, stays preloaded in the host's prompt, and the library, the broader collection, stays on disk and is searched on demand through two lightweight tools on its tool server, search_skills and read_skill. Its diagnostic CLI has doctor, which verifies host connectivity and tool registration, index --root over a folder of local skill directories, and search; trim --dry-run inspects which skills can be safely offloaded from the host's preloaded configuration to the on-demand library, without deleting files; and a standing routing instruction tells the agent: 'before non-trivial work, search relevant skills and read matching instructions; follow host permissions and use only skills relevant to the task.' Why it matters here: per the collection pack, kept skill-trigger-bench (2026-10-23) points to the listing-budget limit: in its author's run, 43 skills had descriptions totaling 22,086 characters against a budget of about 15,000 characters in the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs, a budget that card calls community-measured, not an official constant, so roughly 13 of them may never be shown to the model. Per the pack, we install the shared skills into six homes, and every skill is preloaded, all or nothing, in each seat's skill directory, so as more skills are added the preloaded listing risks blowing the budget and hiding critical skills; this is the architectural remedy, a lean resident core kept in the prompt and the rest queried through fast local tools on demand, and none of it is applied here. We already have: a fleet installer that wires the vault's standing instruction files into the homes of the coding CLIs, and the two shared skill bundles, canonical in the vault, into the skill homes of two seats and the project mirrors (#skills), marked enforced in the controls inventory on the evidence of seven links that resolve to the fleet contract and one copy whose checksum matches, a check run on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory); a byte ceiling on the two files every agent reads before every task, 13,489 B for the fleet contract and 81,155 B for the never-again list, which covers those two files only (#resident-budget); the promotion-gate rule that moves a routine or skill up the autonomy ladder only with three clean runs, a rollback tried once and a complete receipt, a manual control in that inventory (#promotion-gate); and a replay regression check before a skill or prompt change is promoted, marked proposed there because its replay set of our own failures is not built yet (#replay-check, #replay-set). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the small resident core plus on-demand library architecture, tried first in a scratch project: its doctor command run and one skill directory indexed, search_skills and read_skill tested there, and a check of whether on-demand search frees resident context without lowering the trigger rate; and the pack's playbook line: preload the core, route the rest: keep a minimal skill core resident in the prompt and let the model retrieve specialized skills on demand via a local tool server to stay well under listing budgets. The pack's stop condition: if on-demand search adds high latency, more than 3 s per call, or the model fails to search for skills that are not preloaded, keep the skills resident. Installing its tool server or routing skill in a live seat, offloading any skill from a live seat's preloaded listing, adding its routing instruction to a seat's standing instruction file, or changing the fleet installer or the shared skill homes would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and a change to the installer is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, which counts writes to shared state or across repos, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the 43 skills, the 22,086 characters and the estimate that roughly 13 skills may never be shown come from the author's run in the skill-trigger-bench card the pack cites, not ours and not this project's; per the pack, the extra tools add latency, a search and a read before the work, and the model has to recognize when to search for a skill instead of having it resident in its system prompt; version 0.2.0-beta.1 is a pre-release and needs Node 20 or newer; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-22 21:20 PT, pushed 2026-10-24 09:08 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: yardgoat: a verifier frozen by hash decides done, and a blocked task parks its question
entries.why: Task coordination engine, its 'yard engine', for coding-agent CLIs of different kinds (Python 3.10 or newer; a CLI and a task reconciler; adapters for three coding CLIs, all three run by our seats (#roster), and for a plain shell), with three formal guarantees. One owner per task: only the registered owner can dispatch or verify, and ownership is transferred explicitly and survives controller restarts. No duplicate dispatch: re-dispatching an active task returns the existing run, and an exited run must be verified before another attempt. 'A receipt, not a vibe': process exit and task verification are strictly separated, and a task passes only when its verifier command, frozen by hash at submit time, exits 0. Question parking: a worker that is blocked or needs human input writes out/BLOCKED.md, and the task parks automatically; yardgoat inbox displays the pending human questions, yardgoat answer supplies the human decision, and yardgoat reconcile, run from cron or on an event, resumes execution. Its yardgoat quick command, given a prompt and a verify command, generates a complete task card, the frozen verifier and a spec in a single command, and warm execution pools reuse agent sessions across tasks. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it implements three of what the pack calls our core harness locks: code decides done, where the agent's self-report is untrusted and only a deterministic verifier script frozen up front decides success; support for our mixed seats, through adapters for the coding CLIs they run; and the human gate, since, per the pack, the session gate needs Haiyuan's approval before destructive actions or ambiguous choices, and writing BLOCKED.md to park a task until an answer arrives replaces busy-waiting and keeps the agent from guessing. Per the pack, none of it is applied: we use custom shell wrappers and manual prompt dispatches. We already have: code decides done, under which a task is done only when a concrete, deterministic check passes, while agent self-reports and the decision layer's completion check are advisory only (#code-decides-done); a completion claim that counts only if the session record backs it, the EM and each reviewer scanning the diff for test tampering, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record); and done receipts whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that actually ran, each with evidence, and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted (#done-receipt), all three under completion validation, a manual control in the controls inventory (#controls-inventory). We also have exclusive ownership of a run's output, enforced since 2026-10-20 by an ownership guard that gives each launch an attempt ID, lets only the current attempt publish and refuses a restart unless the old process is proven dead (#watchdog-resume-safety); unknown outcomes after a crash or dirty exit parked for Haiyuan or the EM, not auto-retried (#retry-ceiling), and anything that cannot be undone in under a minute parked and asked, under the reversibility tiers (#gyr-authority); a kick ledger whose rows go from posted to launched to PR open or done, or to blocked with a note (#coding-em-kicks); and a decision queue, one file for the irreversible items and judgment calls waiting on Haiyuan, each with the question, options and our recommendation, an item unanswered for 3 or more days re-raised once (#decision-queue). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the frozen verifier hash requirement and the out/BLOCKED.md question-parking convention in our EM dispatchers, and a trial of yardgoat quick for reproducible test receipts, first run as yardgoat quick with a frozen verifier command on a simple task, with BLOCKED.md parking tested in yardgoat inbox; and the pack's playbook line: code decides done, questions park: verify task completion with a verifier command frozen by hash at submit time, and park blocked runs in a structured file rather than letting the agent guess. The pack's stop condition: if frozen verifiers cannot accommodate dynamic test output, or worker session locks fail on restart, adopt the BLOCKED.md convention only. Running it on a live seat or repository, routing a real kick through it, scheduling yardgoat reconcile from cron, or changing how the EM dispatches, verifies or parks work would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and a wrapper, cron or routine change is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the three guarantees are the README's own claims, read by the collector and not tested here; per the pack it is pre-alpha and its schema may change, and running agent sessions inside warm pools needs process monitoring so that crashed workers do not leave orphan locks; Apache-2.0, 0 stars, created 2026-10-23 03:32 PT, pushed 2026-10-24 08:45 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agents-kit: a versioned common block in every repo's instruction file, drift-checked
entries.why: Fleet CLI (Python) against instruction drift, corruption and maintenance friction across many repositories: it structures each repository's agent instruction file into two zones, a canonical common block between two HTML comments, BEGIN:agents-common with a version (v2.1 in the example the pack shows) and END:agents-common, holding the common rules (environment, execution loop, git, security), followed by the project-specific rules, preserved untouched. Its three core commands: audit scans the fleet's repositories and reports drift, that is versions, missing blocks, corrupted markdown and byte weight; check is a fast gate that exits non-zero, for CI or a pre-commit hook, when a common block has drifted from canonical; and sync cleanly updates the delimited block across all registered repositories while strictly preserving every project-specific section. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our fleet contract is synced from the vault to several seats, the home folder and the project roots by the vault's hook installer, and whole-file copying or symlinking has two severe failure modes: either project-specific instructions get overwritten, or repositories silently diverge because agents modify their local instructions; a delimited common block lets canonical fleet rules be updated idempotently without disturbing what is specific to each repository. Per the pack, none of it is applied: the installer does whole-file symlinks or copies, without delimited sections or drift detection. We already have: a fleet installer that symlinks the fleet contract into the homes of three coding CLIs, wires a global standing instruction file from the vault for another, and gives the project repos the vault contract and skill mirrors (#skills), marked enforced in the controls inventory on the evidence of seven links that resolve to the fleet contract and one copy whose checksum matches, a check run on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory), with a how-to-extend step that extends the installer when a new coding CLI has an instruction or skills home (#extend); the fleet contract touched only for fleet-wide standing rules, a Decision note plus a one-line pointer preferred (#vault), a manual control in which nothing checks the reason for an edit, and held to a byte ceiling of 13,489 B (#resident-budget) that it has reached, so an edit that adds bytes needs an equal trim, the size gates that guard it being report-only (#controls-inventory); a same-day sweep that carries a model or seat swap into the playbook, the fleet contract, the role cards and the affected skills (#model-change-sweep); and cited vault paths that must resolve, the Monday card sync checking those cited in the fleet contract and the role cards, with the lint tool not installed (#pointer-check). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): delimited common blocks in the vault's fleet contract and in the hook installer, and the check and audit pattern in our weekly consolidation to catch instruction rot, tried first by wrapping the canonical rules of the fleet contract in a BEGIN:agents-common block and testing sync on a temporary project directory; and the pack's playbook line: delimit the common, preserve the local: sync fleet-wide instruction-file rules inside versioned HTML comment blocks so canonical updates never clobber repository-specific instructions. The pack's stop condition: if delimiter parsing conflicts with markdown renderers or strips comments, drop the tool and keep the delimiter convention. Editing the fleet contract, including the wrap of the pack's first trial, moving the installer from whole-file links and copies to block sync, running sync on any live home or repository, or wiring check into a hook or CI would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and an installer change is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, which counts writes to shared state or across repos, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). entries.title: git-warden: a pre-receive push wall with green, yellow and red verdicts and quarantine
entries.why: External push guard for autonomous coding agents (Go 1.24 or newer; two binaries, push-guard and backup-guard) that intercepts git push before commits reach the remote, so that only checked SHAs get through: its pre-receive hook reads the remote refs fresh with git ls-remote, never trusting the agent's local tracking state, isolates the new objects in quarantine and evaluates its rules, a secret scan among them, keeping push.jsonl as the audit trail and red pushes as bundles under pending/. Its gate has three colors: green is an atomic fast-forward push to the real remote with the guard's own credentials (git push --porcelain --atomic), never with --force; yellow is a rejection returned with exact file:line:reason diagnostics, so the agent can self-repair without human intervention; and red is a hard block that needs human approval ('rejected: waiting for a human'), the commits quarantined in a git bundle and the owner notified by a command or a webhook. A backup guard adds append-only lineage tracking (git-everref) against branch deletion and history rewrites. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, client-side git hooks can be skipped with --no-verify or modified by an agent with shell access, while a pre-receive guard is a boundary the agent cannot bypass, which isolates unreviewed commits, runs secret scanning and cleanly implements our green, yellow and red ladder, enforcing what the pack calls our standing push rules: no exit while waiting, hermetic-first push and never pushing without review. Per the pack, none of it is applied: we rely on client-side checks and review gates before a push. We already have: an EM loop in which the implementer commits, pushes and opens the PR without waiting for reviewers, blind review starting only once a PR exists (#em-loop), and merge by Haiyuan only (#coding); reviews that count only with a verdict line on the current head SHA (#review-verdict-line); no exit while waiting, under which an agent does not end a turn waiting on background CI or live jobs with a dirty tree, but foregrounds to a durable exit or pushes hermetic-first and runs a second pass (#coding), a manual control whose wrapper gates for a dirty tree or an unchanged HEAD are hand-written per kick (#controls-inventory); an always-on play that keeps advisory policy in skills and must-hold rules in hooks, no secrets in a diff and no push to main among them (#em-loop); a test-tamper scan that also looks for commits made with --no-verify, which skips the repo's hooks, policy text only (#check-can-fail); an approval that covers the item as approved, the PR head SHA included, re-checked right before the RED action runs, policy text only (#approval-recheck); and, for vault notes, a manual control with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook (#controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a study of its pre-receive quarantine and its yellow and red feedback as a pattern for a remote push gate, evaluated against a prior push-gate Lab card the pack cites (history not confirmed here); a first trial on a test bare repository with its pre-receive hook, verifying that atomic pushes are accepted and that unreviewed pushes and force-pushes are rejected with yellow or red diagnostics; and the pack's playbook line: guard the remote at the door: place a pre-receive push wall between agents and Git remotes so force-pushes, secrets, and unreviewed commits are quarantined before hitting upstream. The pack's stop condition: if the bare intermediary repository creates excessive push latency or authentication complexity with the code host's remotes, keep the local push gates. Putting it in front of a real remote, handing it push credentials, a permissions change on the RED list (#gyr-authority), letting it notify anyone by command or webhook, running its backup guard on a real repository, or changing any push path or gate would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and a hook or wrapper change is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: per the pack, it needs a bare intermediary repository or a daemon set up, and a secret scanner on PATH for its scans, and an intermediary remote adds setup overhead compared to the code host's standard branch protection; never pushing without review is not a rule in our playbook, where the implementer pushes and opens the PR before review and review gates the merge (#em-loop), while the pack's trial rejects unreviewed pushes; its colors are not our tiers: our GREEN, YELLOW and RED are reversibility tiers, kept apart from the autonomy ladder, and our YELLOW means allowed inside approved tools or lanes, while its yellow is a rejection (#gyr-authority, #autonomy-ladder); the pack speaks of our remote push gates, but no remote push gate is documented on the playbook; license NOASSERTION (MIT-compatible, per the pack, not checked here), 1 star, created 2026-10-02 16:39 PT, pushed 2026-10-24 08:45 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: continuity: a session ledger detects handoffs made stale by its own work
entries.why: Session continuity built around a record and a thin handoff, with a shared engine for a coding CLI and a second coding CLI. Its checkpoint command writes the current session's handoff JSON without ending the session: working directory, session id, git.head at checkpoint, branch, next action, open loops and uncommitted files from a per-session ledger of touched paths. It does not commit, merge or push; a handoff that fails lint is still written with the failure reported. The documented stop hook writes a skeleton without blocking if no handoff exists, but prompts an update and blocks that stop if this session's own work made an existing handoff stale. Staleness comes from touched files and session-owned commits in the ledger, rather than file age. After compaction it restores this session's handoff with a reminder to revalidate against the record; its context guard warns at 50% when usage data is available. Its improve-harness command routes a concrete mistake to its narrowest owning rule, skill, agent definition or memory, and independently reports over-limit instruction files and exact or near-duplicate rules, naming both files and line ranges. Both passes are report-only even unattended; agreed edits stay uncommitted. One CLI adapter refuses checklist and checkpoint writers from headless sessions and subagents; sweep is watch-only with no scheduler. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our handoff packet has no check that it still describes the tree, and the interrupted curate runs required manual state checks before resuming. The playbook confirms those checks and interruptions (#mac-run-lessons, #idempotent-resume). Per the pack, agent-role-contracts rejects stale handoffs at offline preflight and agent-memory lints stale facts after the fact; the proposed delta is staleness computed from this session's own edits at stop, plus a commit the next session can compare. The report-only instruction checks also give the repeat-lesson rule a mechanical proposal path; these checks are not applied here, per the pack. We already have: handoff packet v1, whose artifact holds the detail and whose packet holds the state, with a completeness check that is report-only, shadow only and never blocks, box-side and unverified from the Mac (#handoff-packet, #controls-inventory), rather than only the hand-followed format the pack describes; idempotent resume, which checks live state before each step that writes and skips completed steps, a manual step documented by the curate checks (#idempotent-resume, #mac-run-lessons); repeat lessons routed to a proposed diff at the owning source, a manual control (#repeat-lesson, #controls-inventory), inside daily consolidation, marked enforced in the inventory but box-side and unverified (#vault, #controls-inventory); a resident-policy byte ceiling whose fold size gates are report-only (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory); and replay before a skill or prompt promotion, proposed because the replay set is not built (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the two checks, rather than the plugin: add git.head and a touched-paths ledger to handoff packet v1 so the next session compares rather than trusts, and propose a report-only duplicate/over-limit pass over loaded instruction files. First trial checkpoint and pickup in one scratch repo before any live hook. The pack places the instruction pass in weekly consolidation; our consolidation is daily (#vault), while the Monday sync has the manual kill review (#kill-review, #controls-inventory). The pack's summary line for continuity: a handoff this session invalidated cannot be left standing. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit criterion is supplied for this KEEP; the stated boundary is a scratch-repo trial before a live hook. The playbook requires a pre-written routine kill condition, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Defining that criterion, changing the handoff packet or consolidation, installing a live stop or restore hook, or allowing automatic instruction edits would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work under the review-depth rule, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the blocking and staleness behavior above is read from documentation, not observed, as pack section 4 states; the adapter covers only the two coding CLIs, and per the pack our headless collect/curate runs would not receive the stop protection. A tmux-launched run needs an explicit kill path and a blocked-stop beat-log line. Shell-driven edits need explicit ledger registration and can go untracked; without a user-owned record destination the handoff points to nothing. The playbook now has report-only skill lint (#skills); that checks skills, not this proposed pass over loaded instruction files. Per the pack's collection-time blockers, the Mac had 12 GiB free, below the 15 GB long-launch hold line, and the vault write was refused; neither is a fresh health check here. The disk floor is a manual control outside the one queue that enforces it (#launch, #controls-inventory). entries.title: agent-ops-kit: only explicit IDLE skips a cycle; a broken precheck is WORK
entries.why: Four small pieces for headless scheduled loops, extracted by the author from a system running 119 background jobs (Python 3.10 or newer, standard library only, plus portable shell). Jobs touch a heartbeat file on success; missing or stale heartbeats become append-only alerts.jsonl findings, fingerprint-deduplicated to one unresolved alert per problem: 'Log, don't page.' A deterministic precheck prints IDLE or WORK: <reason>; only explicit IDLE may skip a cycle, while errors fail open into WORK, a corrupt config counts as enabled and a crashing precheck counts as work. Its wrapper orders kill switch, single-instance lock, precheck gate and wallclock budget with hard kill. The repair skill validates, classifies, fixes only if provably safe, verifies, rolls back on doubt and leaves one digest line, with shadow mode, at most 2 attempts, protected paths and human escalation. The author's 7-day audit of one real hourly loop found about 95% no-op runs and about $231 per week in API-equivalent spend for zero changes. This is one author's audit of one loop, not a benchmark and not our number. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, collect and curate decide nothing new by judgment, and a failed, rate-limited or stale lookup can look like a quiet hour. Only explicit IDLE being allowed to skip makes the negative-claim rule part of control flow. Per the pack, overlapping collect runs and runs that never return motivate the single-instance lock and wallclock kill, and the deduplicated alert file could feed the existing sole missed-slot detector rather than create another one. Those are proposed controls, not measured savings or existing per-routine heartbeat files here. We already have: negative claims requiring a successful, fresh lookup and a failed fetch reported as gap:, never zero or quiet, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory); routine receipt lines even when nothing happened, checked in the manual weekly receipts review (#receipt-line, #kill-review, #controls-inventory), rather than this project's success heartbeat file per routine; the sole Field Brief missed-slot detector, marked enforced but box-side and unverified (#controls-inventory); long-run tmux, streaming and stale-log watchdog use, a manual convention (#launch, #controls-inventory), alongside exclusive run-output ownership and refusal to restart until the old process is proven gone, enforced by the ownership guard (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); and run limits stated in policy, with runtime enforcement still a follow-up, not live (#run-limits). The existing shadow launch decision is manual, logs only and never blocks; fixed schedules skip it and always run (#worth-running-scope, #controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the IDLE / WORK: contract in collect and curate prompts backed by a real precheck command for a new live-Lab updatedAt, a new pack file or a new push since the last run; non-zero exit means WORK. Add a heartbeat touch on success and one alerts.jsonl consumer; put the single-instance lock and wallclock kill in the launcher. The pack's summary line for agent-ops-kit: only a deterministic check may say IDLE; a broken check is WORK. The pack's stop/kill condition: no trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; the wrapper's kill switch and wallclock hard kill are mechanisms, not a stated trial criterion. The playbook requires a pre-written routine kill condition, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Defining that criterion and the budget for fail-open work, changing a fixed schedule to permit IDLE skips, choosing the new-material check, wiring heartbeat alerts into a routine, or changing launcher locks or kills would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A launcher or routine change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers); spend is a manual Haiyuan approval gate (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory). Caveats: the 119 jobs and the 7-day, about 95% and about $231 per week figures are the author's, not ours; errors deliberately consume tokens by becoming WORK and need a budget line. New material is ours to define and that check can be wrong; protected paths are prompt-enforced, not sandboxed, and state paths are operator-trusted with no containment. The standard-library scripts would still be code we own. The pack says curate is at 16:30 PT; the playbook says 16:45 PT (#usage). Skipping scheduled cycles would change the playbook's fixed-schedule always-run rule (#worth-running-scope), not merely replace its shadow decision. Per the pack's collection-time blockers, the Mac had 12 GiB free, below the 15 GB long-launch hold line, and the vault write was refused; neither is a fresh health check here. The disk floor is a manual control outside the one queue that enforces it (#launch, #controls-inventory); MIT, 1 star, created 2026-07-03 03:57 PT, pushed 2026-10-25 07:12 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. entries.title: dsh-skill-pack-security: a caller-enforced pre-install scan with named misses
entries.why: Deterministic pre-install supply-chain scan for the open-source agent harness one of our seats runs, with 8 audit skills and a zero-dependency plugin_vet provider. Given an owner/repo or local package, it checks license evidence, a lockfile dependency tree with optional external vulnerability checks and their source annotated, immutable 40-hex commit refs in install manifests and workflow actions, malicious patterns in lifecycle scripts, exfiltration domains and encoded payloads, and data-responsibility findings such as ungated sensitive listeners, undisclosed outbound endpoints and instruction-override payloads embedded in shipped text. A five-dimension risk card scores license, source, dependencies, build scripts and maintenance from 0–100 and folds them into PASS / WARN / FAIL. The default warn policy is non-blocking; deny still depends on the caller wiring the verdict into its installer or CI. It does not intercept the host's plugin-add command. The author's own benchmark in the repo's benchmark/RESULTS.md has 38 samples, 20 malicious and 18 benign, over three pattern checks: micro precision 1.000, recall 0.850, F1 0.919 and FPR 0.000. Per-class recall is 1.000 for install scripts, 0.667 for network exfiltration and 0.833 for obfuscation. The three named misses are the messaging-service webhook samples ne-pos-03 and ne-pos-04, where receiver-domain comparison against the bare URL host fails, and the inline-base64-via-variable sample ob-pos-01. These checks catch shapes, not intent and have no vulnerability database. The benchmark is the author's, not ours; optional dependency vulnerability checks do not change that limitation of the pattern checks. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, shared skills are copied into six homes and third-party plugins and skills run with the seat's file access; the existing adjacent cards address pinned-content identity, install integrity and hook behavior, rather than package safety. Per the pack, no pre-install scan, third-party commit-pin rule or license/SBOM check is applied in those homes. The pack cites kept skill-trigger-bench (2026-10-23) for listing-budget pressure; a measurement of our shared skill homes is history not confirmed here. The refreshed playbook already documents skill lint, so that existing report-only check must be distinguished from the proposed supply-chain scan (#skills). We already have: a fleet installer wiring the vault contract and shared skills into CLI homes and project mirrors (#skills), marked enforced on link and checksum evidence checked on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory); skill lint adopted today for frontmatter, when-to-use triggers, near-duplicate or drifted copies and description budgets, report-only, never editing skills, rerun in Monday sync with alerts only for a rising count or a new error (#skills); untrusted material treated as data rather than instructions, policy text only, classified manual in the inventory (#untrusted-content, #controls-inventory); the open-source harness pinned to 0.2.1-rc.2 or newer on the 0.2.1 line, enforced by the updater skipping it (#controls-inventory); and skill promotion requiring three clean runs, rollback tried and complete receipts, manual, with the replay check still proposed because the set is not built (#promotion-gate, #replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): trial plugin_vet in a throwaway profile against one real third-party plugin and one local skill pack, recording the PASS/WARN/FAIL card before deciding whether it belongs in the fleet installer; verify the provider's own card from a clean profile, since installing the scanner is itself a plugin install. Separately propose immutable 40-hex pinning and instruction-override-payload checks for packages shipped into a seat. Keep the 8 skills out of a live seat for now; use one language edition in one root. The pack's summary line for the package scanner: scan the package before it enters the seat — and print the misses. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; scratch-profile evidence precedes the installer decision. The playbook requires a pre-written routine kill condition, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Defining that criterion, installing the provider or skills in a live seat, choosing or enforcing a deny policy, changing the fleet installer or shared skill homes, or making pinning and payload findings binding would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. An installer, hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: all package counts and benchmark figures are the author's, not our results. The provider is specific to the open-source harness one of our seats runs; the pack's stated verification is release 0.2.1-alpha.1 on 2026-09-25, which does not confirm compatibility with our documented 0.2.1-rc.2-or-newer pin (#controls-inventory). Static pattern checks have no vulnerability database; the gate stays advisory unless the caller enforces it. Two language editions add listing pressure, and one maintainer's 87-plugin family makes version churn a risk, per the pack. The pack calls the webhook pair two named false negatives but lists three missed samples once ob-pos-01 is included; the sample ids and all three misses are retained here. Per the pack's collection-time blockers, the Mac had 12 GiB free, below the 15 GB long-launch hold line, and the vault write was refused; neither is a fresh health check here. entries.title: dsh-ctx-budget: estimate resident context and check contract paths
entries.why: Static-context auditor for the open-source agent harness one of our seats runs (Python 3.10 or newer, standard library only). Its six layers cover standing-rule bytes, memory counts and token estimates, skill counts and frontmatter characters, tool entries with schema tokens reported as null, session count and disk use, and a read-only knowledge database, plus an optional cost layer. Read-only by default, it requires --apply for writes, with backups and atomic replacement, and makes no network or model calls. Its capabilities command checks backticked paths, exiting 1 for broken paths, and looks up single-segment commands without treating an unknown command as broken. Its probe command reads plain or compressed session logs and request tool arrays: cold starts with zero cache-read tokens estimate static context as the first prompt minus the first user message; warm sessions return null rather than a guess. The memory commands audit or archive entries, while skills can compress long descriptions and write backups on --apply. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the collector found one shared contract file reached through two symlinks and loaded twice in the same session; these are collection-time measurements, not re-verified here. Its contract spot check counted 61 backticked path-like tokens, 45 resolving directly and 16 false alarms for a naive run: 7 templates or model identifiers and 9 home-prefixed paths that all existed after expansion, leaving 0 dead pointers. The proposed path check therefore needs home-directory expansion and template skipping. Per the pack, session probing could supply a per-seat static-context usage line; the updated playbook already has resident-policy byte ceilings and a cited-path rule (#resident-budget, #pointer-check), so the delta is per-request estimates and a calibrated report, not inventing those controls. We already have: resident-policy byte ceilings for the two files every agent reads before a task, with daily consolidation recording both sizes and fold size gates classified report-only (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory); cited vault paths required to resolve before a pointer is written, with Monday sync checking contract and role-card paths while skipping placeholders, a manual step described by the rule with the upstream lint tool not installed (#pointer-check); adopted skill-description budget lint and a one-time static config audit, both report-only, neither a measured per-request context cost (#skills); and negative claims requiring a successful fresh lookup, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory). The blanket pack claims of no resident-context measurement and no contract path check overstate the gap: byte checks and the path-check rule already exist, while per-request static-context estimates are not documented on these playbook surfaces. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): run ctxbudget baseline and probe --since 7d read-only on the existing seat, recording an estimate in the usage dashboard as a per-seat static-context line; run capabilities on a copy of the shared contract file after teaching it home-directory expansion and template skipping. Propose a report-only weekly step until it has run clean twice, alongside the existing Monday path-check rule. Keep skills --apply off shared homes and do not use memory-archive until the tool has more than a day of use. The pack's summary line for the context auditor: measure what the seat pays before its first token; a dangling pointer must exit non-zero. Here that number is an estimate, not billing. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; two clean runs before considering a blocker and more than a day of use before the named writes are staging boundaries, not a kill threshold. The playbook's pre-written routine kill condition is policy text only, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Defining that criterion, installing the CLI or plugin in a live seat, adding the dashboard line or weekly step, making path findings block work, or allowing description rewrites or memory archiving would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A routine, hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). entries.title: memcap: heavy commands wait for memory across sessions; light work never queues
entries.why: Shared memory budget and admission queue for every session of two coding CLIs on one Mac, both run by our seats (#roster), plus an always-on background watchdog that retires what agents leave behind (Mac only; shell plus standard-library Python 3.9 or newer). Pre-tool-use hooks see each shell command first: searches, reads and git status never touch the queue; only commands with positive evidence of heavy work (builds, test runners, simulators, containers) go through admission, and unrecognized syntax alone does not queue. A queued command starts only when memory pressure allows it (red always blocks; unknown pressure admits nothing), its reservation fits the physical headroom and the previous start has settled; reservations follow measured peaks of earlier identical workloads, incomplete measurements never shrink an estimate, and missing ones are reported as unknown, never as healthy zeros. Cleanup runs through one kill choke point in narrow tiers (orphaned dev servers past a 300 s age gate, over-budget dev servers, idle simulators and browsers), re-verifying identity before TERM and again before KILL; agent CLIs and its own ancestry are never targets, MC_DRY_RUN=1 previews, and memcap off pauses everything. Each watchdog pass stamps a heartbeat, and past the stale threshold its status prints 'MEMCAP IS PROBABLY NOT RUNNING', added after the author's machine ran 28 hours without enforcement while its status still printed a budget; the founding incident was a 24 GB Mac hard-shut-down with 388 orphaned dev servers and 20.3 GB of swap in use. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, several seats run on this Mac at once, each starting test suites or builds on its own, and the fleet has had the neighboring failures (exec wedge, disk at 99 %, stalls). Per the pack, kept command-silence-watchdog (2026-10-21) asks whether a command went quiet, kept whystuck (2026-10-18) asks why it hung, kept watchdog-kit (2026-10-18) escalates ignored alerts and kept agent-ops-kit (2026-10-25) gates whether a cycle fires; none of those four rations the machine across sessions, so two seats can pass all of them and still push the Mac into swap together. The transferable rules, per the pack: light work must be provably light or it queues; an unknown measurement admits nothing, our own gap: rule in control flow; and a watchdog that cannot prove it ran must say so in its status line. We already have: long launches held while the Mac has less than 15 GB free (#launch), a manual control that only one queue's disk gate enforces (#controls-inventory), a disk floor, not a memory budget per command; after Mac trouble, two timed spawn-ok probes, a failed one meaning nothing is launched and a gap is recorded (#spawn-ok), run by hand, report-only in the inventory (#controls-inventory); long runs in tmux with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s, a manual convention (#launch, #controls-inventory), with a restart refused unless the old process is proven dead, enforced by the ownership guard (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); failed lookups reported as gap:, never as zero, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory); and two report-only Mac checks, installed with no schedule, one reporting the freshness of run logs, packs and receipt lines (#report-only-checks, #controls-inventory). The playbook's heartbeats are run-level (#launch, #em-loop); the nearest local evidence for the pack's watchdog-liveness rule is a run lesson in which a queue's watch loop ended with its tmux session and the stall was found by a manual check (#mac-run-lessons). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a trial in observe mode only, adopting the admission rules before any kill tier. Install it in a scratch window, run its init step but leave enforcement paused (memcap off) and garbage collection at the default GC_MODE=observe, then use its status and classify commands and MC_DRY_RUN=1 for a week to see what it would queue or retire here. Unpausing is discussed only after that dry-run log has been read, and no tier may kill until the protected-process list is extended. The pack's summary line for memcap: heavy work waits for memory across all sessions; light work never touches the queue; an unknown measurement admits nothing. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its negative control is that a plain text search must never enter the queue, which the author treats as a reportable defect ('lightweight-queued'). The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing the package, its background watchdog or its hooks in any seat, even paused; unpausing enforcement; arming any cleanup tier; extending its protected-process list; reconciling its queue wait with our launcher; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, launcher or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: hooks cover the two coding CLIs only; per the pack, four other seats get no admission, and its built-in agent list, extendable through a variable, does not name those seats, so kill classification must be verified before any tier is armed. It is a process-killing, always-on service whose README history includes killing a deliberately daemonized server (a parent pid of 1 is also what nohup produces) and shutting down a simulator a live run was driving (fixed, and logged). Admission is not an operating-system memory limit, so running work can overshoot between samples; hook timeouts fail open in the host, and our run lessons record tool-use hooks stalling two runs (#mac-run-lessons); managed commands default to a 24-hour queue wait and background execution, which per the pack must be reconciled with our launcher walls; the playbook's nearest timing control is the stale-log watchdog at about 540 s (#launch). A package plus hooks in live seats is a third-party install: per the pack, the 2026-10-25 skill-pack security gate card applies, itself a Lab proposal, and one coding CLI's hook trust stays user-approved. The 388 orphans, 24 GB, 20.3 GB of swap and 28 hours are the author's figures, not ours; the pack's spawn-ok and free-disk readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: docgraph: two separate doc graphs flag unlinked, placeless and untracked docs
entries.why: Pre-push or CI gate, a Go binary, over a repository's agent-facing documentation graph, the docs an agent navigates by grep and links rather than the rendered site, built as two graphs that are never unioned: the content graph (findability: prose links plus inline-code path mentions), where orphans flags a tracked doc with no inbound content edge, and the metadata graph (placement: frontmatter links: edges such as part-of or depends-on), where disconnected flags a frontmattered doc with no doc-to-doc edge, edges to covered code not counting. Whole-state checks add broken links, untracked markdown (a forgotten git add), frontmatter well-formedness with a required type, edge targets and cycles, and leaks, a scan of tracked content against a machine-local, never-committed TOML file of deny terms with no hidden built-ins: no config means no rules, a warning and a no-op scan, stated rather than hidden. Its doc-drift stop hook (exit 2, once per finding) checks the session's diff for a dangling reference (a symbol's definition removed while a doc still names it), anchored value drift (a constant's numeric value changed while a doc names the constant and shows the old literal) and covers drift (code changed, its covering doc untouched); suppression lives only in config or flags, and no inline markers are ever read. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the vault is an agent-facing doc graph, measured at collection time to be a git work tree, so the tool's tracked-file scope applies, and seats navigate it by grep plus path mentions. Per the pack, kept agnix (2026-10-26) checks that a doc or skill file is syntactically valid for its host, the 2026-10-26 context-auditor card checks that backticked paths exist and kept continuity (2026-10-25) flags duplicate or over-limit instruction files, but none of the cards it names checks graph position: a Hunt note nobody links to is invisible to the next seat, a Decision with frontmatter but no edges has no place in the structure, and an untracked pack file is one git clean from gone. Per the pack, anchored value drift is the second new mechanism: our docs name constants next to their values (ports, budgets, model ids, thresholds), and nothing notices when a value moves; link health is otherwise checked by eye during curate. We already have: cited vault paths that must resolve before a pointer is written, the Monday card sync checking those cited in the fleet contract and the role cards, a manual rule for which the playbook took only the dead-reference idea from the agent-docs-lint Lab card, whose lint tool is not installed (#pointer-check), so broken cited paths are already checked by hand, more than the pack's by-eye reading; recall that greps each note's one-line summary line, written with the exact names a later search would use, policy text only (#memory-loop), so a note docgraph would call an orphan can still be found by search here; a provenance card (claim, source, owner, status, supersedes, review_after) on new Decision notes, with no checker named (#memory-rules), the nearest thing to declared placement; a same-day sweep of every statement of an old model or seat assignment, with no checker named (#model-change-sweep), the nearest thing to value-drift control, for model and seat names only; skill lint that checks skill frontmatter, report-only (#skills); and a manual no-secrets rule for notes, with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook (#controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the two-graph report and the untracked check first, with no push gating yet. Run docgraph report-only against a copy of one vault subtree, or a scratch repository seeded from it, with --skip frontmatter,leaks on the first pass, and read the orphan, disconnected and untracked counts before deciding what a clean state would even mean here. The stop-hook mode and any pre-push blocking come only after the whole-state report has run clean, or been consciously scoped, twice. The pack's summary line for docgraph: findable ≠ placed: audit both doc graphs, plus untracked markdown, before trusting the vault's shape. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its negative control is to add an unlinked markdown file and a doc naming a deleted symbol and confirm that both fire. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running it on the live vault rather than a copy, conforming vault notes to its frontmatter model, wiring its stop hook into any seat, letting any check block a push, treating its leaks scan as a secret gate, scheduling it, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, pre-push gate, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the default doc model requires a type frontmatter block on every doc except the README, a flood on the vault, and the README's own advice (conform hand-curated corpora, exclude only derived ones, never skip a check repository-wide) implies a real conforming project, not a flag day; leaks is local-only by design, since CI and fresh clones have no rules and scan nothing, so it cannot be the fleet's secret gate; the value check is not proximity-checked, so over-reporting on common numbers such as 30 or 211 is expected; a missing binary fails closed as a push gate, blocking unrelated pushes on machines without Go; and installing the binary and wiring a stop hook is a third-party install under the 2026-10-25 skill-pack security gate card, per the pack, itself a Lab proposal. The git work tree is a collection-time measurement, not re-checked here, and our orphan, disconnected and untracked counts are unknown until a trial runs. entries.title: custodiet: a blocking rule needs a signed law, cases both ways and killed mutations
entries.why: Stop-hook governance gate for one coding CLI (zero-dependency JavaScript on Node 20 or newer; 30 rules, 28 engine and 2 built-in) that judges a turn by its tool-call record, not by what the assistant said: rules read assistant text and tool-call inputs, never tool outputs, so reading a file that mentions git commit is not committing. Its completion rules have the familiar shape; the load-bearing half, per the pack, is how the gate governs itself. Every blocking rule carries a law: anchor to a human-signed clause plus positive and negative cases, and anchors are verified at load time in the production hook, not only in CI, so a rule with no source cannot load. Each rule ships at least 2 break-the-predicate mutations that its fixtures must kill before it may ship; the author records that when this acceptance went live, 40 of 97 existing mutations survived the old suite. Every alarm enters a denominator ledger and claimed false positives are booked with reasons (the author's machine on 2026-10-11: 205 of 2,223 rule hits, 9.2 %, self-claimed); missed detections cannot be measured, so the report prints RECALL=UNKNOWN. The ledgers carry per-row hash chains, known defects carry batch expiry dates, missing required input means UNKNOWN and blocks (fail-closed), and a block cap degrades to a notice so the hook cannot loop forever. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the completion-claim lane is the Lab's most crowded (gatehouse, proof, claimcheck, cliffhanger, kept yardgoat (2026-10-24), and rationguard as a 2026-10-26 runner-up), and what no card covers is discipline for the gates themselves: kept cheat-drill (2026-10-14) attacks hooks from outside with 39 known cheat moves, while custodiet is the inside view, where a rule earns the right to block with a signed source, examples both ways and mutations its own tests must kill, and its error rate is a ledger with the unknown printed. Per the pack, our fleet keeps adding hook rules (an install script, stop hooks, prompt gates) with no equivalent acceptance bar, so a rule that fires wrongly is found by a seat getting stuck, the cry-wolf failure the pack says our locks warn about. We already have: a new check, such as a wrapper gate or a checker script, run once against a deliberately broken input (a mutant or a planted bad line, for example) and seen to fail before it counts toward done, and a check that examined nothing reported as a gap, never a pass, policy text only (#check-can-fail), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); beside it, a rule-record reference format asking for evidence, a reproducer and a dated verdict with its owner, and for a proposed check a proof record with healthy, incident or planted-bad, and empty inputs (#check-can-fail), so cases both ways are already the documented shape; a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed, an enforcing stop hook being a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record); report-only mutation testing on one SDK repository, never a merge gate (#mutation-testing); a controls inventory that pairs each fleet-contract rule with what enforces it, from a trial table pending review (#controls-inventory), the reverse of a law: anchor; and, for the decision layer's shadow gates, a hand check of minority verdicts before a gate goes active, manual (#constant-baseline, #controls-inventory). So the pack's no-mutation-acceptance point holds for a ship gate, not for policy: one seen-to-fail broken input is already asked in policy text, while at least 2 killed mutations per rule, anchors verified at load time and a false-positive denominator are not documented on the playbook. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the rule-acceptance contract, not the gate. Copy its five-part shape (detection over structured context only, a law: anchor, a blocking flag, positive and negative cases, at least 2 mutations) as the bar for any new blocking rule in our hooks, and start a false-positive ledger for the blockers we have, printing the unknown where recall cannot be measured. A trial of the tool itself, if wanted, is its observe mode (records only, never blocks) in one scratch repository, never the copy-mode install into a live repository, which writes agent configuration files: the shared contract file, one coding CLI's standing-instruction file and its settings file. The pack's summary line for custodiet: a blocking rule needs a signed law, cases both ways, and mutations its tests must kill — or it does not load. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named for adopting the contract; its stated boundary is observe mode in one scratch repository, never the copy-mode install. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Making the contract a standing bar for new blocking rules, starting a false-positive ledger for existing blockers, installing the gate in any seat or live repository, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision; a standing rule change gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory), and a hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: its text rules recognize Chinese sentence patterns only, and the author states plainly that in an English repository they will neither false-block nor fire; judge messages are Chinese too, so the shipped rule set is largely inert for this fleet. One user's repository is the whole deployment history, and recall is unknown, though printed; the 9.2 % figure, the 40 of 97 survivors and the stop timings (median 582 ms, p90 1,575 ms over 590 stops) are the author's own ledger, not third-party audited and not ours; the false-completion papers it cites were not re-verified in the collection; it supports one coding CLI only; its hash chain's external anchor sits in the same user's home directory, so it does not resist a process running as that user; and the anchor's install-task command is for another desktop operating system only. No local measurement backs this row; what it says about our hook rules is the pack's. entries.title: codex-config-doctor: resolves what one coding CLI will load, per key and per file
entries.why: Read-only program, zero-dependency JavaScript on Node 18 or newer, that reads one coding CLI's configuration and says what that CLI will do with it, outside the CLI and with no model call; that CLI runs one of our two blind review seats, and the playbook also lists a fallback seat on it (#reviewer-rule, #roster). Its show command lists every layer in the order the CLI applies them (system, user and profile files, then the project's own config files from the project root down to the working folder), each marked read, missing, skipped as an untrusted project, or broken with the parse error's line, and prints the merged settings with the layer each key came from, plus the ten keys a project file may not set, this project's trust entry, the standing-instruction files against the CLI's size cap, the rules files, the hooks and whether the CLI trusts them, and the tool servers and whether their programs exist. Its lint command reports 44 findings, each with id, severity, file and line, what the CLI does and the fix, exiting 1 on an error or warning; per the author, 42 of the 44 rest on the real binary and two on documentation, and a markdown form of at most 12 findings, 500 characters a line, is meant for pasting into an agent. A why subcommand says what the CLI does with a given shell command under the approval policy, sandbox and rules (sandboxed, asks, runs outside through an allow rule, refuses, or splits a script and judges each part) and which rule matched, or why none did; agents prints the standing-instruction order, each file included, cut or left out against the cap, and can emit the text exactly as the CLI sends it; cost estimates the first request's fixed load, marking each row computed, recorded or not measured. Per the pack, the evidence discipline is the second product: every explanation line is marked verified (put to the real binary), documented (the docs say so, the binary was not asked) or not verified. The README counts 300 or 333 tests depending on the operating system and 115 or 148 real-binary tests against a fake model API on the local machine, on three operating systems and the CLI's versions 0.163.0 and 0.165.0, with no model and no token reached. The silent failures it targets are all author-documented: the standing-instruction file cut at 32 KiB with no message; an empty override file hiding the instruction file beside it; a project's config ignored until the project is trusted, with the CLI's headless run printing nothing; a hook without a trust record, or changed since it was trusted, skipped; a hook field the CLI does not read dropped in silence; and an allow rule for a prefix the CLI does not honour (git, rm, a shell, an interpreter, a package-script runner) ignored. The README says the CLI's own built-in doctor command reported 4 of 8 seeded problems and called the other 4 fine. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, that CLI's rules are hand-edited and linked, and a review seat running on rules it thinks are loaded but the CLI skipped is exactly the silent failure our review lock cannot see. Per the pack's collection-time measurements on this Mac, made by the collector rather than by this tool and not re-verified here: the CLI's user config file was 41,741 B; its hook file held no hooks; the instruction file in its home and the one in the collect workdir are links to the shared contract file; and because the vault is a git work tree, a session started there loads the same 13,462-byte file as both its global and its project instructions. Per the pack, the global copy is not counted against the 32 KiB cap, so the text is resident twice, 26,924 B or about 6.7k tokens at chars/4, the double load the 2026-10-26 context-auditor card's pack measured for the open-source harness another seat runs. Per the pack, the adjacent cards ask other questions: kept agnix (2026-10-26) whether a file is syntactically valid for its host, kept deadweight (2026-10-22) which keys the runtime ignores, and kept everyhook (2026-10-19), from the same author, how to translate one hook across agents, a different repo and claim, adjacent rather than a duplicate; none of them resolves the layers and says which source wins, which project folder is untrusted, which hook is skipped, or how much of the instructions actually reached the model. We already have: the fleet installer linking the shared contract file into that CLI's home (#skills), enforced on link and checksum evidence checked on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory), which proves the link, not what the CLI loaded; a 13,489 B byte ceiling on the shared contract file, its size recorded in daily consolidation and the size gates report-only (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory), so the pack's 13,462-byte reading sits under both that ceiling and the 32 KiB cap the author documents, while neither bounds how many times a seat loads the file; an adopted one-time static config audit, report-only, which does not run hooks or prove runtime admission or effective settings (#skills), with declared-versus-effective hook loading not adopted from the byte ceiling's source card, since the watchdog's model check already reports the effective model (#resident-budget); the daily CLI updater checking and restoring model and effort, marked enforced but box-side and unverified, with the report-only model-default check covering the other coding CLI only (#controls-inventory, #report-only-checks), two keys rather than the merged layers; and done receipts that keep VERIFIED, only checks that actually ran with their evidence, apart from NOT VERIFIED (#done-receipt), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory). So per the pack the three evidence labels would add a middle level, documented, between those two, and the delta is effective-config resolution for one CLI: per-key source, project and hook trust, and what reached the model. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): read-only diagnostics, no config writes. Run its show, lint, agents and cost commands against this Mac and against a copy of one project, and compare the text agents emits with the text we think the seat gets; adopt the three-level evidence labels in our own reports, so a claim we did not put to the binary is documented, not verified. Do not paste raw show output into the vault without reading it first: it prints setting values and paths, and a config can hold a secret. The pack's summary line for the config doctor: what that CLI's seat loads is a resolved result, not the file you edited: layers, trust, caps, hook trust, per-key source. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; its stated boundaries are read-only runs with no config writes and no raw show output in the vault unread. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running the package on this Mac at all, even read-only; putting any of its output in the vault; adopting the three evidence labels in our receipts; changing that CLI's config, hooks or trust entries on its findings; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it covers that CLI only, none of our other seats' CLIs; 0 stars and one author; its key and feature tables are from version 0.163.0 while this Mac ran 0.165.0 at collection time, so a newer key can be reported as unknown, with the author's weekly real-binary CI the stated mitigation; a key set on the command line, a different profile or a sandbox flag given there is not seen; tokens are chars/4, not a tokenizer; the terminal interface's hooks, status and debug-config views were not driven, though the app server was; tool servers reached over HTTP are not started and their tools are not measured; managed and requirements config is listed, not merged; and show prints setting values, so sanitize before sharing. The 44 findings, the test counts and the 4 of 8 doctor comparison are the author's, not ours; the playbook's evidence fields, a reference format with no checker named, keep external numbers external until reproduced here (#check-can-fail). The local readings above are collection-time measurements by the collector, not re-verified here.
