entries.title: agent-harness-eval: same tasks, two harness versions, and inconclusive is not a pass
entries.why: Evaluation runner for the harness of two coding CLIs, the files that shape a seat (standing instructions, skills, subagents, hooks, tool servers and model settings), run as distributed on the same tasks and compared against a no-harness baseline or the previous version (Python 3.10 or newer plus PyYAML only; README in Japanese). One command runs tasks × profiles × trials; each trial gets a temporary isolated home, so the seats' real homes are never touched, and calls the real CLI headless, writing an HTML report, a JSON summary and per-trial JSON lines. It reports pass@1 and pass^k, cost, a failure classification and a 95 % interval per task. Its release gate compares the current run with the previous one at a pre-decided margin and returns pass, fail or inconclusive, the third verdict a first-class outcome, not a rounded-up pass. Grading puts code graders first, allows custom scripts and keeps an LLM judge auxiliary only; validate --selftest proves the grader passes the reference answers and fails when nothing is done, a negative control before any spend. Its doctor command checks the CLI version and auth, plan estimates calls, cache savings and cost with zero spend, --max-cost-usd caps a run, and harvest drafts candidate tasks from a seat's own session history for a person to edit and validate. Its run command refuses an output folder inside the repo or the home, because an instruction or settings file in the output folder would be read by the agent and break the comparison. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our promotion rule for skills, prompts and hook changes is Three-Run Proof, but the proof is a person reading two runs, not a measurement; this is the missing arithmetic: is the change better than the last version, by how much, with what interval, at what cost, and is the sample too small to say? The playbook differs on two points: Three-Run Proof is three runs, not two, and it is written for new routines, with the promotion gate covering routines and skills and the replay check skill and prompt changes, none of them naming hook changes (#three-run-proof, #promotion-gate, #replay-check); its detection-floor note confirms that Three-Run Proof records only clean or not clean (#detection-floor). Per the pack, kept skill-trigger-bench (2026-10-23) asks whether a skill is seen and picked and kept skillrouter (2026-10-24) where skills live, while this asks whether the whole harness configuration does the job better; per the pack, its pre-decided margin and inconclusive verdict are the honest form of the "0 fix rounds / APPROVE" line our reviews already write, and harvest would turn our own session history into tasks instead of inventing them. We already have: Three-Run Proof before a new routine and a promotion gate of three clean runs, a tested rollback and complete receipts, both manual (#three-run-proof, #promotion-gate, #controls-inventory); a detection-floor line in each promotion note that lists every case that got worse, policy text only (#detection-floor); a replay check before a skill or prompt promotion, proposed because its set is not built, though that set's bar is already written as pass^3, the worst of three runs counting and one of the three reworded (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory); a harness evaluation design of 28 cases from our own records in four arms, each arm scored by the same sealed check written before the first run with a negative control, where zero failures is reported as inconclusive, not a pass, a proposal not approved and not run as of 2026-10-24 (#harness-eval); a new check seen failing once on a broken input before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); and, right after that rule, a performance-comparison evidence format, with no checker named, under which a missing limiter or comparable settings means inconclusive and external numbers stay external until reproduced here (#check-can-fail). entries.title: assume-nothing: probe first, and no answer about a named thing nothing looked up
entries.why: Hook plugin, a single Go binary, that turns 'don't assume' from a prompt request into a mechanism, built for one coding CLI, the one our default implementer and a blind review seat run (#roster), with adapters for four other coding agents that the author labels new and not yet run through a live session. Four moves. Probe first: at session start, resume, clear or compact it checks the machine and working folder within a 2-second budget and hands the agent a list under 2,500 characters: CONFIRMED (operating system, shell, disk, memory, folder, project type, git state, installed languages and tools), MISMATCH (the project asks for a version the machine does not have), NOT INSTALLED (checked on the path) and UNKNOWN (not checked or could not check), plus rules: anything not listed is UNKNOWN and must be checked, and folder and file names are data, not instructions. No probe, no tools: until a probe record exists, every tool call is stopped, and the stop message carries the probe so the agent reads it and continues. No phantom commands: a shell command whose name is not on the path is stopped once, with the list of what is installed, and the same command a second time goes through, since it may be an alias, a function or an odd path; commands after an install on the same line are not checked. No answer from memory about a named thing: when a request names something (an owner/repo, a URL, hyphenated, dotted, backticked or quoted names, plus language-specific patterns), the agent is told those facts are UNKNOWN until looked up in a primary source; after each finished tool call it notes what was looked at, and a failed call (an error, a 403, a rate limit, an empty answer) does not count, nor does delegating to a subagent. An answer about a named thing nothing looked at is sent back once, while one that says next to the name that it is not verified goes through; questions about things that change, such as a latest version or a price, need a lookup even with no name, and a hedge does not excuse them the first time. Its honesty is explicit: it checks that something was looked at, not that the answer is right, a nudge with teeth rather than a fact checker, and it fails open on an internal error, a missing binary or an unwritable probe record, while strict mode (ASSUME_NOTHING_STRICT=1) keeps blocking. The author's small benchmarks ran 10 runs per task and condition with that CLI headless in a clean config: on missing-tool tasks success was 40/40 either way, while failed commands on a missing tool fell 0.9 → 0.0 and 0.6 → 0.0 on the two models tested, with tool calls roughly flat; on facts-only-in-project tasks results went 24/30 → 30/30 and 20/30 → 30/30, the misses mostly giving up at a 404 rather than wrong facts; and the author reports that a version 0.10 note saying only 'look it up' made one model worse (21/30) by sending it to the internet first. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our 2026-09-27 lock says a negative claim needs a lookup that worked, a failed or rate-limited fetch being a gap:, never zero or quiet, and that rule is still prose a model can skip; this makes the distinction mechanical, looked and found nothing versus did not look, with the failed call explicitly not counting. Per the pack it also stops the phantom-command turn (python versus python3, make without make) that burns the first 2–4 turns of a run; a paper the README cites found the same environment snapshot in its search, which the author correctly calls a hint, not a measurement of this plugin. Per the pack's collection-time readings, the hook settings of both coding CLIs on this Mac were empty, so a negative control is trivial: run a known-bad command and see it stopped once. The playbook's run lessons, though, record a plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hanging 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalling two implementer runs (#mac-run-lessons), so empty hook settings show no hooks configured there, not a seat that has never run hooks. Per the pack, kept agent-ops-kit (2026-10-25) applies the same fail-open rule to scheduled prechecks, where a broken precheck counts as work, and this is the interactive half; the 2026-10-26 context-auditor card checks that paths in a contract exist, while this checks that the agent looked at the thing it is answering about. We already have: negative claims requiring a lookup that worked, a failed, rate-limited, unexpectedly empty or stale lookup reported as gap:, never zero or quiet, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory), the rule the pack cites; a check that examined nothing reporting nothing measured, a gap and never a pass, policy text only (#check-can-fail); a completion claim counting only when the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed, an enforcing stop hook being a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record); instructions found in collected content or tool output treated as data and never followed, policy text only, classified manual in the inventory (#untrusted-content, #controls-inventory), the stance the probe's rules take on folder and file names; and, after Mac trouble, two timed spawn-ok probes before any launch, run by hand and report-only in the inventory (#spawn-ok, #controls-inventory), a launch-level check rather than a per-session inventory handed to the agent. Per the pack, none of its three mechanisms, a session-start probe, a phantom-command stop and a check that a named target was looked up, is applied here; the playbook names none of them. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the probe and the failed-lookup rule in the collection pack contract, with the hook trialed on that CLI first. Install it there only, leave strict mode off (the default fails open), run one known-missing command and one question about a named thing nothing looked up as negative controls, then read its status after a week. Do not put it on the collect seat that wrote this pack, which it does not support, and do not install it on the CLI our other blind review seat runs until that CLI's hook-trust path has been exercised; the author labels support beyond the first CLI new and says it has not been run through a live session. The pack's summary line for assume-nothing: a failed lookup is not a lookup; looked-and-found-nothing must be distinguishable from did-not-look. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its negative controls are one known-missing command and one question about a named thing nothing looked up, and its review point is the status read after a week. The pack's summary table calls the trial warn/default fail-open and its verification section a report-only or warn-first trial, yet as the pack describes the plugin, it stops every tool call until a probe record exists, stops a missing command once and sends an answer back once even with strict mode off, which only decides whether it keeps blocking on its own errors; the pack describes no warn-only or audit mode, while the playbook's path for an enforcing stop hook is a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record). The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it in any seat, even with strict mode off; turning strict mode on; installing it on the other coding CLI or any collect seat; adding the probe or the failed-lookup rule to the collection pack contract; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it covers none of the four other seats the pack lists, including the collect seat that wrote this pack, and the adapters beyond the first CLI are author-labelled experimental and not live-run; it fails open by design and is not a security boundary; it checks looked-at, not correctness; name extraction is heuristic and language-specific, so an unquoted name written only in kanji is not picked up; and, per the author, it reads the request, tool inputs and outputs and the final answer in memory, keeps only extracted names and sends nothing anywhere. The benchmarks are small and trap-built, and the README dates them 2026-10-30, one day after this collect, so both the date and the numbers are the author's, not ours, and the date is unexplained; the cited paper's figures are a citation, not a test of this plugin. Installing it writes hooks into live seat settings, so per the pack the 2026-10-25 skill-pack security gate card applies, itself a Lab proposal; that CLI hosts our default implementer and a blind review seat (#roster). The empty hook settings are collection-time measurements, not re-verified here. MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-29 03:56 PT, pushed 2026-10-29 08:50 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. entries.title: doneguard: a stop hook blocks done until checks pass, yielding after 3 failed fixes
entries.why: Stop hook in zero-dependency, standard-library Python 3.9 or newer (repository size 1,291 KB in the pack's metadata read) that keeps a coding agent from declaring a task finished while types or tests are failing, with hooks for six coding agents, among them the two coding CLIs the pack names for its trial. A start command records when the session began; when the agent tries to finish, the harness fires the stop hook, whose verify command inspects the git changes since then, honoring the repository's ignore rules, and runs only the type checks, linters and related tests that match the changed files. If any check fails, it blocks termination, formats the errors in the agent's native protocol and returns them, so the agent keeps fixing; after 3 consecutive failed fix attempts it yields, letting the agent stop while alerting the human, to avoid runaway token loops. A stats command logs every blocked completion claim and tracks the agent's self-fix rate without storing code or paths, and one config file at the project root picks among four execution modes: files; filter, which counts only errors in modified files so existing repository debt does not block; tests, which runs only tests related to changed code; and command. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our standing rules say code decides done and ask for done receipts with verified evidence, yet 'run tests before declaring done' is prose in the shared contract file that agents occasionally rush past; doneguard moves that invariant to the runtime boundary, and its filter mode keeps existing errors in untouched files from failing a run while new errors from the session are caught. Per the pack's dedupe, the completion-claim cards gatehouse, proof, claimcheck, cliffhanger and yardgoat are adjacent; this one is the mechanical stop hook that runs tests on changed files before it lets the agent say done. We already have: a task done only when a concrete, deterministic check passes, green tests among them, with agent self-reports advisory only (#code-decides-done); a tests-pass or done claim counting only when the session record shows the test command ran against the current head and its last run passed, plus a test-tamper scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer, a prose rule with no hook installed, where an enforcing stop hook would be a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record); a new check seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail); and done receipts whose VERIFIED line names only checks that actually ran, with their evidence (#done-receipt); all four sit within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory). Beside them, three failed correction rounds escalate, the same cap as review fix rounds, a manual control with rounds counted by hand and no enforcing wrapper live (#retry-ceiling, #controls-inventory), the same shape as doneguard's three-attempt valve. So the rule exists in policy and review; per the pack, what is not applied here is the mechanical half, checks run on the session's changed files at the stop boundary with the failures fed back. Per the pack, our existing stop hooks do not run tests on session diffs; the playbook names no installed stop hook and says the completion-claim rule has none (#claim-vs-record). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a trial on one project only, with the two coding CLIs the pack names: install it in one repository with a config holding one linter and one test runner, simulate an agent breaking a test, and verify that the stop hook blocks termination, feeds the error back and allows exit once the test is fixed. The pack's verification section calls all three of its KEEPs scoped, advisory-mode trials, not immediate fleet-wide mandatory enforcement, yet this trial checks that the hook blocks, and the pack describes no warn-only mode; the playbook's path for an enforcing stop hook is a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record). The pack's summary line for doneguard: a Stop hook blocks completion until tests and linters pass on changed files; 3-strike circuit breaker before human escalation. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its negative control is the simulated broken test, which the hook must block and feed back before it lets the agent exit once the test is fixed, and the three-attempt valve is the tool's own escalation, not a trial criterion. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Choosing the trial repository and its checks; installing the package there or in any seat; wiring its stop hook into either coding CLI, or trusting it where that CLI asks; letting it block anywhere beyond the one trial project; making it a fleet gate; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: 0 stars and hours old at collection, created the same morning; it needs its command on the system path; its hooks run local shell commands, so its config must be reviewed before it is committed; on one of the two CLIs, hook integration relies on that CLI's hook trust; the filter mode's handling of existing debt and the self-fix rate it tracks are the author's claims and the tool's own metric, not ours; and our run lessons record tool-use hooks hanging 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalling two implementer runs (#mac-run-lessons). entries.title: rulesift: hidden-text and injection lint, change diff and hash lock for agent files
entries.why: Offline static analyzer and PR gate, a single Rust binary that makes zero network calls (repository size 708 KB in the pack's metadata read), for the files that steer coding agents: standing-instruction files, skill folders, hooks, the configuration of tool servers, and rules, with parsers for the shared instruction-file convention, six coding agents' own formats and the skill-file format. Its reveal command detects and decodes hidden Unicode Tag characters, bidirectional overrides, zero-width spaces, base64 payloads and instructions hidden in HTML comments, all invisible to a human reviewer but parsed by a model. Its scan flags prompt injections ('ignore previous instructions', 'do not tell the user'), piped download-and-run shell commands, hardcoded credentials and tool servers launched unpinned at their latest version. Its diff command summarizes what a branch or PR changes for agents (new permissions, altered hooks, added tool servers, modified rules); its lock command writes a hash manifest, rulesift.lock, and its verify command fails when any agent-steering file changed without an explicit lock update. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our vault and project roots rely on the shared contract file and skill files linked across the Mac CLI seats, and invisible characters or silent rule changes can redirect agents without showing up in a human diff. Per the pack, kept agnix (2026-10-26) validates syntactic schema conformance for host agents and kept custodiet (2026-10-28) gates that blocking rules carry tests and author attribution; rulesift fills the operational and security gap: it checks that human-reviewed markdown has not been tampered with through invisible characters, flags unpinned tool servers and makes agent policy changes obvious in a PR before they are merged into the vault. We already have: the fleet installer wiring the shared contract file and shared skills into the CLI homes and project mirrors (#skills), enforced on link and checksum evidence, seven links that resolve to the vault file and one copy whose checksum matches, checked on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory), which proves where a link points, not what the file says; a 13,489 B byte ceiling on the shared contract file whose size gates are report-only (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory), and edits to that file limited to fleet-wide standing rules, a manual control with nothing checking the reason for an edit, where the inventory notes that the size gates cannot catch a rewrite: the 2026-10-20 probe's unrelated, equal-size replacement passed both (#controls-inventory); skill lint, report-only, which checks frontmatter, when-to-use triggers, near-duplicate or drifted copies and description budgets, and a one-time static config audit, report-only (#skills); untrusted content treated as data, never instructions, policy text only, classified manual in the inventory (#untrusted-content, #controls-inventory); and no secrets in notes, a manual rule with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook (#controls-inventory). So links, sizes and skill headers are checked here, while per the pack the text of the steering files is not: no hidden-character scan, no pin lint for tool servers and no lock verification in our vault sync or PR gates. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack's verdict line reads adopt the scan and the diff in vault pre-commit or CI linting, but its trial is narrower, and on this card it is a proposal to evaluate on the vault, not an adopted gate: run the scan against the vault and check whether any linked contract or skill file triggers findings, and evaluate the diff in PR review templates. The inventory's no-secrets row records no active git hook in the vault (#controls-inventory), so a pre-commit or CI gate there would be new. The pack's summary line for rulesift: offline linter and PR gate detects hidden Unicode Tag text, prompt injections, and unpinned tool servers in standing-instruction files and skills; provides rulesift.lock. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; the playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts (#check-can-fail), and the pack's trial plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Building the binary; running it on the vault, even read-only; adding it to a vault pre-commit hook or CI; adopting its diff in PR review templates; writing or enforcing a lock file; tuning its rules for our scripts; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, pre-commit gate or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: a 0.1.0 pre-release, installed from a local source build with the language's package manager; static rules cannot catch every nuanced semantic prompt injection; legitimate scripts and download commands need false-positive tuning in its config; its zero network calls and its parser coverage are the author's claims, not verified here; and the pack's vault PR gates assume a review flow the playbook does not describe for the vault. No local measurement backs this row; what it says about our vault is the pack's. entries.title: agent-slop: syntax-tree lint and session ratchet for leftover agent comments
entries.why: Deterministic linter written in Rust (repository size 486 KB in the pack's metadata read) that parses code comments into syntax trees in 12 languages and flags the ephemeral commentary coding agents habitually leave behind, across 16 rule categories, among them change-history residue that narrates the edit rather than the code (such as 'updated to handle Y'), session talk and review jargon ('as requested by user', 'temporary workaround'), tautological comments that repeat a function or variable name, TODOs with no actionable removal condition or owner, and unsourced claims or hedging ('ultra-fast', 'efficiently handles'). Its ratcheting stop gate pins a baseline fingerprint of existing comments at session start and at stop inspects only comments added during the session; in block mode it exits with an error only if the session added new slop, so legacy debt never blocks an agent. It reads two hook payload formats on standard input, one coding CLI's and one other agent platform's, fails open on configuration errors and accepts audited inline suppressions that must give a reason citing a URL or a decision record. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, coding agents write conversational filler in comments ('TODO: refactor later') that clutters PR diffs and wastes reviewer tokens in blind review, and agent-slop stops it at the stop-hook boundary at zero model cost, uniquely reading both hook formats. Per the pack's dedupe it sits next to the tripwires (2026-10-22) and continuity (2026-10-25) cards. The playbook differs on two points: the pack speaks of dual blind review, but code our default implementer wrote gets one blind review seat (#reviewer-rule); and the pack lists our coordinating bots as a surface, but no coordinating bot writes code, a manual seat rule (#controls-inventory), so only the coding CLI's format applies to a seat that writes code here. The source behind our converging re-reviews reports that an agent author fixes every nit, so each nit costs another commit and review round (#review-convergence). So, per the pack, nothing here checks comment wording: our linters check formatting and syntax, and nothing ratchets against newly added residue. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): an advisory, warning-only hook trial in one coding CLI's sessions, configured in one seat's settings file on post-tool-use and stop events: an agent edit that introduces a comment starting 'previously we did' should be detected, while existing comments must not trip the ratchet. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack): a verification CLI plus a feature map
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack), part 1, read in the translator's Chinese translation: the guide's author treats a verification skill as critical infrastructure rather than just a skill, because an agent that can verify its own work closes its own loop and keeps going until the task is done instead of making a person the bottleneck, and says that giving agents this ability lets everyone in an organization contribute and verify that their changes work. Per the translated guide, the agent should be able to interact with the app, debug it and capture performance traces with whatever a developer would use by hand: the browser's debugging protocol for a desktop app built on web technology or a web app, a device simulator for a phone app, or, without a rich runtime, tools the agent builds, such as a native debugger or a custom package that runs as a sidecar in development; the author even suggests building rich debugging tools or switching stacks, since the harder a stack is to debug and control, the harder agents are to use well. Under the guide's principle 'Build the Lever', the skill hands the agent a tool, not just Markdown: a small agent-friendly CLI that wraps app interaction and debugging, so the agent runs one command instead of writing a one-off script to click an element, spends fewer tokens, and verification becomes reproducible and testable. The author adds the development basics to think about, seeding the development database, handling authentication, test users and staging API calls, and installing and starting the development environment consistently, and advises polishing the CLI until it is stable before anything more advanced. A Feature Map, a few searchable Markdown files inside the skill whose README is the top-level map, lists every main feature, what it does and how a user reaches it; the skill's generator walks the app and catalogs the features itself. The author calls the map 'materialized memory', a compact form of the codebase, which the author sees as the ultimate memory, recommends running the maintenance step at least once a day, with agents also updating the skill as they develop and the maintenance step filling the gaps, and suggests treating the skill as critical infrastructure, even with an oncall rotation. A typical prompt asks the agent to build a feature, verify the change with the generated app-control skill and show video and screenshots as proof. Why it matters here: per the curating bot's analysis of the posts, the Lab has no feature-map or app-control-CLI card, and our harness has done receipts but no per-repository verification CLI for the SDK repository we ship to or the hub site. We already have: a task done only when a concrete, deterministic check passes, green tests, an expected file, a pushed commit or HTTP 200, with agent self-reports advisory only (#code-decides-done); prose done that needs a mechanical artifact or an independent read-only check (#rules); and done receipts whose VERIFIED line names only checks that actually ran (#done-receipt), all within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); a repro artifact before a bug fix, with exact steps, a command, logs or a failing test, and that failing test as the first commit, a manual control (#coding-em-kicks, #controls-inventory); and the shared notes vault as the team's long-term memory, treated as a context repo (#vault), where cited paths must resolve, a manual check (#pointer-check). The playbook keeps a browser-driving candidate as Lab backlog only, with a note not to install its browser-automation tool (#usage). So, per the curating bot's analysis, what is new here is a tool per repository that an agent drives to prove its change works, and a feature map kept current by a maintenance run. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's analysis of the posts (a proposal, not approved): a trial in which each repository our default implementer ships to, the SDK repository first, gets a verification CLI and a features README, and the implementer's receipts cite a run of that CLI as VERIFIED evidence; a weekly maintenance run is proposed, not scheduled, where the guide's author recommends running the maintenance step at least daily. The analysis's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the curating bot's analysis or the posts. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory); a new routine such as a scheduled maintenance run passes Three-Run Proof before it goes active, a manual control (#three-run-proof, #controls-inventory), and a new check such as a verification step is first seen failing on a deliberately broken input, policy text only (#check-can-fail). Building a verification CLI or a feature map in any repository; letting a receipt count a CLI run as VERIFIED; scheduling a maintenance run, daily or weekly; installing any browser-automation or debugging tool; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A routine change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the guide's productivity figures are the author's claims from the author's own products, not ours, and are left out here; the example CLI commands and the sample feature entry the post introduces are missing from the fetched text; the posts are Chinese translations by the translator, and the English original and the example repository the guide links were not opened, per the curating bot's analysis. Part 1 is dated 2026-09-01 by the guide's author; post 1, the translation, posted 2026-10-29 12:30 PT; verified against the translated posts only. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack): six rules for CLIs that agents call
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack), part 1, read in the translator's Chinese translation: once the verification CLI exists, the guide's author says to think, or have the agent think, about how to design a CLI an agent can use well, and from the many sources online names the traits the author values most: an API that composes easily, after the 'deep modules' design philosophy; a dry-run option on any command that could have destructive side effects; subcommands that disclose features progressively instead of exposing everything at once; error messages that are very specific and tell the agent explicitly what to do instead; rich help text; and output in a machine-readable format such as JSON. The author's case for a CLI over Markdown, the 'Build the Lever' principle, is that one command costs the agent fewer tokens than a one-off script and makes the work reproducible and testable, and the author advises polishing the CLI until it is stable before moving on to anything more advanced. Why it matters here: per the curating bot's analysis of the posts, the Lab does not hold these rules as a set, and our own tools, the launcher, the watchdog, the receipt helper and the curate check scripts, state no CLI contract. We already have: two report-only Mac checks whose exit codes are written down, the freshness check's being 0 fresh, 1 stale, 3 gap, 4 nothing measured, 2 usage or an invalid timestamp format and 5 crash, with nothing acting on either check's exit code (#report-only-checks), report-only in the inventory (#controls-inventory); spawn-ok probes whose exit codes say what went wrong, 142 for a hung program and 127 for one that could not start, run by hand, report-only in the inventory (#spawn-ok, #controls-inventory); the ownership guard, which refuses a stale attempt's publish with return code 3, enforced (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); and a check's own exit status captured without an output-filtering pipe or a forced success, a check that examined nothing reporting nothing measured, policy text only (#check-can-fail). So some of our tools already document what their exit codes mean; per the curating bot's analysis, the delta is one written contract for every new or changed harness script. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's analysis of the posts (a proposal, not approved): new or changed harness scripts follow the agent-CLI contract, a dry-run mode for anything that deletes, moves or pushes, a JSON output mode, errors that name the next command, and help text; existing scripts migrate when next touched; and the contract stays policy only until a lint exists, recorded in the rule-to-enforcer table behind the controls inventory, itself a trial pending review (#controls-inventory). The analysis would put the contract in the shared contract file, which is at its byte ceiling, so an added line needs an equal trim (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory). The analysis's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the curating bot's analysis or the posts. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Writing the contract into the shared contract file or any skill; adding a lint for it; changing any existing script's options, output or exit codes; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A script, launcher or wrapper change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the six traits are the guide's author's preferences, picked from many sources, with no measurement behind them; the example commands the post introduces are missing from the fetched text; the posts are Chinese translations by the translator, and the English original was not opened, per the curating bot's analysis. entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack): plan in code with prototypes and sketches
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack), part 2, read in the translator's Chinese translation: the guide's author plans, but plans in code. For shared code or packages, README-driven development: write the README or a tutorial first, which forces a developer-experience view of how a hypothetical user calls the API, then work backwards to the implementation and architecture; the author's writing skill splits documents into four distinct modes (tutorial, how-to guide, reference and explanation) and strips slop, and a plan written this way gives the agent a concrete target to check its work against. The two planning mistakes the author sees most are accepting the agent's first design and over-deliberating a plan without empirical evidence, and the guide answers both with 'measure twice, cut once' through parallel agents. Its prototyping playbook builds throwaway drafts in the app or a temporary directory, puts two or three variants of a UI interaction behind a simple toggle, drives each with the verification skill, screenshots it and measures real timing or layout. For larger changes its architect skill runs in phases: ground the problem with its how and why skills; sketch, launching several independent candidate runners in parallel, usually across model families, each drafting call-site examples, core types, public function signatures and a short rationale, mostly by sketching type signatures backwards from the call sites wanted, while weighing interface depth, failure modes on weaker models and a catalog of design red flags; cross-judge, where a judge on a model different from the main agent's scores the candidates against a strict rubric and the loop synthesizes one design; implement against the sketch, surfacing any function that turns out to need unexpected parameters or extra state; and scrap the design when it is wrong, the evidence being the same workaround recurring at unrelated call sites or types that need escape hatches such as any or forced casts. The author never bothers with adversarial review of abstract plans, saying agents invent theoretical risks and complex edge cases that never happen, and lets prototypes and verification answer open questions instead. When a plan document is still needed, the guide's multi-phase planning playbook organizes every task around proof and verification, tells the agent that tests alone are not sufficient verification until it actually runs the code and confirms it works, has a script check each plan's structure and format, and executes an approved plan item by item in small, self-contained PRs. Why it matters here: per the curating bot's analysis of the posts, the Lab has no card on sketch arenas, the four-mode documentation framework or README-driven design, and the author's stance on reviewing plans is in tension with our standing rule that drafts get blind review, so the analysis proposes scoping that rule, not replacing it. We already have: intent, spec and plan files written before anything bigger than a one-line fix and committed next to the code, except in the SDK repository, which forbids checking in those file names, so there they stay in the vault or local-only, kept out by an ignore rule and a format check, with Haiyuan accepting intent and spec when the change is consequential and the plan listing ordered slices, a claim map, files to touch, a test plan and a done definition (#em-loop); reviewers who start only once a PR exists and check the PR against the intent, spec and plan (#em-loop); two blind reviewers, each blind to the other, on docs and drafts (Decision notes, cards, role cards) and on other seats' code, and one blind review seat on code our default implementer wrote (#reviewer-rule), the seat assignment a manual control (#controls-inventory); disproof review against 2–3 rejection criteria named before reading the diff, a manual control (#disproof-review, #controls-inventory); review depth in three tiers, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers); a task done only when a deterministic check passes, green tests counting (#code-decides-done), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); a performance-comparison evidence format, with no checker named, under which a missing limiter means inconclusive (#check-can-fail); and a harness evaluation design whose arms test whether blind review earns its cost, a proposal not approved and not run as of 2026-10-24 (#harness-eval). Vetting a measured number is already in the Lab as 'A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026) — seven questions to answer before reporting a number' (2026-10-20), so this card leaves it out. So the guide's view lines up with our code loop, where review waits for a PR, and differs on drafts, which our standing rule sends to blind review, and on proof, where the guide says tests alone are not verification while our rule counts green tests. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's analysis of the posts (a proposal, not approved): for design tasks only, our default implementer first produces two or three sketches or prototypes (types, call sites or a throwaway toggle) and measures them, and the two blind reviews then run on the chosen sketch or artifact with its evidence, not on an abstract plan, while blind review of drafts stays unchanged. This touches our standing rule that drafts get blind review, so any change there needs Haiyuan. The analysis's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the curating bot's analysis or the posts; the guide's scrap rule, recurring workarounds or escape-hatch types, decides when a design is wrong, not when a trial stops. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Changing what our blind reviews read or when, for plans, sketches or drafts; letting any plan or draft skip blind review; running sketch runners or a judge on other models; making README-first design or the four-mode documentation split a standing step; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A review-rule change is a standing rule change, which gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory). Caveats: the workflow is the guide's author's, built on the author's own products, and the guide's monthly PR counts are the author's claims, not ours, and are left out here; the posts are Chinese translations by the translator, and the English original was not opened, per the curating bot's analysis. Part 2 is dated 2026-09-10 by the guide's author; post 2, the translation, posted 2026-10-30 03:06 PT; verified against the translated posts only. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack): ground with how, why, recall and teach
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack), part 2, read in the translator's Chinese translation: the guide's author still sees two failure modes in frontier models, missing the real intent because the request is under-specified or unclear, and lacking the context to do the work right, and says that using agents well comes down to filling their context window with high-quality context. Its grounding moves: an 'indirect prompt', in which the agent reads a whole reported thread and, before anything else, restates in its own plain words what it thinks the underlying problem is; a how skill that traces runtime mechanisms and, for a subsystem spanning several directories or services, launches several explorer agents in parallel on a fast, efficient model; a why skill that queries historical evidence in parallel from many sources, git history and PR review comments, tickets, design docs, chat conversations, monitors, error logs, code lineage and events in an analytics warehouse, because code shows what happened but rarely why; a recall skill that pulls recent context out of past chats so a freshly started agent regains the background; and a teach skill, built on how and why, through which the agent explains intuitively what it did or plans to do and why, its trade-offs included. The author notes that even the newest models often reach confident conclusions without data or without reading the code a mental model of the runtime needs, so explaining back helps the agent as well as the person. The translator's summary of part 2 frames it as two problems, aligning with the agent on requirements and planning and designing effectively, and lists how (how the system runs now), why (why it was designed this way and under what historical constraints) and recall (what context past conversations give); the fetched text of that summary breaks off at its fourth item. Why it matters here: per the curating bot's analysis of the posts, restating and recall are partly ours already, and one card is kept for the multi-source history search and the teach-back. We already have: restate the ask before starting, in which the agent restates the goal and the problem in its own words and the restatement is compared with the intent before work starts, policy text only (#intake-restatement), a rule that came from the card already in the Lab as '@poteto — most used prompt: restate my goals and the problem before you start' (2026-10-04), so this card does not repeat it; reading the fleet contract, the never-again list, recent notes and the Decisions that touch the work before a task, a manual control (#vault, #controls-inventory); a memory loop whose recall scans the notes' one-line summaries, opens only the ones that apply and names them or says nothing applies, policy text only (#memory-loop); a repro artifact before a bug fix, with exact steps, a command, logs or a failing test, a manual control (#coding-em-kicks, #controls-inventory); and a handoff packet that carries the decisions already made, with a shadow-only completeness check that never blocks, report-only in the inventory (#handoff-packet, #controls-inventory). Readable explainers are already in the Lab as '@karpathy — throwaway explainers for hard-to-review changes, built only from the receipt and verified evidence' (2026-10-04), so this card leaves them out. So, per the curating bot's analysis, the delta is a why step that reads history beyond the vault, such as git history and PR review threads, and a teach-back of the plan and its trade-offs before code. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's analysis of the posts (a proposal, not approved): a grounding block in our task-brief template, with runtime (how), history (why: git log, PRs and the vault's Decisions), recall (prior runs and receipts) and a teach-back line before code. The analysis's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the curating bot's analysis or the posts. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Adding the block to any template, skill or routine prompt; giving any seat read access to new history sources such as tickets, chat or monitoring; running explorer agents in parallel on another model; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the failure modes and the claim that explaining back helps the agent are the guide's author's observations, not measured here; the history sources the why skill queries are the services the author's team uses; the translator's summary is cut off in the fetched text, and its image and the English original were not read, per the curating bot's analysis; the posts are Chinese translations by the translator. Part 2 is dated 2026-09-10 by the guide's author; post 2, the translation, posted 2026-10-30 03:06 PT, and post 3, the translator's summary, posted 2026-10-30 07:01 PT; verified against the translated posts only. entries.title: JiTTest: tests written to fail on each risky diff, not only a model review
entries.why: A large company's engineering post (2026-10-29) on just-in-time catching tests, JiTTests, as summarized in the curating bot's drafts: the post reports a system that generates executable tests for each diff, tests that show a concrete behavior difference from the diff's parent, instead of a language model reading the code like a reviewer. It has two workflows: in 'dodgy diff' the whole diff is treated as a mutant and the system writes tests that tell it apart from its parent; in 'intent-aware' it infers the diff's intent from the code, title and summary, lists the risks, builds a mutant for each risk, writes tests that kill those mutants and then runs the tests on the real diff. A failing test is a weak catch, which per the drafts is scored and ranked before it goes further. The post reports that it catches bug classes model code review misses, a 60% true-positive rate as judged by engineers, 74 serious privacy bugs caught at the diff stage in the first half of 2026, and privacy incidents (SEVs) down 20%; the drafts also cite a 2026 conference paper on just-in-time catching test generation. Why it matters here: per the curating bot's notes on the post, our blind reviewers only read code, and a failing test is evidence, not opinion. The curating bot keeps the diff-aware catching tests as new: they overlap our mutation testing and the change-risk loop, but those measure the strength of a test suite, while catching tests write new failing tests against one diff. We already have: report-only mutation testing on one SDK repository, on a schedule or by hand and never a merge gate, with change-risk scores beside it only a proposal, not adopted (#mutation-testing), and the 2026-10-11 Lab card on a code-quality loop with mutation and change-risk hardening; a repro before a bug fix, its failing test as the first commit, a manual control (#coding-em-kicks, #controls-inventory); a new check seen failing once on a deliberately broken input, a mutant among them, before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail); disproof review in which reviewers test unsupported claims and try to break the result, a FAIL returning file and line, a command and its output or a failing input, and a P0 or P1 without such evidence downgraded to P2 or re-asked once (#disproof-review, #review-convergence), a manual control (#controls-inventory), so proposal B below is largely in the playbook already and the drafts' 'only read code' understates what reviewers are asked to do; and a test-tamper scan of each diff by the EM and the reviewers, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record). Reviewers start only once a PR exists (#em-loop), and the small-job seats are advisory and never write real code, while another seat implements only when Haiyuan asks (#roster, #coding). So, per the curating bot's notes, what is new is a pass that writes failing tests against one diff before review. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's proposals (a proposal, not approved): (A) a trial on pull requests to the SDK repository in which, before blind review, a seat that is not a reviewer runs an intent-aware catch pass: infer the intent from the PR's title, body and diff, list 3-5 risks, write tests that would fail if each risk were present and run them on the PR head; any failing test goes into the review packet as evidence the reviewers must address, the receipt gets a catch-tests line, and unexplained failures go under NOT VERIFIED; and (B) a reviewer's P1 claim cites a failing test or a command where possible, extending the disproof framing. The curating bot marks A as a trial that changes the standing review rule, so any change there needs Haiyuan. The proposals' stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the curating bot's notes on the post. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running a catch pass on any repository; choosing the seat that writes and runs its tests; letting its failures into a review packet or a receipt; changing what a P1 must cite; changing the standing review rule; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A review-rule change is a standing rule change, which gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory). Caveats: the 60% true-positive rate, the 74 privacy bugs, the 20% fewer privacy incidents and the claim that it catches bug classes model review misses are the post's, from the company's own code base, not ours; the conference paper was not read; the drafts are the curating bot's summary, and the post's prompts, mutant builders and tests are not in them. No measurement of ours backs this card; the post is dated 2026-10-29 in its link; summarized by the curating bot from the post, not re-read in this run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: JiTTest: several model judges and fixed rules rank and filter false alarms
entries.why: A large company's engineering post (2026-10-29) on just-in-time catching tests, as summarized in the curating bot's drafts: the post reports that each weak catch, a generated test that fails on a diff, is scored by an ensemble of state-of-the-art language models, which see the test code, the failure output or trace, the diff and the inferred intent, and by a deterministic, rule-based false-positive filter that the post names; together they rank the candidates, and only high-ranked ones go further. Per the drafts, the post does not publish the filter's rules. Why it matters here: per the curating bot's notes on the post, model judges are rich but non-deterministic and hard to verify, while rules are verifiable, so pairing them cuts noise before a human is pinged. The curating bot marks the pairing as partly ours already, through blind dual review and mechanical-first evidence, and keeps only one idea as a card: deterministic rules before a model judge. We already have: blind review in which each seat is blind to the other, two seats on docs, drafts and other seats' code and one on code our default implementer wrote, with disproof framing and a VERDICT line, a manual control (#reviewer-rule, #disproof-review, #controls-inventory); prose done that needs a mechanical artifact or an independent read-only check (#rules); a task done only when a deterministic check passes, with self-reports and the decision layer's completion check advisory only (#code-decides-done), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); a shadow model gate that goes active only if it beats the constant majority verdict on hand-checked minority calls, a manual control (#constant-baseline, #controls-inventory); and a harness evaluation design whose arms are all scored by one sealed artifact or report check written before the first run, with no check reading a seat, a verdict or a gate receipt, a proposal not approved (#harness-eval). Already in the Lab: the 2026-10-20 card proposing a deterministic rule-table router in front of our decision layer, from a 2026-10-19 post on the same blog, and 'agent-harness-eval: same tasks, two harness versions, and inconclusive is not a pass' (2026-10-29), which grades with code first and keeps a model judge auxiliary. The playbook does not name a mechanical-first evidence file; that part of the verdict is the curating bot's. So deterministic checks already come before opinions for done claims; per the curating bot's notes, the delta is the same order stated for any model judge we add. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's proposals (a proposal, not approved): only the ordering, deterministic rules before a model judge, which is the curating bot's proposed takeaway, not the post's design, since the post scores each weak catch with the model judges and the rules together; it is kept as a reference card, and the curating bot proposes no harness change for it. The proposals' stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the curating bot's notes on the post. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Adding a model judge or an ensemble to any gate or review; putting a rule filter in front of our reviews or decision-layer gates; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A gate, wrapper or hook change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). entries.title: A model lab's super-agent prototype: restart only what a restart can fix
entries.why: A model lab's research prototype, a bundle for their agent harness that runs a proactive coding agent for one code repository, read with the lab's design article on what it calls a super-agent (in Chinese): in the prototype, recovery rests on three rules about what not to restart. First, its service script under scripts/ exits 0 while the service runs normally; 1 when it is stopped, runs twice, does not answer or its runtime reports an error, which 'a restart may fix'; 2 when it runs but a part other than the runtime, such as an event source or an allowed-list sync, reports an error; and 3 when it runs and waits for setup; a restart fixes neither 2 nor 3, which need a person (docs/006-deployment.md). The hourly check is a prompt, not a built-in monitor: the same document asks the operator to schedule it from their everyday profile, so that it keeps running when the agent service is down, and it tells the agent that runs it how to act on those codes: on 0 it does nothing and says nothing; on 2 or 3 it does not restart and reports each problem once, unless it already reported the same ones; if the status shows a deliberate stop, it leaves the service stopped; and on 1 it restarts with --respect-stop, and if that fails too, it reads the newest log and the troubleshooting table, fixes what it can and says what was wrong and what it did. Second, the documented check leaves a deliberate stop alone, but only through a flag: only stop writes the stop marker, before it waits for the graceful shutdown, so a monitor respects the stop even if that wait times out; start clears the marker, and so does a restart, which ends in a start; only a start or restart run with --respect-stop, as the hourly check runs it, is skipped while the marker is there, so a plain start or restart overrides a stop; stop and restart wait up to five minutes for running work and never force-kill, and the script refuses to start a duplicate or to choose between two running instances (docs/006-deployment.md, scripts/). Third, a run waiting on its own background work is not stalled: the worker preset moves a foreground shell command to a background job after 5 seconds, so a worker can take new messages at its next step; when a turn ends while shell jobs or subagents still run, the ticket keeps its worker slot and stays working instead of waiting, and a finished job wakes the worker with its result in the same slot; after each turn, background work has at most 30 minutes, then the shell jobs are killed, the report names them, and the ticket is reported waiting, while subagents may go on; neither the slot nor the limit applies after a handoff to a person, when subagents stop and shell jobs left for the person, such as a server offered for review, hold no slot, are exempt from the limit and do not wake the worker when they end (docs/003-execution.md; the executor module under src/executor/ sets the 30-minute limit). A host restart also starts each assignment it cut off mid-work again, with a recovery note: inspect the worktree, git history and the code host's state before continuing, and do not repeat an already completed external operation (src/core/assignments.ts). Article vs prototype: the article's section 6 goes further, with an independent watchdog session outside the main system, driven by timed messages as an outside control loop, which handles infrastructure faults such as interface errors and failed state recovery, has the model judge whether each worker is making real progress or drifting from the overall goal, keeps rechecking an outside transient fault until it clears, and, being a full agent session itself, can answer a maintainer's plain-language question about a fault or correct the main system online, such as by adding or removing prompts and adjusting trigger rules. That session is not in the prototype: no file in the repo mentions a watchdog, and its only outside check is the hourly status check above, while the three restart rules are in its code and docs. Why it matters here: per the curating bot's analysis of the repo and article, our stale-log watchdog acts on one signal, a log silent for about 540 s, and its on-stale action resumes the same session (#launch); our run lessons show it restarting what it should have left alone: on 10-15 it re-ran a catch-up collect cold twice, a new conversation each time, while the collect waited up to 15 minutes on its own background task, each run ending with a success result and no pack, and the second re-run left two seats holding the same pack path for about 3 minutes (#mac-run-lessons). A deliberate stop is confirmed layer by layer by hand, the stopped bot's tmux jobs and their watchdogs included (#emergency-stop), and the playbook describes no stop record that the watchdog's resume path reads, by a search of it for a stop marker or an intentional stop. We already have: every long Mac run launched in tmux with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s whose on-stale action resumes the same session, a manual convention that nothing blocks (#launch, #controls-inventory); a resume only after the old agent is proven gone, with a stale attempt's publish refused (rc=3), enforced by the ownership guard (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), and an unknown outcome parked, never retried blind (#retry-ceiling); a resumed routine that checks live state before each write and never publishes twice (#idempotent-resume), the same rule as the prototype's recovery note; two spawn-ok probes after Mac trouble, exit 142 meaning a hung program and 127 one that could not start, run by hand, report-only in the inventory (#spawn-ok, #controls-inventory); report-only Mac checks whose exit codes are written down while nothing acts on them (#report-only-checks); an emergency stop that confirms each layer by a lookup that worked, a manual control (#emergency-stop, #controls-inventory); the EM bot's heartbeat every 15 minutes over live agent tasks (#overview-day, #em-loop); and named long-run failure modes, with loop patterns kept distinct from the stale-only watchdog, which is not fleet-replaced without Haiyuan's ask (#exception-first). Already in the Lab: 'watchdog-kit: change-only alerts for scheduled jobs that escalate once if ignored' (2026-10-18), whose exit codes are its interface; 'whystuck: names why a quiet command stalled and prints the non-interactive fix' (2026-10-18); 'livelock + loopguard — named failure modes + loop/oscillation detect' (2026-09-23), folded into the playbook; and the 2026-10-09 card on a plugin that holds automatic goal continuation while the session still has live background work, for the goal rounds of their agent harness rather than for a watchdog. So, per the curating bot's analysis, what is new here is the restart decision itself: exit codes that say whether a restart can help, a stop marker the recovery loop must honor, and a run that ended its turn on its own live background job counted as working up to a cap. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's analysis of the repo and article (a proposal, not approved): a trial on one routine's watched launches only, in which a deliberate stop writes a stop marker beside the run's log and the watchdog's on-stale path skips the resume, and logs why, while the marker is there; before an on-stale resume, the watchdog first checks whether the agent ended its turn with its own background job still running and, if so, holds the resume until that job ends or a cap passes, then reports it; and the watchdog's own exit codes separate 'a restart may fix it' from 'a restart does not fix it', so that only the first leads to a resume. The prototype's cap is 30 minutes; ours would be set in the trial, and a model that judges progress, as in the article, stays out of it. The analysis's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the repo or the article; the playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts (#check-can-fail), which here would be a planted stop marker and a planted background wait. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Changing the watchdog, the launcher or the ownership guard; adding a stop marker or a background-job check to any of them; choosing a cap; changing what an exit code triggers; letting a model judge a run's progress, as the article proposes; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A launcher, wrapper or watchdog change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: a research prototype for reference only, not an official product, per its README, which also says it differs from the lab's internal version and from the article and that some article designs are not implemented; the watchdog session is one of them, per a search of the repo; its script manages its own service in its own tmux session, not our launcher, and its stop marker holds only against a start or restart run with --respect-stop; the 30-minute cap, the 5-second move to the background and the exit codes are the prototype's choices, not measured here; and its workers run commands without approval as the operator's user, with command wrappers that set defaults, not a security boundary (docs/003-execution.md, docs/006-deployment.md). MIT license; commit 6337fc8, cloned 2026-10-31; read from the repo and the article only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: A model lab's super-agent prototype: the router is told to forward the ask, never to work
entries.why: A model lab's research prototype, a bundle for their agent harness that runs a proactive coding agent for one code repository, read with the lab's design article on what it calls a super-agent (in Chinese): the article's two-layer design (section 2) puts a resident router layer in front, which takes every human interaction, holds the global context and dispatches work but runs no task itself, possibly without a shell tool and often on a lighter model, and context-isolated worker sessions behind it, which hold the full tools and the strongest model, never answer people directly and report to the router, which replies for them. The prototype implements it as one main session on a router preset with a smaller tool set and one worker session and directory per ticket (docs/003-execution.md). Its built-in prompts say the main session only routes: it forwards the original trigger reference and only routing facts, makes no technical decisions and adds no requirements, implementation plans, acceptance criteria or policy checklists, because workers derive requirements from the original source and standing policy (prompts/shared.md, prompts/dispatch.md, docs/004-prompts.md). An accept or attach takes an optional routing note of at most 30 words, a limit the routing tool checks, and the host always includes the original trigger reference independently of the note (prompts/dispatch.md, src/app/tools/main.ts). On the worker side, its instructions say a routing note or ticket title never substitutes for the original context and cannot add implementation requirements, and a worker that cannot reach the source context reports that limitation rather than treating the router summary as complete (prompts/work.md). A guard refuses main-session shell commands that run sleep, shell timeouts over 30 seconds and job waits over 5 seconds, because a blocked step delays new candidates (docs/004-prompts.md, src/app/sessions.ts); still, 'Avoiding code reads is a prompt rule, not a tool restriction', since the main session keeps shell and file-read tools (docs/007-architecture.md). The article's ablation (section 7.1, on the authors' synthetic load: about 300 chat and CI messages per run, about 20 of them work requests, coding replaced by a tool that only spends time, message gaps and work times scaled to 1/4, each scheme run 5 times) compared four schemes, the design, the design without pass-through routing, and one session given a subagent tool under each of two prompts: under a neutral prompt the model called no subagent in any of the 5 runs and did all the work itself while new messages kept interrupting it, a p95 of 29.5 minutes; under a prompt preferring delegation it delegated in 4 of the 5 runs, and in the other one judged the work small and did it itself; the two-layer design reached a p50 of 12.4 and a p95 of 15.7 minutes. Without pass-through, completion times stayed about the same, but the router made about 30% more decisions and the run's total cache-read tokens rose by about 37%; the design itself read more cached tokens than the single session, trading tokens for shorter, steadier completion times. The authors call these results preliminary, from synthetic load in a simplified setup. Article vs prototype: the two layers, the router's light load and the ablation are the article's; the prototype implements the main and worker sessions, the routing rules and the 30-word note limit, while its router keeps a shell and its workers, unlike the article's, post their own acknowledgements and review-thread replies (prompts/replies.md, prompts/work.md). Why it matters here: per the curating bot's analysis of the repo and article, our split has the same shape, and our rule that no coordinating bot writes code is a manual seat rule; the authors' test suggests that a prompt alone does not reliably hold a coordinator to delegating. The prototype also guards the request's own words across the hop, which our handoff rules do not: the playbook names no rule that Haiyuan's original words travel with a kick, by a search of it for verbatim or original-ask wording. We already have: the same two layers, the bots orchestrating, the Mac CLIs executing and the vault as the shared memory across both (#layers, #vault), and no coordinating bot writing code, a manual seat rule, policy only, with nothing checking the pick (#controls-inventory); every handoff and new kick carrying a packet with its objective, artifact paths, decisions already made, constraints, open questions and next gate, passing ownership, not transcripts, report-only in the inventory (#handoff-packet, #controls-inventory); the implementer restating the ask in its own words, compared with the ask, intent.md or the packet objective before work starts, policy text only (#intake-restatement); ambiguous asks going back to Haiyuan, never to a specialist by silent hand-off, a manual routing rule (#rules, #controls-inventory); and reviewers who see only the PR plus intent, spec and plan (#em-loop). Already in the Lab: the 2026-10-20 cards on a large company's thin-orchestrator post, whose router does no domain work and routes by fixed rules; the 2026-10-05 card on hook-enforced subagent routing with an orchestrator write-deny, which would turn our no-code rule for coordinating bots into a gate; and 'Intent-review stage — third oracle blind to PLAN.md' (2026-09-22), which checks the final diff against the verbatim original intent. So, per the curating bot's analysis, the split and the no-code rule are ours, and a gate for the rule has its own Lab card; what is new is the request's fidelity across the hop. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's analysis of the repo and article (a proposal, not approved): a trial on new coding kicks only, in which each kick-ledger row carries Haiyuan's original ask, in Haiyuan's own words or as a link to that message, beside the handoff packet; the EM bot's own note stays a short routing note that adds no requirements, plans or checklists, with the prototype's 30 words as a starting cap; and the implementer reads the original first, restates it (#intake-restatement), and reports when it cannot reach it rather than working from the packet's objective alone. A gate that keeps coordinating bots from writing code stays the 2026-10-05 card's separate proposal. The analysis's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the repo or the article. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Changing the handoff packet or the kick-ledger row; capping or checking the EM bot's notes; changing what the implementer reads first; restricting any coordinating bot's tools; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A handoff-contract change is a standing rule change, which gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory). Caveats: a research prototype for reference only, not an official product, per its README, which also says it differs from the lab's internal version and from the article; the ablation is the authors' own synthetic scheduling test, not a coding benchmark and not ours, and they call it preliminary; the prototype's coordinator is one session of their agent harness, while ours are bots on another platform with a kick ledger, so its tool limits do not carry over as they are; and their agent harness is the harness one of our seats runs for collection and advisory small jobs, never real code (#roster, #coding), while the prototype's workers write and push code. MIT license; commit 6337fc8, cloned 2026-10-31; read from the repo and the article only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
