entries.title: A model lab's super-agent prototype: quiet while working, and a 100-word chat cap
entries.why: A model lab's research prototype, a bundle for their agent harness that runs a proactive coding agent for one code repository, read with the lab's design article on what it calls a super-agent (in Chinese): the article (section 4.2) says chat should disturb people little, messaging like a human colleague only when a decision or acceptance is needed, asking direct questions and giving short conclusions, and reports one simple, effective hard rule the authors verified: no single reply over 100 words, while pull requests, email and documents carry the structured, dense detail. The prototype's founding principle is to take as little human attention as possible and give as much value as possible: a message, a notification, a question, a setting, a panel element or a paragraph of documentation must give more value than the attention it costs, or it is removed, and the agent stays quiet while it works (docs/000-philosophy.md). Its send path enforces the cap in code: a word counter that segments mixed Chinese and English text (src/infra/text.ts) rejects an outgoing chat message of more than 100 words, link labels and addresses counted, asking for a short high-level update and forbidding a split into several messages, and acknowledgements are held to 100 words on any channel (src/app/tools/tool.ts). The prompts call 100 words a hard ceiling, not a writing target, forbid evading it with long compound sentences, semicolon chains, bullet lists or several consecutive messages, and make one short sentence the default: the user-visible result, its link and any necessary next action (prompts/replies.md, prompts/team/communication.md). Per its prompts, an unsolicited chat message needs a ready outcome, a necessary human action or a definitive inability to complete; brief acknowledgements of a request and direct answers to a person's questions are kept; progress, unfinished drafts, pending checks and retries stay internal; and before sending, the agent asks of each clause 'would deleting this prevent the human from understanding the result or taking the required action?' and deletes it if not, and the evidence stays in the pull request and the internal report (prompts/team/communication.md). Its built-in text has a worker put one concrete question in its report for the router to forward unchanged (docs/004-prompts.md), and the setup guide asks one question per message, each message under 300 words unless the operator asks for more, with a recommended answer the operator can accept with one word (SETUP.md). Article vs prototype: the article states the 100-word rule as the authors' finding; the prototype enforces it in its send path and writes the rest into its prompts. Why it matters here: per the curating bot's analysis of the repo and article, the article's thesis is that the limit on productivity is moving to human attention, and the authors observe that one person can follow only 3 to 5 active sessions at once; in our fleet that attention is Haiyuan's, and every bot message to Haiyuan spends it. We already have: chat as a digest, with proof of done in a vault note path or a live URL, a manual control that no script checks (#vault, #controls-inventory); an always-log receipt line for every routine run, with chat quiet on success (#receipt-line); one decision queue for everything waiting on Haiyuan, irreversible items and genuine judgment calls only, each with the question, options and our recommendation, re-raised once after 3 days (#decision-queue), rules with no tooling adopted (#decision-queue-kill-receipts); done receipts that name what was and was not verified, open risks and approvals needed (#done-receipt); and a category Haiyuan approves more than about 90% of the time proposed for policy instead of a prompt, policy text only (#approval-rate). The playbook sets no length for a chat message, by a search of it for a word count or cap. Already in the Lab: 'watchdog-kit: change-only alerts for scheduled jobs that escalate once if ignored' (2026-10-18), which alerts only on a change and escalates an ignored problem once. So quiet success and a queue with a recommendation are ours; per the curating bot's analysis, what is new is a hard cap checked where a message is sent and the clause-by-clause deletion test. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's analysis of the repo and article (a proposal, not approved): a trial on one bot's chat messages to Haiyuan only, in which each message is held to 100 words, counted with a word segmenter so Chinese text counts by words, and checked where the message is sent rather than in the prompt, with the receipt and its evidence left in the vault note the message links; and each decision-queue item put as one concrete question with a recommended answer Haiyuan can accept in one word. The playbook names no point in a bot's chat send path where such a check could run, so the trial would first have to find one. The analysis's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the repo or the article; the playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts (#check-can-fail), which here would be a planted message over the cap. entries.title: A model lab's super-agent prototype: a rule change reaches the work it bears on
entries.why: A model lab's research prototype, a bundle for their agent harness that runs a proactive coding agent for one code repository, read with the lab's design article on what it calls a super-agent (in Chinese): in the prototype every accepted ticket holds a mandate, an immutable record of what the accept granted: the policy version, the scope, the strength, explicit or inferred, the matched rules, the sender's identity on that source and how the source received the message; wider scope means a new ticket, and a ticket's end does not end its mandate (docs/001-domain.md). The policy version covers the assessment rules, the accept mode and each source's allowed list, bot list and admission table, while models, concurrency, the pause and polling intervals leave it unchanged (docs/002-authorization.md, src/policy.ts). A version change discards running evaluations and queues their messages again, and sends a policy-changed input to each live ticket it bears on, saying whether a rule the ticket was accepted under changed, with its new text, or no longer applies, whether the requester may no longer start work, or whether proactive work is no longer accepted; unaffected tickets get no notice, and the change does not immediately revoke live tickets' mandates (docs/002-authorization.md; src/policy.ts works out each ticket's effect). The design rejects cancelling running tickets on a policy change, because a cancelled change leaves half-finished work; the change is recorded and delivered instead (docs/001-domain.md). Before an ended ticket resumes, its mandate is revalidated against the current policy: the source must still listen to the original thread; an explicit follow-up passes; an inferred mandate needs the auto mode and its matched rules still enabled; one admitted by an admission-table cell needs at least its original strength under today's table; a bot's needs the bot still listed; any other needs the sender still on the allowed list; and a ticket that fails stays ended and takes none of its waiting messages, each of which goes to a fresh evaluation if no other ticket owns it (docs/002-authorization.md). Only three operations change a mandate: accept creates it, a person's stop withdraws it, and failed revalidation revokes it (docs/002-authorization.md). Article vs prototype: the article does not describe mandates or a policy version, though its watchdog may adjust trigger rules online; this mechanism is in the prototype only. Why it matters here: per the curating bot's analysis of the repo and article, our standing rules change often: five entries in the playbook's rules list are marked adopted by Haiyuan on 2026-10-31 alone, by a count of that list (#rules), and each standing-rule change gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory). The playbook names no step that tells work already in flight about a change, by a search of it for notices to running or in-flight work; its nearest rules carry a model or seat swap into documents the same day (#model-change-sweep) and re-check current authority right before a RED action (#approval-recheck). We already have: an approval that covers the item as approved, with the item and current authority, a later ruling included, re-checked right before a RED action runs, policy text only (#approval-recheck), within approval validity, a manual control (#controls-inventory); a same-day sweep of every statement of an old model or seat assignment through the playbook, the shared contract file, the role cards and the affected skills (#model-change-sweep); a kick ledger whose rows go posted, launched, PR open or done, or blocked with a note (#coding-em-kicks), each new row carrying a handoff packet with the decisions already made and the constraints, report-only in the inventory (#handoff-packet, #controls-inventory); a resumed routine that checks live state before each write and never publishes twice (#idempotent-resume); and an emergency stop that marks a stopped bot's open kick-ledger rows blocked with a note, so the pickup check does not re-wake them, policy text only (#emergency-stop). Already in the Lab: 'agent-role-contracts: offline preflight that rejects self-review and stale handoffs' (2026-10-19), in which a review or approval must bind the current digest, which covers the policy as well as the task, and 'continuity: a session ledger detects handoffs made stale by its own work' (2026-10-25). So, per the curating bot's analysis, the RED half is ours; what is new is the in-flight half: a rule change that reaches the running work it bears on as a notice, not a cancel, and a resume that re-checks why the work was allowed. What would be adopted, per the curating bot's analysis of the repo and article (a proposal, not approved): a trial on coding kicks only, in which each kick-ledger row records its basis, who asked and when, the approval and the Decision locks it relies on; when a new Decision lock lands, the EM bot lists the live rows it bears on and sends each a short notice of what changed and what remains allowed, never a cancel, while rows it does not bear on hear nothing; and a resumed or retried row re-checks its basis first and, if it no longer holds, stays stopped and goes back to the EM bot and Haiyuan. The analysis's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied, and no negative control is named, in the repo or the article. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Changing the kick-ledger row or the packet; sending notices to live work; letting a failed re-check hold a row; deciding which locks a kick relies on; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A handoff-contract change is a standing rule change, which gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory). Caveats: a research prototype for reference only, not an official product, per its README, which also says it differs from the lab's internal version and from the article; the mandate model is in the prototype only; its policy covers who may ask for work and which proactive rules apply, a narrower set than our standing rules, which also cover seats, reviews and routines; its test list names mandate revalidation among the policy tests (docs/007-architecture.md), which were not run here; and what counts as a lock a kick relies on would need defining before any trial. entries.title: A model lab's super-agent prototype: a test pins the rules each prompt must state

Per its architecture document, one test covers 'The rules the built-in text must state, file by file', another checks everything models read, tools, prompts, skills and inputs, against the tool schemas, the execution environment and the glossary, within a size budget per role, and another checks that numbered documents link only to earlier ones and that every local link resolves (docs/007-architecture.md). entries.title: Success-claim receipts: audit detected claims for a fresh, relevant, correctly counted run
entries.why: Plugin for one coding CLI (JavaScript on Node 18 or newer, zero dependencies, no network; repository size 14,153 KB in the pack's metadata read) that holds the agent's final message against its own transcript. At the stop event, and for a subagent against that subagent's own transcript, a claim such as 'all tests pass' needs a receipt: a matching command that ran after the last change that can affect it, and passed. Its named failure shapes are never run; stale, edited after the green run; failed, where the output is scanned, so a piped test run that prints a failure, or a failure inside a too-long saved output file, still counts as failed; subset, one test file claimed as all; wrong count, '142 pass' when the run reported 140; unchecked, a background run never read back; and weakened, a test skipped or focused or an assertion deleted inside the claimed turn and not disclosed. Honest gaps, hedged and past-tense sentences, quotes and questions are not claims and are never flagged. The default mode is warn, which shows the user; block sends the agent back once, then only warns. After an edit to a shared module, a post-tool-use hint names its dependents and the project's real full-suite command, and a claim is flagged when dependent code that tests exercise was never exercised after the change. A history scan replays past sessions locally; a ledger lists each check as fresh, stale or failed; a PR receipt writes a verification table of what actually ran; and a circuit breaker blocks the third identical re-run of a command that failed twice with nothing changed in between. The author's evidence, not ours: on 4.6 GB of real history (215 success-claim turns, 233 claims), 35 claims had no receipt; read by hand, 11 were real, 19 false alarms and 5 undecidable, a precision of 37 % on the decidable cases, which is why it warns by default. In the author's pre-registered A/B runs over 1,260 real sessions of that coding CLI, the share of cross-package changes that left a working repository went from 43 % to 78–79 %, but the same three session-start rules pasted into that coding CLI's own instruction file in the repository did just as well (57 vs 56, 56 vs 55), figures for which the pack gives no unit or denominator, and the stop hook alone did not measurably help, because no session in any arm made a false claim; the README prints those three rules verbatim. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our done receipts and code-decides-done rule have no measured false-alarm rate and no history scan, and a checker that will send agents back needs both numbers before it may block. Per the pack, the lane is crowded and this is not carded for blocking an unbacked claim: kept proof-of-done (2026-10-06) already decides by the latest matching command after the last relevant edit, kept claimcheck (2026-09-28) already ships measured evals, its new checks blocking only once false alarms are near zero, kept agent-receipts (2026-10-03) already audits offline and kept doneguard (2026-10-30) runs the checks itself. What none of them carries, per the pack, is the claim-semantics layer (staleness judged by relevance per check ecosystem and directory, quoted-count arithmetic across runs, subset against all, a test weakened in this turn, and subagent claims audited before they reach the main thread) joined to a published precision and a baseline rate on real history, about 1 unbacked claim in 20 on the author's machine. We already have: a task done only when a concrete, deterministic check passes, with agent self-reports advisory only (#code-decides-done); a tests-pass or done claim counting only when the session record shows that a test command ran in this session against the current head and that its last run passed, plus a test-tamper scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer for tests skipped, deleted or focused, assertions gutted or a test command changed so it always passes, a green run after such a change being SUSPECT, never PASS: a prose rule with no hook installed, where an enforcing stop hook would be a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first, and no tamper incident is traced in our records yet (#claim-vs-record); the exit code in VERIFIED being the check's own, since a check piped into tail or head reports the last command's status, and a count or an all-or-none statement in a receipt naming how it was counted and over what, policy text only (#check-can-fail); and done receipts whose VERIFIED line names only checks that actually ran, each with its evidence (#done-receipt); all four sit within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory). Two of the adjacent cards already fed those rules: the claim-versus-record rule came from the claimcheck card and the check-can-fail rule in part from the agent-receipts card, as rules only, their tools not installed (#claim-vs-record, #check-can-fail). Beside them, transient errors retry at most twice, a manual control with no enforcing wrapper live (#retry-ceiling, #controls-inventory), the nearest thing here to the plugin's breaker; and the always-on plays in the EM loop section list that coding CLI's own instruction file at each repository root, under one page, and name hooks as the place for must-hold rules such as no weakening tests during a fix (#em-loop), though the claim rule itself has no hook (#claim-vs-record). So the core claim, that a success claim needs a matching run after the last change and that green after a weakened test does not count, is already our policy, a manual control; per the pack, what is not applied here is the mechanical layer and its two numbers: no claim-versus-transcript audit, no freshness judged by relevance, no quoted-count check and no history scan runs on any seat, and our done receipts carry no measured false-alarm rate. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a warn-first trial only, head-to-head with the carded claim checks. First run its history scan offline over our own past sessions of that coding CLI and hand-read every flag, as the author did, before any live use; then install it warn-only on that seat for one project; then compare it with the proof-of-done card's rule on the same transcripts and keep whichever is right more often. Block stays off until our own precision is measured; per the pack, 37 % on the author's history makes it a warning tool, not a gate. Per the pack, the cheap arm of the trial is three sentences, not a plugin: the plugin install could instead be the three rules the README prints, pasted into that coding CLI's own instruction file in one repository. The pack's summary line for the receipts plugin: a success claim needs a run that is fresh for the files changed, covers what "all" claims, reports the quoted count, and did not get there by weakening a test in the same turn. The pack's stop/kill condition: the head-to-head is its only criterion, keeping whichever of the plugin and the proof-of-done rule is right more often on the same transcripts; no precision threshold for turning on block is supplied, only that block stays off until our own precision is measured, and no negative control is named. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts (#check-can-fail); the pack's trial plants none, and in the author's own A/B no session made a false claim for the stop hook to catch. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running its history scan over our session records, even offline; installing the plugin on any seat or project, even warn-only; pasting its three rules into that coding CLI's own instruction file in any repository; turning on block; extending it to another seat; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it is a plugin for one coding CLI only, so none of our other seats is covered; per the pack's local read, one seat's settings file held 0 hook events, a collection-time measurement, which the pack reads as making any hook trial a first install on that seat; the author's live and A/B runs were on another desktop operating system, not the Mac, so Mac-specific verdict bugs are likelier undiscovered; claims are detected by phrase in seven languages, so unusually worded claims slip through and its recall is unmeasured; weakening done by rewriting a whole file or by a shell edit is not compared; checks outside the shell, such as editor compiles or manual device tests, are invisible to it; it is built for honest mistakes, not as a sandbox against a model trying to deceive; the 37 % precision, the 4.6 GB of history and the A/B figures are the author's numbers, not ours; and our run lessons record tool-use hooks hanging 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalling two implementer runs (#mac-run-lessons). It was created the same morning, hours before the collection, and its first release is the shipped arm of its own A/B, with no external use yet. MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-31 00:49 PT, pushed 2026-10-31 08:24 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: verderer: a rule ledger with provenance and dead, derivable or needed ablation verdicts
entries.why: Ledger, in dependency-free JavaScript on Node 20 or newer, for the rules in an agent's standing instruction files, the shared contract file and one coding CLI's own instruction file, built to answer one question: does this rule still earn the tokens it costs every session? Its scan inventories the rules into a ledger file in that coding CLI's project folder, one entry per rule with its text, source file, section, first-seen date, origin and status. Scanning is idempotent and append-only: known rules keep their provenance and verdicts, new rules are dated, and rules that leave the file are marked retired, never deleted. Provenance is decided by version history: for a tracked instruction file, git blame dates each rule, and the date names the model era the rule was written against; for an ignored, private file, which has no history, the first scan records the origin as unknown and dates everything after it, so the ledger can be tracked while the file stays private. Its ablation verdicts, from runs without the rule, are three-valued: dead, the model does it unaided; derivable, unaided but a miss is expensive, so keeping the rule is cheap insurance; and needed. It reports and never auto-deletes; the blast radius stays a human call. The one validation in the README was done before the tool existed: of 3 long-standing rules in one coding CLI's instruction file, probed by ablation in about 1 hour over 3 headless runs, 1 was dead, 1 derivable and 1 reduced to a single clause. Its probe command today only prints the manual ablation recipe; automated per-rule ablation worktrees and headless runs are on the roadmap, as is re-examining rules when the configured model changes. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our rule files only grow: the pack cites the 2026-10-30 publish note as recording the shared contract file held at 13,469 B under a no-growth ledger rule, and reads that as nothing retiring. Per the pack, the cards we have ask different questions: kept tripwires (2026-10-22) judges a guard rule by its denials and a weekly helps-or-hurts report, kept deadweight (2026-10-22) finds config the runtime silently ignores, kept custodiet (2026-10-28) governs which rules may block, and kept agnix (2026-10-26) and kept rulesift (2026-10-30) check validity and integrity; none asks whether a rule that loads, fires and is valid is still needed after a model upgrade, or after the code grew to carry the convention. Per the pack, a blame-dated ledger plus a dead, derivable or needed verdict is the missing retirement path, and it pairs with kept agent-harness-eval (2026-10-29): that card measures a harness change, while an ablation verdict says which single rule to remove next. The playbook differs on two points: the files every agent reads may not grow past their byte ceilings (#resident-budget), so they are capped, not only growing; and retirement is not ad-hoc deletion, as the pack says it is today: adding a line past the ceiling means making room by compressing or demoting another, older line, oldest first, to a learning note with a pointer, and a wrong line goes on a prune list that Haiyuan approves item by item (#resident-budget, #memory-loop). We already have: byte ceilings on the files every agent reads before every task, 13,489 B for the shared contract file, where adding a line past the ceiling means compressing or demoting another, oldest first, and the daily digest records both sizes (#resident-budget), the size gates report-only (#controls-inventory); edits to that file limited to fleet-wide standing rules, a manual control with nothing checking the reason for an edit (#controls-inventory); the rule-to-enforcer table behind the controls inventory, a trial pending review with statuses as of 2026-10-20, which pairs each of the shared contract file's 73 rules with what enforces it, 34 of them policy-only, though the playbook mentions no origin date or still-needed verdict in it (#controls-inventory); a correction already in the never-again list twice or more becoming a proposed skill diff instead of another paragraph, a manual control (#repeat-lesson, #controls-inventory); wrong or outdated lessons, a wrong line in the shared contract file among them, going on a prune list that names each item, why it should go and what replaces it, and deleted only after Haiyuan approves the specific items, policy text only (#memory-loop); a provenance card (claim, source, owner, status, supersedes, review_after) on new Decision notes and standing-rule memories, old notes not bulk-rewritten, with no checker named (#memory-rules); a same-day sweep of every statement of an old model or seat assignment when Haiyuan swaps one, each agent also rewriting its own lessons the swap made wrong or listing them for deletion, with no checker named, where re-running a replay set after a model change is not taken yet and version bumps from the daily update are not swaps (#model-change-sweep); a stated detection floor, three clean runs catching a large regression but not showing that a smaller one is absent, policy text only (#detection-floor); and a harness evaluation design whose arms remove whole components, the blind-review stage or one docs seat, and which reports zero failures in an arm as inconclusive, never as support for removing a component, a proposal not approved and not run (#harness-eval). So retirement here goes by size, age and judgment, with deletions approved item by item; per the pack, what is not applied is a per-rule provenance ledger dated by version history and an ablation verdict per rule: nothing here tests whether a single rule is still needed, and our model-change sweep rewrites statements of the old assignment, not the rules a new model may no longer need. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): run the ledger and run probes by hand. Run its scan over the vault's shared contract file, read-only on the rule files, the ledger being the only write; then hand-ablate the 3 oldest rules, the README's recipe being 3 headless runs, and record the verdicts. Re-probe at the next seat model change; per the pack, that trigger is the pattern worth keeping even if the tool is replaced. The pack's summary line for verderer: a harness rule stays only while ablation still needs it; provenance and a dead/derivable/needed verdict make retirement evidence, not ritual. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; its stated boundary is that the scan stays read-only on the rule files, the ledger being the only write, and its stated trigger is a re-probe at the next seat model change. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). entries.title: task-handoff-check: a handoff whose state contradicts itself is rejected at pickup
entries.why: Small command-line tool and library in standard-library Python 3.10 or newer, with no network (repository size 169 KB in the pack's metadata read), that validates an explicit JSON handoff document before the next person or agent picks it up. Its state model is checked for contradiction: objective, owner, status (ready, in progress, blocked or complete), next action, inputs, evidence, blockers and completion criteria are required; complete requires every criterion met, no open blockers and a null next action; any open blocker requires blocked, and blocked requires at least one blocker, each with an owner, plus a concrete next action; a criterion marked met requires at least one evidence reference by exact label. Unknown fields are errors; blank text and exact placeholders such as TBD, todo, unknown, unassigned and n/a are rejected; reference paths and URLs are validated for shape, a portable relative path with no embedded credentials, but never opened. Freshness is reproducible: staleness is never inferred from the machine clock at read time; the caller supplies an as-of time and, optionally, a maximum age in hours, a future updated-at time is rejected, and the report's freshness field names within limit, stale, future or not evaluated explicitly. The bundled examples include a deliberate failure case, complete with an open blocker, which exits 1. Its README states its scope plainly: 'A passing handoff is structurally consistent. It is not proof that its claims are true, that its references exist, or that anyone is authorized to act.' It changes no task state and executes no command. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, written handoffs are our load-bearing contract, in group rooms, the manager bot's intake, the pack-to-curate-to-publish chain and the EM's intent, spec and plan, and the failure we actually make is structural: done claimed over an open blocker, a next step with no owner, a criterion marked met with no evidence pointer, a stale note picked up as current. Per the pack, kept continuity (2026-10-25) is a live-session checkpoint coupled to two coding CLIs that flags a handoff its own session's work made stale; it is not a portable lint a receiving seat can run on any handoff it is handed. This one is that receive-side check, offline, dependency-free and exit-coded for CI or a pre-accept hook, and per the pack its as-of rule is the correct form of our own fresh as-of discipline. Per the pack, the cost is real: our handoffs today are markdown, so adoption means emitting or generating a JSON sidecar for each handoff we choose to gate. The playbook differs on one point: the manager bot's handoffs and new coding kick rows already carry a machine-readable packet (#handoff-packet), with a different field set from this tool's, while the pack's trial target, the daily Lab pack, is markdown. We already have: every actionable message from the manager bot to a specialist carrying goal, owner, trigger, artifact path, verified, assumptions, waiting-approval, open questions and return shape, the written handoff contract, with no checker named (#grok-patterns); every handoff from the manager bot to a specialist, and every new coding kick row, carrying the artifact path and a machine-readable packet (from, to, job type, objective, artifacts, decisions already made, constraints, open questions and next gate), the artifact carrying the detail and the packet the state (#handoff-packet), report-only in the inventory: the packet's completeness check by our decision layer is shadow only and never blocks, box-side and unverified from the Mac, and a missing field gets a packet-incomplete note and never blocks the kick (#controls-inventory, #coding-em-kicks); a kick ledger on the same box, whose rows move from posted to launched to PR open or done, or to blocked with a note, a kick posted with no seat never counting as idle, its daily pickup check paused since 2026-10-23 (#coding-em-kicks); done receipts listing what was verified and what was not, reusing the handoff's verified, assumptions and waiting-approval fields, within completion validation, a manual control (#done-receipt, #controls-inventory); negative claims needing a lookup that worked, with a fresh as-of time, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory); fast-clock facts such as CI state or a PR's tip SHA re-fetched live before any action or claim, with no checker named (#memory-rules); and cited vault paths checked to resolve before a pointer is written, a manual rule whose lint tool is not installed (#pointer-check), which covers by hand, for vault paths, the referenced paths this tool never opens. So the state our handoffs carry is checked for missing fields at most, in shadow, and, per the pack, nothing rejects a handoff whose own status, blockers, criteria and evidence contradict each other before a seat accepts it; per the pack, the only structural gate on a pack is its closing done line. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a trial as a receive-side gate on one handoff format only. Pick one recurring handoff, the daily Lab pack's curate handoff, emit its state as JSON alongside the markdown, lint it in the curate step with an explicit as-of time, and keep the three bundled shapes (consistent, complete, contradictory) as controls, of which only the contradictory one is a negative control, though the pack calls all three negative controls. Per the pack, a pass is never to be presented as verification; its own README forbids that reading. The pack's summary line for task-handoff-check: a handoff whose status, blockers, criteria and evidence contradict each other is rejected at pickup; freshness is judged only against a supplied as-of. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its controls are the three bundled shapes, of which only the contradictory one is a negative control, and the bundled examples include the deliberate failure case that exits 1; a pass shows structural consistency, not truth. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Choosing the handoff; installing the package, even pinned; hand-writing or generating a JSON sidecar for any pack; wiring the lint into the curate step, or letting a failed lint hold a curate; extending it to the manager bot's intake, group rooms or coding kicks; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: JSON only, it does not parse markdown, so a sidecar, hand-written or generated, is the adoption cost, and a generated sidecar can itself drift from the note it describes; it never opens a referenced path or URL, so missing evidence files still pass; it does not understand free text, so an unhelpful but non-placeholder sentence passes; its first release is days old, and its README notes that the packaged CI results, not every later commit, are the executed-coverage evidence; its package-index release as of 26 Oct 2026 and its state model are the README's claims, not verified here. entries.title: antibody: scan transcripts for an incident's repeats, then block or warn on the command
entries.why: Command guard built backwards from its author's own incident log: one static binary in Rust, with no network and no daemon (repository size 2,748 KB in the pack's metadata read; 16 and 19 test functions in two test files; CI and release workflows). Its scan reads the local transcripts of 14 coding agents, extracts every shell command the agents actually ran and matches each against its 13 detectors, which it calls antibodies, 10 that block and 3 that warn. The scan is read-only, with no cache, no log and no network; it counts hits per antibody with dates, agents, example commands and how many were already blocked or declined, and offers JSON output, filters by date, agent and path, an HTML report with redaction and a share card with counts only. Its check is a pre-tool-use hook: it reads one hook payload of at most 16 MiB, finds the shell command, splits it with a shell-aware parser for three shell syntaxes (quotes, chained and piped commands, substitutions and here-docs, unwrapping bash -c, ssh, sudo, env, timeout and xargs up to 6 levels deep) and refuses a command matching a blocking antibody in the agent's own hook format, an exit code of 2 with the reason or a deny or cancel reply, across 12 hook formats. The denial carries the incident and the alternative: its kill-by-name antibody says an agent once killed a runtime's processes by image name and stopped every other session's servers, and that the fix is to find the PID listening on the port and kill that; an explain command prints the full incident. The incident log is the evidence: 22 incidents between 2026-09-21 and 2026-11-01, each with what happened, the damage, the rule and what enforces it now; 13 became command-shaped antibodies, and the rest stayed written rules because they have no command shape. In the README's own summary, written rules failed at least three times (incidents 7, 8 and 11), and each repeat stopped only when a hook blocked the command. It fails open by design: bad JSON, an unknown tool, oversize input, a config parse error or a panic all exit 0, so a command is refused only by a deliberate block, and it can only take permission away, never grant it. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our never-again list and incident notes are prose, and the same failures recur because a written rule is not a check. Per the pack, kept tripwires (2026-10-22) already carries each rule's incident, its test and a weekly verdict, and kept cheat-drill (2026-10-14) tests hooks against known moves, but neither has the scan step: the missing measurement is how often an incident already happened in our own transcripts before the guard is installed, which the scan answers read-only, and the hook then puts the incident and the safer command in front of the model at the moment it is about to repeat it. Per the pack, for a fleet that runs parallel seats on one Mac, its kill-by-name, recursive-delete-outside-repo, parallel-disk-scan, foreground-sleep-loop and dump-secret-file detectors map directly to failures we already write postmortems about; the pack does not say which of our incidents each would have matched. We already have: a correction already in the never-again list twice or more turned into a proposed fix where the rule is applied, such as a checker or hook spec, instead of another paragraph, a manual control (#repeat-lesson, #controls-inventory), a rule written after that list came to hold 18 near-identical paragraphs because the lesson never became a filter (#repeat-lesson); a byte ceiling on that list, 81,155 B, which it had reached in the inventory's statuses of 2026-10-20, so an append needs an equal trim, a manual control (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory); repeated failures fixed with a hook, a test or a skill, not with a memory line, policy text only (#shared-memory-admission); a rule-record reference format, the incident or evidence, the safer action, a reproducer or test with its tested version and the latest dated verdict with its owner, a missing verdict being a gap, a reference note with no checker named, beside a rule that is policy text only (#check-can-fail), so a rule that carries its incident and its safer action is already the documented shape here, a shape whose dated verdict, per the pack, antibody cannot supply; the always-on plays of the EM loop, which name hooks as the place for must-hold rules such as no secrets in the diff, no push to main and no weakening tests during a fix, with no inventory status and no installed hook named for them (#em-loop); after a test on 2026-10-28 cleaned up with a tmux kill-server command, killing the Mac's shared tmux server twice and ending its own run, a rule that no seat kills the shared tmux server or uses pkill or killall, that a seat stops only processes it started, by PID, and that launch prompts forbid tmux kill commands, logged in the changelog with no hook or checker named (#changelog-2026-10-26), the kill-by-PID alternative that the kill-by-name denial also gives, held here as a written rule and launch-prompt text; deleting anything but junk as a RED action that always goes to Haiyuan, a manual control (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory); a pre-tool gate in our decision layer, which sits in front of the manager bot's routing and whose router the playbook configures in active mode, that returns allow, ask or deny before a high-risk tool-server or shell mutation, a deny at or above its confidence floor meaning stop, a model verdict rather than an incident-derived rule, with no row in the controls inventory (playbook §13, gates table), while a separate per-tool hook, distinct from the decision layer's router, was retired permanently by Haiyuan on 2026-10-25 and is not to be reinstalled unless Haiyuan asks (playbook §13); and, nearest to the scan's count, a replay set meant to start from a count of failure types and to hold 20 to 50 real failures taken from never-again corrections and failed done receipts, policy text with the set not built yet, the replay check proposed in the inventory (#replay-set, #controls-inventory). So the written-rule half and the record shape are ours already, but the playbook names no installed coding-CLI hook that refuses a shell command; per the pack, nothing here scans our own transcripts for how often an incident's command already ran, and no denial carries its incident. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): scan first, install two or three detectors, keep the incident text. First a read-only scan over one week of our own transcripts from two coding CLIs our seats run (#roster), with every hit hand-checked, since the README's own scan hit 11 antibodies on 45 commands in its fixtures, which per the pack is exactly why the examples need eyes; then a dry-run init on one Mac, installing only the 2–3 detectors with real hits; and no pipe-to-shell installer, but a build from source or a release archive checked against its published checksum. The pack's summary line for antibody: a repeated incident becomes a command detector; scan the transcripts first to measure how often it already happened, then block the repeat with the incident and the safer command. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; its stated bounds are the read-only scan with every hit hand-checked, the dry-run init on one Mac, only the detectors with real hits, and no pipe-to-shell installer. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts, and that a proposed check's proof record hold healthy, incident or planted-bad, and empty inputs (#check-can-fail); hand-checked hits would be incident inputs, and the pack names no healthy or empty case. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running the scan over our transcripts, even read-only; installing the binary on the Mac, even for a dry-run init; choosing or enabling any detector; wiring its hook into any seat's settings; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the 13 antibodies (10 block, 3 warn), the 22 incidents, the 14 agents' transcript readers and the 12 hook formats are the author's numbers, not ours; only one coding tool was verified against real data, and the other 13 transcript readers and 11 of the 12 hook formats are built from docs and synthetic fixtures, as the README says, so of the two coding CLIs the trial would scan, one would be read by an unverified reader, and under our negative-claim rule, a manual control, a zero from it counts as zero only once the lookup is shown to have worked (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory); it is shell-only, so an inline interpreter command, a script, an encoded command run through eval or a changed hook config gets through; failing open means a bug lets a command run; the hook logs nothing and keeps no state, so it cannot give a weekly helps or hurts verdict, which per the pack is the tripwires card's job; the incident log mixes the Mac and another desktop operating system and includes a payment-refund rule that may be too specific to its author, a snapshot of one developer's scars; whether its kill-by-name antibody matches the pkill, killall or tmux forms of our own incident is not stated in the pack; and our run lessons record tool-use hooks hanging 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalling two runs (#mac-run-lessons). It was created hours before the collection, by one author. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: Covenant: judge the finished change against the rules at its base commit
entries.why: Rule tool in Python 3.11 or newer (repository size 1,148 KB in the pack's metadata read; 19 checkers; a benchmark with 6 scripted tasks and a 50-repository replay; CI and release workflows) that compiles rules written in plain English into checks over the outcome, then enforces them at the agent's hooks, at git commit and push, and in CI. Its compile step turns sentences into a rules file bound to one of 19 named checkers; the examples: don't change public APIs (exported names and signatures in five languages), don't delete user data (protected files and database rows, restored from a snapshot if lost), no destructive migrations, only allowed dependencies change (majors stay put), only change files under one folder, don't commit secrets, don't skip tests (deleted, skipped or focused tests), keep the change under 200 lines, no debug prints or new lint suppressions, run tests before committing, never force-push, deploy or run destructive SQL (16 refused-command categories), a network allowlist, folder ownership between agents, and time, action and cost budgets. It checks outcomes, not tool calls: the API surface is compared after the edits, however they were made; protected files and rows are compared before and after and restored from a snapshot; and the order check is that tests passed after the last edit and before the commit. An explain command prints the rule, the evidence and the fix, and an undo command puts the working tree back. The governance property: a PR is judged by the rules at its base commit, so a PR cannot weaken the rule that judges it. The author's evidence, not ours: on CovenantBench, instruction alone gave 1.17 violations per task and the tool 0.0, with task success 1.0 in both arms, for a scripted agent on 6 tasks; four live trials of one coding CLI on real Python repositories committed every honest task and refused or blocked every trap; and a replay of 1,446 real commits from 50 repositories flagged 75, of which 72 were real rule breaks per the bench page, while the main README also says 2 were false alarms, which does not add up to 75. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our rules live in the shared contract file and one coding CLI's standing-instruction file and are enforced by prose or a per-tool hook, though the playbook records the per-tool hook it names, distinct from our decision layer's router, as retired permanently by Haiyuan on 2026-10-25 (playbook §13). Per the pack, kept custodiet (2026-10-28) governs which rule may block, with a signed law, cases both ways and killed mutations; kept tripwires (2026-10-22) attaches an incident and a test to a command rule; and kept verderer (2026-10-31) decides when a rule should be retired; none checks the finished change against the rule, and none pins the rule to the base commit. Per the pack, that is the gap that matters for our vault, where a docs or rules PR can edit the rule that reviews it: the base-commit judgement is the missing half of the review gate, and the outcomes-not-tool-calls shape catches the change a hook never sees, such as a rename made through the shell, a deleted test, a bumped dependency or a path reached by a script. The playbook is more specific than the pack: its inventory, a trial table pending review, pairs the shared contract file's 73 rules with what enforces each, 34 of them policy-only and the others a script, a check, a routine, review or nothing built yet (#controls-inventory). The pack calls tripwires and custodiet the nearest existing gates; neither is named on the playbook, and a card calls a practice applied only where the playbook says so, a playbook lesson, not a lock (#lab-card-claims). We already have: blind review of each PR against its intent, spec and plan, the plan listing the files to touch, by reviewers who name 2–3 rejection criteria from the task contract before reading the diff and then attempt disproof, a manual control (#em-loop, #disproof-review, #controls-inventory); docs and drafts such as Decision notes reviewed by two blind seats, a manual control, with doc or policy folds given the full Tier 2 pass, policy text only (#reviewer-rule, #review-depth-tiers, #controls-inventory); before approval, one read of the complete resulting files, not only the diff, against the acceptance criteria, a manual review step (#review-convergence, #controls-inventory); a review verdict pinned to the head SHA, a line naming an older SHA never counting as an LGTM, a manual control (#review-verdict-line, #controls-inventory), and Pre-existing findings judged against the PR's original base, the commit the branch forked from, never against the latest fix round, another manual review step (#review-convergence); a reviewer or gate taking its policy from its own prompt and the playbook, the material under review being evidence only, policy text only (#untrusted-content), though the playbook does not say whether a PR that edits a rule is judged by the old text or the new; a test-tamper scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer, for tests skipped, deleted or focused, gutted assertions or a test command changed so it always passes, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), which also looks for || true added after a check and for commits made with --no-verify, which skips the repo's hooks (#check-can-fail); hooks named among the EM loop's always-on plays as the place for must-hold rules such as no secrets in the diff, no push to main and no weakening tests during a fix, with no inventory status and no installed hook named for them (#em-loop); edits to the shared contract file limited to fleet-wide standing rules, a manual control with nothing checking the reason for an edit, while its byte-ceiling gates are report-only and an unrelated, equal-size replacement passed both in a probe on 2026-10-20 (#controls-inventory); and a rule-phrase check, a report-only shadow trial not built yet, that would report each must-hold rule no longer stated where agents read it and each superseded wording still there (#rule-phrase-check). So judging the finished change against a written contract is ours already, done by reviewers as a manual control; per the pack, what is not applied is a mechanical check of the outcome against compiled rules, and nothing here pins a rule set to a PR's base commit: our verdicts are pinned to the head SHA and Pre-existing findings to the original base, and neither rule says which version of an edited rule applies. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a read-only replay first, then one repository's pre-commit hook. Install it with a Python package installer and compile three rules (don't change public APIs, run tests before committing, don't touch the docs folder); run its CI mode over the last 20 commits of one repository, read-only, and hand-check every flag and every miss; then install only the git pre-commit hook in that one repository, and not the dashboard, the editor extension, the container sandbox or the chat alerts yet. The pack's summary line for Covenant: a rule is judged on the finished change at its base commit, not on the tool calls; a PR cannot weaken the rule it is judged by. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; its stated bounds are the read-only replay with every flag and every miss hand-checked, and then only the git pre-commit hook in one repository. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts (#check-can-fail); the pack's trial plants no broken commit and relies on the replay's real flags and misses. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing the package anywhere; choosing the repository or compiling its rules; running the replay, even read-only; installing its git hook or any agent hook; letting a flag block a commit, a push, a CI run or a merge; judging our rule changes by the rules at their base commit; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the benchmark figures, the four live trials and the 1,446-commit replay are the author's, not ours, and were not reproduced in the collection; the README's 2 false alarms and the bench page's 72 of 75 do not reconcile, so 72 of 75 is quoted here as the bench page's figure and the discrepancy stays open; the benchmark agent is scripted, on 6 tasks; the tool is large (19 checkers, a dashboard, a container sandbox, an editor panel), so a trial must be scoped to the git and CI core; a compiled rule can be wrong, since its offline extractor or a language model chooses the checker, and a wrong compile silently enforces the wrong thing; one live trial reported about 0.9 s per hook on another desktop operating system; the base-commit rule is a governance control, not a security boundary against a hostile agent that can edit the hook config; and a git pre-commit hook is skipped by a commit made with --no-verify (#check-can-fail). It is about a day old, by one author, created one minute after the earliest row of the previous day's pack, which it was not in. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: stay-in-lane: a stop hook flags edits the user's own words don't cover, by keyword
entries.why: Stop-time scope check for one coding CLI, built from the user's own words: a plugin with one skill, in standard-library Python (repository size 25 KB in the pack's metadata read; 14 paths; a built-in self-test, no tests folder and a committed bytecode cache). At session start it snapshots the working tree with git stash create, which touches neither the working tree nor the stash list, so files already dirty before the session are never flagged. At the stop it diffs the working tree against that snapshot, new files included, and sorts each change into a category: formatting-only (whitespace and blank lines, by git diff -w), dependencies (dependency manifests and any lockfile), config, build and CI files, deleted or renamed files, and a change set over 25 files. In-scope is decided by the user's messages, read from that coding CLI's transcript, user messages only, not tool output or compaction summaries: a change is in scope if the messages use one of its category's words (among them format, lint, style or refactor; upgrade, update, bump, install, package, version or CVE; config, CI, workflow, build, deploy or env; delete, remove, clean up, unused, rename, move or refactor) or name the file, and changing only the scripts of a package manifest is not a dependency change. It flags once and never reverts: the agent gets a list, such as a file changed only in whitespace or formatting and a manifest whose dependencies changed, and must undo each change or keep it and say in its reply why the task needed it; a justified change is not re-flagged, so the hook cannot loop. A PR mode prints the same categories for any branch or PR and exits 1 if anything turns up, for CI labelling; it is the same code without the session scoping. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the expensive part of reviewing an agent's PR is often not the bug but the 14-file diff that buries the two-line fix. Per the pack, kept pinwash (2026-10-19) checks whether a change weakened the checks, kept agent-slop (2026-10-30) whether it added comments, and kept swarm-agent-coordination (2026-09-28) checks paths owned by another agent; none answers whether this session changed things the user never asked for. Per the pack, the Covenant card from the same pack can enforce a declared path scope but cannot infer scope from the request, and this is the cheap, config-free complement: a short out-of-scope list, to justify or undo, is the artifact a reviewer wants before reading the diff. The pack ties that list to our blind dual-LGTM reviews; per the playbook, code our default implementer wrote gets one blind reviewer, while docs, drafts and other seats' code get two (#reviewer-rule). We already have: an intent written by research or product, not by the implementer inventing scope mid-build, and a plan listing the files to touch, against which reviewers check the PR, a manual review step (#em-loop, #controls-inventory); reviewers who name 2–3 rejection criteria from the task contract before reading the diff, a manual control (#disproof-review, #controls-inventory); since 2026-10-31, the ask carried verbatim in the handoff packet's source, with the implementer's restated ask and the reviewers' rejection criteria checked against it, its packet check shadow only and never blocking, box-side and unverified from the Mac, report-only in the inventory (#verbatim-ask, #controls-inventory); the agent restating the ask before a non-trivial task, compared with the intent before work starts, policy text only (#intake-restatement); a catch-test pass, adopted 2026-10-31 and policy text only, in which a seat that is not a reviewer infers an analytics SDK PR's intent from its title, body and diff and writes tests for 3–5 risks before blind review (#catch-tests); and the heartbeat's no-progress flag, a report-only shadow trial adopted on 2026-10-31 whose written rule would also flag a run whose log shows it working on something its objective does not cover, logged only and never sent (#no-progress-flag); the playbook leaves the heartbeat text to the bot that owns the heartbeat and records no result from the trial yet. So a written scope and the user's own words already reach the implementer and the reviewers, and a written shadow trial would log a run that drifts from its objective; per the pack, nothing here snapshots the tree at session start or lists, before review, the changes the ask never mentioned, and our reviewers find them by reading the diff against the plan. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a warn-only hook on one repository, then a PR label. First run its built-in self-test; then run its PR mode on five recent agent PRs and hand-count the false positives; only then install the hook in one repository of that coding CLI, warn-only. If the flag rate is high, narrow the keyword table rather than turning it off. The pack's summary line for stay-in-lane: the session's scope is what the user asked for; changes outside it are named and must be justified, never auto-reverted. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP: for a high flag rate the pack says to narrow the keyword table rather than turn the hook off, without saying what rate is high, and no negative control is named; its stated bounds are the self-test, the five-PR hand count and warn-only use in one repository. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts (#check-can-fail); the pack's hand count is of false positives only, so misses go uncounted. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running its PR mode over our PRs, even read-only; choosing the repository or the five PRs; installing its hooks for any seat, even warn-only; adding a PR label or a CI step; changing its keyword table; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it has no test suite, only a built-in self-test, unmeasured here like its flag rate, and it ships 14 files with a committed bytecode cache; scope is keyword matching, so a request to update the button text puts dependencies in scope because of the word update, erring toward staying quiet, which the pack calls the right default; formatting detection is whitespace-only, so a formatter that changes quotes shows up as a normal code change; the user's own manual edits count as changes, and the agent will have to explain them; only that one coding CLI's transcripts are read, so other coding CLIs get the skill only, not the hook; a long session with many requests accumulates a wider scope; and the row does not say how the hook runs warn-only, since by design it asks the agent to undo or justify each flagged change. It was created hours before the collection, by one author. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. MIT, 0 stars, created and pushed 2026-11-01 02:30 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: stay-in-lane: flag suspected out-of-scope edits by keyword matching
entries.whatItIs: A hook for one coding CLI that flags a session's edits of certain types, such as formatting, dependencies, config or deletions, as suspected out of scope unless the user's messages use a matching keyword or name the file. The agent must undo or justify each; nothing is reverted automatically.
entries.whyItMatters: Our reviewers find unrequested changes by reading the diff against the plan. A warn-only trial on one repository, after a hand count of false alarms on five recent pull requests, is only proposed and not installed; it has no test suite, only a built-in self-test, and any change needs Haiyuan.

entries.title: realstop: a stop hook sends polite quits back to work but lets real approval stops pass
entries.why: Stop-time check for one coding CLI, a plugin plus its own command line in Python 3.9 or newer, also published as a Python package (repository size 413 KB in the pack's metadata read; 74 paths, among them tests, scripts and a file of regression pairs), that catches unfinished work handed back to the human at the end of a turn: a polite deferral or closing offer such as 'Want me to add the requested tests?' or 'I have created the plan, should I implement it?', or a command the user is told to run in their own terminal. A caught quit is not let through: the hook returns feedback that keeps the turn going. Its judge has three tiers: a small local model running on the Mac (median 27 ms and p95 33 ms in the author's measurement, 186 ms for the whole hook); a cloud decision model, through a judge mode that per the pack explicitly supports the model behind our decision layer; and phrase rules only, with no model download, which per the author catch 56.7% of quits with 14.6% false interventions. A stop is let through when it matches an explicit harness denial named in the reply, when the user's prompt asked for an approval pause, or when it matches a listed approval step: a production deploy, a force push, destructive SQL, sending email or a payment; replies under 400 characters skip the model and use the phrase rules. A pre-approved list holds steps the user has approved in advance: when the agent asks consent for one of them, the stop is blocked and the agent is told the step is pre-approved. When the user types "no", "that's wrong" or "do this yourself", a second hook records the miss, and a learn command lets the human confirm or flip labels to tune how strict it is, refitting a 4 KB decision head locally. The author's evidence, not ours: scored on 864 test turn ends, 289 quits and 575 valid stops, the default moderate judge caught 67.5% of quits with 15.8% false interventions, and in the author's live trials with two coding models, closing offers dropped to zero. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our agents often end a turn early with a polite offer, such as asking whether to write the tests now, or hand raw shell commands back to Haiyuan. Per the pack, kept proof-of-done (2026-10-06), kept doneguard (2026-10-30) and kept antibody (2026-11-01) check exit codes and command shapes but cannot catch a conversational abandonment in which the agent never ran the tool at all, and this is the stop-time filter that gap needs; its pre-approved list matches our human-gate policies, and it supports our decision layer natively. The pack calls those three existing completion gates, but they are Lab cards: a text search of the playbook finds none of the three names, and a card calls a practice applied only where the playbook says so, a playbook lesson, not a lock (#lab-card-claims). We already have: a task done only when a deterministic check passes, with agent self-reports and the decision layer's completion check advisory only, never declaring done on their own (#code-decides-done), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); that completion check itself, which before a non-trivial task is reported done answers complete, verify more or incomplete, and runs in shadow, logging its verdict and never blocking (playbook §13), the nearest thing here to a cloud judge of how a turn ends; a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed, where a stop hook enforcing that rule would be a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first, and where the playbook records that needing a model call was the objection to an earlier stop-hook candidate, stingray, on 2026-09-27 (#claim-vs-record); RED actions, among them send or publish, spend or pay, merge, deleting non-junk, permissions and production, always going to Haiyuan, with anything that cannot be undone in under a minute parked and asked about, a manual control (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory), and an approval re-checked against the approved item and current authority right before the action runs, also manual (#approval-recheck, #controls-inventory), so its listed approval steps are RED actions here, except the force push, which the RED list does not name; steps approved in advance, kept as standing approvals listed per bot with their evidence, two bots holding one publish blanket each and all others none, also part of that manual approval control (#promotion-ladder, #controls-inventory), standing disk approvals from Haiyuan for clearing a build cache and thinning local snapshots below 15 GB free (#launch), and an ask-versus-allow list for the bot desktop, a draft re-applied after a bot is duplicated, which asks first for send, publish, push, delete and pay and allows vault reads, read-only git and named launches (playbook §12); since 2026-10-31, a run blocked on a question only Haiyuan can answer held on its kick-ledger row and moved only by Haiyuan's answer or an explicit lift, which the owning bots apply once they update their routine prompts (#held-kicks), so a stop that waits on Haiyuan is a recognised state here; among the things the EM does not do, putting Haiyuan back on the critical path of mid-build approval prompts, with no inventory status (#em-loop); no ending a turn while waiting on background work with a dirty tree, a manual control whose wrapper gates are hand-written per kick (#coding, #controls-inventory); the heartbeat's no-progress flag, a report-only shadow trial adopted on 2026-10-31 that would log a live run with no commit, file change or test run for about an hour, and never kills, resumes or re-prompts it (#no-progress-flag); and the verification CLI adopted on 2026-10-31 with nothing built yet, from a guide whose reason is that an agent able to verify its own work keeps going until the task is done instead of waiting on a person (#verify-cli). So the human gate and its advance approvals are ours already, as manual rules and for bots, not as a check on a coding seat's turn, and a stop on Haiyuan's question is a held state; the playbook names no installed stop hook (#claim-vs-record), and per the pack, what is not applied is any check at the end of a turn that tells a polite quit from a real approval stop. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the rules-only judge first, and only then an evaluation of the cloud decision model or the local model. Install it with the rules-only judge, add our fleet's pre-approved commands, such as our launcher and note filing with the vault's note helper, to its pre-approved list, and measure false interventions on 10 turns, which the row puts as the false-intervention rate across 10 tasks of one coding CLI. The pack's summary line for realstop: catch conversational quits and polite closing offers at Stop time without blocking legitimate human approval gates; pre-approve actions via standing.txt. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP: the trial measures a false-intervention rate without saying what rate would end it, and no negative control is named; its stated bounds are the rules-only judge, the pre-approved list and that count. The only reference figure in the pack is the author's own, 14.6% false interventions for the rules-only judge. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts (#check-can-fail); a planted closing offer would be such an input, and the pack plants none. The playbook's audit-mode-first trial is written for a stop hook that enforces the rule that a completion claim must match the session record (#claim-vs-record); it names no path for a hook that judges whether a turn should end, and the pack names no audit or observe mode for this hook. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing the package or its plugin in any seat, even with the rules-only judge; choosing what goes on its pre-approved list; letting it keep any turn going; enabling its learning hook; downloading the local model or calling the cloud decision model; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the 864 scored turn ends, the catch and false-intervention rates, the latencies and the live trials are the author's, not ours, were not reproduced in the collection, and the pack does not say which test set the rules-only figures come from; it judges only the decision to stop and does not inspect whether the code is correct; the local model requires Apple Silicon and about 1 GB of disk, and the cloud judge needs the network; the learning feature refits its decision head on the Mac from the user's corrections, so its strictness follows them; a step on its pre-approved list is one the hook pushes the agent to take without asking, so a RED action on that list would bypass our rule that RED always goes to Haiyuan (#gyr-authority), while the pack's two examples, our launcher and note filing, are YELLOW and GREEN work in that table; 10 turns or tasks is a small sample beside the author's 864; and our run lessons record tool-use hooks hanging 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalling two runs (#mac-run-lessons). It was created the evening before the collection, so the pack's caveat that it was created today holds only in UTC. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.whatItIs: A stop hook for one coding CLI that judges whether an agent ending its turn with a polite offer or a command for the user to run has quit early, and if so sends it back to work. Stops at a listed approval step, such as a production deploy or a payment, and stops the user asked for are let through.
entries.whyItMatters: Per the collection notes, our agents often end a turn early with a polite offer. A rules-only trial over 10 turns is only proposed, not installed; per its author that mode catches 56.7% of quits with 14.6% false interventions, results we have not reproduced, and any change needs Haiyuan.
