entries.title: regista: a commit hook needs a reviewer's verdict fingerprinted to the exact diff
entries.why: Build harness for two coding CLIs, shipped as a plugin for each, that moves rules out of the model's memory and into deterministic hooks (Python 3.10 or newer; repository size 443 KB in the pack's metadata read; 120 paths, among them agents, hooks and tests folders); the whole engine is one standard-library Python script with no third-party dependencies. A pre-tool-use hook on git commit checks for an approving verdict from an independent reviewer, a verdict whose cryptographic fingerprint must match the exact current diff, and any later edit voids the verdict, which per the pack prevents self-approval and tampering after review. The building flow may not delete tests: a commit with fewer tests than the baseline is blocked unless the user approves a tests cleanup by hand, and that cleanup must prove each deleted test redundant by mutating the code it guards. Compaction runs in brackets: at 55% of context capacity the agent is warned to checkpoint, at 65% compaction is triggered, and at 75% a hard pause saves the work if the host's compaction failed; state is saved by a hook before compaction and reloaded at session start. Its hooks fail closed: a config error or a hook crash blocks, so a broken harness script never lets an unverified commit through. Its wider scope includes fleet workers and a milestone planner, and used as a complete harness it needs strict adherence to its own state schema. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, in long EM loops models drift with their context, skip test runs when tired or approve their own changes. Per the pack, kept Covenant (2026-11-01) checks rules against the base commit, and this adds the cryptographic review-to-diff fingerprint and hard blocks on test deletion; the pack's dedupe also places custodiet (2026-10-28) and our blind dual review in this lane, though per the playbook code our default implementer wrote gets one blind reviewer, and docs, drafts and code from other seats get two (#reviewer-rule). Per the pack, its 65% compaction trigger matches our context-engineering standards, but a text search of the playbook finds no compaction threshold or context standard. On self-approval the playbook already has a rule: the agent that wrote the code cannot approve it, and an implementer never reviews its own work (#em-loop, #reviewer-rule), a manual control (#controls-inventory). We already have: every review ending with one machine-readable verdict line on the head SHA, where a review with no parseable line, or with a line that names an older SHA, is UNPARSED and never counts as approval, and dual approval means two approving lines on the current head (#review-verdict-line), applied in the EM's review steps, a manual control (#controls-inventory); an approval re-checked right before a RED action runs, its item check covering the PR head SHA, also manual (#approval-recheck, #controls-inventory); an implementer that, in the EM loop's play-by-play, builds, runs the repository's one-command tests, commits, pushes and opens the PR without waiting for reviewers, who start only once a PR exists (#em-loop), so our verdict comes after the commit, not before it; a scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer for tests skipped, deleted or focused, assertions gutted or a test command changed so it always passes, where a green run after such a change is SUSPECT, never PASS, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), the same scan also looking for commits made with --no-verify, which skips the repository's hooks (#check-can-fail); report-only mutation testing on one SDK repository, never a merge gate (#mutation-testing), and a new check run once against a deliberately broken input, such as the old code or a mutant, and seen to fail before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail), the nearest thing here to proving a test redundant by mutation; hooks named among the EM loop's always-on plays as the place for must-hold rules such as no weakening tests during a fix, with no inventory status and no installed hook named for them (#em-loop); fail-closed acceptance, under which a prose done cannot pass without a mechanical artifact or an independent read-only or diff-only check, complementing blind review rather than replacing it, a rule with no inventory row of its own (playbook §16), and an installed watchdog that holds, with no stale handling, a job whose background deadline it cannot read (#unreadable-deadline); and, for state across a break, a reference format for pause and resume notes that records the checkpoint SHA, the session and the remaining work, with session ids reused per PR or slice (#launch). So a verdict tied to the reviewed revision, an independent reviewer and a scan for deleted tests are ours already, as manual review steps on the pull request; per the pack, what is not applied is a hook that refuses the commit itself without a matching verdict, a mutation proof before a test may go, and compaction brackets, which the playbook does not address. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): inspect the single script and test only its review-fingerprint commit hook, on one repository. Extract the commit hook from the script, test it on a mock repository with a staged diff, and verify that modifying a file after review invalidates the fingerprint and halts git commit; the pack's summary table puts the test as a staged diff with a modified file. The test-retention block and the compaction brackets are not part of the trial. The pack's summary line for regista: block commits unless an independent reviewer's fingerprinted verdict matches the exact diff; forbid test deletion unless proven redundant; automate 65% compaction. That 65% is the author's setting, not a threshold of ours. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its negative control is the file modified after review, which must void the fingerprint and halt the commit, and the pack's steps do not say whether an approved, unchanged diff is then shown to commit, the healthy case. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts (#check-can-fail), and a reference note right after that rule asks that a proposed check's proof record hold healthy, incident or planted-bad, and empty inputs (#check-can-fail); the post-review edit is the planted-bad input. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Extracting or running its commit hook anywhere, even on a mock repository; installing the plugin for either coding CLI; letting any hook block a commit; moving review ahead of the commit in our loop; adopting its test-retention block, its mutation proof or its compaction brackets; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the brackets at 55%, 65% and 75% are the author's settings, not ours, and the pack does not say how context capacity is measured; the pack does not say how the hook knows that a verdict came from an independent reviewer, only that the fingerprint binds it to the diff; as the pack describes it, it is a pre-tool-use hook on the agent's own git commit, so a commit made outside the agent's tool calls is outside its view; failing closed means a crashing or misconfigured hook blocks every commit, and our run lessons record tool-use hooks hanging 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalling two runs (#mac-run-lessons); its workflow scope is large, so a trial has to stay with the one hook; and no gate execution was observed in the collection. It was created and last pushed in the hour before the collection. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: regista: no commit without an independent review of that exact change
entries.whatItIs: A build harness for two coding CLIs that enforces its rules with hooks: a commit is blocked unless an independent reviewer approved that exact change, a test may go only with the user's approval and proof it is redundant, and context is compacted at 65%, its author's setting.
entries.whyItMatters: Our reviewers' verdicts already count only for the exact commit they read, a check done by hand after the push. Its diff fingerprint is now a report-only script the EM must check, by rule, before any dual approval; its commit hook is not installed, and adopting that needs Haiyuan.

entries.title: Context tax: an estimated per-file token bill for what loads before the first prompt
entries.why: Static token auditor in TypeScript and JavaScript, run from its repository with a package runner (repository size 1,052 KB in the pack's metadata read; 100 paths, among them a command-line entry point, sources and test fixtures), that estimates what three coding tools load before the user types a first prompt. It scans repository roots and the home directories of the three tools for standing-instruction files, rule files, skill folders and tool-server declarations, and prints a token bill per file. Its diagnostics name dead rules and legacy config files; manual skills whose documentation is loaded into the startup prompt without need; the exact percentage of overlap between the shared instruction file and one coding CLI's own instruction file; and files that a working-directory boundary or a tool's precedence order suppresses. A comparison sets the token spend of the three tools side by side on the same project tree. The counts are estimates: per the pack, it uses a tokenizer library and character heuristics without calling each provider's own tokenizer for tool-server schemas, and it does not fetch full dynamic tool schemas, though the pack's description of the tool also calls the cost it computes exact. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our seats on the Mac run with heavy instruction suites, the shared contract file from the vault, global hooks, project-level skills and tool-server configurations, and while we watch runtime usage with dashboards and compaction hooks, nothing tells us statically how many tokens a seat spends at turn 0, before the user types; per the pack, this is the exact measurement rule consolidation needs. The two hooks the pack names for that watching are Lab cards in its dedupe, kept memcap (2026-10-28) and the 2026-10-26 context-budget card: a text search of the playbook finds neither name, and a card calls a practice applied only where the playbook says so, a playbook lesson, not a lock (#lab-card-claims). The dashboard is ours: a public usage dashboard with Mac CLI quota and health cards, collection seats among them, and an activity share from local transcripts, labelled not plan dollars (#usage), refreshed three times a day by an enforced routine whose box crons are unverified from the Mac (#controls-inventory). Per the pack we also audit transcript tokens; the playbook describes no such audit. We already have: byte ceilings on the two files every agent reads before every task, the shared contract file at 13,489 B and the never-again list at 81,155 B, set because every task pays the full read; to add a line past a ceiling, another is compressed or demoted, oldest first, and the daily consolidation digest records both sizes (#resident-budget); the contract file's ceiling is held by fold size gates that are report-only, the list had reached its ceiling in the inventory's statuses of 2026-10-20, so an append needs an equal trim, a manual control, and edits to the contract file are limited to fleet-wide standing rules, also manual, with nothing checking the reason (#controls-inventory); the skill lint, adopted 2026-10-25 and report-only, which checks frontmatter, when-to-use triggers, near-duplicate or drifted copies and description budgets in the Monday sync, against a documented baseline of 1,176 finding groups and 1,133 at the latest sync (#skills); the deadweight config audit, adopted 2026-10-25, a local one-time, report-only audit of persistent seat configurations from installed-source, schema and filesystem evidence, whose operative baseline is 5 findings, down from 9, that are not a deletion list, and which does not prove runtime admission or effective settings (#skills), the nearest thing here to the dead-rule and legacy-config diagnostic; the shared contract file linked into the seat homes, 7 links whose check is enforced but run on demand (#skills, #controls-inventory), and one coding CLI's global instruction file supplied from the vault (#skills), so the overlap this tool measures would be between two files the vault supplies; among the advisory jobs of our default small models, on a two-week trial from 2026-10-28, a pre-review lint of the shared contract file's size (#roster); and a six-test charter that accepts measured context bloat as one reason a role may become its own bot or seat, whose check confirms only that an allowed reason is named, with no way of measuring it named (#five-test-charter). So a size budget for the two always-read files, a skill-description check and a dead-config audit are ours already, the first in bytes rather than tokens and the last two report-only; the playbook names no token count per startup file, and its nearest record, that declared-versus-effective hook loading was not adopted from the Lab card behind the byte ceiling and that the adopted static config audit does not establish it (#resident-budget), concerns hooks, not the instruction files whose suppression this tool reports; per the pack, what is not applied is a token estimate per startup file across the coding tools, tool-server schemas included, and an overlap figure between the two instruction files. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): one read-only run over our home directory and the shared notes vault. Run its command-line entry point read-only against the vault and inspect the reported startup token breakdown and the overlap between the shared contract file and one coding CLI's instruction file. The pack's summary line for the context-tax tool: measure pre-flight startup tokens consumed by instructions, rules, skills and tool-server schemas before turn 0; flag dead rules and overlap between the shared contract file and one coding CLI's instruction file. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; its stated bound is one read-only run. entries.title: memrot: flag dead paths, contradictions and decaying time words in agent instructions
entries.why: Zero-dependency local linter, one JavaScript script for Node 18 or newer that uses only the standard library (repository size 52 KB in the pack's metadata read; 6 paths), for the standing-instruction files, memory files and memory folders of coding agents. It resolves backticked paths against the real project root and flags references to deleted or moved files as stale paths; checks the run commands a file names against the scripts in the project's package manifest and flags missing ones as stale commands; catches conflicting instructions within one document, such as an always rule against a never rule for the same thing, with a simple regex and heuristic; flags relative time words that decay, among them today, yesterday and currently, plus a Chinese word for currently; and estimates tokens with a CJK-aware count, about 1 token per character for CJK text, flagging a document over 200 lines or 25 KB. It exits 1 on error findings, for use in CI, and a fix mode strips duplicate lines and repairs character encoding, per the pack without losing content. It needs a root option to resolve paths accurately. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the shared contract file and the never-again list in the vault are updated all the time by several bots, and stale references to scripts or paths that moved weeks ago mislead agents into edits on files that are not there. Per the pack, kept agnix (2026-10-26) and kept rulesift (2026-10-30) check markdown syntax and hidden tags but do not verify referenced paths against the real filesystem or check for temporal decay, and the pack's dedupe also places verderer (2026-10-31) in this lane; the pack calls the first two existing linters, but all three are Lab cards: a text search of the playbook finds none of their names, and a card calls a practice applied only where the playbook says so, a playbook lesson, not a lock (#lab-card-claims). Per the pack, it is an instant, zero-AI sanity check for the daily consolidation. The playbook records a failure of the kind it targets: since at least 2026-10-07 a shared-memory line has cited a 2026-10-06 Decision note that is not in the vault (#pointer-check). We already have: cited vault paths that must resolve: before writing a pointer to a vault path, in a note, a card, the shared contract file or shared user memory, the writer checks that the file exists, and the Monday card sync also checks every vault path cited in the shared contract file and the role cards, skipping placeholders such as a dated-slug template, and fixes or reports each one that no longer resolves; only the dead-reference idea was taken from the agent-docs-lint card, its lint tool is not installed, and the manager bot adds the check to the Monday sync prompt after publish (#pointer-check), a rule applied by hand with no row in the controls inventory; memory rules under which slow-clock rules may be remembered while fast-clock facts, such as whether the Mac is connected, a PR's tip SHA, quota or CI state, are re-fetched live before any action or claim and hourly status lines are not memory, with a provenance card of claim, source, owner, status, supersedes and review_after on new Decision notes and standing-rule memories and no checker named (#memory-rules); shared memory written one line per fact with the date and the source, policy text only with nothing enforcing it (#shared-memory-admission), a rule that asks for a date on each line but says nothing about relative time words; a memory loop in which the daily consolidation merges lessons that say the same thing and wrong or outdated lessons go on a prune list that names each item, deleted only after Haiyuan approves the specific items, policy text only (#memory-loop); a correction already in the never-again list twice or more turned into a proposed skill diff instead of another paragraph, a manual control written after that list came to hold 18 near-identical paragraphs (#repeat-lesson, #controls-inventory); byte ceilings of 13,489 B on the shared contract file, held by size gates that only report, and 81,155 B on the never-again list, where an append needs an equal trim, a manual control (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory); the rule-phrase check, a report-only shadow trial adopted on 2026-10-31 and not built yet, which would report each must-hold rule no longer stated where agents read it and each superseded wording still there (#rule-phrase-check), the nearest thing here to a contradiction check; and doc and README drift among the advisory jobs of our default small models, on a two-week trial from 2026-10-28 (#roster). So the dead-path check is ours already, as a written rule applied by hand when a pointer is written and to the paths the shared contract file and the role cards cite, and shared-memory lines are to carry a date, a rule silent on relative time words; per the pack, what is not applied is a linter that resolves every backticked path mechanically and flags relative time words, contradictions and stale run commands in the instruction and memory files. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): an offline, read-only run of its script over the shared contract file, and per the summary table over the never-again list too, to flag broken backticked paths or time words that decay; the row also names our vault notes as the target. The pack's summary line for memrot: verify backticked paths against filesystem ground truth; detect missing package scripts, rule contradictions, and temporal decay phrases in the shared contract file. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; its stated bound is the offline, read-only run. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts (#check-can-fail); a dead path planted in a copy would be such an input, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running it over the vault, even offline and read-only; using its fix mode on any vault file, since stripping duplicate lines from a durable note is a delete that needs Haiyuan's approval of the specific items (#memory-loop); adding it to the daily consolidation or the Monday sync; acting on any finding; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: its contradiction detector is a simple regex and heuristic, so differently worded conflicts can slip past it and each finding needs a person's read; a run over vault files has to point its root option at the vault, and our pointer rule skips placeholders such as a dated-slug template while the pack does not say whether memrot does; its stale-command check reads the scripts of a package manifest, so it applies only where a project has one; by its stated thresholds its size flag at 200 lines or 25 KB would fire on the never-again list, which the inventory records at its 81,155 B ceiling (#controls-inventory), so that finding is known in advance; its token count is an estimate; the paths, commands, contradictions and time words it would find in our vault are unknown until a run; and the pack's heading says it detects broken links, which its list of checks does not describe. It is single-author and was created about an hour before the collection. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: hookjack: a static pre-clone scan of what a repo would auto-run when an agent opens it
entries.why: Static scanner, one Go command-line program (repository size 569 KB in the pack's metadata read; 49 paths, among them its command, scan, remote, report and source packages, tests, CI, release and scorecard workflows, a CI action and a pre-commit hook), for every project-supplied entry point that a coding agent or an editor runs on its own when it opens a repository. Its twelve rules cover one coding CLI's hooks and command-valued settings (session-start and pre-tool-use hooks, an API-key helper command and trust-widening settings), tool-server declarations in the settings files of several coding tools and an editor, one tool's custom commands, an editor's tasks set to run when a folder opens and its auto-run settings, a development-container initialize command, which runs on the host, agent-instruction files (hidden Unicode, hidden HTML comments and phrasing that tells the agent not to tell the user), package install hooks (post-install scripts, a PHP package manager's scripts, command expansion in a native-addon build file and download-and-execute make recipes), obfuscated JavaScript and multi-megabyte scripts in hidden directories, and encrypted native-addon sidecar blobs. It follows each entry point to the script it launches and grades the command by what it does: a download piped to a shell, an encoded shell command, base64 fed to an interpreter, a raw-IP URL or a launcher that falls back from one script runtime to another raises the severity, while a plain package-runner call to a tool server stays informational; commented JSON is handled, and line numbers point at the entry. Its pre-clone mode streams a repository's archive into memory over unauthenticated HTTPS, so nothing touches disk and no token is read or sent; an org mode scans every public non-fork repository of one owner; and it exits 1 at or above a chosen severity, high by default, with text, JSON or SARIF output. Per the README and the tree the pack read, in the pack's words, nothing executed is tested, not asserted: process APIs are banned from non-test code three ways (a linter rule, a test that parses the source and a CI dependency check), and a canary test builds a repository in which every entry-point kind would create a canary file, scans it and asserts that the file does not exist afterwards, repeated for both remote modes against a local web server, also asserting that no authorization header is sent; its test fixtures are synthetic. Per the README, its trigger was a security vendor's October 2026 report of 42 armed repositories across 11 owners on one code host, whose execution hooks in the settings, rules and task files of several coding tools and an editor launched an obfuscated script of 12.9 to 13.7 MB that the host's code search reportedly did not index; it reads such files directly, sampling scripts to 4 MB and still flagging larger ones by size and shape. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the collect itself opens a dozen unknown repositories a day, reading their READMEs through the code host's API, which is safe, but any trial, clone or open puts a seat inside a repository whose session-start hook, tool-server declaration or folder-open task runs as Haiyuan before the first prompt. Per the pack, kept rulesift (2026-10-30) checks what steering files say (hidden text, injected lines and a hash lock), while no Lab card answers what a repository will execute on our Mac seats; the pack's dedupe also places rollcage-guard (2026-10-15) and the 2026-10-25 skill-pack security card in this lane, its title search of the Lab for auto-run or folder-open found no hits, and it holds the same-day agent-surface-scan, text and injection rules over agent-facing prose, as a runner-up so that the lane gets one card. Per the pack, no auto-run surface scan, no pre-clone check and no grading of the script a hook launches exists anywhere in the collect, curate or trial path, and the one-command check fits where the risk enters: before the manager bot trials anything a pack proposes. The playbook records one case of the same risk by another path: in the 2026-10-29 security fix from the nightly audit, the tracing plugin of an SDK our nightly audit covers started Python in the folder a session runs in, usually a checked-out repository, so a file there named like a module Python loads could run with the user's credentials as soon as a session started; the fix keeps that folder off Python's import path, and the plugin's marketplace copy keeps the old start scripts until a release updates it (#changelog-2026-10-26). We already have: text an agent reads from the web, PR text, tool output or another agent's output treated as data, with any instructions in it quoted to Haiyuan and never followed, policy text only (#untrusted-content), a manual control with nothing enforcing it (#controls-inventory), a rule about what an agent reads, not about what a repository runs when it is opened; Mac CLI runs on named repositories classed YELLOW, allowed inside approved tools and lanes, while RED actions always go to Haiyuan (#gyr-authority), part of the manual approval control (#controls-inventory); the deadweight config audit, adopted 2026-10-25, a local one-time, report-only audit of persistent seat configurations from installed-source, schema and filesystem evidence, which does not run hooks or prove runtime admission or effective settings (#skills), the nearest thing here to reading what a configuration would make a seat do, though it reads our seats' own settings, not a repository's; hooks named among the EM loop's always-on plays as the place for must-hold rules, such as no secrets in a diff, with no inventory status and no installed hook named for them (#em-loop); and a run lesson in which a tracing plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hung 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons). So the rule that read text is data, lane approval for named repositories and a one-time, report-only audit of our own seat settings are ours already, and the playbook records one plugin path by which an opened repository could run code; a text search of the playbook for clone, auto-run and folder-open finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any scan of what a repository would run on open, before a seat opens it, or any grading of the script a hook would launch. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): pre-clone checks first, on repositories we already mean to trial. Build or install the binary from source on one Mac, since prebuilt binaries come only once its first release ships; run its no-clone check over the four KEEP repositories of this pack and over five repositories already installed in our seat homes, and hand-read every low or medium finding that something auto-runs, which the README warns about; only then consider it as a standing pre-trial step in the collect skill, and do not wire its CI action into the vault in the same step. The pack's summary line for hookjack: what a repo will auto-run on open, named with file and line before clone; a scan that provably executes nothing. That proof is the author's canary and import tests, read from the README and the tree, not reproduced here. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control of ours is named: the canary test is the author's, and the trial's only stated check is the hand-read of low and medium findings. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, with the expected results written first and no live records touched, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a scratch repository planted with one known auto-run entry would be such a copy, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Building or installing the binary on the Mac, even for the no-clone mode; scanning the repositories installed in our seat homes; making it a standing pre-trial step in the collect skill or any routine; wiring its CI action or its pre-commit hook into the vault or any repository; letting its exit code block a trial or a clone; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it is heuristic by design, so a payload fetched at run time by a clean-looking command may rate only low or medium; its remote mode reads one code host only, unauthenticated, at 60 API requests an hour and from the default branch or a named ref only, and our rule that a rate-limited lookup is reported as a gap, never as a zero (#negative-claim-check), would apply to a scan that hits that limit; native addons are not disassembled; new tools keep adding new auto-run files; and the 42-repository campaign figure and the canary-test results are the author's, read from the README and the tree, not reproduced in the collection. It has 0 stars and was created the morning of the collection. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: find-my-session: a read-only cross-harness session finder that hands off a bounded digest
entries.why: Local, read-only session finder and handoff-digest tool for coding-agent harnesses, in Python 3.9 or newer with the standard library only, also published as a Python package (repository size 1,104 KB in the pack's metadata read; 256 paths, among them one adapter module per harness, a skill form, a read-only local browser panel, and CI and release workflows). It has 18 ready adapters and 2 planned, one module and one documented store each, among them, per the pack, the stores of several coding CLIs our seats run, with a per-harness compatibility matrix of verified versions, surfaces and caveats, and store-schema references for adding one. Its commands are shaped for the moment a seat exits at its quota: a keyword search that can be filtered by harness; the latest session for the current folder; a show command that prints a low-token handoff digest with caps on messages and characters, plus the raw source path so an agent can grep the original when the digest is not enough; a prompts command that counts the human prompts and then pages them with their original indices kept; and a doctor that reports decoder availability, readable roots and per-harness health, with a fingerprint option that adds a content-free shape summary for drift reports. Filters cover the working directory, a start date, and a limit with an offset; archived sessions are left out unless asked for; a deep scan reads full transcripts but still prints metadata only; and a verbose flag warns about skipped sessions on standard error without changing standard output, so JSON consumers stay clean. A session reference is the harness name plus a session-id prefix, and a raw path from a supported store also works. Per the README, read-only is structural: the command line makes no network calls, SQLite stores are opened read-only, nothing is edited or deleted, and search output is metadata only, while show and prompts print conversation content, which the README says to treat like the transcript itself. Compressed stores need Python 3.14 or newer or the zstd command-line tool, or those sessions are skipped, and the verbose flag exists so that a skip is never silent. It supports the Mac and Linux, with another desktop operating system as an experimental, non-blocking CI job that is not supported yet; the agent skill and a human browser panel on the local machine, same-origin JSON only, share one core; and its tests are unit tests, a compile check and artifact builds, per the README. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our weekly failure is not losing the transcript but not knowing which seat and which store holds it when a seat exits at its quota or a session is resumed days later, and then paying for a full-transcript re-read to find out; the playbook records quota stops, such as a writer seat reaching its weekly quota on one brief (#exception-first), and the weekly failure itself rests on the pack. Per the pack, kept conspectus (2026-10-21) maps live sessions to terminal panes and repositories, and the 2026-11-02 pack's agent-recall runner-up answers with a refreshed SQLite index behind a tool server; the pack's dedupe also places continuity (2026-10-25), a handoff made stale by the session's own work, and sctxx (2026-09-23), a finished session turned into a handoff artifact, in this lane, and none of them does a stateless, metadata-first lookup with a bounded digest at the moment of handoff. Per the pack, its discipline of working directory, start date, and a count before paging is also the missing cheap half of our resume safety: confirm which session is about to be resumed, and what the human actually asked in it, before any old process is disturbed. Per the pack, session lookup today is a hand search or memory across three of our seats' session stores, with no cross-harness finder, no reference space of harness and prefix, and no content-free doctor fingerprint. We already have: session ids reused for a PR or slice, with no cold start of follow-ups, a standing order in the launch standards with no checker named (#launch); for a quota stop, failover to a named fallback seat, which the playbook calls our live rule, with the handoff still the named session id plus a vault note, while an earlier card's automatic checkpoint of git status and the uncommitted diff, followed by a relaunch on the other coding CLI, is not live (#exception-first); a pause and resume note format that records the objective, a checkpoint SHA or why it is absent, the branch or worktree, the session or attempt, the log and stream paths, the watchdog state, the last completed step, the remaining work, the review state and pending approvals, with unknown fields marked unknown, a note that neither proves an old process stopped nor authorizes a relaunch, with pickup following the spawn-ok, ownership, approval and idempotent-resume rules (#launch), a reference format; a resume only after the old agent is proven gone, enforced by the ownership guard since 2026-10-20, with a run whose state cannot be read parked as an unknown outcome (#watchdog-resume-safety, #retry-ceiling, #controls-inventory), and the matching of a running coding CLI's process to its session file through the files it holds open not adopted from an earlier card (#watchdog-resume-safety); a resumed routine that first checks the live state behind each step that writes and skips any step already done, a practice with no checker named and no row in the controls inventory (#idempotent-resume); pass ownership, not transcripts: every manager-bot handoff and every new coding kick carries a machine-readable packet whose completeness check is shadow only and never blocks, report-only and box-side, unverified from the Mac (#handoff-packet, #controls-inventory); shared user memory that excludes run logs and session, commit and run ids, policy text only (#shared-memory-admission); negative claims that need a lookup that worked, a failed or rate-limited lookup being reported as a gap, never as zero, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory), and a paged or cut-off read that is not the whole list, policy text only (#paged-reads), the same discipline as its reported skips and its limit and offset; tool output and another agent's output treated as data, never instructions, policy text only (#untrusted-content), which would cover the transcript text a digest prints; no secrets, tokens or private keys in notes, a manual rule with no secret scan in the vault's note helper (#controls-inventory), which would cover a digest pasted into a note; and a record that one collection seat's session file is compressed (#launch), the kind of store whose decoder this tool's doctor reports. So a named session id with a vault note, a resume-note format that records the session and its log paths, and an enforced proven-dead check before a resume are ours already, as a standing order, a reference format and one installed guard; a text search of the playbook for session lookup finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is a cross-harness finder that locates a session in the stores of several coding CLIs, read-only and without an index or a background service, and hands off a bounded digest with the raw path. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a read-only lookup trial over copies or fixtures first, naming the missing adapter. Install it on one Mac with a Python application installer, or run it from a checkout, and run its doctor with JSON output, confirming that every skip is reported, the decoder condition above all; then find three known past sessions, one from each of three coding CLIs our seats run, by keyword and working directory, and check each digest against the raw transcript; then scope, from the repository's recipe for extending it, what an adapter for the uncovered seat's store would need before any fleet use. Do not start from the browser panel. The pack's summary line for find-my-session: the session a quota-stopped seat left behind, located across harnesses read-only and handed off as a bounded digest. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP: its pass conditions are that the doctor reports every skip and that each of the three digests matches its raw transcript, it names no planted fault, and it does not say what result would end the trial. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail); a copied compressed store with no decoder present would be such an input, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it on the Mac or running it from a checkout, even read-only; pointing it at any live seat's session store rather than at copies; writing an adapter for the uncovered seat; using it for real handoffs, in a skill or in a routine; starting its browser panel; pasting any digest into the vault; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: its 18 ready adapters do not include the session store of one of our own seats, so that seat is not covered until an adapter is written, and until then, per the pack, it covers the other seats only; it has 1 star, was created the evening before the collection and was still being pushed during it, at 10:00 and 10:03 PT, so its README is a moving target to re-fetch at trial; only the surfaces in its compatibility matrix are verified, the rest built from documentation; its JSON contract is pre-1.0, with a documented stability policy; show and prompts print transcript content, to be handled as such; its browser panel is a local server and stays out of the trial; compressed stores are skipped where no decoder is present; and its verified-surface claims and its tests are the author's, read from the README and the tree, not reproduced in the collection. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: sluice: a hook shunts bulk reads to a cheap worker; its meter never prints savings alone
entries.why: Bulk-read shunt for coding CLIs in standard-library Python (repository size 83 KB in the pack's metadata read; 60 paths, among them adapters for three coding CLIs our seats run, a Phase 0 corpus study, stub and live benchmark outputs, and tests for its hooks, worker and meter) that blocks the coordinating agent from absorbing bulk reads, sends them to a cheap worker and reports its own effect. Two pre-tool-use hooks close the shell bypass: one denies a file read over the threshold, 350 lines by default, and redirects it to a bulk-read skill, while targeted reads with an offset and a limit pass untouched; the other catches an unpiped cat, less or another shell's file-reading command against files totalling over the threshold, while piped or targeted commands pass. It ships as a plugin for one coding CLI, a manual adapter for a second and a native plugin bundle for a third; for the third, whose adapter also covers head and tail over the threshold, the author reports that CLI's own offline hook test passing 9/9, blocking a big cat or a big read and passing small, piped, windowed and edit calls, while the second CLI's adapter is one script for the shell-read surface whose README lists its gaps: reads through sed, awk or an inline interpreter, tool-server argument names, and a live authenticated session check still owed. The worker contract is narrow: files and a question in, structured bullets out, with exact names, types and line numbers taken from a numbered prompt, so the worker cites instead of counting, and nothing unasked; a second worker that writes generated code straight to disk is out of scope for any trial here, and both refuse debugging, architecture decisions and safety-critical work by task type. The backend is one client for a widely used chat-completions interface, configured from the environment: the model id is mandatory, the worker refuses to call without one, and keys come from the environment only. The meter is the claim: every delegation appends a record, and its report prints coordinator-context savings, worker tokens and worker dollars together; by a rule enforced in code, the avoided figure is labelled an estimate and is never printed without the measured pair of coordinator tokens, worker tokens and worker dollars, and worker dollars are null, never 0, when prices are unset. The README's own correction stays up front: total tokens go up with a shunt, and the saving is coordinator context, with dollars only when the worker is cheaper per token: 'if the coordinator is subscription-billed, token savings are not dollar savings, and this README does not claim they are'. The author's measured evidence, not reproduced in the collection: a Phase 0 study over a public 28-session proxy corpus of 4,262 tool results found that bulk reads of 350 lines or more were 39 calls but an estimated 20.6% of tool-result payload, with the threshold's sensitivity printed (a 200-line threshold gave 33.6% and a 1000-line one 0.95%); a pre-registered live benchmark of three extraction tasks, under a $0.05 approved cap with $0.002021 measured spend, reports identifier accuracy of 100% and coordinator-context savings of 95.0–98.9% against a kill bar of at least 50%, and discloses the first attempt's unmeasured-usage bug, its fix and one off-by-one line citation. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the 2026-11-02 pack already recorded the naive version of this idea failing: its tiered-workers runner-up, a runner-up in that pack and not a Lab card, raised total tokens by 26.7% per its author, who marked it NO-SHIP; and per the pack our usage reporting keeps seeing claims of tokens saved that silently move spend to another model. The playbook records no such claim: a text search of it for savings finds only our decision layer's shadow savings tally, run inside the Monday sync, with no counting method given (playbook §12). Per the pack, sluice is the first in-window tool that enforces the shunt at the hook on our actual seats and makes the false-savings claim unprintable, the estimate and the measured pair travelling together or not at all, and that meter discipline transfers even if the shunt itself is never adopted fleet-wide: it is the reporting shape our usage dashboard and weekly token claims need. Per the pack, kept context-tax (2026-11-02) measures the static load at turn 0, not run-time read payload or delegation cost, and the pack's dedupe also places the 2026-10-26 context-budget card and memcap (2026-10-28) in this lane; per the pack, a title search of the Lab for bulk-read, shunt or cheap-worker found no hits. We already have: a public usage dashboard with Mac CLI quota and health cards and an overall activity share for the bots from local transcripts, labelled not plan dollars, plus a routine fire proxy labelled as a proxy, not dollars or tokens (#usage), refreshed three times a day by an enforced routine whose box crons are unverified from the Mac (#controls-inventory), so our proxies already say what they are not; a reference note asking count or cost evidence to state its counting unit, population, window and a lookup that worked, and keeping external numbers external until reproduced here (right after that rule, #check-can-fail); a count or an all-or-none statement in a receipt, Decision or Lab card that names how it was counted and over what, where a claim with two parts counts both, policy text only (#check-can-fail), the rule nearest to never printing an estimate without its measured pair; among the advisory jobs of our default small models, on a two-week trial from 2026-10-28, a pre-review lint for estimates stated as measured, where they never implement real code and the owning seat accepts or drops their output (#roster), so a cheaper model working for another seat is a known shape here, as advisory work only; per-token list prices recorded for our two default small models (#providers); run limits under which long fires default to $0 spend and 0 external actions without Haiyuan's approval, a manual control (#run-limits, #controls-inventory); byte ceilings on the two files every agent reads, the shared contract file at 13,489 B and the never-again list at 81,155 B, the first held by size gates that only report and the second by hand (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory), static load in bytes, not run-time reads; a paged or cut-off read that does not count as the whole list for a count or a none claim, policy text only (#paged-reads), which would apply to the windowed reads the hook lets through; a post-tool-use trim of noisy tool output from an earlier Lab card, listed among the Lab follow-ups as a new practice that is not installed (#usage), the nearest thing here to cutting tool-result payload; and a run lesson in which a plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hung 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons). So labelled proxies, the count-and-cost evidence fields and an advisory lint for estimates stated as measured are ours already, as a reference note, policy and advisory work; per the pack, what is not applied is any bulk-read block or redirect hook on any seat and any ledger of coordinator against worker tokens. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): meter and dry-run first, bulk reads only, no code-write worker. Run its 46 standard-library tests and the $0 stub benchmark from a checkout; run its Phase 0 study over a copy of one seat's real session logs, since the author's own stated gap is that Phase 0 ran on a proxy corpus, not on the owner's sessions; then install the native hook pair for one of our seats' coding CLIs in one scratch project, with a local or an explicitly priced worker, and check that the meter report never shows an estimate alone. The pack's summary line for sluice: bulk reads blocked at the hook and shunted to a cheap worker, with savings never printed without the measured worker cost. The pack's stop/kill condition: reject the trial if the bulk-read share on our own logs is under the author's kill logic, a small share meaning the hooks are not worth their friction; the pack gives no number for that share, and the author's kill bar of at least 50% belongs to the live benchmark's coordinator-context savings, not to it. Its other check is that the meter report never shows an estimate alone; the playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail), and a delegation record stripped of its measured pair would be such an input, which the pack does not plant. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running its tests or benchmark on the Mac; running Phase 0 over a copy of any seat's session logs; installing any hook pair, even in a scratch project; choosing a worker model, endpoint or price, or spending anything on one, since long fires default to $0 spend (#run-limits); taking its meter's reporting rule into our usage dashboard or weekly token claims; enabling its code-write worker; or setting the share that would end the trial would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: every percentage, savings figure, test count and benchmark number above is the author's, from a proxy corpus, three synthetic extraction fixtures and one live run capped at $0.05, and none was reproduced in the collection; its own README says total tokens go up, and the saving is coordinator context, not dollars unless the worker is cheaper per token; its install text still carries placeholders, so a trial installs from a clone, not from the marketplace lines; a live real-model session check is still owed for every host, the third CLI included; worker setup needs a model and endpoint decision, where cost and routing are ours to make and keys stay in the environment; and the code-write worker, which writes code the coordinator never reads, is explicitly not part of this proposal. It has 0 stars and was created the morning of the collection; the pack read its README in full and its tree listing. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-11-03 08:54 PT, pushed 2026-11-03 09:44 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: sluice: send big file reads to a cheaper helper, and show what that costs
entries.whatItIs: Hooks that stop a coding agent from reading whole files over a line limit itself and send those reads to a cheaper helper model that answers a set question. A meter shows the estimated context saved only beside the helper's measured tokens and cost.
entries.whyItMatters: Per its author, total tokens go up, and the saving is the main agent's context, with money saved only when the helper costs less per token. Its tests, a free stub run and a scan of copied logs are only proposed, not installed; its figures are the author's, and any change needs Haiyuan.
entries.statusNote: A Lab proposal only: no hook redirects bulk reads and no meter pairs a saving with its cost, and the nearest rule is that a count names how it was counted (#check-can-fail; #usage).

entries.title: baton: cross-machine agent handoffs as append-only records on one git branch
entries.why: Coordination for coding agents on more than one machine through git alone, with no server and no shared database, in one Rust program (repository size 494 KB in the pack's metadata read; 50 paths, among them a 33-line README, a 214-line design document, sources for its board, guard, hooks, notes and secret scan, tests for its board, hooks, notes and setup, and a plugin with skills for one coding CLI; the README gives its status as v1, under trial, with commands 'tested end to end against real git'). Its design decisions D1 to D3 make a dedicated board repository append-only, with one branch as the compare-and-swap: every message and every status change is a new file, so racing posts never touch the same file and a rebase cannot conflict, and rule-bearing records (plan, take, release, close, handover and close-task) re-check every rule against the exact fetched tip before they push, with up to 3 compare-and-swap retries; order is first-parent commit order, never timestamps. D4 is one lead per task: the machine where the human started the task posts the plan and leads; a second plan for the task is refused, and a machine cannot post a plan while it has an unanswered plan from the other machine; only the addressee changes a message's status, a won't-do needs a reply in the same commit, a closed task's slug cannot be reused, and branch ownership follows the latest handover carrying the repository, the branch and the commit. D5 makes waking cost no tokens: a stop hook with an asynchronous re-wake polls the remote's refs every 30 s, through git, not the model, about 120 calls an hour per session, backing off to 5 min on error and keeping errors in state, never printing them; it fetches only when the tip moves and wakes an idle session only for a message that needs action from it. Nothing starts on its own: the human runs its command in the session they choose, a wake for new work still asks the human before taking it, the newest waiter owns the session, and the waiter exits with its coding CLI process; the design records why a session-start hook was not used, as tested. D6 gives the board no authority: a message is another agent's note, the inbox shows ids and metadata only, a body prints inside a nonce fence marked untrusted, wake lines carry no subject or body, posts are scanned for known token patterns and refused with exit 11 unless a human overrides, a message is never treated as the human's approval, and identity checks are stated conveniences, not a boundary; its pre-tool-use guard is written for honest mistakes by a cooperating agent, such as raw git in the notes repository, pushes to main or writes into the board clone, and never grants anything, only denying, asking or staying silent. D7, optional, syncs a git-held notes vault shared by the same machines: a sync command commits only the paths an agent changed, after a snapshot backup, integrating in a private worktree with a journal and a reset that keeps local changes, then a fast-forward push; it never puts conflict markers in notes or overwrites uncommitted work, and it warns against running a file-sync service on the same files. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our fleet is this topology, with always-on bots on a cloud box, a Mac full of coding-CLI seats and a shared notes vault staged between the box and the Mac, coordinated today by room messages, kick ledgers and tmux pokes, where two seats can plan the same work and a handoff can sit unseen until a heartbeat notices. The playbook records both kinds of failure: an unacked handoff, a room-only kick the heartbeat never read, on 2026-09-24 (#coding-em-kicks), and, on one machine, a re-run collect and its replacement seat holding the same pack path for about 3 minutes on 10-15 (#mac-run-lessons), the fail case the ownership row of the controls inventory cites (#controls-inventory). Per the pack, the Lab already has the single-machine halves: kept agent-sync (2026-10-20), whose task leases the pack's own dedupe says are decided by a git-ref compare-and-swap, dibs (2026-10-03), single-machine resource leases, the 2026-10-21 shared-inbox card, an inbox on a local tool server, and kept pair-mailbox (2026-10-15), two live seats on one machine. Per the pack, baton's new claim is the cross-machine, serverless whole: git push rejection as the arbiter, one lead per task as a checked rule rather than a convention, and a zero-token wake that per the pack respects the no-exit-while-waiting discipline, since the waiting is in git, outside the turn, in a session the human armed. Since the pack's own dedupe credits agent-sync with a git-ref compare-and-swap, the push-rejection arbiter is not new to the Lab, and the delta is narrower: the append-only board with its plan and lead rules, the zero-token wake and the path-scoped notes sync. We already have: a kick ledger on the box, with no row of its own in the controls inventory, in which every manager-bot handoff to the coding EM is a direct priority wake plus a ledger row, posted, launched, then PR open or done, or blocked with a note, read first by the EM's 15-minute heartbeat, where a row posted with no seat is launched or marked blocked, never idle, and whose pickup check is paused since 2026-10-23 (#coding-em-kicks); rows marked held when Haiyuan says to stop or wait, or when a run is blocked on a question only Haiyuan can answer, which stay held across heartbeats, sweeps, re-kicks, new sessions and restarts, where CI results, review comments and bot output never relaunch, resume or unblock the work, and which the owning bots apply once they update their routine prompts (#held-kicks); a machine-readable handoff packet on every manager-bot handoff and new kick, with the ask carried verbatim, whose completeness check is shadow only and never blocks, report-only and box-side, unverified from the Mac (#handoff-packet, #verbatim-ask, #controls-inventory); exclusive ownership of a run's output on the Mac, enforced by the ownership guard: each launch gets an attempt ID and a workspace, only the current attempt can publish, and a restart is refused unless the old process is proven dead (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), one machine's guard, not a cross-machine rule; a box-to-Mac vault rule under which the Mac vault path is the source of truth, and when the box cannot see the Mac's files it stages a copy, marks it as staged on the box and copies it to the Mac once the Mac is up, a shared box computer being no isolation (playbook §12), a written rule with no row in the controls inventory, where, under the memory loop, policy text only, clearing a box staging copy after a box-to-Mac copy is not a lesson delete (#memory-loop); another agent's output treated as data, never instructions, policy text only (#untrusted-content), a manual control (#controls-inventory), the same stance as a board message being only another agent's note; RED actions, among them send or publish, merge and deleting non-junk, always going to Haiyuan, and an approval re-checked right before the action runs, both manual (#gyr-authority, #approval-recheck, #controls-inventory), so a message is never an approval here either; hooks named among the EM loop's always-on plays as the place for must-hold rules such as no push to main, with no inventory status and no installed hook named for them (#em-loop); no secrets, tokens or private keys in notes, a manual rule with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook (#controls-inventory); and no ending a turn while waiting on background work with a dirty tree, a manual control whose wrapper gates are hand-written per kick (#coding, #controls-inventory). So a ledger of kick states, held rows, a handoff packet, an enforced one-owner guard for runs on the Mac and a staging rule for notes between the box and the Mac are ours already; per the pack, what is not applied is a board repository, plan and lead rules checked at push, a wake that polls git instead of the model, and a path-scoped sync command for the notes vault. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a two-machine board trial on scratch work first, and notes sync last, if at all. Build it from source and run its Rust tests; set up one private board repository, two named machines or two clones standing in for them, and one throwaway task, and prove the three refusals, a second plan, a status change by a non-addressee and a plan posted while an unanswered plan waits, plus one offline queued post delivering on the next write; arm the waiter in one designated session and time a wake; only after those steps, trial its sync on a copy of a notes repository and try to make it produce a conflict marker or overwrite uncommitted work. The pack's summary line for baton: cross-machine handoffs as append-only git records with one lead per task, woken at zero token cost. That zero cost is the design's claim: the polling is done by git, not the model. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its negative controls are the three refusals, each of which must be refused, and the attempt to make the sync produce a conflict marker or overwrite uncommitted work, with one offline queued post delivering on the next write as the healthy case, and the pack does not say what result would end the trial. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, with the expected results written first and no live records touched, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); the planted refusals and the healthy delivery fit that shape, and the pack names no empty-input case. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Building it or running its tests on the Mac; creating any board repository; arming its waiter in any session; letting any agent plan, take or hand over work through it; replacing any part of the kick ledger or the box-to-Mac staging rule with it; trialing its sync on any copy of the vault, let alone the vault itself; installing its hooks, plugin or skills; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it has 0 stars and calls itself v1, under trial; its design decisions are dated the day of the collection, on a repository created at 01:05 PT that morning, and credited to the author's same-day use; it supports one coding CLI only today, with identity read from that CLI's child-session variable and hooks and skills shaped for it, so our other seats would need adapters; the waiter is a long-lived git poll every 30 s, capped by the hook's timeout and the session's lifetime and armed by a human in each session, never a fleet-wide default; its guard is explicitly not a security boundary, and its identity checks are conveniences; our watchdog treats a log silent past about 540 s as stale and counts a stated background wait as alive for at most 30 minutes (#launch, #background-wait), and the pack does not say how a session idling under the waiter would look to it, while the fit with no-exit-while-waiting is the pack's reading, not a playbook ruling; the README is thin, and this verdict rests on the design document, the tree and the tests being present, all read in the collection, with nothing executed; and its name is unrelated to kept ai-baton (2026-10-08), a workspace kit, a different repository with a different claim, so the two must not be confused or merged. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. Apache-2.0, 0 stars, created 2026-11-03 01:05 PT, pushed 2026-11-03 08:58 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: baton: hand work between agents on different machines through one git repo
entries.whatItIs: A tool that lets coding agents on several machines coordinate through a shared git repository: each message is a new file, one machine leads each task, and a hook that checks git, not the model, wakes an idle session only when a message needs it.
entries.whyItMatters: Per the collection notes, two agents can plan the same work and a handoff can wait unseen. A two-machine trial on scratch work is only proposed, not installed; it supports one coding tool today, its guard is not a security boundary, and any change needs Haiyuan.
entries.statusNote: A Lab proposal only: no board repository links our machines, and handoffs still go through the kick ledger, with one owner per run enforced on the Mac alone (#coding-em-kicks; #watchdog-resume-safety).

entries.title: hookfuzz: payload tests, a fuzzer and a bypass search for hooks, plus a dead-path scan
entries.why: Test harness, spec runner and fuzzer for one coding CLI's hooks, which it treats as black boxes in any language, written in TypeScript for Node 20 or newer (repository size 64 KB in the pack's metadata read; 47 paths, among them its sources, its tests, example hooks for shell, Node and Python plus a set named buggy, and an example suite file) and published as a package with one runtime dependency per the README. Its run command fires one realistic event at a hook and derives the decision the way that CLI's own decision table does, per the README: exit 2 blocks only on blocking events, not on post-tool-use or notification events; valid JSON on standard output decides whatever the exit code; JSON counts only if standard output is a single object; and invalid JSON or a schema violation becomes an error. Its decisions are allow, deny, ask, defer, block, stop, none, error, timeout and spawn-error, over 33 known events, with per-event rules modelled too, such as any non-zero exit failing a worktree-create event. Its test command runs suites written in YAML or JSON in CI, with expectations on the decision, the exit code, whether the call was blocked, standard output and standard error, the reason (a substring or a regular expression), valid JSON and a maximum duration, and it exits 1 on any failure and 2 on spec errors. Its fuzz command fires 20 malformed and edge-case payloads, among them an empty object or empty input, malformed and non-object JSON, every common field missing, null or wrong-typed fields, 1 MB strings, emoji, right-to-left text and NUL bytes, traversal paths, shell metacharacters, 200-deep nesting, unknown future fields and tool-server tool names, and reports a crash, a hang or invalid output per case; a hook passes only if it exits 0 or 2, or prints valid JSON, within the timeout and with schema-valid output. Its bypass command takes a command the guard should block and generates about 24 equivalent variants (an absolute path, privilege, environment or command prefixes, quoting tricks, a nested shell, eval, command substitution, backticks, chaining, pipes to a shell, an argument-list runner, and split, reordered or long flags), then prints every variant the hook does not block. Its scan command audits the configuration instead: it reads that CLI's user, project and local settings files, expands the project-directory variable and other environment variables, resolves executables on the PATH and the script argument of a shell, Node or Python call, and prints a MISSING line, file not found or not on PATH, exiting 1; per the pack, this is the silent case the README names first, a path that does not exist, so a policy hook silently never runs. Per the README and the tree the pack read, that nothing is executed is itself tested: variants are only ever placed inside the JSON on the hook's standard input, never executed or shell-interpreted, and a test runs canary variants, a file touch and a recursive delete inside a temporary directory, against an allow-everything hook and asserts that the canary never appears and that the temporary directory is byte-identical; timeouts kill the whole process tree, and standard output and error are capped at 16 MiB, with cut output reported as an error. The README also compares it with seven alternatives and claims to be the only policy-bypass fuzzer and the only tool combining black-box runs, declarative specs, a payload fuzzer and schema validation in one command line, the author's claim, not checked in the collection. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, every rule we care about is enforced by a hook, among them stop-claim gates, commit gates, command guards and edit fences, and there is no test for any of them, so two failure modes are invisible today: the hook file that moved and now silently never runs, while the settings still say the policy is active, and the hook that crashes or hangs on a payload shape it did not expect and so fails open; per the pack, hook health today is 'the session behaved, so it must have run'. The playbook does not show those guards installed: it names hooks as the place for must-hold rules but names no installed hook for them (#em-loop), it keeps its completion-claim rule as prose with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), and a text search of the controls inventory for hook finds only the vault's installer that wires the shared contract file into the seat homes and, in the secrets row, the note that there is no active git hook (#controls-inventory). What it does record is one hook hang, a tracing plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks that hung 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalled two runs, turned off for that run only (#mac-run-lessons), and the removal of four dead hook commands and their leftover trust-state entries, from a per-tool hook retired for good on 2026-10-25 (playbook §13). Per the pack, kept cheat-drill (2026-10-14) already scores a fixed set of 39 cheat moves against pre-tool-use hooks, cheats blocked next to legit actions blocked, and this is the complementary half: test the hook we wrote at the payload level, and prove that the configured hook is wired at all; per the pack, 30 Lab titles mention a hook, its stop-claim gates and commit or review gates among them, cards that decide done and do not test a hook, and its search for a hook test or fuzz card found only a mock-binary card for model-free end-to-end runs and gatehouse, neither of which tests a hook's own decisions, and this is the only in-window item that can be run against hooks we already have without touching the fleet. We already have: hooks named among the EM loop's always-on plays as the place for must-hold rules, such as no secrets in a diff, no push to main and no weakening tests during a fix, with no inventory status and no installed hook named for them (#em-loop); a completion-claim rule kept as prose, where a stop hook enforcing it would be a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory), and a test-tamper scan in review that also looks for commits that skip a repository's hooks (#check-can-fail); a new check counted only once it has been seen failing on a deliberately broken input, policy text only (#check-can-fail), and, adopted 2026-11-02 as standard practice, a gate, any check whose result something acts on, run on a planted broken copy and a healthy control before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy), whose definition of a gate would reach a blocking hook, though it names no hook among its examples; the deadweight config audit, adopted 2026-10-25, a local, one-time, report-only audit of persistent seat configurations from installed-source, schema and filesystem evidence, whose findings baseline is 5 after a hooks fix, down from 9, and which does not run hooks or prove runtime admission or effective settings (#skills), the nearest thing here to its scan, though the playbook does not say whether that audit resolves each configured hook's script; declared-versus-effective hook loading, not adopted from an earlier card, with the adopted static config audit establishing neither declared-versus-effective hook loading nor runtime enforcement (#resident-budget); the rule that a cited vault path must resolve before it is written, with a Monday card-sync check of those cited in the shared contract file and the role cards that the manager bot adds to the sync prompt, the lint tool not installed and no row in the controls inventory (#pointer-check), the same dead-path idea for notes, not for hook settings; and the shared contract file and shared skills wired into the seat homes, marked enforced on a link and checksum check that is run on demand, not on a schedule, and fails on any missing, broken or stale link (#controls-inventory), a wiring check for that file, not for hooks. So a named place for must-hold rules, a seen-failing rule that would reach a blocking hook, a one-time report-only audit of our seats' configurations, a dead-path rule for cited vault paths and an on-demand wiring check of the shared contract file are ours already, as policy text, one report-only audit and one enforced check; a text search of the playbook for fuzz and bypass finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any test suite for a hook, any payload fuzzing or bypass search against a guard, and any check that each configured hook is wired. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a read-only scan first, then one guard's suite. Run its scan in one seat's home, read-only, where per the pack every MISSING line is a policy that never ran; write a 6-case suite for one hook we already rely on and check that the cases pass; run its bypass command against the same guard, with a recursive delete of a scratch path as the command to block, and hand-read each bypass it prints; then fuzz the same hook; only then consider a pre-merge suite for new hooks. The pack's summary line for hookfuzz: test the hook you wrote at the payload level, fuzz it for crashes/hangs, fuzz its blocking rule for bypasses, and prove the configured hook is wired rather than silently absent. Wired here means that the configured path and executable resolve: the tool does not evaluate matcher or if filters, so whether the hook is selected for a given tool call is not tested. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP: its checks are that the six cases pass and that each bypass is read by hand, it names no planted fault, and it does not say what result would end the trial.
