entries.title: undo-ticket: a destructive command runs only against a ticket with a rehearsed restore
entries.why: Agent skill plus a fail-closed pre-tool-use hook, in Python 3.8 or newer with the standard library only (16 paths, among them the skill file and a Chinese translation of it, one script and its tests, example settings and hook files for two coding tools, an edit fence, a ready ticket and a cases file), that asks one question before an irreversible command: how exactly do we put it back, and have we checked that the way back works? It sorts a command into four reversibility classes, GO, TICKET, BLIND and ONE-WAY, with exit codes 0, 10, 20 and 30, and a compound command takes the class of its worst piece, so changing into an app folder, deleting a legacy source folder and force-pushing to main together are ONE-WAY. It reads commands the way a shell does: it splits on semicolons, and-or chains, pipes and newlines, strips privilege, environment, timing, no-hangup and timeout prefixes, opens nested shells, command substitution, backticks and an argument-list runner, finds SQL inside two database clients' command options and deletes inside inline Python, and keeps quoted text as data. Per the pack, its coverage runs from recursive and wildcard deletes, find with delete, git resets, cleans, checkouts, stash clears, forced branch deletes and history rewrites, force-pushes and remote deletes, and SQL drops, truncates and deletes or updates without a WHERE clause to a key-value store's flush-all, cluster and chart deletes, container volumes, infrastructure destroys, cloud object-store deletes, a sync with delete, disk-level copies, formats and shreds, recursive permission changes, a crontab removal and package publishing. The ticket is the claim: drafts come with a recipe per family, among them an archive, a git branch plus a stash, a database dump, an exported manifest, a volume archive, a crontab export and infrastructure state, and a linter checks the fingerprint match, the scope, preview evidence, a snapshot artifact on disk, a restore plus a verify, a recorded rehearsal, that the class was not understated, the expiry and a named approval for one-way doors; its ticket check must print READY. Its drill runs 43 tricky built-in cases plus your own cases file, with under-calls counted separately, 'because they are the dangerous misses' in the words the pack quotes, the asymmetry being the point, and the repository has 37 unit tests. The hook, shaped for one coding CLI and offering another coding tool's output format, has a warn-only mode and an edit fence for edit, write and notebook-edit calls. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our GREEN, YELLOW and RED reversibility lock is applied by the agent, in prose, and nothing checks that a RED action actually has a way back, let alone a tested one. Per the pack, the Lab's command-guard cards, among them kept tripwires (2026-10-22) and kept antibody (2026-11-01), the dates on their published Lab cards, decide block or allow from command text, as do vector-gate, which the pack's own dedupe lists as a 2026-11-02 runner-up and not a Lab card, and glove, which this pack discards as a duplicate in that lane; none requires evidence that the undo works, and none tells a snapshot taken from a restore rehearsed. Per the pack, that distinction is the whole card: a backup never restored is not a way back, and our human gate currently approves on a promise; its search of the Lab for undo, reversibility, rollback and restore found no reversibility check, the cards it returned including bounded-agent-runtime, with its tool risk tiers, and Proof, with its tamper receipts; and per the pack destructive commands are guarded only by keyword rules. We already have: three lanes set by how easy an action is to undo, under which RED actions, among them send or publish, spend or pay, merge, delete non-junk, permissions, production and accepting terms, always go to Haiyuan, and an action that cannot be undone in under a minute is parked and asked about (#gyr-authority), part of the manual approval control (#controls-inventory), with a reversibility line required on every bot charter, a manual control that, per the inventory, only one of the four always-on bots' cards carries today (#controls-inventory); an approval that covers the item as approved and is re-checked, item and current authority, right before the RED action runs, policy text only (#approval-recheck); a promotion gate under which a routine or skill moves up the autonomy ladder only with three clean runs, complete receipts and a tested rollback, a documented way to undo the routine's effects that has actually been tried once, such as a revert commit, a restored backup, a paused routine or a deleted draft (#promotion-gate), a manual control (#controls-inventory), the one rule a text search of the playbook for rollback finds that asks for a way back that was tried, a rule for promoting a routine, not before each destructive command; install records that name a backup and a rollback of one or two file copies for the ownership guard and for the daily update's busy check (#watchdog-resume-safety, #cli-update-busy-check), without saying whether either rollback was tried; a dry run on anything our harness scripts delete, move or push, which shows what would change and changes nothing, policy text only until a lint exists, an existing script moving over when a change next touches it and the real run keeping its lane, with RED still needing Haiyuan (#agent-cli-contract); run limits that are policy in charters and skills, where an earlier card's tool risk tiers, read, write, external and irreversible, map to our three lanes, and a wrapper that enforces them outside the agent loop is a Lab follow-up, not live (#run-limits), a manual control (#controls-inventory); deletes of durable lessons only after Haiyuan approves the specific items, an approved delete removing them rather than archiving them, policy text only (#memory-loop), so one-way doors in the vault already wait on a named approval; an ask-versus-allow draft for auto-review that asks first before send, publish, push, delete or pay (playbook §12), with no row in the controls inventory; and, in our decision layer's gate table, a pre-tool gate that scores destructive risk before high-risk shell or tool-server mutations and answers allow, ask or deny, never authorizing send, pay or merge (playbook §13), with no inventory row either. So the reversibility lanes, the approval re-check, a tried rollback before a promotion, install records with a named rollback, a dry-run rule for our own scripts and allow, ask or deny decisions on a command are ours already, as manual controls, policy text and one decision-layer gate; a text search of the playbook for rehears finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any classifier for commands, any ticket artifact, any restore rehearsal before a destructive command and any under-call metric. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): classify and drill first, hook in warn-only. Run its classifier over about 30 real commands pulled from our own session transcripts and hand-check the under-calls; run the 43-case drill; cut one real ticket for a genuinely destructive task, in a scratch directory, including the rehearsal; and only then install the hook in its warn-only mode, before any fail-closed use. The pack's summary line for undo-ticket: a destructive action needs a rehearsed, verified way back, not a promise; under-calls are the number that matters. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP: its checks are the hand-check of the under-calls and the rehearsed ticket, and it does not say how many under-calls would end the trial. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail); a ticket whose restore was never rehearsed, which its linter must refuse, would be such an input, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it on the Mac, even to classify commands; reading our session transcripts for its classifier; cutting a ticket outside a scratch directory; installing its hook in any seat, in warn-only mode or fail-closed; letting its classes block or allow any command; writing adapters for our other seats; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it parses command text and does not sandbox, so a command assembled entirely at run time can still hide, which is why its BLIND class still needs a human; its recipes are best-effort examples, not guarantees for our stack, with, per the pack, nothing for background-service state or for our notes vault's semantics; the hook is shaped for one coding CLI, so our other seats would need adapters; its class thresholds are the author's, not tuned to our incident history; and the 43 drill cases and the 37 unit tests are the author's, read from the README and the tree, not reproduced in the collection. It has 0 stars and was created minutes before the collect closed, then pushed 7 seconds later, by a single author, with no forks or tests outside the repository, so per the pack its README is unverified beyond the pack's one read. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: harness-diff: paired A/B runs for rule changes, with the detectable effect printed first
entries.why: Paired A/B harness for changes to an agent's instruction file, plus the published result of running it on nine of the most-shared instruction-file lines on one social network, in Python 3.10 or newer with no dependencies (repository size 2,863 KB in the pack's metadata read; 3,228 paths, because its run receipts are committed, among them its package, a task battery, an experiment file, its runs, a results chart, a preregistration file, a lines file and 15 tests). The result, plainly, per the author: the same 30 tasks and the same agent, with and without each line, many runs, with the plan pushed before the first counted run; none of the nine changed how often the agent finished by more than rerunning the agent does, and on the first of its two cheap models the control that compares the baseline with itself read +6.7 percentage points, pure noise at that sample size and bigger than most of the effects measured. It publishes what the run could see: the second model passes 95.9% of the tasks with no instruction file, so there is no room to see a line help there, while a line that hurt by 12 or more points would have shown; the first model would have shown a short line that helped by 13 or hurt by 16; and 'too small to see' is stated as smaller than that, not zero. The one effect it could see is positional: a rule placed at the very end of a 52 KB instruction file was followed 89% of the time, against 100% when it was the only rule (−10.6 points, interval −19.6 to −1.5), cutting a quarter of the file did not get it back (−6.7, interval −17.3 to +3.8), and the same rule alone took compliance from 0% to 96.6% on the second model. Behaviour moved where outcomes did not: the line 'when docs and code disagree, follow the code' cost +0.62 turns per task on the second model (interval +0.56 to +0.67), while the placebo moved turns by 0.00. The workflow is the product: its plan mode, given an old and a new instruction file, prints the smallest help and hurt a run could detect before any spend, at a sample setting of 10 on the second model about +4.5 and −5.7 points for 600 runs, about $0.84 at list price; runs resume where they stopped; every run leaves a receipt with the model's full transcript and usage; and its preregistration was pushed at one commit before the first counted run, and an independent reviewer caught a bias before the freeze. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our consolidation keeps making exactly this claim, that we cut something and things improved, and this is a measured floor for how big that improvement has to be before it means anything: +6.7 points of pure noise at a sample of about 10, which per the pack is larger than most of the nine effects and larger than most of our rule edits. The playbook records no such claim: a text search of it for improv finds no match, and the comparison with our own rule edits is the pack's. Per the pack, the positional finding is a second, cheaper rule: a new rule appended to the bottom of a 52 KB instruction file is followed about 11 points less often than the same rule standing alone, so where a rule goes is a measurable variable, not a style choice; our corrections are appended to the never-again list (#vault), which is at its 81,155 B ceiling (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory), but the author's long-file arm is another project's file, not ours, so how a line placed at the end of ours fares is not measured. Per the pack, context-tax (2026-11-02) measures the static load at turn 0, Harness Wrangler (2026-10-14) repeats graded runs with a confidence interval and a no-headroom baseline, and verderer (2026-10-31) keeps a rule ledger with dead, derivable and needed ablation verdicts, and none of them publishes a measured baseline-against-itself delta or a plan that prints the smallest effect a run could see before money is spent; the pack holds the in-window rulelab, a per-rule ablation on one's own repository, as a runner-up behind this card and Harness Wrangler. We already have: a detection-floor rule under which a promotion note says in one line that three runs catch only large regressions, not a smaller one, and lists every case that got worse even when all three runs passed, policy text only (#detection-floor), written because our Three-Run Proof records only clean or not clean, the nearest rule here to a stated floor, though it states the floor in words and measures none; Three-Run Proof before a new routine, a manual control (#three-run-proof, #controls-inventory); a replay check before a skill or prompt promotion, proposed because its set is not built, that set's bar already written as the worst of three runs, one of them on a reworded instruction (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory); a harness evaluation design of 28 cases from our own records in four arms, each scored by the same sealed check written before the first run with a negative control, where zero failures is reported as inconclusive, not a pass, a proposal not approved and not run as of 2026-10-24 (#harness-eval); a reference note under which a performance comparison states its alternating-run count, median and range, a missing limiter or comparable settings means INCONCLUSIVE, and external numbers stay external until reproduced here (playbook §13, after #gate-broken-copy), with no checker named; a count or an all-or-none statement in a receipt, Decision or Lab card that names how it was counted and over what, policy text only (#check-can-fail); byte ceilings on the two files every agent reads, the shared contract file at 13,489 B and the never-again list at 81,155 B, the first held by size gates that only report and the second by hand (#resident-budget, #controls-inventory), sizes, not effects; a rule-phrase check on trial, report-only and in shadow and not built yet, that would report each must-hold rule no longer stated where agents read it (#rule-phrase-check), presence, not effect; and run limits under which long fires default to $0 spend and 0 external actions without Haiyuan's approval, a manual control (#run-limits, #controls-inventory). So a stated detection floor, a proposed replay set, an evaluation design that calls zero failures inconclusive, a comparison-evidence note, a counting rule and size ceilings are ours already, as policy text, proposals and report-only gates; a text search of the playbook for placebo and noise floor finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any measured noise floor, any placebo arm and any habit of writing down the detectable effect before a rule change. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): its free plan mode first, and one paid run only if the floor is small enough to matter. Run its plan mode on today's shared contract file against the version before our most recent rule addition, which costs nothing and prints the detectable effect; if that floor is acceptable, make one paid run at a sample setting of 10 on the second model, about $0.84 per the author, on the same pair, and read the receipts, not the headline; and treat 'too small to see' as the default verdict in consolidation until a run says otherwise. The pack's summary line for harness-diff: a rule change must beat a measured noise floor (+6.7 pp in the author's run), and the tool prints the detectable effect before any spend; a rule buried at the end of a long file is followed less often. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP: the paid run waits on the free plan's floor being small enough to matter, the pack gives no number for that floor, and the control that compares the baseline with itself is the author's design, not a check of ours. The playbook asks that a new check be seen failing once on a deliberately broken input before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail); for a measurement, a pair of instruction files with a known large difference, which the tool must report as a detectable effect, would be such an input, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it on the Mac, even for its free plan mode; pointing it at the shared contract file or any other instruction file of ours; any paid run, since long fires default to $0 spend (#run-limits); choosing the model, the sample setting or the pair of versions; taking the too-small-to-see verdict into the consolidation routine as its default; moving any rule within our files on the strength of its positional result; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: every figure above, the +6.7 points of noise on the control, the 89% against 100% end-of-file effect and its intervals, the extra turns, the 95.9% pass rate and the cost estimate, is the author's, read from the README and the committed results, not reproduced in the collection; it runs on macOS only, through the system's sandbox tool and one package manager's Python; it measures a fixed battery of 30 short Python tasks with a 4-turn budget, so it can tell whether a rule changes behaviour on those tasks, not whether it helps on our real work; it uses two cheap models only, a stronger model passing 97.9% of the tasks and leaving nothing to detect; its long-file arm is another project's instruction file, not ours, and its 25% cut is random; and one vendor's models run through that vendor's coding CLI with its tools and settings off. It has 0 stars and was created the night before the collection, by a single author. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: locus: one human-set account pin per session; children get only the pinned credential
entries.why: Identity plane for coding agents, in Rust 1.89 or newer (repository size 4,586 KB in the pack's metadata read; 593 paths, among them crates for its command line, its core and its tool server, a local dashboard, adapters, a red-team script, its documentation and an agent contract), built on one idea: one pin, and every tool acts only as that client until a person pins again. The pin is human: entering an alias seals the session, with an HMAC, to one binding, and the command line, the tool-server tools and the local dashboard then act only as that client; unpinned sessions get control tools only, and agents cannot pin, its tool server offering a request-pin tool that asks a person, with no fallthrough to a personal account. The child does not inherit the other client: its exec, run and CI-run commands scrub ambient code-host, cloud, database-platform and hosting tokens from the environment and redirect HOME to a private per-binding config, so the credential files of the code host's command line, a cloud command line, netrc, git and the package manager are not reachable through HOME, and an exec for the code host's command line injects only the pinned credential. Frozen ids stay frozen: a binding freezes the project reference, the team id, the org and the repository, and a model argument naming a different one is denied; destructive names can require approval, and its approve command is labelled as advice that does not itself release provider execution. It publishes its own red team: on a plain launch, 48 of 48 ambient credential variables were reachable, across 16 variables and 3 trials, and under a bound run 0 of 48; credential files read through HOME, 0 of 15; an agent's attempt to pin, refused 3 of 3; and it states the limit itself: 'This is not a sandbox. The same files opened by their real absolute path stayed reachable (15 of 15, same as a plain launch).' Its doctor returns SAFE, WARN or UNSAFE as JSON and can exit 0 while ok is false, which it calls advisory-only; a session-verify and claim-text pair adds a small verification plane; and a forensics export ships a pack with no secrets. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our seats share ambient identity: every bot acts through the same code-host credential, any second account or project token present in the environment is inherited by every child process a seat spawns, so a wrong-tenant push is one unset variable away, and nothing in the fleet notices which account an action used. The playbook records part of that: all always-on bots share one cloud computer, files and logins, so a shared box is no isolation (playbook §16), and one seat's model-gateway key is reused by the backup seat, loaded by the launcher of the first default small model and reused by our decision layer (#providers; playbook §13). Per the pack, the Lab has no card in this lane at all, its search finding only Preflight (2026-09-21), an outbound secret-redaction proxy marked backlog, and even if locus is never adopted whole, the transferable rule is worth having: the credential a child gets is the pinned one, and only a person can change the pin, the same authority shape as our human gate, applied to identity instead of to posting. We already have: RED actions, among them permissions, always going to Haiyuan (#gyr-authority), and an approval re-checked right before the action runs, against the approved item and current authority (#approval-recheck), both part of the manual approval control (#controls-inventory), the human gate whose shape the pack's transferable rule borrows; no secrets, tokens or private keys in notes, a manual rule with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook (#controls-inventory); no keys in the vault or in hub pages, and anything pasted into chat rotated (#extend), with secrets and credentials kept out of group posts (playbook §12); errors that never echo secrets, a value read from an environment variable whose name contains KEY, SECRET, TOKEN or PASSWORD never being printed, adopted 2026-10-31 as policy text that nothing enforces until a lint exists (#agent-cli-contract-5-6); and, in a reference section on another team's agent prototype, not adopted, that team's warning that a credential reaching the model's context can leak in normal work, so agents need a way to use credentials without touching them, and its note that its credential wrappers and directories are defaults, not a security boundary, since a worker can still run a program by absolute path and isolation needs a dedicated OS account (#superagent-reference), the same limit locus states of itself. So a human gate on permissions, rules that keep secrets out of notes, chat, posts and error text, and a reference design's warning that credential wrappers are no boundary are ours already, as manual controls, policy text and a reference; a text search of the playbook for tenant finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any pin, any per-binding scratch home and any record of which account an action ran as. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): an isolated quickstart only, and no real seat pinned yet. Run its quickstart under a throwaway home and confirm that a run expecting a different binding is refused with a pin mismatch before the child starts; export a canary code-host token and a canary cloud profile and confirm that neither reaches the child of a run; read its routing document before pointing it at a real code-host command line; and treat the dashboard and the tool server as out of scope for the first trial. The pack's summary line for locus: one human-set pin per session; the child inherits only the pinned credential, and an agent cannot re-pin. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP; its negative controls are the mismatch check, which must be refused before the child starts, and the canary credentials, which must not reach a child, and the pack does not say what result would end the trial. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, with the expected results written first and no live records touched, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); the planted canary and the mismatched binding fit that shape, while the pack names no healthy control and no empty-input case. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it on the Mac by either route, even for the throwaway quickstart; exporting any canary credential; pinning any real seat or pointing it at a real code-host command line; starting its dashboard or its tool server; letting a binding decide which account any action uses; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, permissions being RED (#gyr-authority). A wrapper or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it is not a new item: it is about three months old, with its latest release on 2026-11-01, 3 stars, 1 fork, 93 open issues and a 4.6 MB repository, installed through a Rust toolchain or a package manager, and per the pack its other install tap still serves the release before; it is explicitly not a sandbox, absolute-path reads by an allowed process staying reachable, so per the pack it complements rather than replaces permissions; a pin needs a live broker, and recovery after the broker exits is documented but manual; one credential scheme fails closed until a scoped bridge exists, in the version the pack read; our fleet currently uses one code-host identity, per the pack, so the benefit is prospective and the trial cost is the real cost; and the red-team figures, 48 of 48 to 0 of 48, 0 of 15 and 3 of 3, are the author's, from one machine with canary credentials, and none was reproduced in the collection. The pack read its README up to the install and command-line sections. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: agent-load-brake: headless sessions queue at start until the host has capacity
entries.why: Admission control for headless agent runs, as a session-start hook for one coding CLI, the one our default implementer and a blind review seat run (#roster): a single Python script for Python 3.8 or newer that uses only the standard library (os, sys, time, json and subprocess), with a Node 20 or newer installer that registers the hook in that CLI's settings file (repository size 411 KB in the pack's metadata read; 31 paths, among them the hook script, the installer and a shell test; published as a package at version 0.1.0, whose registry entry answered HTTP 200 at collection time). Per the README as the pack reads it, when orchestrators, schedules or scripts start headless agents in parallel, every session competes for CPU, memory and disk, so before a session makes its first model call the hook samples load averages, memory pressure, swap use and free disk. It caps concurrent headless sessions on a ladder, 8 normally, 4 under moderate load and 0 when the host is heavy, holds the others in a local first-in-first-out queue until capacity clears, and recognizes interactive sessions and never delays them. If the host stays loaded past its --max-wait limit, whose default the pack gives only as configurable, the hook ends the session cleanly with exit 2 before any tokens are spent, and the orchestrator gets a structured pause-or-retry code with its queue position kept, so a launcher can reschedule instead of letting the machine thrash. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our seats' scheduled and catch-up kicks start on the one Mac through our launcher, and when they overlap, host load rises and runs wedge or stall; per the pack, this hook would queue headless starts until the machine recovers, at no model cost. The playbook records the 10-15 exec wedge, in which newly started programs hung before running and timed probes ended with exit 142, without naming a cause, and ties a 10-11 app-level disconnect, as likely, to a nearly full disk (#mac-run-lessons), so the link from overlapping load to a wedge is the pack's reading, not a measured one. Per the pack, kept mac-dev-janitor (2026-10-22) kills a runaway process group after the fact, a Lab card the playbook does not mention, so not a control of ours, and a 2026-11-02 runner-up the pack names reserves session quota; neither queues a headless start at zero spend, the gap the pack says this card fills. We already have: long launches held while the Mac has less than 15 GB free, a disk floor rather than a load or memory gate, manual in the inventory, where one queue's disk gate enforces it and the shared launcher has no disk check (#launch, #controls-inventory); after Mac trouble, two timed spawn-ok probes before any launch, relaunch or resume, a failed probe meaning nothing is launched and the slots are recorded as owed, run by hand and report-only in the inventory (#spawn-ok, #controls-inventory); long runs in tmux with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s, a manual convention, since nothing blocks a bare or unwatched launch (#launch, #controls-inventory), with a restart refused unless the old process is proven dead, enforced by the ownership guard (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), and a stated background wait counted as alive for at most 30 minutes after its line (#background-wait); max throughput, under which reviewers and catch tests launch in parallel on each PR head and an idle seat pulls the next item, the 15 GB floor and tmux isolation still applying (#max-throughput), so parallel starts are standing policy; run limits of 50 items, 2 retries, $0 spend and 0 external actions without Haiyuan's approval, policy in charters and skills, a wrapper that enforces them outside the agent loop being a Lab follow-up, not live (#run-limits), a manual control (#controls-inventory); exit codes that say whether a restart can help, listed in the help of any script a watchdog, routine or retry may act on, policy text only (#agent-cli-contract-5-6); and, from earlier Lab cards, a pre-flight quota check before a coding-seat launch, listed as a new practice not installed, and runtime-enforced run limits in the wrapper, listed as not built (#usage). So a disk floor, probes after trouble, a stale-log watchdog, an ownership guard and written run limits are ours already, as manual and report-only controls and one enforced guard; a text search of the playbook for load average and memory pressure finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any gate at session start on host load, memory or swap, any automatic disk check in the shared launcher and any queue for headless starts. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): status and a dry run first, then one synthetic hold. Run its installer with --dry-run to see the change it would make to one seat's settings file; run its status command to check its load thresholds against this Mac; then start one synthetic headless session under simulated load, to confirm that the queue holds it and that it exits cleanly. The pack's headline for agent-load-brake: admission control at SessionStart so parallel agents don't freeze the Mac. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP: its checks are the dry run's proposed change, the status reading and one held synthetic session, and it does not say what result would end the trial. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, with the expected results written first and no live records touched, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); the simulated load is such a planted fault, while the pack names no healthy control, an unloaded session that must pass straight through, and no empty-input case. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it on the Mac, even for its dry run or its status command; letting its installer touch any seat's settings file; registering its hook in any seat; reconciling its queue, its wait limit and its exit 2 with our launcher, watchdog and retry rules; calibrating its thresholds for this Mac; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, launcher or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it hooks one coding CLI's session-start contract only, so per the pack two of our other seats' CLIs need wrapper integration, and the pack names no others; per the pack its thresholds need calibration for this Mac, where memory pressure and Unix one-minute load averages read differently; our stale-log watchdog treats a log silent for about 540 s as stale unless its last line states a background wait in the form it recognizes (#launch, #background-wait), and the pack does not say what a held session writes while it waits; the playbook already records hooks that held our runs: a tracing plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hung 1.5–6+ min per tool call and stalled two runs, turned off for that run only (#mac-run-lessons); and the 8, 4 and 0 ladder, the pass-through for interactive sessions and the clean exit 2 before any spend are the author's description, read from the README, not reproduced in the collection. entries.title: rufix: secrets masked in tool output, restored in shell commands just before they run
entries.why: A single Go binary that acts as a pair of hooks for one coding CLI, the one our default implementer and a blind review seat run (#roster), to keep credentials and internal host names out of the model's context and the session transcript, working offline with no proxy, daemon or network bridge, per the README as the pack reads it (repository size 56 KB in the pack's metadata read; 34 paths, among them its main program, packages for the hook, redaction, secret values and env files, and an install script). Its post-tool-use hook reads each tool result before the model gets it, file reads, shell output and errors, and tool-server results among them, and replaces known environment secrets, private keys, API tokens and internal domain names with reversible placeholders of the form [S:hash8]. Its pre-tool-use hook works the other way: when the model later writes a shell command that contains a placeholder, it puts the real secret or host name back just before the process runs, so legitimate automation proceeds while the value stays out of the model's view. It matches standard token formats, JSON web tokens, code-host personal access tokens, cloud access keys and generic hex or base64 bearer tokens, plus values the user defines in an env file, and checks a domain's top-level part so that ordinary text is not replaced by mistake. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our fleet contract forbids secrets, tokens and private keys in notes and our untrusted-content rule treats tool results as evidence only, yet when agents run diagnostic shell commands, inspect repository configs or read local files, raw tokens and internal host names 'frequently enter the model's context window and transcript logs', a frequency the pack states and does not measure. Per the pack, command blockers such as kept antibody (2026-11-01), the date on its published Lab card, and vector-gate can only allow or deny a whole command (vector-gate has no Lab card: the published undo-ticket card records it as a 2026-11-02 runner-up), and kept Preflight (2026-09-21), an outbound secret-redaction proxy marked backlog, was never built; per the pack, this card does the redaction at the hook layer, both ways, in one dependency-free binary and with no proxy. The nearest statement of the problem in the playbook sits in a reference section, not adopted: another team's design notes that a credential reaching the model's context can leak in normal work, so agents need a way to use credentials without touching them, one of that design's open questions (#superagent-reference). We already have: no secrets, tokens or private keys in notes, a manual rule with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook, blind reviewers checking new text case by case (#controls-inventory); hooks named among the EM loop's always-on plays as the place for must-hold rules, no secrets in a diff among them, with no installed hook named for it (#em-loop); untrusted content, tool output included, treated as data and never as instructions, policy text only (#untrusted-content), a rule about what an agent does with text it reads, not about which values reach it; errors that never echo secrets or whole argument lists, a value read from an environment variable whose name contains KEY, SECRET, TOKEN or PASSWORD never being printed, adopted 2026-10-31 as policy text that nothing enforces until a lint exists, while our launcher's run log and the watchdog's resume line still print a whole command line (#agent-cli-contract-5-6); a report-only Mac check with a known open issue that a credential value could appear in an error message (#report-only-checks); and, from an earlier Lab card, a post-tool-use trim of noisy tool output, at the hook position this card uses, listed as a new practice not installed (#usage). So rules that keep secrets out of notes and out of error text, the place where a must-hold hook would go and the data-not-instructions rule are ours already, as manual controls and policy text; a text search of the playbook for redact and mask finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any masking of tool output before the model reads it and any restore at execution. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a dry run with a dummy secret, then one non-production repository. Build the binary from source; run its redact step on a sample of command output carrying a dummy token and check that a [S:hash8] placeholder replaces it; check that its restore step puts the dummy token back into an echo command; and only then try it on one non-production repository, before it is enabled in any seat's settings. The pack's headline for rufix: bidirectional secret and internal host redaction at the hook layer. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP: its checks are the dummy token's replacement and its restore, and it does not say what result would end the trial. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, with the expected results written first and no live records touched, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); the dummy token is such a planted input, while the pack names no healthy control, output with no secret that must pass unchanged, and no empty-input case. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Building or installing it on the Mac, even for the dry run; giving it any real secret or env file; registering either hook in any seat; trying it on any repository, non-production or not; writing adapters for our other seats' CLIs; or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: per the pack, its placeholder map lives in process memory or a local cache, so an evicted cache or a restarted process can miss a restore when a session runs long; its hooks target one coding CLI, so per the pack another seat's CLI needs an equivalent adapter; masking keeps a value out of what the model reads, not out of the commands it writes, since a placeholder in a model-written shell command is restored before the command runs, and the pack does not say whether restore is limited to particular commands or destinations; the pack lists what it matches, standard token formats and the user's env-file values, and does not say what happens to a secret in another form; and the redaction rules and the false-positive guard are the author's description, read from the README, not tested in the collection. It has 0 stars and 0 forks, is at version 0.1.0 and was created the same morning as the collect, in PT. entries.title: parallel-agents-safety: blocks broad kills, detaching and main-checkout resets
entries.why: Pre-tool-use command guard for several coding agents working side by side on one workstation, shipped as the parallel-agents-safety plugin in the agent-plugins repository: one Python script of 43.5 KB, hook definitions for three coding CLIs, each one a CLI that one of our seats runs per the roster (#roster), and a test file (repository size 46 KB in the pack's metadata read; 39 paths; Python 3 and shell). Per the README as the pack reads it, it splits each shell command the way a shell does, at semicolons, pipes and subshells, and blocks four kinds of command. Sweeping process kills: pkill, killall, fuser -k, kill fed by a pgrep substitution, pgrep piped into xargs kill, a port lookup with lsof piped into xargs kill, and kill -1, any of which can end a neighboring agent's session or a shared service, while a kill of one known process, such as kill 1234, kill $! or kill %1, is allowed. Detaching from the session's supervision: nohup, setsid, disown and a trailing or lone &, while && chains, |& and & followed by wait are allowed. Destructive git in the main checkout: git reset --hard, git clean -f, git checkout -- ., git checkout -f, git restore ., git stash and git branch -D are blocked when the command runs in the primary working tree, which it tells apart from a linked worktree, and allowed inside a linked worktree. And force pushes: a plain git push --force or a +branch refspec is blocked and --force-with-lease is required, so unmerged upstream commits are not overwritten. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, several seats share our Mac, and an uncoordinated broad kill or a forced checkout in the main repository risks ending a background watchdog or destroying staged work; per the pack, this hook turns our operating rules into an enforceable pre-tool-use gate on two of our seats' CLIs. The pack quotes the shared contract file for strict isolation, but the lines it joins are the no-exit-while-waiting rule, the rule that coding goes to the Mac's coding agents through our launcher and the wrapper gates on a dirty tree, none of them about one agent stopping another's processes; the playbook's own isolation rule is a different one, below. Per the pack's dedupe, simpool, a 2026-11-02 runner-up, leases ports and simulators, and kept undo-ticket (2026-11-04) asks for a rehearsed restore before a destructive command; neither bans broad kills or detaching or keeps destructive git out of the main checkout, and per the pack this card supersedes a discarded guard that filtered process kills and layout formatting. We already have: tmux isolation on the Mac, logged on 2026-10-29 after a test that cleaned up with tmux kill-server killed the Mac's shared tmux server twice and ended its own run: a test or script that uses tmux first unsets TMUX and TMUX_PANE and puts every tmux call on its own private socket, no seat kills the shared tmux server or uses pkill or killall, a seat stops only processes it started, by PID, and never touches another agent's sessions, and launch prompts forbid tmux kill commands (#changelog-2026-10-26), restated in part under max throughput (#max-throughput), with no row in the controls inventory and no hook named, so this card's first rule, broad kills blocked and a kill of one known process allowed, is already our rule, in prose and launch prompts; one agent per run or worktree, a stale run resuming only after the old process is proven gone, enforced by the ownership guard (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), which keeps two of our runs off one worktree across a resume, not an agent's own git commands out of the main checkout; long runs started through our launcher in tmux, never with a bare nohup from the always-on bots' shell (#launch), after a nohup watch loop died with its launching shell and was relaunched in tmux (#mac-run-lessons), a manual convention, since nothing blocks a bare or unwatched launch (#controls-inventory), which covers how a run is launched, not what an agent detaches inside it; no ending a turn while waiting on background jobs with a dirty tree, with per-kick wrapper gates on a dirty tree or an unchanged HEAD written by hand for each kick, a manual control (#coding, #controls-inventory); hooks named among the EM loop's always-on plays as the place for must-hold rules, no push to main among them, with no installed hook named for it (#em-loop); and, in our decision layer's gate table, a pre-tool gate that scores destructive risk before high-risk shell or tool-server mutations and answers allow, ask or deny, with no row in the controls inventory (playbook §13). So a ban on broad kills with stops by process id only, one owner per worktree across resumes, launches kept in tmux, hand-written dirty-tree gates, a named place for must-hold hooks and a decision-layer allow, ask or deny gate are ours already, as prose rules, manual controls, one enforced guard and one gate with no inventory row; a text search of the playbook for git reset, git clean, force-with-lease, setsid and disown finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any runtime check of an agent's commands against these rules, including the kill ban we already have in prose. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the author's tests and synthetic commands first, then log-only in a test workspace. Run the author's test suite to check its command parsing; check how it judges synthetic command strings, pkill and a git reset --hard in a main checkout and in a linked worktree; then register its hook definitions in a test workspace with log-only output before any blocking mode. The pack's verdict names warn or log mode on our Mac CLIs as the goal; its trial puts the test workspace first, and on a live seat that would be a hook install. entries.title: Parrhesia: separate overclaim and underclaim reviews, then one adjudicator, no averaging

It separates three jobs a single model does badly at once: an overclaim reviewer that flags only level jumps, unexcluded confounders and reasoning gaps, asking what is the highest level the evidence actually supports, and is explicitly forbidden from using 'does the tone sound humble' as a metric; an underclaim reviewer that finds contributions weakened without cause and no-information disclaimers, asking what the evidence already robustly supports, and is forbidden from scoring 'how many disclaimers were deleted'; and one adjudicator, with no voting and no averaging, that rules adopt, partially adopt or reject per item and gives one verdict plus observable re-decision conditions, such as narrowing the scope to the original population if a cross-centre calibration slope leaves the range 0.8 to 1.2. entries.title: signoff-cli: five exit-code gates and a tree-bound verdict, optionally signed
entries.why: Git-hook-centric command line in JavaScript (Node 18 or newer only; repository size 9.3 MB in the pack's metadata read; version 4.1, renamed at 4.0.0 and moved to its current repository at 4.1.0) whose first use case, per the pack, was a coding-agent harness one of our seats runs, later generalised to any git repository. It runs five gates plus a release gate, each a command, with no partial pass: exit 0 on a pass, 1 when any gate is red, 2 on a usage or environment error. The gates: P1 verification, whether the tests actually ran, within a time budget, and how many cases; P2 coverage level, verified to scenario, harness, smoke or missing; P3 queue, whether cards are complete, concurrency collisions, and who overstepped or did not deliver; P4 ledger, whether a dangerous action had a ticket and its rollback point still exists, with signed checkpoints and a one-line publishable anchor; and P5 anti-slop, empty phrases, absolute claims and 'verified' with no number. Before P1 it scans for 16 secret shapes and prints only a prefix, the rule and the line, so the log does not become a second leak. Its commit-message hook writes a pass trailer naming the tree, plus an optional ed25519 key and signature over the full tree; its audit command re-checks each commit, and an allowed-signers anchor separates verified from self-signed, never reporting the latter as verified. Its coverage command, with a minimum of 80 on the diff, reads an existing coverage file and reports 'not tested' when none exists rather than passing. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our done receipt's VERIFIED line does not say at what level something was verified, so a smoke check and a scenario check both read as VERIFIED, and P2 grades exactly that. Per the pack, our review rule depends on the head SHA, and the trailer and signature bind the verdict to the full tree, so a marker copied from another commit, or a bypass with --no-verify or SIGNOFF_SKIP=1, is detectable after the fact, a stronger property than any receipt card the Lab holds. Per the pack, the author's own case study is unusually honest about what did not work: P1 missed the actual frontend bug, P3 never ran, and P4 caught the author's own fake rollback point only after the fact. Per the pack, the completion-gate lane holds kept gatehouse (2026-10-01), kept tamperproof (2026-10-10) and kept undo-ticket (2026-11-04), which covers rehearsed restore tickets rather than a signed commit gate, and this card adds coverage-level grading and a signed verdict with a bypass audit that survives after the fact. We already have: the done receipt, whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that actually ran, each with its evidence (an exit code, a CI URL, an HTTP 200 or a commit) and names the command and its exit code, with no field for the level a check reached among its objective, changed, verified, not verified, risks and approval lines (#done-receipt; #claim-vs-record), part of completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory), and the rule that a passing check says what it examined, files, rows or cards, policy text only (#check-can-fail), the nearest thing to a level; a completion claim counted only when the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed, and a test-tamper scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer that also looks for || true added after a check and for commits made with --no-verify, which skips the repository's hooks (#claim-vs-record; #check-can-fail), so a skipped-hooks commit is already looked for in review, by hand; a verdict line pinned to the head SHA, where a line naming an older SHA is UNPARSED and never counts as an approval (#review-verdict-line), a manual review step (#controls-inventory), so a verdict carried onto a later commit already fails by rule; the rule that a count or an all-or-none statement names how it was counted and over what, policy text only (#check-can-fail), the nearest rule to its anti-slop gate; a promotion gate that asks for a rollback actually tried once (#promotion-gate) and reversibility lanes that send RED actions to Haiyuan (#gyr-authority), both manual controls (#controls-inventory); and a manual no-secrets rule for notes, with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook (#controls-inventory), beside the agent-CLI rule that errors never echo secrets, policy text only (#agent-cli-contract-5-6). So listed checks with evidence, a review-time scan for skipped hooks, a verdict pinned to the head, a tried rollback before promotion and a no-secrets rule are ours already, as manual controls and policy text, which narrows the pack's point that we have no bypass audit; a text search of the playbook for scenario and ed25519 finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any grading of the level a check reached, any signed verdict bound to the commit tree and any after-the-fact audit of bypassed commits. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP. Per the pack it fits the commits of the bot that runs our coding loop far better than a collector's read-only packs, and its machine layer rewrites the git hooks path for all repositories, which per the pack is a Haiyuan decision, not a collect action. entries.title: RetroHound: Sigma-style rules audit coding agents' raw tool calls, with exit codes
entries.why: Offline command-line tool in TypeScript (Node 22.13 or newer; repository size 1.89 MB in the pack's metadata read; published on a package registry, per the pack) that audits coding agents after the fact and can also run as a live guard hook, with no network access, per the pack. The high-risk behaviors it flags: a secret read followed by network egress, a script piped into a shell, config or hook files modified, unapproved subagents spawned and blocked actions retried. entries.title: lodeline: one static scan scores permissions, hooks, sandboxes and tool-server reach
entries.why: Single-binary static scanner in Rust (1.88; repository size 14.9 MB in the pack's metadata read; formerly named Sigil; prebuilt binaries for three desktop operating systems; described in the pack's source line as an alpha on a zero major version and in its caveats as pre-alpha status) that, in one command, parses and scores the configuration, permissions, hooks, sandbox flags and tool-server settings of five coding CLIs, runs locally with zero external network access and has machine-readable output. It calculates a unified risk score from 0 to 10, bucketed low, medium, high or critical, and reports specific structural misconfigurations: an agent running without host boundary isolation; a wildcard regular expression on a pre-tool-use hook that catches all tools or allows unintended execution; a hook that invokes a destructive command; a tool server configured to auto-launch an arbitrary shell binary; untrusted repository settings that override environment variables or helper commands; and a permission block that specifies no deny patterns. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, we manage multi-CLI configurations through the vault's hook installer and shared instruction files; kept haloguard (2026-11-05) detects when configuration files change between snapshots but does not evaluate whether the configuration itself is safe, and kept context-tax (2026-11-02) counts tokens, not permissions. Per the pack, lodeline evaluates the reach of the configuration: whether a pre-tool-use hook matcher is dangerously broad, whether a tool server launches local shell commands and whether sandbox boundaries are disabled, and running a single binary over the seats' home and project settings before launches would give immediate configuration posture visibility. Per the pack's dedupe section, it does what none of the config-inspection lane's cards do, among them the snapshot diff, the token bill, a config doctor and a schema lint. The Lab's own cards narrow that absence: the 2026-10-22 deadweight card, adopted 2026-10-25 as a one-time report-only audit of seat configurations, finds permission rules that never match and hooks that never fire, per its own summary, so what remains new is scoring how broad a live hook or permission is. So the wiring check, the one-time config audit, the skill lint and the RED list are ours already, as an enforced on-demand check, report-only audits and a manual control; a text search of the playbook for matcher and for the word broad finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any scored, multi-CLI review of what a seat's permissions, hooks and tool servers can reach. entries.title: agent-constraint-auditor: declared rules over event logs exit 0 CLEAN or 2 DECAY
entries.why: Deterministic auditor in Python (3.10 or newer; repository size 784 KB in the pack's metadata read; CI passing, per the pack) that checks agent execution journals or JSON-lines event transcripts against declared YAML constraints to detect constraint decay, which the pack defines as the progressive failure of an agent to maintain standing rules as context lengthens. Per the pack it makes zero model calls and uses no model-graded heuristics, running entirely through deterministic regular-expression and predicate evaluation over event streams. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our fleet operates under strict standing constraints (foreground-only, $0 external spend, no background processes left running, no hub HTML edits), agents frequently observe constraints during initial steps but instruction following degrades as context approaches 30+ tool calls, which the pack calls 'constraint decay' and does not measure, and detecting it today requires human post-task inspection. Per the pack, a deterministic exit code can run inside CI or post-task receipts to prove an agent adhered to constraints from step 1 to finish. Per the pack's lane, neighbouring Lab cards are the 2026-10-31 verderer card, a rule ledger, and the 2026-11-02 memrot card, which flags decaying temporal words; this adds a decay slope and first-violation index over a session's events. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP. entries.title: claude-codex-orchestration: typed subagents, a gate hook and required cross-family review
entries.why: Orchestration skill, typed subagents and a hook suite in Python (3.9 or newer; repository size 988 KB in the pack's metadata read; Turkish and English documentation) for two coding CLIs, which enforces multi-agent task execution and cross-family critical review, per the pack. The main session only plans, briefs and reviews and is prohibited from direct file editing and exploration. Four single-purpose subagents do the work: an explorer for read-only judgment, a worker that applies code and runs tests, a researcher for API and docs checks and a scanner for fast regular-expression searches. A fresh subagent conducts a same-family task review, and a cross-family critic script is mandatory for multi-task plans, multi-file changes and schema updates: work produced in one CLI is dispatched to the other for independent critique. An agent-type gate hook automatically denies generic agent types and blocks unapproved models, keeping subagents within their assigned type and model tier, and an irreversible-action gate blocks pushes, deletion of untracked files and external writes until a human approval is recorded. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this matches our team's architecture, the standing decision under which one seat drafts artifacts and two others review them blind, and the repository provides the shell scripts, hook definitions and model-dispatch bridges to run that cross-family review programmatically on the Mac without manual human relay; per the pack, the agent-type gate also enforces that subagents cannot silently switch models or run unconstrained general-purpose prompts, and our review rules are enforced via prompt instructions and manager-bot orchestration, not local hook-mediated cross-CLI invocation scripts. The Lab's own cards narrow the lane: a 2026-10-05 card on hook-enforced subagent model routing with an orchestrator write-deny, set aside in the 2026-10-13 triage as a deny-gate hook install, and a 2026-10-04 cross-vendor review-jury card, set aside there because a review fan-out costs tokens and a third review seat needs Haiyuan, per their status notes. We already have: named reviewer seats, with one blind reviewer on code one seat implemented and two blind reviewers on docs, drafts and other seats' code, each blind to the other and the implementer never reviewing its own work (#reviewer-rule; #em-loop), the seat pick being policy, with per-review launch scripts and nothing checking the pick, a manual control (#controls-inventory); the EM requesting those reviewers itself on the PR URL (#em-loop); blind disproof review with 2-3 rejection criteria and a verdict line on the head SHA, where a missing line is UNPARSED and never an approval, a manual review step (#disproof-review; #review-verdict-line; #controls-inventory); three fix rounds, then escalation to Haiyuan (#review-convergence), a manual control (#controls-inventory); and RED actions such as merge, send, deleting non-junk and permissions always going to Haiyuan, with an approval re-checked right before it runs, manual controls (#gyr-authority; #approval-recheck; #controls-inventory). So the review seats, the blind verdict pair, the fix-round cap and the RED list are ours already, as manual controls and policy text, and the EM's own review launches mean the pack's 'without manual human relay' is only partly the gap; a text search of the playbook for cross-family, cross-model and agent-type finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is local hook-mediated invocation across the CLIs: a hook that denies generic agent types or blocks unapproved models, or one that hands a seat's finished work to the other model family for critique. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP. It singles out the cross-family dispatch and the agent-type gate, and it notes that the critic script needs both coding CLIs authenticated locally. A hook, launcher or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers), and a reviewer-seat change is a standing rule that gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory). entries.title: speckit-agents: hooks block test edits, gate code on a spec verdict and audit each lane
entries.why: Team of eight specialized subagents (the pack names seven roles) for one coding CLI, governed by lifecycle hooks in one script (JavaScript on Node 22 or newer; repository size 16.3 MB in the pack's metadata read), covering the path from idea to pull request: a product owner that writes the spec, an architect that writes the plan and task list, a spec auditor that independently emits a pass or fail verdict, an implementer and a test writer working from stubs to failing tests to a passing implementation, a spec gatekeeper for final review, and a patcher as a fast track for up to 30 lines in 2 files. Per the pack, hooks rather than prompt instructions enforce phase separation: a pre-tool-use hook stops the implementer from modifying test files; another allows the test writer to touch only test files; a gate blocks implementation entirely until the spec auditor has emitted a pass verdict; a retry gate halts the implementer after 3 consecutive failing red rounds; and a subagent-stop hook inspects the agent's full git diff, catching out-of-lane writes made through the shell. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our engineering-manager loop is built on intent, spec and plan files, dual approval and a rule against test tampering, and prompt instructions alone regularly fail when an agent edits a test to make its implementation pass; per the pack, this solves that deterministically at the hook layer, where the implementer receives an error if it tries to edit a test path and the architect cannot write code, and the 3-failure retry ceiling and the mandatory pass verdict before code are exact mechanical implementations of our standing process locks. The pack cites the 2026-10-10 tamperproof Lab card, which blocks agent edits to existing test files, as our test-tamper rule; per the playbook that rule is the manual scan below, and per its own status note the tamperproof card was set aside in the 2026-10-13 triage as a hook install, noting that our claim-versus-record rule already covers the test-tamper scan. We already have: the artifact chain of intent, spec and plan committed before anything bigger than a one-line fix is implemented, with Haiyuan accepting intent and spec when a change is consequential and the implementer working from the accepted plan (#em-loop); a test-tamper scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer for skipped, deleted or focused tests, gutted assertions or a test command changed so it always passes, where a green run after such a change is SUSPECT, never a pass, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), part of completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); a failing test first for bug jobs, the EM holding the implementer until a repro is linked, a manual control (#coding-em-kicks; #controls-inventory); three fix rounds, then escalation to Haiyuan, and three failed correction rounds escalating the same way (#review-convergence; #retry-ceiling), a manual control (#controls-inventory); and the playbook's standing play of skills for advisory policy and hooks for must-hold rules, including no weakening tests during a fix (#em-loop), a recommendation on the page, not an installed control. So the spec and plan gates, the tamper scan, reproduce-before-fix and a round cap are ours already, as manual controls and policy text; those are nearby rules, not the same mechanisms: the playbook's cap counts review fix rounds and correction rounds, not an implementer's failing test rounds. A text search of the playbook for out-of-lane and test-writer finds no match, and per the pack what is not applied is any installed hook that denies test-file writes based on subagent role. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). entries.title: agent-escape-bench: tries to break each written rule through every tool path
entries.why: Pair of commands (Python 3.9 or newer, no dependencies) that measure what actually stands behind an agent's written rules, per its README. The verify command reads each forbidding rule in one coding CLI's standing-instruction file, the shared contract file and an editor's rules format (rules such as do not touch CI, do not edit applied migrations, do not read the local secrets file, no force-push) and tries to break it: through the edit, write and read tools and through several shell forms of the same action (an append redirect, a cd then a redirect, an in-place sed, an inline interpreter). Hooks are run for real exactly as the agent would invoke them; permission rules are modeled from that CLI's documentation; a code-owners file is reported as a merge gate, not a session gate. Each rule is graded CONCRETE (every probe stopped), PARTIAL, REVIEW (open in session, covered at merge) or OBEDIENCE (nothing stops a violation, so the rule rests on the model following text), with a control action per rule that must stay allowed. The bench command grades a shell guard against 164 commands: 123 escape techniques (direct writes, subshells, variables and eval, xargs and find, downloads, patches and archives, interpreters, git tricks, links and copies, outside-repo writes, secret exfiltration) plus 41 ordinary commands that must keep working, reporting escaped and false-block counts. Nothing from the corpus is executed: the bench only asks the hook what it would do, in a throwaway repository with a fake home. The author's reference results: no hook, 123/123 escaped; a typical hand-written case or grep guard, 98/123 escaped with 1/41 false blocks; a shell-parser guard, 0/123 and 0/41. Both commands can run as CI gates that exit 1 on regression (a maximum-escapes setting for the bench, a maximum-obedience setting for verify), and a third command statically maps which rules mention any mechanism at all, explicitly a heuristic map, not proof. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our standing rules live in the shared contract file and the never-again list and are enforced mostly by prompt discipline plus a few installed hooks, and we have no mechanical answer to which of these rules would actually stop an agent that tried. Per the pack, kept ctxlock (2026-11-07) checks whether rules load, kept lodeline (2026-11-08) scores whether configuration looks safe and kept Ruttla (2026-10-06) demands a broken probe per rule but does not generate one; this tool derives the probes from our own rule text, runs our own hooks and names the rules that rest on obedience alone, which per the pack are the rules most likely to be violated silently on a long autonomous run. Its escape corpus would also be, per the pack, a ready-made regression suite for any pre-tool-use guard we adopt (it names parallel-agents-safety and speckit-agents scope hooks). We already have: a controls inventory that pairs each contract rule with what enforces it, so a rule nothing enforces shows up, from a trial table pending review that counts 73 rules, 34 of them policy-only, statuses as of 2026-10-20 (#controls-inventory), the nearest thing to the OBEDIENCE grade, but built by reading and checking the enforcers it could reach, with a few rows recording planted probes that were run and with box-side enforcers marked unverified, not by trying to break each rule through every tool path; a new check run once against a deliberately broken input and seen to fail before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail), with the Ruttla card one of the rule's five Lab sources and its tool not installed, and since 2026-11-02 the same proof for any gate before it is trusted, on a planted broken copy, a healthy control and an empty input, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a fleet installer that wires the contract file and shared skills into each seat's home, and a one-time deadweight config audit, report-only, which per the playbook does not run hooks or prove runtime admission or effective settings (#skills), the nearest thing to the pack's point that a rule can load without holding; and a rule-phrase check that would report a must-hold rule no longer stated where agents read it, a trial in report-only shadow that is not built yet (#rule-phrase-check), which tests wording, not whether a rule holds. A text search of the playbook for obedience and bypass finds no match, and per the pack we lint and count rules but never probe whether a rule survives contact with the edit, write and read tools plus shell variants. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP; it describes the value as deriving probes from our own rule text, running our own hooks and naming the rules that are obedience-only, and the corpus as a regression suite for any guard we adopt. The pack's summary line for agent-escape-bench: verify each stated rule by trying to break it through every tool path. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named for adopting it; the project's own control actions, which must stay allowed, and its 41 ordinary commands belong to the tool, not to a rollout here. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running it against our own contract file and hooks, installing it in any seat, wiring its CI gates, adopting its corpus as a regression suite, adding or changing any hook, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: 0 stars and created the day of the pack; per the README the 164-case corpus comes from auditing one team's guard, which it names as its main limit; verify models permission rules from documentation rather than running the CLI and does not see the sandbox or permission modes; rules it cannot parse into a path or command are listed as not probed. The 123/123, 98/123 and 1/41 results are the author's, not ours, and per the pack its CONCRETE and OBEDIENCE grades on our own contract file and installed hooks are unconfirmed (not run; no installs).
