entries.title: session-watchdog: wakes only stuck sessions; a dead-man switch watches the watchdog
entries.why: Agent skill meant to run on a schedule (every 1 to 2 hours) that reads every other session from the outside and sorts each into DONE, WAITING-ON-USER, WAITING-ON-BACKGROUND, STOPPED-MID-TASK, ERROR or HUNG from two signals: the last result line and the last assistant text. It wakes only ERROR, stale WAITING-ON-BACKGROUND (45 minutes or more) and STOPPED-MID-TASK sessions (a result of success but a last text that promises a next step, idle 20 minutes or more), with a message that quotes the session's own pending step and tells it to reply 'nothing pending' rather than redo finished work. When unsure between DONE and STOPPED-MID-TASK it chooses DONE, because per the author a wrong wake costs money and can redo work while a missed one is caught next run. Hard limits are enforced in code before every wake (a can-wake command that exits 0 or 1): at most 1 wake per session per 3 hours, 2 per day and 5 per run, and never a DONE, WAITING-ON-USER, HUNG or archived session or one typed in within 5 minutes. A dead-man switch watches the watchdog: every run ends with a beat, and a prompt-submit hook surfaces one line in any session the user types in when the last beat is over 5 hours old. The design comes from a real failure the author reports: its first 6 scheduled runs died silently on a permission prompt while the app still marked them 'succeeded', so the skill requires an exact-letter allow list and demands that the first run be verified to end in done with a beat, not trusted from the scheduler's status. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our stale-log watchdog fires on about 540 s of quiet and resumes the pane and kept antiloop (2026-11-07) catches the loud stall, but neither can tell a finished idle session from one stopped mid-task, which per the pack is how a rate-limited or interrupted seat loses hours until someone asks whether it is stuck. Per the pack this supplies the missing classifier plus two transferable disciplines we do not mechanically enforce today: wake budgets checked in code before acting, and a heartbeat that makes a dead watchdog visible in the next session a human types in; it also reads the project's runs-marked-succeeded failure as a warning for any scheduled run of our coding CLIs whose done signal is the scheduler's status word. We already have: the rule that coding agents must not end a turn waiting on background CI or live jobs with a dirty tree, foregrounding to a durable exit or making a hermetic-first push followed by a live second pass (#coding), a manual control in the inventory with hand-written per-kick wrapper gates for a dirty tree or unchanged HEAD on push-required kicks only; these read the work tree and HEAD, not the session's last turn, and the engineering-manager re-kick is box-side and unverified (#controls-inventory); long runs in tmux with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s with resume of the same session, a manual convention with nothing blocking a bare launch (#launch, #controls-inventory); a stale run resumed only after the old agent is proven gone, enforced by the ownership guard (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); since 2026-11-01 a stop marker that keeps a run stopped on purpose from being resumed, a last-line reader that counts a stated background wait as alive for at most 30 minutes, and a hold with no stale handling when that wait's deadline cannot be read (#intentional-stop, #background-wait, #unreadable-deadline), so the watchdog is no longer purely a staleness timer, but none of these tells a finished session from a stopped one; a 15-minute heartbeat over live agent tasks from the engineering-manager bot (#em-loop), and on it a no-progress flag, a trial in report-only shadow that is logged only and never kills, resumes or re-prompts a run (#no-progress-flag); a pickup check that compares the coding kick ledger with tmux and pull requests and sends one re-wake for a stuck kick, paused since 2026-10-23, which looks at kicks, not sessions (#coding-em-kicks); an interrupted run resuming automatically since 2026-10-31, after state checks so that nothing runs twice (#auto-resume); default run limits of 2 retries and transient errors retried at most twice, policy in charters and skills, a wrapper enforcing them outside the agent loop being a Lab follow-up, not live, with rounds counted by hand (#run-limits, #retry-ceiling, #controls-inventory); and a claim that a scheduled job ran checked against outside receipt lines, never the job's own report, policy text only, the check script not installed or scheduled (#claim-vs-receipts). On the pack's watchdog-watcher point, a text search of the playbook for dead-man and for watcher finds no match, and the report-only freshness check that reads run logs is unscheduled (#report-only-checks). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP; it names three transferable pieces, the idle classifier, wake budgets checked in code before acting and a heartbeat that makes a dead watchdog visible, and says porting the classifier to our tmux and tee-logged seats needs an adapter that does not exist yet. The pack's summary line for session-watchdog: wake only the sessions stuck mid-task; a dead-man switch watches the watchdog. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Building the adapter; letting any classifier wake a session; installing the skill or its prompt-submit hook in any seat; adding a wake budget or a heartbeat to the launcher or watchdog; replacing or bypassing the stale-log watchdog, which the playbook says is not replaced fleet-wide without Haiyuan (#exception-first); or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, launcher or watchdog change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: 0 stars and created the day of the pack. It is built on one vendor desktop app's session tools (list sessions, list events, send message), so porting the classifier to our tmux and tee-logged seats needs an adapter that does not exist yet, and per the pack whether an equivalent last-turn signal can be read reliably from our logs for every seat is unconfirmed (no adapter exists; no probe was run against live panes). Its thresholds and limits are the author's design values, not ours. Per the pack the collector also read the skill file and its wake-log script besides the README. entries.title: apiary: file-based task claims with fencing tokens, leases and a hash-pinned check
entries.why: Coordination for coding agents sharing one repository, built from plain files and a written spec (a demo export of a larger repository). A task is a small text file and the folder is the status: pending, active or done. Claiming is one atomic rename, so of two simultaneous claims exactly one wins. Every claim gets a fencing token and a lease: only the current token can renew or close, and a crashed session's lease expires so that a resume call returns the task with the old token invalidated. Each task carries one acceptance command, and the close call runs it and refuses unless it exits 0. The claim records the SHA-256 of the task file, so rewriting the check after claiming makes close refuse. A guard hook for one coding CLI refuses direct edit, write and shell-redirect access to the ledger, task folders and decision log, forcing every state change through its tool-server calls (claim, renew, close, resume and others), each returning a status word (CLAIMED, DONE, REFUSED, CONFLICT). Every operation appends one line to an append-only ledger checkable against git. The spec names every requirement and a black-box conformance suite tests any implementation from the outside: the author reports the reference passing 49/49 and the textbook design it started from 8/49, and claims 673 unit tests. The author's own write-ups report that the original colony design cost 7.7× a plain session's tokens for the same score, redesigned to about 0.90M for parity ('the claim I was testing lost'), and that an earlier guard hole, another tool server able to write the ledger, failed 42 of 71 new guard tests before the fix brought it to 101/101 with 30/30 planted bugs caught. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our handoffs are vault files and git with ownership by convention: nothing stops two seats from taking the same kicked task, a dead session's claim has no lease to expire, and done is a self-report the receipt discipline then audits after the fact. Per the pack this project moves those three properties into mechanism (an exactly-once claim, a reclaimable lease and close only on a green check pinned at claim time), the mechanical form of our code-decides-done rule applied to the task lifecycle rather than to a single turn. Also per the pack, its split of spec and conformance suite means the requirements, under a share-alike documentation license and implementable under any license, could be a checklist for our own handoff tooling without vendoring its copyleft code, and the cost write-up is a measured caution against defaulting to multi-agent fan-out. We already have: a handoff packet on every manager-bot handoff and new coding kick (from, to, job type, the ask verbatim, objective, artifacts, decisions, constraints, open questions, next gate), checked only in shadow and never blocking, report-only in the inventory (#handoff-packet, #verbatim-ask, #controls-inventory); a coding kick ledger with rows moving from posted to launched to pr_open or done, or blocked with a note, read first by the engineering manager's heartbeat, and a hold rule, adopted 2026-10-31, under which a held row moves only on Haiyuan's answer or an explicit lift (#coding-em-kicks, #held-kicks); the ownership guard, enforced: each launch gets an attempt ID and a workspace, only the current attempt can publish and a stale attempt is refused, and a restart is refused unless the old process is proven dead (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), the closest thing to a fencing token here, though it fences one run's output, not the claiming of a task; and a concrete deterministic check as the only thing that makes a task done, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory), with a test-tamper scan of the diff as a prose rule and no hook installed (#claim-vs-record). Per the playbook the fail case has happened at run level: a 2026-10-15 overlap in which two seats held one pack path for about 3 minutes (#controls-inventory). A text search of the playbook finds the word lease only inside release, and per the pack our task claiming is by kick text and vault notes, with no lease expiry and no acceptance check pinned at claim time. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the requirements of its written spec as a checklist for our own handoff tooling, taking the spec and the pattern and not the code, because per the pack the code is a spec and pattern source, not code to vendor without a license decision. The pack names no trial or adoption step beyond that, and no implementation of any claim, lease or pinned check on our side. The pack's summary line for apiary: file-based multi-agent coordination: fencing tokens, leases, and a hash-pinned check that cannot be rewritten after claim. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named for adopting the checklist. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). entries.title: honest-done: a stop hook with no model calls judges only this turn's diff
entries.why: A prompt-submit and stop hook pair for one coding CLI with zero model calls (Python 3.8 or newer, standard library only). At prompt time it snapshots the working tree into a temporary git index (the real index is never touched; untracked files are included and ignore rules respected). At stop time it diffs old to new, this turn only, so pre-existing TODOs and the user's own uncommitted work are never judged, reads the transcript for commands run, exit codes and files touched, and applies six deterministic checks: unfinished code (TODO or FIXME, empty bodies, not-implemented errors, placeholders claiming the rest of the code is unchanged); unverified claims (the final message claims tests or a build pass but no matching command ran this turn or the last one exited non-zero, while hedges such as 'should pass' never fire); silent shortcuts (a test file deleted, skip, xfail or only markers added, assertions removed, blanket type-ignore comments or a bare except that passes); skipped context (a path named in the prompt that exists but was never read, searched or edited this turn); partial task list (a numbered or bulleted prompt item whose specific names appear nowhere in this turn's tool use); and leftover debug calls in non-test source. On a finding it blocks with one short specific sentence, never repeats a reason already given this turn (an intentional-stub reply passes the next stop), blocks at most a configured maximum, and is fail-open on any crash or non-git folder. A command-line mode runs the same checks by hand or in CI (exit 1 on findings). The author's bench: 34 author-written cases (18 incomplete caught 18/18, 16 false-positive temptations allowed 16/16; median about 625 ms per stop on another desktop operating system) plus a real-history replay of 213 commits across five open-source libraries flagging 2 (1%), both genuine test removals. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the done-gate lane is dense, and this still earns its slot on two deltas no card in it has. First, turn scoping: kept doneguard (2026-10-30) gates on whether checks pass and kept claimtrace (2026-11-07) audits a finished report, but per the pack neither isolates this turn's diff, so both must either judge pre-existing mess or trust the agent's framing; the temporary-index snapshot makes added-in-this-turn exact. Second, coverage of the brief itself: per the pack the skipped-context and partial-task-list checks catch the failure our kicks actually suffer, a multi-clause task where clause 3 is silently dropped and the named file never opened, which test-based gates cannot see. Per the pack its published 1% real-history flag rate, with every early false positive turned into a bench case, is also the false-positive accounting our receipt cards mostly lack, kept success-claim-receipts (2026-10-31) admitting its miss rate is unmeasured. We already have: done as a deterministic check passing, with self-reports advisory only, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory); a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it, and a test-tamper scan of the diff by the engineering manager and each reviewer for skipped, deleted or focused tests, gutted assertions or a test command changed to always pass, where a green run after such a change is SUSPECT, a prose rule with no hook installed, an enforcing stop hook being a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); done receipts that list what was verified and what was not and a review verdict line pinned to the head commit, both manual (#done-receipt, #review-verdict-line, #controls-inventory), which is the pack's prompt-text point; restating the ask before a non-trivial task, policy text only, and the ask travelling verbatim in the handoff packet (#intake-restatement, #verbatim-ask), the nearest rules to covering the brief itself; and blind reviewers searching for missing cases against rejection criteria named before reading the diff, a manual control (#disproof-review, #controls-inventory). A text search of the playbook for partial task list, skipped context and temporary git index finds no match, and per the pack no hook diffs the turn or checks the brief's items off mechanically. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP. The playbook's stated route for a stop hook that enforces the claim-versus-record rule is a separately drafted, blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record), and a trial of this hook would fall under it. The pack's summary line for honest-done: a zero-token Stop hook that judges only this turn's diff and blocks "All done!" with one specific sentence. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named for adopting it; the project's own bench of 34 cases belongs to the tool, not to a rollout here. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing the hook pair in any seat, letting any stop hook block a turn, running its check mode as a gate, writing an adapter for another seat, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: 0 stars and created the day of the pack; the 34-case bench is author-written, and the README says plainly that 18/18 proves the checks do what they claim, not that they catch everything; timing was measured on another desktop operating system; it supports one coding CLI only, and an adapter for another seat would need the equivalent transcript and snapshot wiring; pattern-based checks can be evaded by unusual phrasing; it is fail-open by design on any crash or non-git folder. Per the pack the 2-in-213 flag rate replays human commits as pseudo-turns (diff checks only, no transcript), so the false-block rate on real autonomous turns with transcripts is unconfirmed and the author-written bench cannot establish it; these figures are the author's, not ours. entries.title: AssertLedger: runs one regression test against fixed code, a known fault and a control
entries.why: Verifier for a single question: does this regression test actually detect the bug it claims to prevent? The operator supplies three worlds, fixed code, a known fault and a neutral control, and it runs the identical candidate test bytes in all three, plus an unchanged base test and repeated attempts for attribution. A test that passes everywhere, for example a type check against an inverted implementation, is verdicted WEAK_ORACLE for that fault; a test that passes on fixed and control but assertion-fails on the fault is eligible for selection. Campaign verdicts are VERIFIED, REJECTED, INCONCLUSIVE or ENGINE_ERROR, and a timeout, crash or collection failure never counts as detection. The output is a replayable evidence manifest (observations, digests, execution limits), and a replay command re-checks integrity and decision consistency without re-running tests or calling a model. A git workflow qualifies a committed regression test directly from history: a buggy commit, a fix commit and a neutral control with a stated reason. Setup is conflict-checked and dry-run first, with partial failures reported under their own exit code and an explicit unresolved-file list. TypeScript on Node 22.15 or newer, version 2.1.0 with a CLI, an SDK and a tool-server interface, and adapters for two test runners; repository size 2,434 KB and 58 open issues in the pack's metadata read. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our locks already demand reproduce-before-fix and a replay-regression check before promoting changes, and the 2026-11-08 pack's claim-audit finding (93% accuracy for test-pass claims against chance-level holistic report truth) is, per the pack, the claim this strengthens: a green test the agent wrote alongside its fix proves little if the test would also pass on the buggy code. Running the candidate against the pre-fix commit turns 'tests pass' into 'this test discriminates bug from fix', with an evidence file a blind reviewer can replay instead of re-running. Per the pack it complements honest-done, in this same batch, rather than duplicating it: that hook catches deleted or weakened tests at stop time, and this tool catches a present, passing but semantically weak test at review time. We already have: reproduce before fix on bug jobs, where a repro artifact is linked before the implementer starts and its first commit is the failing test, a manual control held by the engineering manager, box-side and unverified in the inventory (#coding-em-kicks, #controls-inventory); a new check, a test written for a fix among the examples, run once against a deliberately broken input such as the old code, a mutant or a planted bad line and seen to fail before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail), and the same proof for gates since 2026-11-02, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy), so the pack's statement that nothing re-runs a new test against the buggy base holds for tooling, not for policy: the rule exists, and no tool runs it; the test-tamper scan of the diff, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); on analytics SDK pull requests, catch tests written to fail if a named risk were present, run on each pull request head in parallel with the reviewers, adopted as policy text with nothing enforcing them yet (#catch-tests); report-only mutation testing on one SDK repository, never a merge gate (#mutation-testing), a different question from whether one new test discriminates; and a replay regression check before promoting a skill, prompt or gate, whose replay set is not built, proposed in the inventory (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory), and which replays saved agent runs, not test runs. A text search of the playbook for neutral control, known fault and replayable finds no match. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP; it suggests that running the candidate against the pre-fix commit would turn a green test into evidence that the test discriminates bug from fix, in a file a blind reviewer can replay. The pack's summary line for AssertLedger: prove a regression test would catch its bug: same test vs fixed code, known fault, and neutral control. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named for adopting it; the neutral control in its three worlds belongs to each campaign, not to a trial here. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it in any repository or seat, running its unsandboxed execution backend on anything but a trusted checkout, requiring a discriminating test before a bug job closes, putting its evidence file in the review packet, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: 2 stars and 58 open issues, which the pack counted but did not triage; its execution backend is explicitly unsandboxed and for trusted checkouts only; the first git workflow is narrow (a committed JavaScript test-runner candidate, no declared runtime dependencies, the same file paths across revisions apart from the candidate), and per the pack whether the three-world check scales to dependency-bearing or multi-file regressions is unconfirmed; the operator must supply a meaningful fault and neutral control, and the tool does not invent them; replay verifies integrity and consistency, not the honesty of whoever produced the observations. Its numbers and claims are the author's, not ours. MIT, 2 stars, created 2026-09-07 17:40 PT, pushed 2026-11-09 09:30 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Say who owns the code: an ownership sentence can change what a newer coding model edits
entries.why: Prompting guidance from a documentation page for a newer coding model, quoted in the pack and not run here: say whether the coding model owns the codebase it is changing. Per the source, the newer model 'responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on.' When a prompt 'said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else's, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. It also tended to report nearby problems instead of fixing them.' 'When the prompt says the code base is the model's own, the model often merges repeated code and makes related fixes without being asked.' To have the model improve the structure as it works, the source says to state that the code is its own, with this sentence: 'This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it.' In the author's testing on small coding tasks (the author's numbers, not ours), the model 'merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it.' 'The rate varied by task.' 'The result held when the sentence stood inside a long system prompt.' 'The requested feature worked in nearly every try either way.' In the same testing, again the author's numbers, 'the model also used about 1.5 times the output tokens with the sentence and made several changes that nobody had asked for, many of them new tests and documentation.' 'Apart from bug fixes, it changed how an existing feature behaves in one try in six to ten, and more often at higher effort.' 'Its closing summary named the larger changes but often left out small ones, so review the diff and not only the summary.' 'Leave the ownership sentence out where the user owns the code and wants it changed as little as possible.' 'A rule elsewhere in the prompt that limits scope doesn't cancel the ownership sentence': with 'No drive-by refactors, renames or cleanups' earlier in the same prompt, 'the model still merged repeated code in about a third of the tries.' Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our implementer prompts already separate the writer from the reviewer (the writer implements, the reviewer does not), but they do not say the codebase is the implementing model's own, and they do not say to leave that sentence out when the user wants the smallest possible change. We already have: an implementer that is never a reviewer of the same change, with each blind reviewer seeing only the pull request plus intent, spec and plan, never the other review (#reviewer-rule, #em-loop), part of blind review, a manual control (#controls-inventory); per the pack that split is a different idea, who may write against who may review, and not a sentence telling the writer the codebase is its own. An implementer that works from the accepted plan, which names the files to touch and the done definition, with the launch prompt pointing at that plan, intent written by research or product and not by the implementer inventing scope mid-build, and reviewers checking the pull request against the plan (#em-loop), through the same manual control. Before a non-trivial task, a restatement of the ask compared with the intent and, since 2026-10-31, with the ask carried verbatim in the handoff packet, policy text only (#intake-restatement, #verbatim-ask). Reviewers who read the diff and try to disprove the change, with the approving round also reading the complete resulting artifact, not only the diff (#disproof-review, #review-convergence), a manual control (#controls-inventory), so a reviewer reads more than a summary. A done receipt that reports what the harness can prove happened, not what the model claims, within completion validation, a manual control (#done-receipt, #controls-inventory). Maximum-effort defaults per seat, enforced with stated limits in the inventory (#controls-inventory), which matters here because the source reports behavior changes more often at higher effort, our reading and not the pack's. A replay regression check before promoting a skill or prompt change, which a prompt change like this would fall under, whose replay set is not built, proposed in the inventory (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory). A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for codebase is yours, owns the code and say who owns finds no match. Per the pack (checked 2026-11-09 ~22:10 PT), the shared contract file and the skill for implementing and then reviewing carry the role split but no ownership sentence, and the implementer's standing instructions and the handoff and rule contracts carry no ownership sentence. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the ownership sentence quoted above, in implementer prompts, if Haiyuan decides to add it; the pack names no adoption step, rollout or trial. The pack's verdict: documentation only / never run, not adopted unless the live playbook already contains this same idea, proposal only, and any prompt change needs Haiyuan; the text search above shows no sign of that idea in the playbook. The pack's summary line for Say who owns the code: prompting guidance: say whether the coding model owns the codebase it is changing. The pack's stop/kill condition: no criterion is supplied, because the source supplies no stop or kill condition; its negative control is to leave the sentence out where the user owns the code and wants it changed as little as possible. Whether to add the ownership sentence to implementer prompts, and in which repositories, is a separate Haiyuan decision; it would never go into reviewer prompts. Caveats: the test rates, the token ratio and the one-in-six-to-ten figure are the author's, from small coding tasks, and are not ours; the pack gives no sample sizes or task list, and the rate varied by task; the guide's figures are for its own model, which is not the model our default implementer seat runs (#roster), so whether they carry over to our seats is unconfirmed; the pack's checks of our prompts are collection-time readings from 2026-11-09 ~22:10 PT, not a fresh check; not a repository, so no license stated in the fetched text, no stars and no created or pushed dates; fetched 2026-11-09 ~22:00 PT; documentation only, never run. entries.title: Which model should you build with? Verify, raise effort, then move up
entries.why: Which model should you build with? A documentation guide by Addy Osmani on choosing a model and effort level: start most work on the default coding model at medium. The author's numbers, not ours: on FrontierCode 2.0, the next model up at high scored about level with the default coding model at max (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task. Before pushing the default coding model past high on a hard task, test the next model up at high. On SWE-bench Pro, the default coding model at medium scored about 2.5 points lower for about 70% of the cost of high; at low it scored about 8 points lower for about a third of the cost; at xhigh it scored about 1.4 points higher for 2.5 times the cost of high. Higher effort helps longer thinking, more tool calls and self-checking but adds latency; it cannot supply knowledge or skill the model lacks. When a model falls short, first give it self-verification with a test, build or endpoint-checking script, then raise effort one level, then move to the next model up at a lower effort than used on the smaller model. If outcomes are automatically checkable, run low and re-run only failures at high: on a SWE-bench Pro subset, the author reports about 97% passed for about $0.17 each, against 95.3% for $0.29 with every task at high. Keep small helper models on file search, log reading and summaries where a mistake is cheap to spot; keep code edits and judgment calls on the main model. The built-in explore helper runs on the session model, capped at the default coding model on the direct API; define a custom explore helper on a small model to reduce exploration cost. On that provider, the small-model helper alias resolves to the new small model and needs coding CLI 2.1.293 or later; on the other providers listed in the source, the same alias still resolves to the previous small model. Keep the main context lean for decisions, especially on bigger models. Switch only at a natural break: compact first or start a fresh session with a short written plan; the first turn on a new model pays the cache-write price on the whole conversation. A move down a tier loses earlier thinking; other moves can lose it too. Measure candidates on our own tasks with an outcome check per task, two or three effort levels per candidate, each in its own session; plot score against spend, retain multiple models only if they beat every single-model point, then run the winner in shadow before cutover. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, long coding runs are pinned at maximum effort, the opposite policy to starting at medium and escalating only as needed. The default coding seat hit a seven-day usage limit at 23:14 PT 2026-11-09, resetting at 14:00 PT 2026-11-10; the pack therefore recommends spending less budget per finished task. Per the pack's collection-time checks, there is no user-level helper-agent directory and no installed small-model explore or log-reader helper. We already have: maximum-effort defaults per seat, enforced with stated limits in the inventory (#controls-inventory); the daily updater checks and restores model and effort but is box-side and unverified, and the patch-based seat requires the patch to be passed on launch. The model-default backup check is report-only, unscheduled and never edits settings or blocks a launch (#report-only-checks, #controls-inventory). Completion validation, meaning deterministic checks rather than self-report, is manual (#code-decides-done, #done-receipt, #controls-inventory); the requirement that a new check be seen failing on deliberately broken input is policy text only (#check-can-fail). Promotion needs three clean runs, tested rollback and complete receipts, a manual control (#three-run-proof, #promotion-gate, #controls-inventory). Replay before skill or prompt promotion is proposed, with the replay set not built (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory). Searches of the staged playbook's raw page and visible text find no start-at-medium escalation ladder, low-then-rerun-failures pattern or natural-break model-switch rule; the maximum-effort pin is the opposite policy, not adoption of this idea. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): self-verify, raise effort one level, then move up a model at lower effort; medium for drafts and high for fix rounds on the default coding model; try the next model up at high before going past high on a hard task; low with only failures re-run at high on auto-checked lanes; read-only small-model explore and log-reader helpers; switch only at a natural break. Measure on our own tasks, then shadow before cutover. The pack's summary line for Which model should you build with?: a 2026-11-09 guide on picking a model and an effort level, and on how to raise them when a run falls short. The pack's stop/kill condition: no criterion is supplied, because the source supplies no stop or kill condition. Negative controls: do not raise effort or switch models until self-verification is in place; do not switch mid-turn; do not put code edits on a small helper. Changing the live maximum-effort pin under the 2026-09-24 lock, installing the proposed small-model helpers, and permitting low-then-rerun-failures on auto-checked lanes each need a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the benchmark rates, point gaps and dollar figures are the author's, not ours; documentation only / never run, with no eval rerun here. The pack attributes figures to the author's FrontierCode 2.0, Terminal-Bench 3.0 and SWE-bench Pro runs; transfer to our seats is unconfirmed. The guide's default effort is not our live policy. Harness and helper absence statements are collection-time checks from 2026-11-10 ~01:33 PT against the staged snapshot, not a fresh live audit. The source gives no numeric stop threshold; not a repository, so no license stated in the fetched text, no stars and no created or pushed dates; fetched 2026-11-10 ~01:28 PT; documentation only, never run. entries.title: Safely scaling multi-agent teams: claim work, split tasks, bound seats
entries.why: Safely scaling multi-agent teams: a documentation guide by Barry Zhang, Tianyi Peng, Elle Najt, Keller Scholl and Lance Martin. The authors' toy experiment, not our result: 1,000 agents on an early version of the stronger coding model reproduced a formal proof of Fermat's Last Theorem with general tools, a shared transactional database and layered safety controls, without the earlier domain-platform scaffolding or researcher steering. The authors report 28.7 hours, one-third as many output tokens and a proof one-seventh the length of the September formalization; that earlier run used a researcher and dozens of agents for 11 days, roughly 6 billion output tokens and 13 million lines in the proof language. Inputs were 60 statements (the final theorem and 59 intermediate milestones), a one-sentence sketch of the classical route, their definitions and 47 already-proved lemmas; no other guidance on proofs or team organization was supplied. One lead and 999 helpers coordinated through a transactional store. In the first 10 minutes the lead built five tables: announce for team orders, assign for ownership, notes for an open board, subtasks where any agent (lead or helper) could add a task and the first helper to claim it owned it, and landed for finished work. By the third hour, idle helpers pulled the next item without waiting for the lead. Pieces too big for one helper became task trees: the hardest remaining statement grew to 2,418 tasks up to 10 levels deep, was proved at hour 28.4, and the final theorem at 28.7. The authors count 54 of 60 statements finished, with five alternatives no longer needed and one dropped. Helpers had judged 47 of the 60 statements infeasible within the budget, yet the team proved most of them. The lead encouraged continued work; the harness sent the lead 19 automatic time-remaining reminders. A single shared machine hit its limits at about 100 agents: more than half of the 100-agent runs stopped or restarted because memory, disk or CPU ran out. The 1,000-agent run instead gave each agent its own sandbox on a lightweight virtual machine. Each sandbox had no network; its only link out was a pipe to a gateway. Agents could push only to their own branch and open merge requests; a separate job merged changes into main, refusing them only for a conflict or a fault. The gateway stamped identity outside the sandbox to prevent impersonation. A fail-closed classifier checked every shell command and file edit before execution. In this particular run, only a block on the lead would have ended the run; a helper block removed only that helper. A stricter design described in the guide stops the whole team for human review after any block; do not conflate it with this run. An offline monitor reviewed all actions, and the tools prevented agents from reading or changing their own agent loop. Across more than a million tool calls, none met the authors' blocking bar in this run; this does not establish safety for our seats or replace domain-specific harnesses. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the workstation has session hangs; the authors' roughly 100-agent single-machine limit is a reason to propose a measured cap on concurrent seats, not a safe local count or a target to reach. We already have: file-based human decision state in the decision queue (#decision-queue, #decision-queue-kill-receipts), done receipts (#done-receipt), launch/attempt IDs and an ownership guard with the watchdog (#watchdog-resume-safety, #launch). Map announce to lead instructions and human decisions in the queue, assign to lane resume notes tied to owner and attempt ID, notes to lane resume notes, subtasks to a lane-local claimable worklist, and landed to a finished-work log linked to receipts and attempt IDs. The queue remains for irreversible decisions and genuine judgment calls; reversible tasks do not enter it. Lane resume notes are a local pattern, not a playbook-enforced table, and these file surfaces are not a transactional store. The existing max-throughput rule says an idle seat pulls the next item (#max-throughput); that adopted component is not adoption of the guide's coordination-and-safety system. Run limits and session isolation are nearby controls (#run-limits, #launch), not a concurrency cap derived from this finding. The no-progress flag is report-only shadow, logged and never sent, and never kills, resumes or re-prompts a run (#no-progress-flag); it is not a time-remaining keep-going nudge. Own-branch pull requests and Haiyuan-only merge are the nearest integration controls (#reviewer-rule); we have no automatic merge job, and merging still needs Haiyuan's ask or explicit approval. Safety gaps: the ownership guard, attempt IDs and watchdog prevent stale workers from sharing a worktree (#watchdog-resume-safety), but they are not a fail-closed classifier on every tool call, an externally identity-stamping gateway or a lead-block team-stop rule. The staged controls do not supply a no-network sandbox per agent, gateway-stamped identity, a fail-closed pre-tool-call classifier that can stop the team, an offline monitor of all actions, or a guarantee that agents cannot read or modify their own loop. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): map the five tables onto the existing queue, lane resume notes, receipts and attempt IDs without installing a database; any agent (lead or helper) can add a task to the worklist; claim-before-work so the first helper to claim it owns the item and a second worker does not duplicate it; keep a landed log linked to deterministic receipts; let idle helpers pull the next eligible unclaimed item under #max-throughput while preserving holds, reviewer blindness and ownership. Split oversized pieces into task trees with parent/child dependencies and checked completion. Do not park on a self-judged infeasible verdict without one attempt within authority and budget; safety stops, held work and unknown outcomes still take precedence. Keep lead-side time-remaining nudges within the approved budget; this does not authorize extending runs or altering the report-only no-progress flag. Propose a measured concurrent-seat cap for the workstation and shared session server, with the value and rollout needing Haiyuan; the author's 100 is not our safe cap and no removed disk floor is restored. Keep the safety-gap list explicit against our ownership guard, watchdog, own-branch pull requests and owner-only merge; no equivalent safety stack is claimed or installed. The pack's summary line for Safely scaling multi-agent teams: a 2026-11-09 write-up of a toy experiment: 1,000 agents on an early version of the stronger coding model reproduced a formal proof of Fermat's Last Theorem with general tools, a shared database, and layered safety controls, without the earlier domain platform or a researcher directing the work. The team took 28.7 hours, used one-third as many output tokens, and wrote a proof one-seventh the length of the original. The pack's stop/kill condition: no criterion is supplied as a numeric threshold; the source's monitor-block behavior is described above, not a rollout threshold for our harness. Negative controls: do not start a second worker on claimed work, do not park on an infeasible verdict with no attempt, and do not call nearby controls adoption of this safety stack. Coordination changes, time nudges, a concurrent-seat cap and any safety implementation each need a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: toy experiment; the authors' figures are not ours; documentation only / never run, with no eval rerun or safety-stack test here; transfer to our seats is unconfirmed. Existing controls and gaps describe the staged snapshot, not a fresh live audit; not a repository, so no license stated in the fetched text, no stars and no created or pushed dates; fetched 2026-11-10 ~02:09 PT; documentation only, never run. Known limit, NOT VERIFIED / open risk, deferred to a later round: proposed/install-haiku-agents.sh never parses its arguments (:7/:64), so --dry-run/--help still back up and replace, which conflicts with checks/playbook.txt:549-554. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: evalid: seals a test run by content hash, re-runs it clean, logs claim against evidence
entries.why: Runtime verification layer for coding agents (JavaScript; version 0.3.1 of 2026-11-04, renamed from OpenFlow; repository size 14.4 MB and 5 open issues in the pack's metadata read). When tests run, the whole tree is hashed and sealed together with the command, exit code and output. Verification copies the sealed snapshot to a clean directory and actually re-runs it, comparing exit codes and failure classes, and in the green phase test files must hash-match the seal, so if the agent edited the tests after the run, the seal breaks. Its pipeline is zero-judge: spec clarification, code review and test verification are plain deterministic code, with no model judge anywhere in the chain and zero tokens spent on checking, and every stage leaves an artifact. Every delivery carries one record: what was claimed, what the replay showed and what each phase cost in time and tokens; when the phase ledger disagrees with wall-clock time by more than 5%, the record flags itself as untrustworthy. Its command line runs the same workflows from several coding CLIs or a plain terminal, and a hosted CI action verifies the seal on every pull request and upserts the claim-against-evidence ledger as a pull-request comment. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this is the closest thing to our code-decides-done rule and replay regression check, but with the evidence made the product: the seal is a hash of the tree, the replay is a real re-run and the claim is a separate record, a deterministic, zero-token gate and the opposite of a model judge. Per the pack, the author's 22/25 and 0/11 are the honest version of a gate that catches the failure and does not punish the honest, and the project maps to our engineering-manager loop artifacts, the replay check and the done gate. The pack also calls a test edited after the run the exact failure mode we have seen in our own done receipts; it cites no receipt, and the playbook's rule on test tampering records that no tamper incident is traced in our records yet (#claim-vs-record), so that reading stays the pack's. We already have: done as a concrete deterministic check passing, with self-reports advisory only, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory); a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it, and a test-tamper scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer for skipped, deleted or focused tests, gutted assertions or a test command changed so it always passes, where a green run after such a change is SUSPECT, never a pass, a prose rule with no hook installed, an enforcing stop hook being a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory); done receipts whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that actually ran, each with its evidence, and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted, manual (#done-receipt, #controls-inventory); a new check run once against a deliberately broken input and seen to fail, and a check that examined nothing reported as a gap, never a pass, policy text only (#check-can-fail); and a replay regression check before promoting a skill, prompt or gate, which replays saved agent runs rather than a sealed test run, whose replay set is not built, proposed in the inventory (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory). So deterministic done, the tamper scan and a receipt that separates verified from not verified are ours already, as manual controls and policy text. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for content hash, clean snapshot, claim-vs-evidence and zero-judge finds no match; the word sealed appears once, for a scoring check in the harness evaluation design, a proposal not run (#harness-eval); and per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP; it singles out the seal, the real re-run and the separate claim record. The pack's summary line for evalid: "claimed ≠ verified": seal the run, replay it from a clean snapshot, and make the claim-vs-evidence gap the deliverable. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named for adopting it; the project's own seal break on an edited test and its 36-episode benchmark belong to the tool, not to a rollout here. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a test file edited after the run, which must break the seal, would be such a copy, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it in any seat or repository, wiring its CI action or pull-request comment, letting a seal or replay result count toward done or block a merge, using it as the replay step before a promotion, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the seal is a content hash, not a cryptographic signature, so a fully self-consistent forged snapshot could still pass, which the README says openly; it is built to catch misreporting and test tampering, not to defeat a determined forger. Plausible-but-wrong expected values are still open; per the pack, the I6d assertion-execution gate closed the callback class. The 36-episode benchmark (22/25 faulty episodes caught, 0/11 honest ones wrongly rejected), the 3 of 12 runs that hit the 20-minute cap while still running and the 0.2.1 SWE-bench run of 4/6 against a 3/6 plain-agent baseline, n=1, with caveats, are the author's, not ours. Per the pack, the test-edit detector was not exercised on our own repositories, and whether the seal survives a real worktree, stash and checkout sequence is unconfirmed. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. Harness statuses above are read from the staged playbook, whose inventory is dated 2026-10-20, not from a live audit. The pack gives the created date without a time, so it stays as given; the pushed time is converted to PT. entries.title: agent-covenant: no verdict file means not done, and a CI gate rejects a stale verdict
entries.why: Collaboration verification protocol (Python; repository size 3.0 MB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) under which no deliverable is done until an independent reviewer has produced a machine-checkable verdict that passes a gate. It is two standard-library tools, a gate script and a lint for card schema and naming. Task cards are namespace-prefixed and carry Context, Deliverables, Owned files and Acceptance. An artifact map declares every file the reviewer is judging, and a change outside the map raises an UNMAPPED_CLAIM_SURFACE warning. The gate's freshness rule rejects a verdict that predates the code. The reviewer writes a review note and a verdict file and must not touch the files under review. The gate exits 0 on a pass, 1 on a fail and 2 on a usage error. The README says 'signed off by four independent review rounds' and includes a FAIL round. Per its README it is not an orchestrator, a swarm library, a model router, a memory store or a vector database, and it is not bound to one vendor's plugin API: it is a file-schema spec plus a CI-runnable gate. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this is the closest thing to our blind dual review as a file: the reviewer is a separate role, the verdict is a file, the artifact map is the freshness check and the gate is what decides, with 'no verdict' meaning 'not done' as our verdict line on the head SHA made machine-checkable. Per the pack, the namespace is a real anti-hijack measure, since a bare task file name can be claimed by another agent, and the project maps to our chief-of-staff rooms, written handoffs, engineering-manager loop and review gate. We already have: a blind reviewer that starts only once a PR exists and sees only the PR plus intent, spec and plan, never the other review, with an implementer never reviewing its own work and two blind seats on docs, drafts, Lab cards, full-team tests and code (#reviewer-rule, #em-loop), part of blind review, a manual control (#controls-inventory); rejection criteria named before reading the diff, with a FAIL returning evidence (#disproof-review), manual too (#controls-inventory); every review ending with one machine-readable verdict line on the head SHA, where a review with no parseable line, or a line naming an older SHA, is UNPARSED and never counts as an approval, and dual approval means two approving lines on the current head (#review-verdict-line), applied in the EM's review steps, a manual control (#controls-inventory); a plan file whose claim map and files to touch the reviewers check the PR against, through the same manual review (#em-loop, #controls-inventory), the nearest thing to an artifact map; a handoff packet on every manager-bot handoff and new coding kick, checked only in shadow and never blocking, report-only in the inventory (#handoff-packet, #controls-inventory), with kicks tracked on a ledger that has no inventory row of its own (#coding-em-kicks), the nearest thing to its task cards; and the ownership guard, enforced: each launch gets an attempt ID and a workspace and only the current attempt can publish (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), which fences one run's output, not who may claim a task. So a separate reviewer, no approval without a parseable verdict, a stale verdict never counting and the files under review named in a plan are ours already, as manual controls; per the playbook an approval means agent-complete and not shipped, and done itself is decided by a deterministic check (#em-loop, #code-decides-done), so the pack's equation of no verdict with not done is close but not the same rule here. The Lab already holds four nearby cards: Covenant (2026-11-01), a different repository and a different mechanism, compiled rules judged on the finished change at its base commit; agent-role-contracts (2026-10-19), an offline preflight that rejects self-review and a task changed after review; regista (2026-11-02), a commit hook that needs a verdict fingerprinted to the exact diff; and signoff-cli (2026-11-07), exit-code gates with a verdict bound to the commit tree. The delta here is therefore narrow: a file schema for the verdict and the task card, an artifact map and a CI-runnable freshness gate. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for verdict file, artifact map, task card and machine-checkable finds no match, and per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP; it calls the project a spec, not a product, and honest about what it is not. The pack's summary line for agent-covenant: a file-schema spec + CI gate: "no verdict" means "not done". The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named for adopting it; the project's own FAIL round and freshness rejection belong to the tool, not to a rollout here. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a verdict file older than the code, which the gate must reject, would be such a copy, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running its tools in any repository or the vault, adopting its card or verdict-file schema, letting a script read a verdict in place of the EM, requiring namespaced task ids, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). A change to the reviewer rules is a standing rule that gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory). Caveats: it is a file-schema spec plus a CI-runnable gate, not a product we installed; the 546 tests and the README's claim of four independent review rounds are the author's, not ours. Per the pack the artifact map is the freshness check, and the pack does not say how the gate dates a verdict against the code; a change outside the map is a warning in the pack's description, not a failure. Per the pack, whether the namespace and freshness model works on a multi-agent vault with a shared contract file is unconfirmed. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: Tego: a Linux-only contract held outside the agent, with a human pause and a hash chain
entries.why: Runs any AI agent that is a Linux process under a short YAML contract listing the files, programs and hosts it may use (Go; version 0.1.0; repository size 21.2 MB and 2 open issues in the pack's metadata read). The Linux kernel and its supervisor enforce the contract from outside the agent: it refuses what the contract rules out, can pause a file open or a connection until a person answers, and keeps a hash-chained record of each run. Commands start a contract from presets, print its rule table and propose one from a finished run; others read the record, verify it and report drift; and others pause, resume, stop or block a running run. Run limits cover tokens, cost, time, stall and repeats, with exit 124. A watch mode runs any command as a black box, and a local dashboard is served on request. Per the pack there is no telemetry, update check or crash report. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this is the strongest rules-outside-the-agent formulation of the window, since the agent cannot talk its way past a kernel rule, and the project maps to our routines and Mac seat health, on sandboxing. Per the pack, its known-limits section is unusually honest, and for our Mac fleet the fit is the blocker: it is Linux-only and a Linux virtual machine is a real cost, so the mechanism is worth keeping even if the install is not. We already have: run limits of 50 items, 2 retries, $0 spend and 0 external actions, with abnormal volume meaning stop and escalate, policy in charters and skills, a wrapper enforcing them outside the agent loop being a Lab follow-up, not live, with rounds counted by hand, a manual control (#run-limits, #retry-ceiling, #controls-inventory); reversibility lanes that send RED actions such as send, spend, merge, deleting non-junk and permissions to Haiyuan, a manual control (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory); text found in pages, posts, pull requests or tool output treated as data, never instructions, policy text only, a manual control in the inventory (#untrusted-content, #controls-inventory); the ownership guard, enforced: each launch gets an attempt ID and a workspace, only the current attempt can publish, and a restart is refused unless the old process is proven dead (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), and an installed stop marker that keeps a run stopped on purpose from being resumed (#intentional-stop), which govern a run's output and restarts, not the files, programs or hosts it may reach; long runs in tmux with streaming logs and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s, a manual convention with nothing blocking a bare launch (#launch, #controls-inventory); and one sandbox limit the playbook records, under which two collector seats can write only under their own workspace (#field-brief-12h), with no inventory row of its own, beside its statement that a shared box is not isolation (playbook §16). A per-tool hook, distinct from our decision layer's router, was retired permanently by Haiyuan on 2026-10-25 and is not to be reinstalled unless Haiyuan asks (playbook §13). So reversibility lanes, run limits as policy and one enforced ownership guard are ours already. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for kernel-enforced, hash-chained, tamper-evident, Linux and virtual machine finds no match; the word kernel appears only where the update busy check reads process paths (#cli-update-busy-check); and per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP; it says the mechanism is worth keeping even if the install is not. The pack's summary line for Tego: keep the rules outside the agent: kernel-enforced, hash-chained, with a pause for the human. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it on any machine, standing up a Linux virtual machine on the Mac for any seat, running a seat under a contract, letting it hold a seat's file open or connection for a person's answer, turning on its dashboard or relay, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it is Linux only, so on this Mac it would need a Linux virtual machine. Its known limits are the README's own: not every rule is the kernel's at every tier; tier 1 is user space and best effort, and a racing thread can change what the kernel then acts on; reads are not recorded by default at tier 1; the record is tamper-evident against an agent held by a contract, not against the person who started the run; it does not stop what an allowed program does inside its own memory or data leaving through a destination you allowed; it is not a sandbox that hides the machine and limits only what the contract names; and its tool-server relay is a preview. Per the pack, whether the hash-chained record is stable across a real tmux and launcher run is unconfirmed. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: harness-engineering-kit: a deletable scaffold with a self-test that proves gates go red
entries.why: Project scaffold for harness engineering (Python; repository size 481 KB in the pack's metadata read) built as five subsystems, Instructions, State, Verification, Scope and Session Lifecycle, which generates agent rules, gates and an evidence chain for a coding project. It is not a framework or a dependency, and the product can be deleted wholesale. Static gates check docs, agent rules and hygiene; an evidence script and a claim verifier give one of three values, PASS, FAIL or UNVERIFIED; host sensors, a standard XML test-report adapter and CI and pre-push adapters sit around them; one entry script covers status, start, intake, verify, release and handoff; and a doctor mode sits beside a skill installer with drift reporting. The State subsystem is a plan template with front matter and one active plan, an evidence schema and a handoff summary. The Verification subsystem adds evidence bound to a clean tree and commit. A negative self-test, injections M1-M9, manufactures a violation for each gate and asserts that the gate must go red. The author reports 175 tests. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the negative injection is the strongest idea in the repository, the discipline of proving a gate fails on a broken copy applied to a whole scaffold, and the project maps to our routines and seat health. entries.title: kakapo: a desktop diff reader with review threads under .git, out of tracked files
entries.why: Desktop diff reader for what an AI actually changed, run from the terminal in the repository at hand (JavaScript; macOS on Apple Silicon; repository size 17.8 MB in the pack's metadata read). Its premise: the diff is the source of truth, not the chat log, and an agent's done is a claim. It opens the actual git diff in a side-by-side view with expandable folded context, hunk navigation and a per-file Viewed state, so the reviewer sees what landed, not what was reported. One key on any line asks a question or requests a change, with one comment per line; another walks every thread until none is left open; a third assembles every open comment into one document to copy. A thread is a plain file, so an agent told its path can append answers onto the cards that asked. It never writes into tracked project files: review threads live under .git/, which git never tracks, so git status stays clean and an agent sandboxed to the working directory can still reach them; everything else lives in the operating system's application-data directory, keyed by absolute workspace path, as plain JSONL, Markdown and JSON, fully local, with no account and no telemetry. Its stated design principles include separating confirmed impact from candidates worth checking, keeping review evidence next to its file and line, and staying independent of any single AI, editor plugin, worktree strategy or hosting service. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our code-decides-done rule is about the agent's self-report and this is about the human's review; the storage under .git/ is a real trick, a review thread that a sandboxed agent can still read and git status never shows; the merge-base rule is the same lesson as a diff against main showing other people's commits as deletions; and one comment per line and a walk over every thread are the mechanics of a review that does not lose a thread. Per the pack, it is the closest thing to the diff being the artifact, and the project maps to our engineering-manager loop artifacts and review. We already have: blind reviewers on the pull request, each seeing only the PR plus intent, spec and plan, never the other review (#reviewer-rule, #em-loop), part of blind review, a manual control (#controls-inventory); a reviewer who checks the change against the task contract, with a FAIL returning evidence such as file and line (#disproof-review), a manual control (#controls-inventory), and each P0 or P1 citing file and line or a command with its output, a manual review step (#review-convergence); a test-tamper scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record); the EM's per-PR open-findings list, on which an unfixed finding stays open and still counts for the verdict until it is fixed, a manual review step (#review-convergence) and the nearest thing to walking every thread; before approval, one read of the complete resulting files, not only the diff, a manual review step (#review-convergence, #controls-inventory); Pre-existing findings judged against the PR's original base, the commit the branch forked from, never against the latest fix round, another manual review step (#review-convergence) and the nearest rule to comparing against a merge-base; merge only on Haiyuan's ask or a standing order for that repository, with approval meaning agent-complete and not shipped, a manual control (#em-loop, #controls-inventory); and done as a deterministic check with self-reports advisory only, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory). entries.title: cassandra: remembers failed tool calls and warns before an agent repeats one
entries.why: Plugin (TypeScript; repository size 516 KB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) for one coding CLI that one of our seats runs (#roster): it remembers failed shell and tool-server calls and warns before an agent repeats one without an intervening project change. It hooks the tool-call lifecycle, before and after each call, fingerprints the structured call data and keeps one record per distinct failure: the command, exit code, error and repository commit. It deliberately stays quiet inside an intact context window, where the agent can still see the failure a few turns back in its own transcript, and earns its place at the boundaries where context is destroyed: a compaction, a new session, or a subagent spawned fresh with no memory of its parent's failed attempts. When a subagent starts or a conversation compacts, it hands over one note listing the project's live dead ends. A slash command opens an interactive side pane with four tabs (History, Warnings, Stale, Denied), live counters and the option to retest or inspect evidence. The author reports 623 passing tests. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, when an agent hits a tool failure, compacts its context or hands off to a subagent, the error context is lost and the agent repeats the exact same failing command, which the pack calls a persistent, expensive failure mode across our multi-seat Mac fleet; it reads the tool's boundary-aware design, quiet in normal flow and active across compaction and subagent spawn boundaries, as a match for our exact operational boundaries. The pack maps it to Mac seat health for that coding CLI, routines, and subagent isolation and context compaction; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. The pack cites no incident of a repeated failing command here, and an earlier Lab card on compaction, compaction-stress-lab (2026-10-11), was set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage on the reading that our runs rarely compact, so how often this failure mode occurs here is unconfirmed. We already have: lessons filed as vault notes that open with a one-line summary, with recall at the start of a task that greps those summary lines and opens in full only the notes that apply, policy text only and manual in the inventory (#memory-loop, #controls-inventory); a never-again list every agent reads before every task, where a correction already there twice becomes a proposed skill diff instead of another paragraph, a manual control (#vault, #repeat-lesson, #controls-inventory); handoffs that pass ownership, not transcripts, in a packet that carries the decisions already made, the constraints and the open questions, report-only in the inventory (#handoff-packet, #controls-inventory); a pause and resume note reference format whose fields include the last completed step and the remaining work, but no field for failed attempts, policy text only with no inventory row of its own (#launch); a launch standard to reuse a tool's session id for a PR or slice instead of cold-starting a follow-up, policy text only with no inventory row of its own (#launch); and a retry ceiling of at most two transient retries, three failed correction rounds before escalation and unknown outcomes parked, with rounds counted by hand, a manual control (#retry-ceiling, #controls-inventory). Our run lessons record one such boundary: a watchdog resume that re-ran a collect cold twice, each time in a new conversation (#mac-run-lessons). The Lab already holds nearby cards: clear-resume (2026-10-12), a handover note with the failed attempts written before a chat is cleared; Context Guard (2026-09-30), a forced handoff note past a context ceiling; and continuity (2026-10-25), a session ledger that flags a handoff the session's own work made stale. So lessons that outlive a session are ours already, as vault notes, policy text and manual controls; what the playbook does not have is a record per failed call, with its command, exit code, error and commit, handed over automatically when a context is compacted, a session is new or a subagent starts. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for compaction, dead end, failed tool call and fingerprint finds no match; subagent appears only in the reference summary of another team's prototype and in the test for creating a new bot (#superagent-reference, #five-test-charter); and per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. entries.title: huqan: a local pre-execution gate that holds risky commands and signs every decision
entries.why: Local-first pre-execution gate and emergency brake (JavaScript; repository size 35.3 MB and 2 open issues in the pack's metadata read) that sits on the execution path of shell, git, infrastructure and memory-write calls before they change state. Read-only commands such as git status, git diff, file reads, directory listings and searches pass straight through with no latency and no prompt; mutating commands, the pack's examples being a package test run, an infrastructure plan and a forced recursive delete, are held for human review; and destructive calls, such as a forced git push, an infrastructure apply or a cluster delete, are blocked. Every decision produces a verifiable local Trust Receipt (ALLOW, REVIEW, QUARANTINE, DRY-RUN ONLY, BLOCK or REJECT) recording the exact evidence and the policy evaluation. Per the author it runs 100% locally, with zero model-judge calls, no cloud dependency and no API keys, and it ships pre-execution guard profiles for six named coding agents, three of them CLIs our roster runs (#roster). Its operator tools, approve and emergency stop, are hidden from the model behind scoped, short-lived operator capabilities of at most 60 seconds. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our standing rules strictly forbid automated git pushes, deploys or destructive actions without a human gate's approval, and this is the cleanest implementation of an out-of-band pre-execution gate, with deterministic receipts and an emergency stop, taking model judges and token costs out of the safety layer entirely. The pack maps it to engineering-manager loop artifacts, the done receipt, the review gate and routines; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. Per the playbook, RED actions go to Haiyuan and the bots' automatic-review draft asks first before a push, but an implementer commits and pushes its own PR branch and runs the repository's tests as part of the coding loop (#gyr-authority, #em-loop, playbook §12), so for coding runs the pack's rule against automated pushes is broader than the playbook's, and the tool's example classes would hold a package test run for human review. We already have: GREEN, YELLOW and RED lanes set by how easy an action is to undo, where RED (send or publish, spend or pay, merge, delete non-junk, permissions, production, accepting terms) always goes to Haiyuan and, when in doubt, anything that cannot be undone in under a minute is parked and asked, a manual control (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory); an approval that covers only the item as approved, re-checked against the item and current authority right before the RED action runs, policy text only (#approval-recheck); an emergency stop confirmed layer by layer, policy text only and a manual control (#emergency-stop, #controls-inventory), with an installed stop marker that the launcher writes before it ends a run and that the watchdog and every automatic resume respect (#intentional-stop); run limits of 50 items, 2 retries, $0 spend and 0 external actions, policy in charters and skills, a wrapper enforcing them outside the agent loop being a Lab follow-up, not live, a manual control (#run-limits, #controls-inventory); a canonical ask-versus-allow draft for automatic review that asks first for send, publish, push, delete and pay and narrowly allows vault reads, read-only git and named launches, re-applied after a bot is duplicated or on a new desktop, a manual step with no inventory row of its own (playbook §12); the manager bot's decision layer, whose pre-tool gate answers allow, ask or deny before high-risk shell or tool-server mutations and is honored only above a confidence floor, a typed model answer rather than a fixed rule, never authorizing send, pay or merge, set to active mode on the box and called by the manager bot's own session recipe, with no inventory row of its own and unverified from the Mac (playbook §13); and run-level records, one receipt line per routine run written by a box helper, with no inventory row of its own (#receipt-line), and done receipts that list what was verified and what was not, a manual control (#done-receipt, #controls-inventory). A per-tool hook, distinct from that decision layer's router, was retired permanently by Haiyuan on 2026-10-25 and is not to be reinstalled unless Haiyuan asks (playbook §13). The Lab already holds nearby cards: bounded-agent-runtime (2026-09-24), hard run limits outside the model, which the playbook cites as a source for our written limits; Tego (2026-11-10), rules enforced from outside the agent with a human pause, Linux only; and undo-ticket (2026-11-04), a risky command allowed only with a rehearsed restore. So human approval for hard-to-undo actions, a stop that stays stopped and run-level receipts are ours already, as manual controls, policy text and one installed marker; what the playbook does not have is a local gate on each command's execution path that holds or blocks it by class and signs a receipt for every decision. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP; it singles out an out-of-band pre-execution gate with deterministic receipts and an emergency stop, with no model judge and no token cost in the safety layer.
