The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it or its approval-authority service on the Mac, wiring a guard profile into any seat, letting it hold or block any class of command, mapping our lanes onto its command classes, giving any agent or bot its operator capabilities, adding a per-tool hook after the 2026-10-25 retirement, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. The first is output compaction: it intercepts the output of test, build, lint, git and infrastructure commands and compacts verbose logs before they enter the model's context, by 69.4% in bytes across a 113-fixture benchmark, the author's measurement. Clean output is compressed aggressively, while failure lines, stack traces and exit codes are kept verbatim, and the full raw output is archived locally by a recovery feature and can be retrieved on demand. The author also reports compacting desktop accessibility trees, with a 53 to 97% byte reduction. The second is subagent model and effort routing: it intercepts subagent spawn boundaries to enforce operator-declared model and reasoning-effort policies, so that mechanical subtasks go to cost-effective models rather than burning frontier-model tokens; that kind of routing is already the subject of an earlier Lab card, named below, and is not this card's delta. entries.title: agent-pulse: alerts on silence, per-target failure streaks and undelivered work
entries.why: Zero-dependency command-line tool, library and tool server (JavaScript; repository size 169 KB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) that answers one question: is anything missing right now? Agents append one JSON line per action to an event log, and a rules file declares the expected cadence: a heartbeat interval, a minimum number of outputs per window and delivery deadlines. It alerts on no_events, silent, below_expected, failure_streak and undelivered, and on first-occurrence auth, config and quota failures, while it deliberately does not alert on input-class failures or on designed caps (at_cap is information, not an outage). Failure streaks are tracked per target and action, so succeeding inbox reads cannot mask failing sends. It evaluates once and exits, with exit 1 only on an alert; a job scheduler or a service manager runs it. Per the author's limits, it reads the log, it does not watch the agent: a total instrumentation failure still shows as no_events or silent, but it cannot say why. It does not schedule itself, rotate the log or keep history or graphs, and it reads the whole file each run; the author says to keep a day or two. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our harness already has heartbeat-style machinery (the terminal-session watchdog at about 540 s, the EM heartbeat and the miss-watch), but agent-pulse names the exact semantics, the pack says, that we keep re-deriving: silence is a finding, designed caps are not outages, auth and quota failures alert on the first hit while transient failures need a streak, and streaks must be scoped so that healthy reads cannot hide broken writes. entries.title: runvouch: missed-run, no-evidence, retry-storm and budget detectors with a proof per run
entries.why: Watchdog service for scheduled and headless agents (repository size 2.7 MB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read): one coding CLI's routines and its non-interactive mode, a workflow-automation tool and the system job scheduler. Agents report through a zero-dependency command-line wrapper, a hook plugin for that coding CLI, a tool server or a plain ping URL. Its detectors are MISSED (an expected run never started), FAILED, NO_EVIDENCE (a run said ok but the required proof, a file written, a URL returning 200 or an assertion, is missing: green is not done), RETRY_STORM (the same tool with identical input N or more times), BUDGET_RUN and BUDGET_DAY (a cost or token cap; on paid plans the agent is paused and its next run refused until it is resumed), DRIFT (duration or output off a 7-run median-absolute-deviation baseline) and STALLED. Every finished run gets a sha256 record; each UTC day's records form a Merkle root chained to the previous day and stamped through an open timestamping service, verifiable with a standard-library-only script. Self-hosting is documented, the server is a Python web service on an embedded database, and the README claims 123 tests. Per the pack's reading, the team sells a hosted service, budget enforcement (pause and refuse) is a paid-tier behavior per the README, and the pack did not verify the self-hosted path, the proof verifier or the test suite, which are README claims only; no account was created. It observes only runs that report to it: an agent that never pings shows up as MISSED only if a cadence was declared. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this is our own doctrine shipped as a product: code decides done (NO_EVIDENCE), the done receipt (a sealed proof per run), run limits and cost ceilings (BUDGET, with the next run refused) and skipped-run payback detection (MISSED). Even without adopting it, the pack says, its detector taxonomy is a checklist our miss-watch and EM loops can be audited against, in particular RETRY_STORM, which our current watchdog, staleness-based, does not name. entries.title: wayside: hash-checked session checkpoints that refuse a bundle changed between reads
entries.why: One local Rust binary, plus a thin Python binding (repository size 296 KB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read), that checkpoints a session's full working state into a store: the state directory's files, declared environment pairs, a memory document and declared database bundles (the main file plus its -wal and -journal files; the -shm file is deliberately never recorded). Capture hashes every member, copies it, then hashes it again: a bundle whose second read differs refuses the checkpoint and consumes no sequence number. Restore verifies every payload against its recorded hash before it places a byte. The checkpoint format, wayside-checkpoint/2, is a plain JSON manifest with a sha256 per file, and a session can be resumed, forked or rewound from a checkpoint. Per the author's limits, capture takes no lock and freezes nothing, so a change a writer makes and undoes between the two readings is not detected; it is a primitive, not a scheduler or an agent, so something else must decide when to checkpoint; and it builds from source only, with Rust's own package manager. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our session state today is version control, vault notes and the terminal-session manager's scrollback; runtime state that lives outside version control (embedded-database stores, environment, harness working directories) has no verified snapshot story, which, the pack says, is exactly what long Mac CLI runs lose when a session wedges or the Mac sleeps. The pack reads the two-read bundle rule and the verify-before-place restore as the careful version of simply archiving the directory, and the resume, fork and rewind vocabulary as a direct match for watchdog resume and EM re-kicks. The pack maps it to routines, the vault and box-to-Mac staging, and Mac CLI seat health (session resume); that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. A knowledge graph records how the organization works, each fact carrying its source and authority, confirmed by the human in short review batches. Nothing goes out under the user's name (a chat reply, a merge, a ticket change) until the user approves that exact action, in one line, from a phone. A watchdog checks every five minutes that everything is alive; every evening a learning pass reads the day's sessions and ledger and proposes fixes, with quoted evidence, for approval. Each session reaches only the connectors named for it. Per the pack's reading, today it serves one engineer and team sharing is roadmap; it is built first for the Mac, one package manager and one vendor's coding CLI; and the code host's API detects no license file, so we can study the design but not adopt code, study-only until a license appears. entries.title: agent-power-guard: sleeps the machine only when every enabled condition is quiet
entries.why: Native Rust watchdog (repository size 849 KB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) for three desktop operating systems, macOS among them, using under 15 MB of memory and no desktop web-app framework, that replaces the operating system's sleep timer with activity awareness: a sampling thread at 1 Hz watches 11 guard conditions (user input, compiling agents, GPU work, calls, media and stuck power requests) through a signal-conditioning layer and an intent state machine, and suspends the machine only when every enabled condition is quiet. Its agent-ready surfaces are a run wrapper, a tool server over standard input and output, a REST API, 8 built-in agent profiles (coding agents from several vendors and a local model runner among them), a mobile dashboard paired by QR code with a fleet view across machines, and a Wake-on-LAN relay. It sends no telemetry, and its local API is token-authenticated. Per the pack's reading, it governs sleep and suspend only: it does not keep a powered-off or network-down Mac reachable, and it cannot fix an offline machine after the fact. All condition and profile claims are README-stated, and its macOS behavior was not verified. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this pack exists because the Mac was offline at two consecutive 09:00 PT collects (mac-offline on 2026-11-11 and on 2026-11-12), and skipped-run payback is now a standing lock. Per the pack, our current answer is process-side (the watchdog, spawn-ok and catch-up scouts), while this tool attacks the machine-side half of the same failure: never suspend mid-run, never burn all night after the run ends, and surface which power request is stuck; its fleet view and Wake-on-LAN relay also speak, the pack says, to box-to-Mac staging. Per the playbook, that process-side list leaves out a machine-side practice: a run lesson has a terminal session run the operating system's keep-awake command (#mac-run-lessons), listed below. The pack maps it to Mac CLI seat health, the terminal-session manager and the watchdog (machine availability) and routines; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. The pack does not say why the Mac was offline at either collect, so whether sleep played any part in either skip is unconfirmed, and the playbook times the daily Lab collect at 08:55 PT, which the pack calls the 09:00 PT collect. We already have: after any Mac trouble, two timed spawn-ok probes that must both exit 0 before a launch, relaunch or resume, run by hand and not wired into the launcher, report-only in the inventory (#spawn-ok, #controls-inventory); runs skipped while the Mac was offline, down or exec-wedged logged as owed and, once spawn-ok passes, paid back by one catch-up run for the whole missed window that first checks what already exists and then logs the payback receipt, with the Monday kill review flagging any owed skip still open, a manual control in the inventory (#kill-condition, #kill-review, #controls-inventory), the Lab collect's own case being one catch-up pack for the whole window (playbook §12); the stale-log watchdog at about 540 s, a manual convention (#launch, #controls-inventory), and the enforced ownership guard, which refuses a restart unless the old process is proven dead (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); the vault on the Mac as the source of truth, with a copy staged on the box and marked as staged when the box cannot see the Mac's files, then copied over once the Mac is up, a locked rule with no inventory row of its own (playbook §12); and, on the machine side, a run lesson, not a Decision lock: because changing the Mac's power settings needs the admin password, a terminal session runs the operating system's keep-awake command, and the 10-09 drop at about 17:05 PT was a lid-closed sleep on battery (#mac-run-lessons), while the launcher's load brake, in harness since 2026-11-10, never holds a keep-awake helper (#lab-adopted-tools). entries.title: Build once, run on any agent: one skill source, per-client packages, a verifier
entries.why: Practitioner guide on a vendor's blog to agent skills as versioned directories centred on one skill file, by Andrea Griffiths, from a session at the vendor's 2026 conference with Shishir Tewari (Senior Manager, Data Engineering, at another company); per the pack it is a method post, not a package. It names four mechanisms. First, self-verification is not verification: the proof-agent example spawns an independent verifier that never sees the coding agent's own assessment, returns PASS, FAIL or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files; its CI action does a static review of the diff and does not execute code or run tests, and in the demo it was set not to block on a failure (advisory), while by default a FAIL fails the check. Second, project facts live in a manifest, not in the skill: an init skill discovers a resolved manifest once (project name, store, engine, paths) and the other skills read it, and discovered repository patterns are kept separate from team standards and stay reviewable, since 'a pattern found in a repository isn't automatically a rule to preserve'. Third, one execution path per platform: one skill reads the manifest and picks the adapter for one of two data engines, so every other skill uses the same query path; the manifest picks the engine, but the host still provides access, and a skill 'doesn't grant access' to a database. Fourth, per-client packaging with a CI check: the skill files are the source, and a script generates a plugin manifest for each of two clients and agent files for a third, and runs in CI in a check mode. The post also draws a scope line: skills fit bounded, repeatable work, and a workflow that needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control or permissions enforced outside the model is a better fit for an application. Per the pack, it is a vendor blog with one team's examples, not a benchmark; the verifier is an illustration and its static diff review is explicitly weaker than tests; the packaging script is not published as a reusable tool in the post; and no claim is made about how skills behave across models or effort levels. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our fleet already ships the same skill set into several seats through the vault's hook installer, maintains those copies by hand and has no check that the clients agree; the pack calls the split between project facts and standards the missing discipline behind our shared contract file and per-folder notes, where project facts drift into standing rules because nothing separates what a repository does from what we require; and it reads 'self-verification is not verification' as the citable version of our blind-review rule, with one addition the pack says we lack: a verifier that must cite the evidence line and may return PARTIAL, not only pass or fail. Per the playbook, the installer links the shared contract file into seat homes and copies the shared skill bundles into two seats' skill homes and into project mirrors, and a report-only skill lint already reports drifted copies (both below), so the copies are not wholly unchecked; and our blind reviewers already return evidence for a failure and cite evidence for every blocker (below), so of that addition the PARTIAL outcome is the part the playbook's verdict line lacks. The pack maps it to routines (skill to test to active, skill packaging), EM loop artifacts (independent review) and Mac CLI seat health (multi-client installs); that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the vault's hook installer as the one fleet-wide installer, which links the shared contract file into seat homes, gives one seat a global instruction file from the vault and copies the shared skill bundles into two seats' skill homes and into project mirrors (#skills), and an on-demand check that seven links to the shared contract file resolve to the vault file and one copy's checksum matches, enforced in the inventory, run on demand and not scheduled (#controls-inventory); a skill lint that checks frontmatter, when-to-use triggers, near-duplicate or drifted copies and description budgets, report-only, never editing skills and rerun in the Monday weekly sync (#skills); Three-Run Proof before a routine goes active and a promotion gate of three clean runs, a tested rollback and complete receipts, manual controls (#three-run-proof, #promotion-gate, #controls-inventory), with a replay check before a skill or prompt change is promoted, proposed in the inventory because its replay set is not built (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory); blind review by the two reviewer seats, each seeing only the pull request plus intent, spec and plan and never the other review, with an implementer never reviewing its own work, a manual control (#em-loop, #reviewer-rule, #controls-inventory), in which a reviewer tries to disprove the change, a FAIL returns evidence (file and line, a command and its output, a failing input) and a PASS lists what was tried (#disproof-review), every blocker cites file and line, a command and its output or a failing input, or is downgraded or re-asked once (#review-convergence), and each review ends with one verdict line on the head SHA whose values are APPROVE, REQUEST_CHANGES and ESCALATE (#review-verdict-line); done only when a deterministic check passes, self-reports being advisory, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory); a small verification tool and a features README for each repository our coding seat ships to, adopted 2026-10-31 with nothing built or scheduled (#verify-cli), and, among the EM loop's always-on plays, a standing-instruction file of under a page at each repository root with build, test and lint commands and conventions, with no status given (#em-loop); memory rules that route every fact to one of five buckets and keep fast-changing facts out of memory, with no inventory row of their own (#memory-rules), and a shared-memory admission rule that admits only enduring, fleet-wide facts, policy text only (#shared-memory-admission); and run limits written as policy in charters and skills, a wrapper that would enforce them outside the agent loop being a Lab follow-up, not live (#run-limits), beside reversibility lanes in which hard-to-undo actions always go to Haiyuan, a manual control (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory). The Lab already holds nearby cards: tackroom (2026-11-11), one versioned repository of skills, tool servers, hooks, roles and instructions written into each coding agent's own files, a Lab proposal; cinch (2026-09-29), one skill file translated into the formats of many agent harnesses with an audit of what each run wrote, set aside in the 09-30 and 10-13 triages because one link-based installer serves all our tools and no skill-dialect problem had been seen; agnix (2026-10-26), a linter for agent setup files such as skill headers and hook settings, a Lab proposal; and agent-orchestra (2026-10-21), a task done only when an independent verifier, never the implementer, passes it with a recorded witness, kept as background only in the 10-25 weekly Lab review, since independent proof stays our rule and its capability scoring conflicts with fixed seats. So one fleet-wide installer, a report-only lint of drifted skill copies, blind reviewers who return evidence for a failure and done decided by a deterministic check are ours already, as an enforced on-demand link check, a report-only lint and manual controls; the delta is a script that generates each client's package from one skill source and runs in CI as a check, a per-repository manifest discovered once and read by every other skill, with discovered patterns kept apart from team standards, and a PARTIAL verdict. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for manifest, verifier and self-verification finds no match, and per the pack nothing from the post is installed or adopted here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP; it singles out a check that the clients' skill copies agree, a split between discovered project facts and the standards we require, and a verifier that cites the evidence line and may return PARTIAL, and its unconfirmed list keeps the check a pattern, not a tool we can adopt today, because the packaging script is not published in the post. The pack's summary line for the vendor blog post: "Build once, run on any agent": the skill is portable, the verification and permissions are not. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a skill copy changed in one seat's skill home only, which an agreement check must flag, would be such a copy, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Building a package generator or an agreement check for the seats' skill copies, changing the vault's hook installer or any seat's skill home, adding a per-repository facts manifest, adding a PARTIAL verdict or a new evidence rule to the reviewer prompts, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers), and a change to the review rules is a standing rule that gets a dated Decision lock, a manual control (#controls-inventory). Caveats: the post is a vendor blog with one team's examples, not a benchmark; its independent verifier and its packaging check are illustrations, the static diff review is explicitly weaker than tests, and the packaging script is not published as a reusable tool, so a client-agreement check is a pattern, not a tool we can adopt today; it makes no claim about how skills behave across models or effort levels. Its client list and package formats are the post's, and how they map onto our seats is the pack's reading, not a measurement here. entries.title: rashomon: its own record of each turn, and a check that its steering notes arrived
entries.why: Alpha hook harness for one coding CLI (Go; repository size 15.5 MB and 7 open issues in the pack's metadata read; its tagged pre-release is v1.2.0-alpha.1, and the README describes the main branch, which is ahead of that release) that keeps its own record of every tool call, subagent and failed command and, at the end of each turn, answers one question: did a test or build pass after the last edit? If the agent claims done and no test or build ran after its last edit, it says so in one line ('done was claimed; the record shows 1 file edited, no test or build run after the last edit'). Before a request, its steering layer shows the agent what the repository declares about the named files (trusted spec rules, gates before done), and it never blocks a call. The part the pack calls genuinely new is a delivery check on its own notes: at turn end it reads the coding CLI's transcript in memory, storing none of it, and checks that each note it sent appears there; if a note is missing at two turn ends, it stores one small evidence file for that hook event, holding only the coding CLI's version, and stops sending notes for that event until a delivery check passes or the CLI is newer, with a one-line notice explaining why. Per the author's limits, it requires version 2.1.280 or newer of that coding CLI (a note after a successful call from 2.1.280, after a failed call from 2.1.304), a Mac or Linux system and Go 1.25 to build; notes are not sent for subagents, SDK sessions, older versions, a version that failed the delivery check or an unreadable surface, and it says so once per session instead of pretending; it does not learn architecture or conventions by itself, its lessons-import layer is manual, and the automatic layer that finds lessons in past sessions is explicitly not in this build. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this is our done receipt and code-decides-done rule with the evidence attached, plus a failure mode the pack says we have not named: we assume a steering message that was sent was also received. Per the pack, our agent-to-agent messages, watchdog resumes and the manager bot's handoffs all send, and none of them checks that the receiving session's transcript actually contains the instruction before the handoff counts as done; it calls the evidence file and stopping notes on an event that cannot be verified cheap patterns we could adopt report-only, without installing anything. Per the playbook, the after-the-last-edit verdict is close to our rule that a done claim counts only if a test ran in this session against the current head and its last run passed, a rule with no hook (below), and an unacked handoff, a room-only kick the heartbeat never read, is already a named failure mode (below); what the playbook does not name is a check that a note injected into a session reached that session's own transcript. The pack maps it to EM loop artifacts (the done receipt and verdict evidence), routines (heartbeat, miss-watch) and Mac CLI seat health; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the rule that a claim of tests passing, a commit, a push or done counts only if the session record backs it, a test command having actually run in this session against the current head with its last run passing, a prose rule with no hook installed, an enforcing stop hook being a separate drafted and blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record); done only when a deterministic check passes and done receipts that list VERIFIED, only for checks that ran, with their evidence, and NOT VERIFIED, within completion validation, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #done-receipt, #controls-inventory); a report-only claim checker, installed 2026-11-10, that checks each claim in a done report against the run's own transcript and marks it VERIFIED, UNVERIFIED, CONTRADICTED or UNPARSED, called by an EM closeout rule that has not run in a real closeout yet (#lab-adopted-tools); coding kicks sent as a direct priority wake with a row in the kick ledger, a room post alone never being enough, read first by the engineering manager bot's heartbeat every 15 minutes, a kick posted with no seat being launched or marked blocked, never idle, with no inventory row of its own (#coding-em-kicks, #em-loop), the unacked handoff named as a failure mode for the exception-first skills, whose rule is a manual control (#coding-em-kicks, #exception-first, #controls-inventory), and a daily pickup check of the ledger against live sessions and pull requests, paused since 2026-10-23 (#coding-em-kicks); a handoff packet on each new kick and manager handoff, carrying the ask verbatim since 2026-10-31, report-only in the inventory (#handoff-packet, #verbatim-ask, #controls-inventory); on every long Mac run, streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s that resumes the same session, a manual convention (#launch, #controls-inventory), with the ownership guard, enforced, refusing a restart unless the old process is proven dead (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); and, among the EM loop's always-on plays, a standing-instruction file at each repository root with build, test and lint commands and conventions, and skills for advisory policy beside hooks for must-hold rules, with no status given (#em-loop). The Lab already holds nearby cards: proof-of-done (2026-10-06), a stop hook that blocks a tests-pass, build or deploy claim unless the transcript shows the command ran after the last relevant edit and succeeded, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage as a stop-hook install because its after-the-last-edit rule is already our claim-versus-record rule; claimcheck (2026-09-28), a stop hook that refuses a done claim the session record contradicts, whose rule is adopted while its hook is not installed; claimtrace (2026-11-07), each claim in an agent's report checked against a transcript line, adopted as the report-only claim checker above; a 2026-10-21 card on a shared inbox in which agent handoffs move from queued to accepted to completed, parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review because a server-backed state machine would duplicate our kick ledger; and agent-pulse (2026-11-12), alerts on silence, per-target failure streaks and undelivered work, a Lab proposal. So a done claim held to the session record, done decided by a deterministic check, a report-only claim checker and a kick ledger with a named unacked-handoff failure are ours already, as a prose rule, manual controls, a report-only tool with no real run yet and a ledger the heartbeat reads; the delta is a record of every tool call kept by the harness itself, the after-the-last-edit verdict printed at every turn end, and a delivery check that each injected note appears in the agent's own transcript, with notes stopped for a hook event that fails it at two turn ends and one small evidence file kept for that event. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for steering, acknowledge, received and delivery check finds no match, and per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): no install; the pack names two cheap patterns it says we could adopt report-only, without installing anything: an evidence file kept for an event whose sent instruction cannot be found in the receiving session's transcript, and stopping sends on an event that cannot be verified. The pack's summary line for rashomon: an independent record of what the agent did, and a delivery check on the harness's own steering notes. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a planted note missing from the transcript, which the delivery check must report, would be such a copy, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Building or installing it for any seat, wiring its hooks into a live coding session, letting any tool read session transcripts for delivery, adding a delivery check or an evidence file to the watchdog's resumes, the agent-to-agent messages or the manager bot's handoffs, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it is alpha, and the README describes the main branch, which is ahead of the tagged pre-release it installs; it requires a recent version of one coding CLI (2.1.280 or newer), a Mac or Linux system and Go 1.25 to build; notes are not sent for subagents, SDK sessions, older versions, a version that failed the delivery check or an unreadable surface. The delivery check was not exercised against our seats, and whether its hooks coexist with our streaming-output logging is untested; it does not learn architecture or conventions by itself. Its turn-end verdict and its delivery check are the author's design, read from the README, not tested here. entries.title: mstar-harness: three independent QC seats, then acceptance mapped to evidence
entries.why: Delivery-process plugin, Morning Star Harness (mstar), at v4.6.0, released 2026-11-13 after v4.5.3 the same day and v4.5.2 on 2026-11-11 (TypeScript; repository size 37.4 MB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read), with native packages for several coding CLIs and agent hosts, among them the host one of our collect seats runs, plus a command-line init. A project-manager agent clarifies the request, writes a plan, runs the work on a feature branch, then drives implement, independent QC review, PM Acceptance and done. Plan-level QC is three independent seats by default, and multi-task plans add per-task review. PM Acceptance is the sole acceptance route for every scope: each required criterion maps to relevant evidence and an honest result, and 'QC approval alone is not test proof'; a named gap may be filled with a short bounded acceptance check, not implementation, test authoring, long suites or ops. It states that plan completion, merge-ready and merged are three different facts, and that only a verified merge followed by a post-merge close ends a delivery. Process state (plans, workflow records, findings, review reports) lives in a project folder that its scaffold keeps out of version control; iterations run through start, drive and loop commands, and its audits are read-only and report. Per the author's limits, its engine checks the mechanically checkable parts (state transitions, branch and worktree alignment, dispatch preconditions, bookkeeping), and those checks are advisory by default: a project can opt into hard enforcement, but 'whether a violation can actually block depends on the host'. A review verdict can be incomplete on exactly three conditions (a run stopped before synthesis, a required domain seat never opened, an unreadable diff basis), and a wall-clock overrun is explicitly not one. Per the pack, all of this is README-stated; nothing was run here, and the per-host install matrix was not exercised. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this is our EM loop (intent, spec and plan, independent review, done receipt) shipped as a multi-host plugin, including a native package for the host one of our collect seats runs, seen from the workflow and acceptance side rather than from the worktree ownership of a 2026-11-11 Lab card for that host. The pack singles out two phrases that would tighten our harness: acceptance is a separate route from QC, since per the pack we sometimes let a review LGTM stand in for the proof that the deliverable was checked, and three facts, not one, since per the pack we blur plan done, merge-ready and merged in handoffs; it reads the advisory-by-default engine as an honest calibration, checks that report but do not block until a host can enforce. Per the playbook, the EM loop already keeps approval apart from merge, approval meaning agent-complete and not shipped (below), so of the three facts the playbook already separates the last two; and the pack cites no instance of a review LGTM standing in for that proof. The pack maps it to EM loop artifacts (intent, spec and plan, dual LGTM), chief-of-staff rooms and written handoffs, routines and Mac CLI seat health; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the EM loop's artifact chain from intent to spec to plan to a pull request with tests, blind review, Haiyuan's merge and the pipeline, each stage committing an artifact the next can read, the spec holding the acceptance criteria the reviewers check against and accepted by the product owner before plan mode, and the plan holding the done definition (#em-loop); blind review by two reviewer seats, each seeing only the pull request plus intent, spec and plan and never the other review, one leading on behavior against the spec and acceptance criteria and the other on state, interfaces and recovery, with an implementer never reviewing its own work, a manual control (#reviewer-rule, #disproof-review, #controls-inventory); approval as agent-complete, not shipped, dual LGTM plus the product owner's merge triggering ship and approval alone not being a merge (#em-loop), under the manual approval-validity row (#controls-inventory); before the approving verdict on every pull request, a final acceptance check in which the approving reviewer reads the complete resulting artifact against the intent, spec and plan acceptance criteria, one pass and not another round (#review-convergence); done only when a deterministic check passes, with done receipts that list VERIFIED, only for checks that ran, and NOT VERIFIED, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #done-receipt, #controls-inventory); on analytics SDK pull requests, catch tests written and run by a seat that is not a reviewer, in parallel with the reviewers, their failures reaching the reviewers as evidence, adopted 2026-10-31, policy text only (#catch-tests); a review with no parseable verdict line, or one naming an older head, counted as UNPARSED and never as approval (#review-verdict-line), and a check that examined nothing reported as nothing measured, never a pass, policy text only (#check-can-fail); report-only checks that only report, nothing acting on their exit codes, installed with no schedule (#report-only-checks, #controls-inventory), and trials that start in shadow, such as the heartbeat's no-progress flag, a trial, report-only and in shadow, logged and never sent (#no-progress-flag); and review depth that scales with consequence in three tiers while the seats stay the same, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). The Lab already holds nearby cards: the 2026-11-11 card on worker agents in separate worktrees, logged takeovers and review-gated merges for one session of an open-source agent harness, a Lab proposal; seanswarm multiagents-workflow (2026-09-23), whose fail-closed acceptance rejects a prose done unless a test, an exit code, a screenshot or an independent read-only review of the diff backs it, adopted that day; agent-orchestra (2026-10-21), a task done only when an independent verifier passes it with a recorded witness, kept as background only in the 10-25 weekly Lab review; and signoff-cli (2026-11-07), five pass-or-fail gates and a verdict over the commit's files that it can sign, a Lab proposal. So an artifact chain with acceptance criteria in the spec, two blind reviewers with split focus, approval kept apart from merge, a final acceptance read by the approving reviewer and done decided by a deterministic check are ours already, as manual controls and policy text; the delta is acceptance as its own route, separate from review, that maps each required criterion to evidence and an honest result, three review seats by default, plan completion named as a fact of its own beside merge-ready and merged, a delivery that ends only after a verified merge and a post-merge close, and engine checks that stay advisory until a host can enforce them. entries.title: orchestra-plugin: an ask ledger the stop hook enforces, after cutting most machinery
entries.why: Plugin for one coding CLI, Orchestra 3.0 (TypeScript; repository size 4.0 MB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read), for prompts that contain more than one ask. The main session writes one line per ask to a ledger file kept per session inside the repository's version-control folder: an id, the files touched, what it waits for, a check that passes or fails, and a status mark, one of four, the last meaning dropped with a reason. Asks are packed into 3 to 6 units, each built by an agent that checks against its asks and commits its own files; the ledger is the spec. One review loop runs before the pull request, with a test gate: unit tests in full once per pull request, then scoped to the repaired files, and its gate-status command must exit 0 before a push. Its goal mode keeps working without asking; while it is active, a stop hook blocks the session from stopping until every ledger line is checked off or dropped, the changes are committed, the gate holds, the branch is pushed and a pull request with the current head is open, and it stops blocking after 60 continuations. Its guard denies the code host's command-line merge and its API merge calls, pushes to the default branch, and a force-push or delete of that branch, and during a run it also denies pushing a branch until the test gate passes; 'Everything else runs': it is a safety net, not isolation. The author's retrospective for 3.0: it removed the Python card engine with leases, reservations, receipts, gates and an autonomy mode, the 7,000-line board mod, three guard modes, size tiers, eight role skills and twelve agents. In the author's benchmark on long multi-request prompts (three tasks, 5 to 6 runs per arm), the smaller design delivered about the same quality as the plain coding CLI in about a third of the time and cost of version 2.15.3, 7.4 min and $2.76 per task against 21.4 min and $8.03; its first round looked faster than the plain CLI, later rounds measured 5 to 18 % less, 'within the benchmark's noise margin', so no speed claim over the plain CLI is made, and the author concludes that the removed parts 'cost time without a measured quality gain'. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our skipped-run payback and miss-watch have exactly this shape, a run being done when the ledger says so, not because the agent stopped, and its stop hook is a concrete implementation of not stopping with open lines, with an explicit continuation cap. The pack reads the 3.0 retrospective as the counterweight our Lab needs: we keep adding receipts, gates and checkpoints, and this is a public case where deleting them measured about the same quality for about a third of the cost, which, applied to us, argues that any new gate should come with a measured delta, or it is ceremony. Per the playbook, the payback rule covers runs skipped while the Mac was offline, down or exec-wedged, owed until one catch-up run's payback receipt closes them, and done is decided by a deterministic check rather than by a ledger (both below); the author's figures measure the author's plugin, not our gates. The pack maps it to EM loop artifacts, routines (miss-watch, skipped-run payback) and the terminal-session manager and watchdog (stop-hook continuation); that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the rule that a claim of tests passing, a commit, a push or done counts only if the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed, an enforcing stop hook being a separate drafted and blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record); done only when a deterministic check passes, self-reports being advisory, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory); no ending a turn while waiting on background work with a dirty tree, a manual control (#coding, #controls-inventory); runs skipped while the Mac was offline, down or exec-wedged logged as owed until one catch-up run for the whole missed window logs the payback receipt that closes them, a manual control in the inventory (#kill-condition, #controls-inventory), and the publishing bot's miss-watch, the sole detector of a missed Field Brief, enforced by box scheduled jobs unverified from the Mac (#field-brief-12h, #controls-inventory); RED actions, merge among them, always going to Haiyuan, a manual control (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory), merges by Haiyuan only (#coding), and, among the EM loop's always-on plays, hooks for must-hold rules, among them no push to main, with no status given (#em-loop); entries.title: mcp-attest: replays recorded tool calls against the written policy, offline
entries.why: Conformance harness for agent access control over the tool-server protocol (Python standard library only, version 3.10 or newer, zero dependencies; repository size 68 KB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read; published as a Python package), created hours before the pack. It takes two inputs, the policy you wrote and the trace of what actually happened, and runs nine checks. The key check (C6) re-evaluates the policy locally against every recorded call; when the policy denies a call the gateway allowed, it reports the exact tool, arguments and decision, and a fix. That failure mode, 'policy accepted but not enforced', is invisible in dashboards 'because dashboards show what the gateway believed'. It is explicitly not a gateway: it never sits on the request path and holds no upstream credential; it reads evidence that already exists, offline, with no network calls or telemetry. Exit codes are the interface, 0 clean, 1 blocking finding and 2 bad input, 'a CI gate without a wrapper script', and it can add optional hash-chained, HMAC-signed receipts for every allowed call. Per the pack, it reads tool-server traces and its own policy format, enforces nothing and cannot see calls that were never recorded; its spec is in the repository, and no third-party audit was seen. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our seats declare permission modes, tool allowlists and hook matchers in config, and nothing proves the runtime honored them; the pack calls it our rule that a negative claim needs a lookup that worked, applied to access control, since a config that says deny is not evidence that anything was denied. It reads the replay-and-exit-code shape as a model for our report-only checks, run against recorded traces without blocking, and the tamper-evident receipt as the same primitive as our done-receipt lane, aimed at allowed actions rather than completed ones. Per the playbook, our own static audit of seat configurations does not run hooks or prove runtime admission or effective settings, and the playbook says that audit does not establish declared-versus-effective hook loading or runtime enforcement (both below), which agrees with the pack; our done receipt is a short report of what was and was not verified, not a hash-chained record (below), so the shared primitive is the pack's reading. The pack maps it to routines (gates), EM loop artifacts (evidence) and Mac CLI seat health (permissions); that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: a one-time, report-only audit of persistent seat configurations from installed-source, schema and filesystem evidence, with an operative findings baseline of 5, which does not run hooks or prove runtime admission, effective settings or remote acceptance, any schedule, gate, cleanup or wider execution needing Haiyuan's OK (#skills), and, in the byte-ceiling rule, the note that declared-versus-effective hook loading was not adopted and that this static audit does not establish declared-versus-effective hook loading or runtime enforcement (#resident-budget); a report-only check, installed with no schedule, of whether the coding CLI's default model and effort match the pins and whether a run's streaming model events show the expected model, a declared-versus-effective check for the model only (#report-only-checks, #controls-inventory); the rule that a zero, none or quiet report needs a lookup that worked, a failed or stale lookup being reported as a gap, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory); done receipts that list VERIFIED, only for checks that ran, with their evidence, and NOT VERIFIED, a short report within completion validation, a manual control (#done-receipt, #controls-inventory), and one receipt line per routine run through a box helper that always exits 0, with no inventory row of its own (#receipt-line); and RED actions, permissions among them, always going to Haiyuan, a manual control (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory), with an approval re-checked against the item and current authority right before the action runs, policy text only (#approval-recheck). The Lab already holds nearby cards: lodeline (2026-11-08), one static scan of the settings, permissions, hooks and sandbox flags of five coding CLIs that gives a risk score, a Lab proposal; huqan (2026-11-11), a local gate on the execution path of the commands wired through it that lets reads pass, holds changing commands for a person, blocks destructive ones and signs a receipt for every decision, a Lab proposal; Titan Receipts + POAW (2026-10-05), signed, hash-chained commit receipts checked by an independent verifier, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage because a verifier outside the repository needs a shared signing secret; and cheat-drill (2026-10-14), known agent cheat moves fed to guard hooks and permission rules and scored, set aside in the 10-18 Lab triage because we have adopted no tool-use guard for it to probe. So a static audit of seat configurations, a report-only model check, the rule that a quiet answer needs a lookup that worked and receipts that report what was verified are ours already, as a report-only audit and check, manual controls and a box helper; the delta is a replay of the written policy against every recorded call, offline and off the request path, that flags each call the policy denies but the runtime allowed, with exit codes a CI step can read and optional signed receipts for allowed calls. Against lodeline, which scores what a configuration permits, this checks what recorded calls actually did; against huqan, which decides on the execution path, this never sits on the request path and only reads evidence afterwards. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for conformance, hash chain, hash-chain, permission mode and matcher finds no match, and per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no adoption step or trial for this KEEP; it singles out the replay-and-exit-code shape as a model for our report-only checks, run against recorded traces without blocking, and its unconfirmed list adds that mapping its policy format onto our actual seat configs is unproven. The pack's summary line for the conformance harness: replay the trace against the policy: an accepted rule that the runtime never enforced shows up as CRITICAL. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a planted recorded call that the policy denies and the trace shows allowed, which the key check must flag, would be such a copy, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing the package on the Mac or the box, recording tool-call traces from any seat for it, writing our seat permissions in its policy format, letting its exit code drive any routine or CI step, turning on its signed receipts, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. entries.title: 5 Tips for Writing Good Agentic Tests: goals, outcome waits, independent assertions
entries.why: Method post on a vendor's blog by Kacper Kapuściak (published 2026-11-13): five tips for end-to-end tests a team can trust, written for tests in which an agent carries out user flows; per the pack it is a method post, not a package to install, and the author still requires the writer of the test to decide what to assert and what counts as success. The running example is a project-management app where users generate a monthly activity report. First, describe user goals instead of implementation: tests tied to widgets and locators break when the implementation changes even if the user can still finish the flow, so the test describes a specific goal and the agent works out the actions (through the author's act helper); a vague goal such as 'Test reports' leaves too much room to interpret, and generating the report is only half the test: assertions must prove it was generated and that its contents match the correct data, read from the underlying activity independently of the report under test, since an empty report is a bug, and so is a report with the wrong records, including tasks from another workspace. Second, wait for outcomes instead of sleeping: an arbitrary delay (the article's example is a 5 second sleep) can hide flakes and slows every successful run, so the test waits for a result, with a timeout as a ceiling, and moves on when the condition holds, picking a ready signal that means the next step can start (a loading spinner disappearing is a weak signal, the report being available a stronger one); the author's immediate-assert helper checks the current screen without waiting, a wait helper is for when the app needs time to reach the state, and a deterministic poll of a value is also offered as an alternative to a model-judged wait. Third, make assertions specific, against an independent source of truth: clicking generate is an action, and getting a report with the data is an outcome; a vague assert such as 'The report looks correct' makes the judge guess; the judge evaluates fresh evidence from the current screen, a false or inconclusive judgment fails the test, and the acting agent saying it completed the task is not enough; know how much each assertion proves, since a 'Report ready' message proves a status, not the contents, and checking a preview does not prove a downloaded file has the same contents. Fourth, keep tests focused and independent: a report test should not need a 'complete a task' test to run first; each test arranges the state it needs and cleans up after itself (per-test or per-suite cleanup, matching how the data was created), another test must not change the data between the source-of-truth read and the action, shared fixtures are fine when they keep important behavior consistent, and the author would split generate, download and email into separate tests, each with its own setup and a specific name. Fifth, make failures easy to debug: a test name should state the expected behavior ('Monthly activity report includes the workspace's completed tasks' rather than 'reports test'), agent goals should stay small enough to check separately, and the log should show what the agent tried to do, what it expected and what happened instead; the author's failure traces add the steps leading to the failure, app logs, recent agent turns and a screenshot or screen snapshot when available, which does not guarantee a perfect reproduction or identify the faulty line of application code. The article restates Arrange, Act, Assert (set up the state, perform the action, check the result): the agent works out how to carry out the action, and the test writer still decides where the test starts and what counts as success. It closes by asking the reader to pick one flow, write it this way, then break something on purpose and see if the test catches it. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the article's rules for a trustworthy agentic test line up with several controls we already have, among them catch tests, the rule that code decides done, Three-Run Proof, two independent blind reviews and the harness eval design (28 cases, where zero failures is inconclusive), and they also name a few gaps; the pack maps each tip onto our controls for this card and for the adoption proposal, and that mapping is the pack's, not a decision. Per the pack, the gaps sit in how tests and catch tests wait, how catch tests and other new tests arrange and clean up their own state, how a catch test or regression test is named and what a failing run records, how a catch test states its goal, and what a catch test, a wrapper gate or a receipt line says it can and cannot support. We already have: done only when a concrete, deterministic check passes (tests green, an expected file, a commit pushed to the remote, a live URL answering HTTP 200), agent self-reports advisory only, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory), and a claim of tests passing or done that counts only when the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), and, since 2026-11-10, a report-only checker that compares each claim in a done report with the run's own transcript, called by a rule in the closeout of every agent kick on our local machine but with no run record yet, so not yet wired in practice (#lab-adopted-tools); tip 3's point that the acting agent saying it completed the task is not enough is therefore ours already; a new check (a test written for a fix, a wrapper gate, a checker script, a review grep) run once against a deliberately broken input and seen to fail before it counts toward done, a check that examined nothing reported as nothing measured under NOT VERIFIED, never a pass, and a passing check that says what it examined (files, rows, cards), policy text only (#check-can-fail), within completion validation, a manual control (#controls-inventory), plus, adopted 2026-11-02, a gate seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and, where it reads an input, an empty one, before it is trusted, the proof never touching live records or sessions and using a scratch HOME, a private socket for the terminal-session manager and copies of the inputs where they apply, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy), so the closing advice to break something on purpose and see if the test catches it is ours already, as policy text; catch tests, adopted 2026-10-31 for analytics SDK PRs: in parallel with the reviewers on each PR head, a lightweight coding seat that is not a reviewer on the PR infers the change's intent from the PR title, body and diff, lists 3 to 5 risks, writes a test for each that would fail if that risk were present and runs the tests on the PR head; each failing test goes to the reviewers as evidence they must address, a passing catch test supports VERIFIED only once it has been seen failing, a reviewer's P1 cites a failing test or a command with its output wherever possible, and catch tests are never committed automatically, policy text only, nothing enforcing them yet (#catch-tests); two independent blind reviews by the reviewer seats on docs, drafts, Lab cards, full-team tests and code PRs, each seeing only the PR plus intent, spec and plan and never the other's review, with an implementer never reviewing its own work (#em-loop, #reviewer-rule), in which each reviewer tries to disprove the change, a FAIL returns evidence and a PASS lists what was tried (#disproof-review), every blocker cites file and line, a command and its output or a failing input, or is downgraded or re-asked once (#review-convergence), and each review ends with one verdict line on the head SHA (#review-verdict-line), a manual control (#controls-inventory); the harness evaluation design: 28 cases cited from our own records (17 real past failures and 11 real successes, 21 dev and 7 held out, split by incident family so a held-out case cannot be a near-copy of a dev case), every arm scored by the same sealed artifact or report check written before the first run with a negative control, no check reading a seat, a verdict or a gate receipt, and zero failures inconclusive, not a pass: an arm with zero failures or zero escaped defects on a metric is reported as INCONCLUSIVE, with no numeric confidence claim, and cannot support removing a component, a proposal, not approved and not run as of 2026-10-24 (#harness-eval); Three-Run Proof before a new routine is enabled (Observe, Correct on a second input, Release after a third consecutive clean run, never automating the first successful run) and a promotion gate of three clean runs, a tested rollback and complete receipts, manual controls (#three-run-proof, #promotion-gate, #controls-inventory), with the caveat that three clean runs catch only large regressions, policy text only (#detection-floor); and done receipts whose VERIFIED line names only checks that actually ran, each with its evidence, and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted, a manual control (#done-receipt, #controls-inventory), which the pack calls already close to the article's log of what was expected and what happened instead. Nearer to single tips: for tip 1, the EM loop's spec states the observable behavior and acceptance criteria the reviewers check against, and the product owner accepts it before plan mode, a manual gate (#em-loop); the pack also points at plan in code, adopted 2026-10-31, but that rule is about sketches and measurements on design tasks, policy text only (#plan-in-code), not about how a test states its goal. For Arrange, Act, Assert, the nearest text is a Given / When / Then done-when for coding kicks, each Then a check code can run or tagged for review, a design note, not adopted, beside report-only mutation testing on one SDK repository, never a merge gate (#mutation-testing). For tip 2, the watchdog counts a run whose last log line states a background wait as alive until that wait ends, and never for more than 30 minutes after the line, built into the installed watchdog since 2026-11-01 (#background-wait), and the no-exit-while-waiting rule is a manual control (#controls-inventory); both are about agent runs, not about how a test waits for an app. For tip 4, a test or script puts every call to the terminal-session manager on its own private socket, and no seat kills the shared session server or another agent's sessions, a prose rule whose kill ban is also in launch prompts, with no row in the controls inventory and no hook named (#max-throughput, #changelog-2026-10-26), and a gate proof works on copies of its inputs (#gate-broken-copy); neither asks a test to arrange its own data and clean up after itself. The Lab already holds nearby cards: an engineering post on just-in-time catching tests (2026-10-30), the source of our catch tests; an agent-workflow rulebook in which a guard must be able to fail and a detector reports what it examined (2026-10-08), one source of the rule that a check must be able to fail; a public agent-workflow plugin guide (2026-10-20), the source of the broken-copy proof; a verifier that runs one regression test against fixed code, a known fault and a control (2026-11-09), a Lab proposal; an evaluation runner that compares two harness versions on the same tasks, with inconclusive not a pass (2026-10-29), a Lab proposal; and a five-stage code-quality loop for coding agents (2026-10-11), with Given / When / Then acceptance; none is this article. So done decided by a deterministic check, a check seen failing before it counts, catch tests aimed at a change's risks, two independent blind reviews that return evidence, Three-Run Proof and an eval design in which zero failures is inconclusive are ours already, as manual controls, policy text and an unrun proposal; the delta, narrowed against the playbook, is how a test waits (a ready signal with a timeout as a ceiling, not an arbitrary sleep), a sentence on how much each assertion proves, tests that arrange their own state and clean up after themselves, failure names and logs that state the behavior and what was expected versus observed, and catch-test goals kept specific and behavioral. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for ready signal, arrange, locator, spinner and test name finds no match, and per the pack nothing from the article is installed or run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): only the deltas we do not already have. (1) When a test or catch test has to wait, it waits for a condition that means the next step can start, with a timeout as a ceiling; an arbitrary sleep is not that condition, and a weak signal (a spinner gone, a "ready" toast) is named as such and is not treated as proof of the outcome. (2) A catch test, a wrapper gate or a receipt line names the claim it can support and the claim it cannot: a preview does not prove a downloaded file, a status message does not prove contents, and a self-report does not prove a check ran; per the pack this is the missing sentence on top of the rule that a passing check says what it examined. (4) A catch test or regression test is named for the behavior it protects, and a failing run records what was expected and what was observed, not only that something went wrong. entries.title: Groove: capped pools of reusable Git worktrees whose reservations survive crashes
entries.why: Command-line tool and portable agent skill (Rust 1.89 or newer; repository size 1.36 MB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) that gives parallel coding agents and CI runners bounded, reusable Git worktree pools with no background daemon. A pool is set up at a fixed capacity (the pack quotes groove init --capacity 4); a task acquires a checkout, works on a detached HEAD and releases it, and its reservation survives shell exits, subagent crashes and harness aborts until it is released explicitly, so a failed task's slot can be inspected, reset or recovered. Releasing with --save pins a local snapshot before the slot is freed, which can later be restored to a path without a commit or any change to the main branch's history. Every command supports --json and returns a versioned JSON envelope (ok, the worktree path and a lease id) with idempotency keys for safe retries. Per the author's limits as the pack reads them, it needs Linux or macOS 13 or newer (APFS recommended) and Git 2.40 or newer; pools share Git branches, objects and repository configuration; the author states that it is not a security sandbox or multi-tenant boundary; and it allocates and bounds workspaces, while the caller remains responsible for concurrency limits, process lifecycles and test execution. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our Mac runs several coding seats at once, plus multi-agent workflows in which worktree proliferation risks dirty trees, disk inflation or detached-HEAD confusion, and Groove handles that mechanically with bounded capacity, daemonless crash recovery and JSON contracts; the pack also reads its bundled skill file as an example of packaging worktree management into agent context. That risk is the pack's reading: no count of worktrees, leaked checkouts or disk they take backs this row. Per the playbook, exclusive ownership of a run's output, one agent per run or worktree, is already enforced, and low disk has held no launch since the free-disk floor was removed on 2026-11-07 (both below). The pack maps it to Mac CLI seat health (worktree management, resource bounding), EM loop artifacts and routines; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the ownership guard, enforced since 2026-10-20, under which each launch gets an attempt ID and a workspace, only the current attempt can publish and a restart is refused unless the old process is proven dead (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), the inventory's control for exclusive ownership of a run's output, one agent per run or worktree; unknown outcomes after a crash or dirty exit parked for Haiyuan or the EM, who inspects the worktree and log before anything re-fires, a manual control (#retry-ceiling, #watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); the idempotent-resume rule, under which a re-run or resumed routine first checks the live state behind each step that writes and skips any step already done, so a resumed run never publishes twice, a rule with no status given that sits beside the ownership guard and whose sources include the 2026-09-15 routine audit asking every routine for idempotent retries (#idempotent-resume); no ending a turn while waiting on background work with a dirty tree, with per-kick wrapper gates for a dirty tree or an unchanged HEAD written by hand, a manual control (#coding, #controls-inventory); the agent-CLI contract for our own harness scripts, which asks for a dry run on anything that deletes, moves or pushes and for a JSON output mode, policy text only until a lint exists (#agent-cli-contract, #agent-cli-contract-5-6); a load brake inside the launcher, installed 2026-11-10 with its pull request not merged, that holds a headless launch while the host is busy and logs free disk without ever holding on it (#lab-adopted-tools); and no free-disk floor since 2026-11-07, its inventory row retired (#launch, #controls-inventory). The playbook's list of Lab follow-ups that are not installed names automatic worktree checkpoint and relaunch as not built (#usage). The Lab already holds nearby cards: dibs (2026-10-03), resource leases for parallel sessions on one machine with no background service, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage, in part because each kick already gets its own worktree; agent-sync (2026-10-20), time-limited task leases decided by an atomic file create or a pushed git ref, parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review because our installed ownership guard comes before another lease system; sandbox-run (2026-10-06), checks run in a detached temporary worktree with the main tree verified byte-identical afterwards, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage; apiary (2026-11-09), file-based task claims with fencing tokens and expiring leases, a Lab proposal; and a 2026-11-11 card on worker agents in isolated worktrees with logged takeovers and review-gated merges, a Lab proposal. So a workspace per launch, one publishing attempt per run and a refused restart beside a live old process are ours already, enforced by the guard, a rule with no status given already asks a resumed routine to check live state so that it never publishes twice, and two earlier lease cards were set aside or parked; the delta is a fixed-capacity pool of reusable checkouts that tasks lease and return, a reservation that outlives a crash, a snapshot on release that needs no commit, and idempotency keys in a versioned JSON envelope, a mechanism for safe retries where our rule relies on checking live state before each write. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for worktree pool, reservation and idempotency finds no match; every hit for idempotent is the idempotent-resume rule above or a mention of it, and per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no install, trial or rollout step for this KEEP; what it singles out is the mechanism, bounded capacity, daemonless crash recovery and JSON contracts, and the skill packaging. The pack's headline for Groove: reusable Git worktree pools with crash-resilient reservations and detached checkouts for concurrent coding agents. entries.title: cc-notify-hooks: seconds-then-minutes alerts, cancelled when the host reports activity
entries.why: Tiered notification hooks (shell and POSIX scripts; repository size 168 KB and 3 open issues in the pack's metadata read; release v2.5.0 on 2026-11-14) for three coding-agent CLIs, each one a CLI that one of our seats runs per the roster (#roster), plus a gateway's hooks, sending to 11 channels from one state-file primitive. Short notifications fire after seconds, for a quick context switch such as moving to another browser tab (per the pack's reading of the README, a native Mac notification at 3 s and two push channels at 5 s and 15 s); long notifications fire after minutes, for unattended background runs or a person out of the room (three team-chat webhooks at 5 min each). When an agent waits for input or finishes a long turn, its notify script writes a timestamped pending file, and each channel checks that the file still exists before it fires; when the host reports later user input, a tool run or a continued turn, its clear script removes the marker and so cancels the scheduled long notifications, and per the author an answer in the terminal within 3 seconds sends no webhook alert at all. It is packaged natively for the three hosts, through plugin marketplaces for two of them. Per the author's limits as the pack reads them, it needs jq and curl; it relies on host lifecycle events (a user-input request and the events before and after a tool call), so if a host emits no resumption event on an abort or an unprompted steering message, a pending flag can linger until the next session clears it; and it is not a scheduling daemon. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, long runs (over 5 minutes) across the always-on bots, the Mac CLIs and tmux sessions often need a person's approval or attention, while too many alerts cause alert fatigue; it calls the two-tier pending-file mechanism a zero-dependency, crash-safe pattern, a short local notification first and a long team webhook only if a run is still unattended after 5 minutes, cancelled the moment input arrives, and notes that it targets three of the CLIs our seats run. How often our runs wait on a person is the pack's reading, not a count, and the author's own limits (jq and curl; a flag that can linger without a resume event) qualify the pack's zero-dependency and crash-safe wording, and the cancellation it describes as coming the moment input arrives happens only when the host reports that input. Per the playbook, asks waiting on Haiyuan go to one daily decision queue, emergencies still go to chat, and routine chat stays quiet on success (below). The pack maps it to tmux and the watchdog, routines (heartbeat, miss-watch), the chief-of-staff rooms and written handoffs, and Mac CLI seat health; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the daily decision queue, one file holding every item waiting on Haiyuan, irreversible or judgment calls only, checked once a day on the morning PR board sweep and re-raised once after 3 days, with emergencies still going to chat (#decision-queue, #decision-queue-kill-receipts), one of three rules taken with no tooling adopted from their source; an always-logged receipt line for each routine run, written box-side through a helper that always exits 0, with chat quiet on success (#receipt-line); holds that wait for Haiyuan, adopted 2026-10-31: a run blocked on a question only Haiyuan can answer is marked held and listed in reports, and CI, review or bot output never relaunches it, applied as each routine owner updates its prompt (#held-kicks); the heartbeat's no-progress flag, a report-only shadow trial that logs a stuck run and sends nothing until a new approval (#no-progress-flag); a ping to the product owner once both blind reviews approve, a review step the EM runs, manual (#em-loop, #controls-inventory); the kick pickup check that told Haiyuan about a kick still stuck, paused since 2026-10-23 (#coding-em-kicks); on long Mac runs, streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s that resumes the same session, a manual convention (#launch, #controls-inventory); a report-only freshness check of run logs, packs and receipt lines, installed with no schedule, whose exit code nothing acts on (#report-only-checks); escalation to Haiyuan after three failed fix or correction rounds, a manual control (#retry-ceiling, #controls-inventory); and the reversibility lanes, under which sending or publishing always needs Haiyuan, a manual control (#gyr-authority, #controls-inventory). The playbook's reference section quotes another team's principle that every message and notification costs someone's attention, a reference that changes no rule (#superagent-reference). The Lab already holds nearby cards: Gate Inbox (2026-09-26), a terminal board that surfaces sessions blocked on you, set aside in the 09-27 triage because Haiyuan works from chat and the decision queue, not from a terminal board; a 2026-10-06 card on tmux window marks for a session that is working, done with a background command still running, or waiting on you, whose window marks were never adopted; watchdog-kit (2026-10-18), change-only alerts for scheduled jobs that escalate once if ignored, whose proposal became our report-only freshness check; agent-pulse (2026-11-12), alerts on silence, failure streaks and undelivered work read from an event log, a Lab proposal; and a 2026-10-31 card on a model lab's prototype that keeps chat quiet while working, whose 100-word chat cap Haiyuan skipped, so no word cap applies to chat. So one queue for asks, quiet chat on success, held runs and a stuck-run flag in shadow are ours already, as rules, a box-side log line and a shadow trial; the delta is a seconds-then-minutes alert for a seat waiting on input, cancelled through one pending marker only once the host reports later activity, so a missed resume event can leave it armed. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for notify, webhook and pending flag finds no match; its one hit for notification is the reference section's quoted principle above, and per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no install, trial or rollout step for this KEEP; what it singles out is the pattern, a short local notification first and a long team webhook only after 5 minutes unattended, cancelled, in its words, the moment input arrives, which holds only when the host reports that input. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). entries.title: Spec-to-PR: spec to draft PR, with an author's pilot pricing each harness layer
entries.why: End-to-end coding harness (Python; repository size 1.10 MB and 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) that turns a spec or an issue into a draft pull request through spec, plan, failing test, fix in a sandbox, test pass, a fresh-eyes review and the draft PR. It never merges on its own: the draft carries the approved plan, a diff summary, test proof showing the test fails without the fix and passes with it, the reviewer's verdict and the cost. The repository also publishes an ablation on SWE-bench Live that adds harness components rung by rung and measures resolve rate and cost; per the pack, the author's figures are: bare loop 65% resolved at $0.106 per resolved task (a minimal baseline agent: 55% at $0.104); with verification 65% at $0.171 (+61% cost, no resolve gain); with skills 65% at $0.179 (+69% cost, no resolve gain); with planning 60% at $0.231 (+118% cost, -5% resolve rate); and with context 50% at $0.365 (+244% cost, -15% resolve rate). The author's own takeaway: 'No component raised the resolve rate over the rung before it in this run; the components added cost only.' Per the author's limits as the pack reads them, this is a pilot run on 20 SWE-bench Live tasks, one run per task, with $12.41 total spend, so a 5% difference is a single task, and the author labels it a pilot that indicates the noise margin, not statistical finality; the context rung ran out of API credits on 6 of 20 tasks. The pack names the model behind the run inconsistently, one vendor model family at two different versions in two lines, so this card leaves the model unnamed.
