entries.whatItIs: A message service for agents on different machines: they send messages, wait for a reply with a time limit and confirm what they read, and a message not confirmed before a crash comes again. Each message is marked as coming from another agent, to be treated as information, not instructions.

Only proposed, not installed, and only if we replace the ledger or staging rule: no test suite found in its tree, no TLS, one shared token, self-declared addresses; any change needs Haiyuan.

entries.title: take-once: a git task queue where the first push wins and done waits for the merge
entries.why: Git-native task queue on a branch of the repository itself (Node 22 and git; 27 KB; 1 open issue in the pack's metadata read), as the pack reads its README and its file tree, which holds a main source file, a test file and a CI workflow. Each task is a Markdown file with Blocked by, Touches and Branch headers. Its pick command says which tasks are ready and why; take moves one into the taken folder in a commit pushed without force, so if two machines race, git keeps one and the other is told it lost; the worker renews a lease; and done moves the task into the done folder with a report, while anything blocked on it waits until its branch is merged into main. Two tasks whose Touches overlap never run at the same time, and after a 3-hour window with no push and no lease renewal another machine may reclaim a task. Per the pack's own limits line, it does not recognize squash or rebase merges, so a merged branch reads as unmerged; it does not check that an agent changed only its Touches, which per the pack the related touchset-gate does; a clock hours off can reclaim live work early; it cannot tell a dead agent from one that works 3 hours without pushing; the queue branch needs protection if agents can force-push; and it never runs the agent or merges. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our dispatch has no installed cross-machine atomic claim, so two seats can pick the same pack or work item and a stale claim can hold a path indefinitely; take-once is the smallest zero-service claim, with git as the arbiter, the queue living next to the code and a done state that waits for the merge, which the pack matches to our code-decides-done rule plus the merge gate, and it is easy to trial on a scratch repository without touching the vault. Per the playbook, one agent per run or worktree is enforced on the Mac by the ownership guard (below), and the fail case its inventory cites, two seats holding one pack path for about 3 minutes on 2026-10-15, came from a watchdog re-run of a seat waiting on its own background task, fixed by the background-wait rule installed 2026-11-01 (#mac-run-lessons, #background-wait); how often seats pick the same item is the pack's reading, not a count. Per the playbook, a stale run is resumed only after its old process is proven gone, because a timeout does not prove the old worker stopped (#watchdog-resume-safety), so, as we read it, take-once's 3-hour reclaim rests on the kind of evidence our resume rule does not accept on its own. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the EM loop and routines; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the ownership guard, enforced since 2026-10-20, under which each launch gets an attempt ID and a workspace, only the current attempt can publish, a restart is refused unless the old process is proven dead and each lock use carries its own marker token, the inventory's control for exclusive ownership of a run's output, one agent per run or worktree, on the Mac (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); a stale run whose old agent may still be running, or whose state cannot be read, parked as an unknown outcome for Haiyuan or the EM, never resumed on top of it (#retry-ceiling); a stop marker that keeps a run stopped on purpose from being resumed or relaunched by any automatic path, installed 2026-11-01 (#intentional-stop); idempotent resume, under which a resumed routine checks the live state behind each step that writes and never publishes twice, a rule with no status given (#idempotent-resume); a pause and resume note format, objective, checkpoint, session or attempt, logs, watchdog state and remaining work, with unknown fields marked unknown, which neither proves an old process stopped nor authorizes a relaunch, with no status given (#launch); the coding kick ledger on the box, one row per kick moving from posted to launched to pr_open or done, or to blocked, read first by the coding EM's 15-minute heartbeat (#coding-em-kicks); the rule adopted 2026-11-15 that two kicks on the same source event asking for the same work start one run, not two, for new kick-ledger rows (#source-event-dedupe); holds that wait for Haiyuan (#held-kicks); max throughput, under which each pull request runs as its own lane and an idle seat pulls the next item, a rule that names no claim mechanism (#max-throughput); done only when a deterministic check passes, such as a pushed commit or a live page, with done receipts that list what was and was not verified, within completion validation, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #done-receipt, #controls-inventory); and approval that is agent-complete, not shipped, with a merge only on Haiyuan's ask or a standing order for that repository (#em-loop), a merge being a RED action (#gyr-authority). The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names baton (2026-11-03), cross-machine coordination with one lead per task and a zero-token wake, a Lab proposal; agent-sync (2026-10-20), expiring task leases decided by a git ref or an atomic file create, parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review because our installed ownership guard comes before another lease system; and swarm-agent-coordination (2026-09-28), paths-owned and merge-batch gates, set aside in the 09-30 triage because merges are Haiyuan's alone and no seam defect is traced on our stacked pull requests. The Lab also holds apiary (2026-11-09), file-based task claims with fencing tokens, expiring leases and a hash-pinned check, a Lab proposal; dibs (2026-10-03), resource leases for parallel sessions on one machine, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage; Groove (2026-11-14), capped pools of reusable worktrees whose reservations survive crashes, a Lab proposal; and a 2026-11-15 card on expiring per-path write locks across one coding CLI's sessions, a Lab proposal. So one owner per run on the Mac, a parked unknown outcome, a box-side ledger row per kick, one run per source event, an idle seat pulling the next item and Haiyuan's own merge are ours already, as an enforced guard, manual rules, a ledger, a new rule and a manual gate, and two earlier lease and paths-owned cards were set aside; the pack calls take-once simpler than baton but less complete, and its narrower delta is the task-queue shape: pick, take and done, blocked-by dependencies, overlapping Touches never run at once, a claim settled by a push without force, and a done state that waits for the merge. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for task queue, atomic, reclaim, squash and force-push finds no match, and lease as a word of its own finds none either; per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): nothing yet; per the pack, chattrs and take-once are worth taking up only if we decide to replace the kick ledger or the box-to-Mac staging rule, and even then baton, with git records and a zero-token wake, and agent-sync, with git-ref leases, both closer to our existing shape, are to be compared first. The pack flags it as one of two narrower deltas that the manager bot can skip without losing the two clear new lanes, and says it is easy to trial on a scratch repository without touching the vault. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Running it against any repository our seats push to, giving it a queue branch there, letting a claim or a reclaim decide which seat works on what, letting its done state stand in for our done receipts or Haiyuan's merge, replacing the kick ledger or the box-to-Mac staging rule, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). entries.title: Verification loops: diff-triggered checks, gates a change cannot edit, no flake retries
entries.why: Engineering post on a vendor's blog by Addy Osmani (published 2026-11-16) on how the team behind the vendor's coding CLI verifies its agents' work; per the pack, a paraphrase of the post's 22 points, with the author's numbers labeled as the author's. The author says about 90% of that team's code is written and reviewed by its own agent, and that verification loops are what let one person run dozens or hundreds of agents instead of one or two (the author's claim, not ours). In the team's internal testing on structured file generation, a separate grader checking against a rubric raised task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems (the author's number). A test failure that repeats becomes a hook or a more explicit rule in the repo's agent-instructions file; flaky tests teach the agent to re-run instead of fixing, slow tests mean fewer runs, and heavier tests belong before commit. End-to-end tests come first, because they are hard to fool and show what is broken while unit tests can pass on a broken feature; a skill that boots, drives and inspects the app gives the agent hands and eyes on the running system, with a feature map as guide and grading rubric, and how to start and run the app is codified in a skill named verify, kept close to the code, used before each commit and stress-tested. Property tests let a property-testing library generate thousands of inputs to disprove something that cannot fail (round trips, invariants, doing it twice equals doing it once, an optimized path equals the naive one), and their edge cases are not made with the agent's own bias; differential tests, the old and the new version of a migration on the same inputs, have their own Lab card. Checks still failing after three rounds bring in a human; code owners write their own checks, and a check that pulls in a reviewer says why. A reliability checklist triggered by the diff has 39 items, each with a trigger readable from a diff, a check and the incidents or PRs behind it (one example: when session storage or message types change, ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts lack it), and the agent checks only the matching items, usually 3 to 10 (the author's numbers). The team runs one reviewer over several rounds and does not stack reviewers, since a second, more expensive reviewer on top is often worse than tuning the primary one; a review file says what to watch, and rounds build on earlier rounds' context and past failures. Changes cannot modify their own checks: the review reads its review file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request, and gating rules live on a branch the change cannot modify; a review of a commit since pushed past means nothing. Tests, build and linter run before a pull request is opened; a verification stamp on each commit and a commit gate with off, observe and enforce modes have their own Lab card, as does grading the reviewers with an incident-replay eval. Misses become rules only if seen in at least two PRs and identifiable from a diff, after three agents try to disprove them and a human approves them; flaky tests may not be skipped, given sleeps or retried until they pass, and a test whose root cause the agent cannot find is deleted with a written reason; test suites, verification steps and rule files are pruned on a routine. The post closes by keeping the verification layer out of reach of the changes it judges. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, Haiyuan asked on 2026-11-16 at 20:55 PT to add the post to a Lab card and to our harness, and the pack diffs the post's points against the live playbook as a first pass. A three-seat decision vote then sorted 19 of the post's practices, unanimous for a diff-triggered checklist and for checks a change cannot edit, 2 to 1 for a flaky-test rule and for property tests, and Haiyuan's pick at 21:44 PT takes those four into the harness as policy text in a separate change; the post's single tuned reviewer is recorded here as a contrast to our standing two independent blind reviews, not adopted. We already have: three failed correction rounds, then escalate, and three fix rounds, then Haiyuan, with rounds counted by hand, a manual control (#retry-ceiling, #review-convergence, #controls-inventory); converging re-reviews that read only the new diff and carry open findings forward, findings tagged Important, Nit or Pre-existing, and a short review file per repo, policy only (#review-convergence); each review ending with one verdict line on the head SHA, a line naming an older SHA being unparsed and never an approval, a manual control (#review-verdict-line, #controls-inventory); a verification CLI and a features README per repo, adopted 2026-10-31 and not built (#verify-cli); a play-by-play step in which the implementer builds and runs the repo's one-command tests before it opens the PR (#em-loop), which covers the post's cheap checks in part, since it names no linter; a correction already in forbidden.md twice turned into a proposed fix where the rule is applied, a manual control (#repeat-lesson, #controls-inventory), which covers the post's misses-into-rules idea in part, without its two-PR, diff-readable, three-disprover and human-approval bar; catch-test item E, a rule approved 2026-11-14, aiming a catch test at the user-visible or contract outcome with a named wait rather than an arbitrary sleep, policy text only, nothing enforcing it yet (#catch-tests); done only when a deterministic check passes, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory); tests skipped, deleted or focused counted as test tampering and a green run after them SUSPECT, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), but, in the playbook as staged before this change, no rule for a test that fails and then passes; a new check seen failing once before it counts, policy text only (#check-can-fail), and a gate seen failing on a planted broken copy before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); pruning rules for memory and resident policy only, all policy text (a Monday prune pass that only proposes, a daily consolidation, byte ceilings on the two files every agent reads), with nothing for tests or verify steps (#shared-memory-admission, #memory-loop, #resident-budget); two independent blind reviews, each blind to the other and each attempting disproof, a manual control (#reviewer-rule, #disproof-review, #controls-inventory), which covers the post's separate grader; and a reviewer eval, proposed, not built (#review-convergence). So the new items, narrowed against the playbook, are the four Haiyuan picked: a reliability checklist triggered by the diff, each item with a diff-readable trigger, a check and the incident record behind it, seeded from our own incidents, since per the pack our forbidden.md and lessons are not indexed by trigger; a change judged by rules it cannot edit, with review rules, gate and checker scripts and repo instruction files read from the base or a template copy, never from the change, so that per the pack, our daily Lab curate run, whose writer edits the run-specific parts of its own verifier script before that verifier judges its cards, is a live instance, and Haiyuan's pick names a second, a reviewer seat started with a flag that loads the checkout's own instruction files; a flaky-test rule, with no arbitrary sleeps and no retry-until-green, a test that fails and then passes on the same head reported as a flake, and a skip or delete only with Haiyuan's OK and a written reason, while an unexplained skip or delete stays tampering under the session-record rule; and property tests as a catch-test kind where they fit, with a seeded, time-boxed generator. entries.title: treeproof: working-tree-bound signed test receipts; stop gate yields after three blocks
entries.why: Command-line tool, library and agent host plugin in Rust (1.89 or newer, 2021 edition; crate version 0.1.0; 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) that turns a claim that all tests pass into a cryptographically checkable fact bound to the repository's files, as the pack reads its README, its manifest, its root tree and its docs. It computes the git tree digest of the working directory, uncommitted edits and untracked files included, so a file modified after the test run makes the receipt stale at once. Its run command runs the test suite and signs an in-toto test-result predicate in a DSSE envelope with Ed25519, so, per the pack, an agent cannot forge a passing receipt in chat or hand-write a JSON artifact. Its done-gates plug into two coding CLIs, both of them, as we read the roster, CLIs our seats run (#roster): stop and task-completed hooks in one and stop, post-tool-use and pre-tool-use hooks in the other. When an agent tries to stop or declare completion, the hook runs its gate command; if no valid passing receipt exists for the current tree, completion is blocked and the agent is told to run the tests and fix the failures, and after three consecutive blocks on the same tree it lets the agent exit with a visible warning, so a session in a broken environment is not trapped. Passing receipts go into a content-addressed cache keyed on the tree digest, the test command and the environment variables, so parallel agents in separate worktrees whose trees match run the suite once, and identical concurrent runs single-flight while the others wait. Zero collected tests, filtered-out tests, non-zero exits and unrecognized test runners all evaluate as FAILED, and failures are never cached. It emits OpenTelemetry evaluation events for the exit code, the file-system diff and a test rerun, each tagged verified, contradicted or unknown, over OTLP/HTTP JSON linked by a trace parent, and its FileGuard refuses edits to files that changed since the agent read them. Per the pack's own limits line, it does not prevent an agent from modifying tests or planting a fake test runner, which the author's threat model answers with pinned commands in its config file and a CI rerun; its signing key resides in the user's config directory, not an isolated sandbox; and network- or database-dependent tests may drift unless their environment is pinned. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our harness mandates code decides done and done receipts with VERIFIED and NOT VERIFIED lines but currently relies on agent self-reports or after-the-fact script runs, and agents frequently commit unverified trees or declare a task complete after a partial run; per the pack, treeproof provides 'the exact cryptographic and hook-level enforcement we need': an Ed25519 attestation tied to the working tree's hash, an automatic stop gate in both coding CLIs and deduplication across worktrees for our Mac seats. Per the playbook, self-reports are advisory only and never declare done on their own (#code-decides-done), so the rule asks more than the pack credits, though nothing mechanical enforces it: completion validation is a manual control (#controls-inventory); how often an agent here commits an unverified tree is the pack's reading, not a count. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the EM loop, routines, the Mac CLIs and the vault; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: done only when a concrete, deterministic check passes, such as green tests, an expected file, a pushed commit or a live page, with self-reports and our decision layer's completion check advisory only, within completion validation, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory); done receipts whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that actually ran, each with its evidence, and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted, manual (#done-receipt, #controls-inventory); a completion claim that counts only when the session record shows that a test command ran in this session against the current head and that its last run passed, plus a test-tamper scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer, a green run after a weakened test being SUSPECT, never a pass, a prose rule with no hook installed, an enforcing stop hook being a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record); entries.title: claude-deploy-kit: default-deny policy gate, destructive-command block, redacted audit log
entries.why: Production-control kit in Python (3.10 or newer; 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read; 39 offline tests and no network use, per the pack) that, per the pack, packages five generalized, dependency-light enterprise controls extracted from a production organization of about 38 agents, for deploying one model vendor's agents, as the pack reads its README, its project file and its test suite. PolicyGate is one configuration-driven chokepoint that answers allow, deny or require_approval per action kind and defaults to deny, so an irreversible action can never be a silent allow and needs explicit human approval. CommandGuard is a hard deny-hook that blocks destructive shell commands, among them rm -rf /, git push --force, DROP TABLE, curl | sh and dd writes to a device, and per the pack it stays active even when an agent runs under --skip-permissions or other automated CLI flags. EvalGate is a pluggable judge gate, such as a rubric score, whose threshold output must clear before it is accepted; it fails closed, so a judge that errors or does not answer blocks delivery instead of waving the output through. AuditLog is an append-only JSONL journal of every dispatch attempt, policy-gate decision and execution result, with an automatic credential redactor that strips API keys and secrets before anything is written to disk, and SecretsProvider is a one-method contract, get(name), that swaps environment variables, a cloud provider's secrets manager or a vault service without changing agent code, so secrets never appear in an object's printed form or in log strings. One Deployment class wraps the five into a single guarded call, an act() on an Action that names its kind, its command and whether it is reversible. Per the pack's own limits line, it relies on the caller wrapping tool calls through that call or plugging it into agent middleware, and it is not an operating-system sandbox: it does not containerize processes. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our harness 'strictly enforces' human gates for external publishing and irreversible actions and forbids leaking secrets, while our Mac CLIs occasionally use high-autonomy flags, so its command guard would be a tested layer that catches destructive commands, force-pushes and dangerous deletes among them, even in unattended runs, and its pre-write redactor would enforce our no-secret rule in telemetry. Per the playbook, those human gates are manual controls, not enforced ones (#controls-inventory), so the pack's word is stronger than the inventory's; one collect seat's launch line in the playbook does pass a disable-approval flag (#launch). Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the EM loop, routines, the Mac CLIs and the manager bot's chief-of-staff role; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the green, yellow and red split, under which a red action, such as sending or publishing, spending, merging, deleting non-junk, permissions, production or accepting terms, always goes to Haiyuan, and anything that cannot be undone in under a minute is parked and asked (#gyr-authority), an approval being re-checked against the item and current authority right before the action runs (#approval-recheck), within approval validity, a manual control (#controls-inventory); the decision queue, which holds only irreversible items and judgment calls and re-raises an unanswered one once after 3 days (#decision-queue); default run limits of 50 items, 2 retries, $0 spend and 0 external actions without Haiyuan's approval, policy in charters and skills, an enforcing wrapper outside the agent loop being a Lab follow-up, not live, a manual control (#run-limits, #controls-inventory); the tmux isolation rule logged 2026-10-29, under which no seat kills the shared tmux server or uses pkill or killall and a seat stops only processes it started, by PID (#changelog-2026-10-26, #max-throughput); the EM loop's always-on plays, which name hooks for must-hold rules such as no secrets in a diff and no push to main (#em-loop), while the inventory records no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook for the no-secrets rule, a manual control (#controls-inventory); the agent-CLI contract adopted 2026-10-31, under which our harness scripts get a dry run on anything that deletes, moves or pushes, and errors and logs never echo secrets or whole argument lists or print a value from an environment variable whose name contains KEY, SECRET, TOKEN or PASSWORD, policy text only until a lint exists (#agent-cli-contract, #agent-cli-contract-5-6); one receipt line per routine run in one log, written even when nothing happened (#receipt-line); review and done rules that fail closed: two blind reviews by seats that did not implement the change, each ending in a VERDICT line on the head SHA, a review with no parseable line being UNPARSED, never an LGTM, a manual control (#reviewer-rule, #review-verdict-line, #controls-inventory), and prose done needs a mechanical artifact or an independent read-only check (#rules); untrusted content treated as data, never instructions, policy text only (#untrusted-content); our decision layer's pre-tool gate, which can answer allow, ask or deny before a high-risk shell mutation on the manager bot's side, sends a verdict below its confidence floor to the chief of staff rather than to deny, and never authorizes send, pay or merge, its mode active in a live-session config dated 2026-09-20, while a separate per-tool hook beside it was retired for good on 2026-10-25 (§13); the bots' auto-review intent list, which asks first before a send, publish, push, delete or payment and narrowly allows vault reads, read-only git and named tmux launches, a draft re-applied after a bot is duplicated or on a new desktop, with no status given (§12); and three always-on rules adopted 2026-11-15 that install nothing: a credential a run needs is injected by a broker or proxy outside the agent, so its environment and readable files hold no live secret (#secrets-not-visible); an unattended run gets hard bounds held in trusted code, among them a network allowlist, writes only in its work directory, process isolation and no unrestricted full-access mode (#trusted-control-plane); and each persistent agent has its own identity, so each action can be audited as the agent's or the user's (#agent-identity). The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names three 2026-11-15 cards, all Lab proposals: one on repetition loops in one coding tool, observe by default, whose separate check before risky commands is off by default; one on expiring path locks that refuse other sessions' edits; and ai-dev-guild, in which one agent builds and a different one inspects, whose separate guard plugin blocks risky edits, reads and commands. The Lab also holds vibeguard (2026-10-07), a hook runtime that blocks a few destructive commands, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage as a hook runtime install, the triage keeping host permissions and our reversibility lanes as the control; rollcage-guard (2026-10-15), one secret-guard rules file for four coding-agent tools that asks before risky commands and scans commits and pushes for keys, set aside in the 10-18 Lab triage; parallel-agents-safety (2026-11-05), undo-ticket (2026-11-04) and huqan (2026-11-11), which block broad kills and main-checkout resets, let a destructive command run only against a rehearsed restore, and hold risky commands for a person with signed decisions, all Lab proposals; Preflight (2026-09-21), an outbound secret-redaction proxy, set aside in the 09-27 triage; and authority-demo (2026-10-08), whose dispatch-time re-check of an approval is in our approval re-check rule, the demo not installed. So red actions going to Haiyuan, an approval re-checked before it runs, default run limits, a ban on broad process kills, scripts that never echo secrets, fail-closed review verdicts and rules that keep secrets out of the agent's reach are ours already, as manual controls, written rules and policy text that installs nothing, and earlier command-blocking and redaction cards were set aside as installs; our decision layer's pre-tool gate can deny a high-risk shell mutation but does not default to deny, no hook here blocks a destructive shell command, and no redactor strips secrets before a log is written. The delta is one dependency-light library that puts a default-deny policy gate, a destructive-command deny-hook, a fail-closed judge gate, a redacting append-only journal and a secrets interface behind a single guarded call, binding only the code that goes through that call; the pack's delta line also calls it dependency-free. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no trial, install or adoption step for this KEEP; its why line, that the guard would be a tested layer for unattended runs and the redactor would enforce our no-secret rule in telemetry, is the pack's reading, not a recommended step. The pack's headline for the deploy kit: enterprise controls for deploying one vendor's agents: policy chokepoints, destructive command deny-hooks, and redacting audit logs. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; the pack suggests no trial. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a planted destructive command that must be denied, and a judge that errors and must block delivery, would be such copies, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it in any seat, wrapper or repository, routing any seat's tool calls through its guarded call, letting its policy gate or command guard stand in for a red-action approval, putting its judge gate in front of a review or a done, writing its audit journal anywhere, choosing a secrets backend for it, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision; choosing a broker or proxy, and the seats it covers, is already a separate decision under the 2026-11-15 secrets rule (#secrets-not-visible). A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it has 0 stars and 0 open issues, as the pack's metadata read gives them; per the pack it was extracted from production but newly open-sourced, and it was created and pushed on the pack's own day, less than an hour before the pack was written. All four repositories among this pack's KEEPs were created on the pack's own day. Its 39 offline tests are the author's and were not run here, and the production organization of about 38 agents it comes from is the author's description, not ours. It binds only calls that go through its guarded call or middleware, so a command a seat runs directly never reaches its guard, and per the pack it is not an operating-system sandbox and does not containerize processes, so, as we read the 2026-11-15 rule, it would not on its own give an unattended run the process isolation that rule asks for (#trusted-control-plane). Its judge gate fails closed, so delivery waits on a working judge. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: MemoraOS: dated facts, point-in-time recall, sentence evidence and refusal without it
entries.why: Local-first memory engine for agents in Python (3.10 or newer; package version 0.2.0, an alpha; 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) designed, per the pack, to eliminate agent memory hallucinations and context bloat, as the pack reads its README, its project file, its test suite and its benchmark suite. It stores both raw text documents and dated structured facts (subject, predicate, object and a valid-from date) in one local SQLite database and answers point-in-time questions through a recall call that takes an as-of date. When it refuses a question it cannot ground, it returns insufficient_evidence instead of a guess: per the author, it refuses 83% of unanswerable questions, against 28% for standard retrieval with abstention gates and 0% for plain retrieval. It returns the exact supporting sentences and dated fact records rather than whole chunks, which the author measures at 4.6 times fewer evidence tokens per answer, 143 against 656 in benchmark measurements. It picks a retrieval strategy per query, exact, temporal, hybrid or vector, from the question's intent and attaches provenance metadata (kind, source type, reliability and effective date). It runs entirely on a local CPU and offline, and ships 284 unit tests and benchmarks on real Python release history (PEPs 693, 719 and 745) scored by mechanical checkers, all the author's. Per the pack's own limits line, the author's disclosure is that on general unstructured prose its overall accuracy is on par with well-tuned retrieval (60.9% against 70.3%), and that its main advantage is on temporal queries (21 of 21 against 6 of 21) and on refusing unanswerable questions. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our shared notes vault relies heavily on dated notes, decision locks and memory retrieval under our memory rules (#memory-rules), agents often struggle with temporal validity, such as which rule superseded which, or invent answers when the notes are silent, and its calibrated refusal and sentence-level evidence match our parsimonious context guidelines and prevent token waste. Per the playbook, recall here is a grep over each note's one-line summary line, written in the exact names a later search would use, the full note opened only when it applies (#memory-loop), not a retrieval engine, and the nearest context rules are byte ceilings on the two files every agent reads before every task (#resident-budget) and, adopted 2026-11-15, reading only the slice of a large file a run needs (#official-per-bot-usage); how often an agent here mistakes a superseded rule or answers past silent notes is the pack's reading, not a count. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the vault, routines, the EM loop and the Mac CLIs; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: memory rules under which slow-clock rules may be remembered while fast-clock facts, such as whether the Mac is connected, a pull request's tip, quota and CI state, are re-fetched live before any action or claim, every fact routes to one of five buckets, and each new Decision note and standing-rule memory carries a provenance card of claim, source, owner, status, supersedes and review_after, with no checker named (#memory-rules); the memory loop: write only what is new, a one-line summary on top in the exact names a later search would use, recall as a grep over those lines, deletions only after Haiyuan approves the specific items, and an explicit statement that nothing applies rather than stretching an unrelated lesson to fit, policy text only (#memory-loop), the post-task note row being a manual control (#controls-inventory); a zero, none or quiet report that counts only with a lookup that worked, a failed fetch being reported as a gap under NOT VERIFIED, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory); in a multi-file fold, the newest dated source winning and an open conflict written as TBD, not guessed (#review-round-breaker); shared memory that admits only enduring, fleet-wide facts, one line each with its date and source, a superseded fact forgotten in the same turn, policy text only (#shared-memory-admission), and, adopted 2026-11-15, a pointer to where a fact lives instead of a copy (#pointer-not-copy); cited vault paths that must resolve, a manual rule that took only the dead-reference idea of an earlier lint card (#pointer-check); a report-only linter, installed 2026-11-10, that flags dead paths, contradictions and decaying time words in agent instruction and memory files, wired as a Monday step with no run recorded in the playbook yet (#lab-adopted-tools); and, in the docs-lane reviewer trial, an adjudication with one ruling per item, insufficient_evidence among them (#lab-adopted-tools). The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names pstack-decision-log, which it says logs step decisions, a 2026-10-20 card on a per-step decision log for long or overnight runs, parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review; learn-from-mistakes (2026-10-11), which it says counts repeated error causes, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage; and contitext, which per the pack stores project continuity metadata but is not a card in the Lab: a search of every card's id, title, link and text fields finds no contitext. entries.title: Beyond Leaderboard Ranks: 27 of 35 Pareto steps unresolved; successive halving cuts cost
entries.why: Empirical study by Srinath Srinivasan and Tim Menzies (North Carolina State University), submitted to arXiv as 2611.21515v1, of 58,197 run-task records from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL) across SWE-bench and six other software-engineering benchmarks, on how teams choose AI agents under cost limits, as the pack reads its record through the arXiv export API. Across the seven benchmarks, 27 of 35 steps along the accuracy-cost Pareto frontiers are statistically unresolved; on SWE-bench, an agent configuration costing $34.16 trails the $170.78 leader by 14.6 percentage points, yet the benchmark's sample size cannot statistically tell their true accuracy apart. Self-reported execution costs differ from standardized token-based estimates by up to 11.7 times, and evaluating agents on selected task subsets puts substantial bias into full-benchmark cost projections. For choosing agents under explicit evaluation budgets and deployment cost ceilings, an adaptive successive-halving strategy reaches uncertainty-aware selection targets on SWE-bench with only 6.6% of the spend exhaustive evaluation needs, and has the lowest cost on 6 of 7 benchmarks, which the pack restates as a 93.4% cost reduction; all of these figures are the authors'. Per the pack's own limits line, it is an empirical study of the leaderboard's archive data, and successive halving needs advance estimates of task costs to reach the full 6.6% efficiency, its advantage narrowing when task costs are unknown before dispatch. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the paper directly informs our model and seat allocation, such as running small default models for routine triage while reserving the default implementer's model for high-leverage implementation, warns against taking vendor leaderboard ranks at face value, quantifies how far reported costs diverge from token realities, by up to 11.7 times, and offers an adaptive successive-halving method to benchmark candidate seats without blowing our token budget. Per the playbook, two small default models handle first-pass triage, pre-review lint, one-file chores and doc drift, advisory only, never real code, the Field Brief or review, in a two-week trial from 2026-10-28 judged on fewer P1s from one reviewer seat and shorter fix rounds without added false alarms, while the default implementer seat does the implementing (#roster); how our seats would rank on these benchmarks is not measured here. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the usage dashboard, the EM loop and routines; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: a harness evaluation design of 28 cases in four arms, filed 2026-10-20 and, as of 2026-10-24, a proposal not approved and not run, under which zero failures on a metric is reported as INCONCLUSIVE with no numeric confidence claim and cannot support removing a component, 0 of 9 against 0 of 9 being inconclusive, not a pass (#harness-eval); for our decision layer's shadow gates, a hand check of minority verdicts before a gate goes active, so a gate must beat the constant majority verdict, a manual control (#constant-baseline, #controls-inventory); the performance-comparison evidence fields in the note that follows the rule on checks a change cannot edit, under which a missing limiter or comparable settings means INCONCLUSIVE, a count or cost states its counting unit, population, window and successful lookup, and external numbers stay external until reproduced here, a reference note with no status given (#check-out-of-reach); entries.title: Agent Host Protocol (AHP): host-owned session state, action replay after a disconnect
entries.why: Engineering post on a vendor's blog by Connor Peet and Rob Lourens, an 8-minute read, on the open Agent Host Protocol behind that vendor's coding assistant's session continuity: start a session in one place and pick it up in another, an editor, an app, a phone or the cloud, as the pack reads it from the blog's feed and the full article page. The failure it removes, per the post: the vendor's old editor extension bundled its own harness, so an agent lived only as long as one window; closing the window ended the agent, an editor update stopped every agent, and a remote connection got a new, version-locked host, while each other client, the vendor's app and its phone apps among them, was building its own one-off cloud-agent integration. The protocol is organized around channels identified by URI: every server must implement the root, session and chat channels and may add more, with terminal support, additions for a common tool protocol and OpenTelemetry reporting named as examples. Inside each channel sits a reducer-based state object; the server arbitrates the state, and each client sends a sequence of actions that change it or trigger side effects. Reconnecting is then mechanical: a returning client re-sends its queued actions, shows a loading state and waits for the server to reconcile and acknowledge them before it confirms them. The post stresses that the protocol stays out of agent behavior, standardizing how you interact with agents, not how agents work, with escape hatches in the style of that tool protocol, custom methods and a metadata field. Its portability test was two independent hosts, both the vendor's own, built by different teams and then reconciled: the editor's host, in TypeScript, which runs locally, can be dropped onto other machines over SSH or into containers and replaced an assistant extension that the post says had grown past 400,000 lines of TypeScript, and the vendor's cloud agent host, in Rust; the post is candid that the variance exposed real gaps in the protocol, such as shell-type tool output not backed by a pseudo-terminal and a client assuming the shape of a session URI. Per the post, the same protocol now serves local sessions in the vendor's app, cloud sandboxes and the editor, and client and server libraries are listed for six languages. Per the pack's own limits line, it is a vendor field note centred on that vendor's assistant and editor; its portability claim rests on two of the vendor's own implementations reconciled by their own teams, the post's framing, not independently verified; it does not specify agent behavior, verification or spend controls; and nothing shows it fitting tmux and command-line seats without an adapter host we would have to build. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it is the reference design for the fragility our tmux, stream-json and watchdog stack works around: a seat's life is a tmux session on one Mac, and continuity across a dead window, a sleeping machine or a hop between the box and the Mac is rebuilt from watchdog resumes and log files, while the protocol gives the session state to the host, makes clients replaceable views and turns disconnect recovery into action replay rather than transcript archaeology. Per the pack, its required channels, root, session and chat, are a useful checklist for what a seat must expose before the manager bot can supervise it from anywhere, even without adopting the protocol, and the protocol is the layer the Lab's session tools would sit behind. Per the pack, it also informs what our EM 5-minute heartbeat and miss-watch should expect from any future session layer, actions the server acknowledged rather than a pane that went quiet; per the playbook, the EM heartbeat has run every 15 minutes since it was stretched from every 5 on 2026-09-21 as a token save, and it does not replace the Mac watchdog (#em-loop), the Field Brief's only missed-slot watch is one bot's check at :44, the manager bot's own watch paused since 2026-09-21 (#field-brief-12h), and urgency stays keyword-only, with no standing 5-minute poller (§16), so the pack's heartbeat figure is out of date. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to tmux, the Mac CLIs, the manager bot's chief-of-staff role and routines; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: long Mac runs launched through the tmux launcher with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s that resumes the same session, a manual convention, since nothing blocks a bare or unwatched launch (#launch, #controls-inventory), and the thesis that long Mac jobs survive reconnects through tmux, streaming heartbeats and that watchdog (§1); a stale run resumed only after the old agent is proven gone, each launch with its own attempt ID and workspace and only the current attempt able to publish, enforced by the ownership guard since 2026-10-20 (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); a stop marker, installed 2026-11-01, that the watchdog and every automatic resume or relaunch respect (#intentional-stop), and a stated background wait counted as alive for at most 30 minutes after its line, installed the same day (#background-wait); since 2026-10-31, an interrupted run that resumes on its own after state checks, so that nothing runs or publishes twice (#auto-resume, #idempotent-resume), and a run whose state cannot be read parked as an unknown outcome, never resumed blind (#retry-ceiling); a pause or resume note whose fields include the objective, the checkpoint, the session and attempt, the watchdog state, the remaining work and the pending approvals, and which never itself proves an old process stopped or authorizes a relaunch, a reference format with no status given (#launch); spawn-ok probes after any Mac trouble before a launch, relaunch or resume, run by hand, report-only in the inventory (#spawn-ok, #controls-inventory), and a run skipped while the Mac was offline owed until a single payback run covers the whole missed window, a manual control (#kill-condition, #controls-inventory); the Mac vault as the source of truth for the box, a file staged on the box not backed up until its Mac copy exists and the hashes match (§12, #staged-on-box-not-backup), and, adopted 2026-11-15, a current copy kept of anything we would have to rebuild after a box wipe (#shared-box-not-permanent); the EM's 15-minute heartbeat over live agent tasks, which reads the kick ledger first (#em-loop), with a no-progress flag in a report-only shadow trial (#no-progress-flag); and the playbook's reference on another team's agent-team prototype, which lists compute kept apart from state, with sessions and tasks in a database so that the agent outlives any one machine, as an idea the article describes and the prototype does not implement, reference only, not adopted (#superagent-reference). So survival of a dead window through tmux and the watchdog, a one-owner resume, a stop marker and background-wait handling, resumes that check state first, a resume note, spawn-ok probes, owed-run payback, the Mac vault as the source of truth and the 15-minute heartbeat are ours already, as a manual convention, an enforced guard, two installed watchdog changes, written rules, a reference format, report-only probes and a manual control, and the playbook records another team's idea of keeping state apart from compute as reference only; the delta is a protocol in which a host owns each session's state behind required channels, clients send actions that the host reconciles and acknowledges after a disconnect, and clients can be replaced or versioned on their own, so a session outlives the window or device that started it. The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names hoply (2026-11-15), a Mac menu-bar view of agent sessions waiting on you with their cost and plan limits, chattrs (2026-11-16), a cross-machine agent mailbox with at-least-once delivery, the pipeline-bot card (2026-11-17), a peer bus inside the runtime of the agent harness one of our seats runs, and approximately (2026-11-15), a per-step run recorder with replay, as session tools with no host protocol behind them, all four Lab proposals. entries.title: slack-dispatch: ledger-first chat intake, rule routing to agent lanes, a human queue

The chat app's live-socket event envelopes are acknowledged, normalized and recorded in a SQLite ledger before any routing, deduplicated by event ID and by a source, channel and timestamp identity; an hourly reconcile pass reads history and thread replies through an allowlist of read methods and advances each channel's read position only after its events commit, and a socket disconnect is recorded as a gap that triggers a reconcile on reconnect, posts that the pass finds within a 30-minute window waking their lane like live posts. Message bodies are stored only when the ledger is configured to store them. Routing is deterministic and first-match, in 11 steps: a membership filter at intake, excluded channels, a bot-post policy, an attention flag for protected authors or exact mentions after which routing continues, a mention-only exclusion unless the post replies in a bound thread, the bound thread's lane, a confirmed scope claim, the first explicit tag, a channel or direct-message default, the first person-channel rule and, last, a human queue, where no classifier runs when the attention flag is set and otherwise an optional classifier may only suggest a lane, never assign one. entries.title: Herdworks: non-coding coordinator, separate verifier and evidence reviewer, script gate
entries.why: Local system in Python, for one machine or a small always-on Linux server, in which you address work to a Project, one per repository with its own coordinator, task list and memory, the way you would message a teammate, as the pack reads its full README and its repository tree, its briefs, its automation and server docs, a bundled verify skill and planted-fault fixtures among them. You send a message with a Done when clause through its say command and follow up with read, tasks and status; each message becomes a task such as MY-1, the Project's repository is cloned for you, and each task starts from the newest base branch, its draft pull request targeting that branch. It separates four roles plus a non-agent gate: the coordinator, an agent that never writes code, turns your message into a task and reports back; the builder writes the change in its own git worktree; the verifier, a different agent, runs it and saves proof; the evidence reviewer checks that the proof is real; and the gate, a plain script, decides verified or not, so, in the README's words, no agent can mark its own work as done. Every task ends as a draft pull request and agents never merge; when a check needs something the machine lacks, such as a simulator or a paid account, the pull request says so and is marked for manual verification. Its agents run in another project's persistent terminals, so they keep working when you close the window and can be watched live, and its server doc covers an always-on server, so tasks run while a laptop sleeps. Its behavior is governed by plain-Markdown house rules, how to work, how to prove a change and what counts as evidence, a Project's copy overriding the machine's copy and the bundled defaults, and updates never overwrite your copies. It lists the skill folders of the user and of the repository and flags house-rule lines that name a skill that is not installed, but it does not install, fetch or edit skills. entries.title: AgentSkill-scan: offline pre-install scan of skill and tool-server bundles, with SARIF
entries.why: Static scanner in TypeScript (Node 22 or newer, with zero runtime dependencies per its README; 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read; published as a package whose command is skill-scan) for what an agent will follow with your permissions, skills, slash commands, sub-agents and tool-server definitions, typically installed after reading a description rather than the 40 files behind it, as the pack reads its full README, its rule and feature tables and the example output for its bundled malicious-skill fixture. Pointed at a folder, a file or a zip or skill archive, it loads everything into memory through a built-in ZIP reader, skipping git and dependency folders; nothing is executed or extracted to disk, and per the README it makes no network call and has no telemetry or account. Its 34 built-in rules, in five groups, prompt injection, exfiltration, shell, agent configuration and manifest, report the rule ID, severity, file, line, column, offending text and a Fix line, and every report masks credentials and neutralizes control characters. The bundled malicious fixture shows the catches it intends: a command that pipes a private SSH key into a network upload, rated CRITICAL as secrets over the network, a reverse shell through the shell's network device, 'ignore all previous instructions' and 'Do not tell the user about the setup step'. It also checks hidden text, invisible Unicode with tag characters decoded in the report, bidirectional overrides and zero-width runs, and instructions hidden in HTML comments, and in tool-server and settings files it flags unpinned package-runner servers, shell wrappers, literal credentials, plain-HTTP servers, auto-approval, shipped hooks and API-endpoint overrides. Its outputs are shaped for a gate: text, JSON, SARIF 2.1.0 and Markdown reports, CI exit codes from a fail-on severity, a policy file that disables rules, changes severities or excludes paths, a baseline that accepts today's findings and fails only on new ones, an installed mode that scans what is already on the machine, a rule explainer, a CI action for the code host that writes SARIF, and a regression corpus, per the README 14 samples: honest skills that must pass, disguised attacks that must fail and known false positives. The README reports the action run on the code host, with SARIF in its code-scanning view and the fixture's 27 findings, and names its untested edges: its skill-install mode is 'not tried with a live agent session', and its Markdown rendering on the code host is 'not checked yet'. Per the pack's own limits line, it is in early development by its README banner; static patterns cannot see runtime behavior, obfuscated payloads beyond its rules or a benign-looking skill that phones home only when invoked, so it is a gate, not a proof; organization policy, a dashboard and signatures are planned as paid features, not present; and all its efficacy numbers are the author's fixture results until someone runs it. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our hooks installer copies shared skills into many harness homes and seats routinely pull third-party skill bundles, with hundreds of new skill repositories surfacing in-window in today's search alone; per the pack, an offline, zero-dependency scan before install is the missing Test step in our skill, Test and Active routine, and it would enforce two standing rules mechanically, untrusted content as data, never instructions, through its injection and hide-from-the-user rules, and no secrets in notes or logs, through its exfiltration rules and masked reports, while its installed mode would give the manager bot a one-command audit of what each Mac seat already trusts. Per the playbook, the installer that wires the shared contract file and the shared skills into the seats' homes is enforced only by a link and hash check run on demand, not scheduled (#controls-inventory, #skills); our routine ladder is Observe, Correct and Release before a routine goes active, with no step named Test (#three-run-proof); and the untrusted-content and no-secrets rules are manual controls, policy text only (#untrusted-content, #controls-inventory); how often seats pull third-party bundles is the pack's reading, not a count. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the vault, routines, the Mac CLIs and the EM loop; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the fleet-wide installer that wires the vault contract and the shared skill bundles into each seat's home, enforced in the inventory by a link and hash check that runs on demand, not on a schedule (#skills, #controls-inventory); skill lint, adopted 2026-10-25, which checks frontmatter, when-to-use triggers, near-duplicate or drifted copies and description budgets, report-only, rerun in the Monday sync and never editing skills, with trigger evaluation, hidden-skill claims and blocking CI not adopted (#skills); a one-time, report-only audit of persistent seat configurations from installed-source, schema and file-system evidence, adopted 2026-10-25, which does not run hooks or prove runtime admission (#skills); a rule-phrase check in a report-only shadow trial, which would report must-hold rules no longer stated where agents read them and is not built yet (#rule-phrase-check); routine steps kept in versioned skills since 2026-11-15, a change going in as a reviewed diff and a box copy being only a mirror of the approved revision (#versioned-routine-skills); Three-Run Proof before a new routine goes active, a manual control (#three-run-proof, #controls-inventory), and a replay check before a skill or prompt is promoted, proposed in the inventory because its replay set is not built (#replay-check, #controls-inventory); untrusted content treated as data, never instructions, with a reviewer or gate taking its policy from its own prompt and the playbook, policy text only (#untrusted-content); the rules adopted 2026-11-15 that a credential a run needs is injected from outside the agent, so its environment and readable files hold no live secret (#secrets-not-visible), and that an unattended run gets hard bounds held in trusted code (#trusted-control-plane), both installing nothing; the agent-CLI contract's points that errors and logs never echo secrets or whole argument lists, policy text only until a lint exists (#agent-cli-contract-5-6); a manual no-secrets rule for notes, with no secret scan in the vault's note helper and no active git hook (#controls-inventory); and a gate seen failing on a planted broken copy before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy). So wiring shared skills into seat homes with an on-demand link check, a report-only skill lint and configuration audit, versioned routine skills, staged promotion and untrusted-content and secrets rules are ours already, as one enforced installer check, report-only tools, manual controls and policy text that installs nothing, but none of them scans a third-party bundle for injected, hidden or exfiltrating content before it is installed; the delta is an offline pre-install scanner for skill, command, sub-agent and tool-server bundles, archives included, with file-and-line findings, SARIF and CI exit codes, a baseline and an installed-scan mode. The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names the deploy-kit card (2026-11-17), which guards runtime actions through a policy chokepoint, and ingrain (2026-11-16), which lints a repo's own code from repeated corrections, both Lab proposals, and a same-day neighbour, a static permission, injection and egress checker seen only at search level and not deep-read, which it lists so that the idea is not double-carded without a comparison. Per the pack's delta line, no existing card covers install-time vetting of third-party skill and tool-server bundles with SARIF and CI gating; the Lab does hold two close cards: a 2026-10-25 card on a pre-install scan of one open-source agent tool's plugin and skill packages that checks licenses, commit pins, install scripts, data-leak domains and encoded payloads, rates each pass, warn or fail and blocks only if the caller wires that verdict in, parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review until scanner trust, pinned-build support and a rejection criterion are resolved; and rulesift (2026-10-30), an offline checker for the files that steer coding agents that decodes hidden characters and flags injected instructions, risky commands and unpinned tool servers, a Lab proposal. It also holds hookjack (2026-11-03), a static pre-clone scan of what a repository would run on its own when an agent opens it, agnix (2026-10-26), schema rules that lint skills and hooks before the copy, and lodeline (2026-11-08), one static scan that scores permissions, hooks, sandboxes and tool-server reach, all three Lab proposals. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for SARIF, exfiltration, reverse shell, zero-width, bidi, invisible, pre-install, third-party, vetting and HTML comment finds no match, and its one hit for prompt injection is in the reference's account of another team's open security questions (#superagent-reference); per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no trial, install or adoption step for this KEEP; its why line, that the scan is the missing Test step and that its installed mode would give the manager bot a one-command audit, is the pack's reading, not a recommended step, and its unconfirmed list asks for a run receipt before any adoption wording. The pack's headline for AgentSkill-scan: scan a skill or tool-server bundle before you install it: prompt injection, secret exfiltration, and dangerous shell, reported with file and line. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named for a trial of ours; the pack suggests no trial. Its README's regression corpus of honest skills that must pass and disguised attacks that must fail is the author's and was not run here. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a planted malicious skill, which must fail, an honest copy that differs from it only by the planted line, which must pass, and an empty folder, which must not report a pass, would be such copies, and the pack plants none. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it in any seat or on the Mac, running its package unpinned, scanning the shared skill homes or a seat's installed skills, wiring it into the hooks installer, the Monday sync or any CI, letting its verdict block an install or stand in for review, accepting a baseline of findings, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it has 0 stars and 0 open issues, as the pack's metadata read gives them, was created early on the pack's own day, about four and a half hours before the pack was written, and last pushed less than twenty minutes before it, and it is in early development. Its 34 rules, the 14-sample corpus, the action run with SARIF in the code-scanning view and the fixture's 27 findings and severities are the author's, from the README, and were not reproduced here; the pack did not run its package, under the collection's no-install rule. Static patterns cannot see runtime behavior, obfuscated payloads beyond its rules or a skill that phones home only when invoked, so a clean scan would not prove a bundle safe. Installing the scanner is itself a third-party package install, a point the 2026-10-25 pre-install scan card also made about its own scanner. Organization policy, a dashboard and signatures are planned paid features, not present. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. entries.title: wissensdatenbank (wb): notes stay Markdown; section hits priced before the agent reads
entries.why: Knowledge base for coding agents in Rust (1.91 or newer; a single local binary with no server and no account; 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) that an agent searches before every task and writes to after it: notes in a folder you own, plus a small command-line tool that finds the one section that answers a question, as the pack reads its full README, with its benchmark table, its command table and its design and limits sections. Its commands, flags and JSON are language-neutral, while its help texts and messages are German for now. Files are the truth and the index is derived: the vault is plain Markdown, a project overview note as the map, one note per topic, web sources and a monthly journal of one line per change, with three-line frontmatter, type, status and checked_on, and Status, Open, Decisions, Dead ends, Tests and Sources headings recognized in English and German; its index, a bundled SQLite FTS5 store in WAL mode so that several processes can read and write at once, can be deleted and rebuilt with a full sync, and stemming and folding, Snowball for German and English plus diacritic folding, run in Rust before FTS5, so that, in the README's example, differently spelled forms of one German word match. Every hit is a section, a heading-to-heading passage with snippets cut at sentence ends, carrying an address, a line range and a token price, so the agent sees the cost of a lookup before paying it. Its commands include a one-call project briefing (status, open points, one line per topic with its age and price, and the latest journal lines), search and read, a note creator that writes valid frontmatter, links the note into the overview and never overwrites, a journal append that is safe with several agents at once, under a lock, a rename that rewrites every inbound link and finishes on the next start if it is interrupted, a check for dead links, broken frontmatter, orphans and oversized notes, and a sync that runs on its own before every read. Every read takes a token budget as a hard limit, and whatever is cut is named by a line that gives the exact command to continue; its JSON mirrors the fields, and the same state gives byte-identical output, with timings only on request, on stderr. On a real vault of more than 1,000 notes with 28 held-back pre-task questions, the README reports its search and read at 28 of 28 answers in the top 3, 24 of them at the top, and 1,016 tokens until the answer, against 26 of 28 (17 at the top) and 1,896 tokens for a fast text-search tool ranked by matched terms and 7 of 28 (7 at the top) and 2,737 tokens for plain file search with whole-file reads, about 45% fewer tokens until the answer, at 20 to 40 ms a call including process start; the README is precise that the text-search tool ties when you already know a rare identifier, and the gain it claims is everything else, plus tokens; these are the author's numbers, not reproduced here. Per the pack's own limits line, which credits the README's own list for candour: it matches words, not meaning, so a question that shares no word, stem or part-word with a note misses it, with no embeddings; a same-size edit that resets the modification time stays invisible until a full sync; a vault should be copied with its timestamps preserved, or notes without checked_on look changed today; only fenced or backticked code is recognized as code; note creation writes German headings; and it was developed and tested on another desktop operating system, so on a Mac local time is currently taken as UTC, journal dates can be a day off near midnight, and paths compare case-insensitively, which, per the pack, would need fixing or accepting before adoption. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it is our vault contract, recall first, file the learning after, a one-line summary and never overwrite, turned into priced primitives: today recall costs whole-file reads of the shared contract file, the Decision locks and the delivery notes, while it would let a seat ask for one briefing, read only the section that answers, with the budget enforced by the tool rather than by agent discipline, and file its post-task line through a multi-agent-safe append that cannot clobber a peer's note. Per the pack, its derived-index rule also matches the staging between the box and the Mac: Markdown syncs by any tool or git, and each machine rebuilds its own index. Per the playbook, recall is a grep over the one-line summary line that opens each new note, written in the exact names a later search would use, and reads the title of each older note, which is not rewritten, the full note opened only when it applies, policy text only (#memory-loop), and the two files every agent reads before every task have byte ceilings (#resident-budget), so whole-file reads apply to those two files and to the notes that apply, not to every note; how many tokens recall costs us is not measured here. The never-overwrite item is the pack's reading: the playbook names no never-overwrite rule, and its memory loop says to update the existing note if it is yours, or cite it (#memory-loop). Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the vault, routines and usage; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the shared notes vault as long-term memory, a context repository rather than a chat log, with a fixed folder layout and a lifecycle of reading the shared contract file, the never-again list, recent notes and the Decisions that touch the work before a task (#vault); the memory loop: write only what is new, a one-line summary on top in the exact names a later search would use, recall as a grep over those lines, or a read of an older note's title, with the full note opened only when it applies, and deletions only after Haiyuan approves the specific items, policy text only (#memory-loop), the post-task note a manual control (#controls-inventory); memory rules with two clocks, five buckets and a provenance card on each new Decision note, with no checker named (#memory-rules), shared memory admitting only enduring, fleet-wide facts, policy text only (#shared-memory-admission), and, adopted 2026-11-15, a pointer to where a fact lives instead of a copy (#pointer-not-copy); byte ceilings on the two files every agent reads before every task (#resident-budget), and, adopted 2026-11-15, a routine that reads only the slice of a large file it needs (#official-per-bot-usage); cited vault paths that must resolve, a manual rule that took only the dead-reference idea of an earlier lint card, whose lint tool is not installed (#pointer-check); a report-only linter, installed 2026-11-10, that flags dead paths, contradictions and decaying time words in agent instruction and memory files, wired as a Monday step with no run recorded in the playbook yet (#lab-adopted-tools); the Mac vault as the source of truth for the box, a copy staged on the box not backed up until its Mac copy exists and the hashes match (§12, #staged-on-box-not-backup); a dated note in the agent's default folder, the vault's note helper enforcing only the filename date and a real top-level folder (#controls-inventory); and a zero, none or quiet report that counts only with a lookup that worked, a manual control (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory). So summary-first recall in exact names, byte ceilings on the always-read files, slice-only reads of large files, pointers instead of copies, a dead-path rule and a report-only memory linter are ours already, as policy text, manual controls and one report-only tool, and nothing here prices a read in tokens before it happens or returns a single section; the delta is section-level search over the existing Markdown vault, a token price on every hit, hard per-read budgets with an exact continuation line, a one-call briefing, a note command that never overwrites and a journal append safe for several agents at once. The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names MemoraOS (2026-11-17), a local memory engine of dated facts with refusal and sentence evidence, which it calls a second source of truth beside the vault, a Lab proposal, and says no existing card prices retrieval before the read; the nearest the Lab holds is context-tax (2026-11-02), an estimated per-file token bill for what loads at startup, a Lab proposal. The Lab also holds vault-memory (2026-10-20), a local index over a notes vault that returns the exact paragraph with no network or model, ranks stale notes down and flags contradictions, parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review until missed recall is measured; wordcell (2026-09-29), which returns only the vault notes scoped to the file an agent is about to change, set aside in the 09-30 and 10-13 triages because summary-first recall covers the cheap half; agent-memory (2026-10-22), a warn-only linter for memory rot, parked in the 10-25 review; skillrouter (2026-10-24), a small resident skill core with the rest of the library searched on demand, parked in the same review; and memrot (2026-11-02), partly in the harness as the report-only linter above. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for SQLite, FTS5, stemming, embedding, token price and journal finds no match; per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no trial, install or adoption step for this KEEP and says its time and path handling on a Mac would need fixing or accepting before adoption; its why line, that a seat would ask for one briefing and read only the answering section, is the pack's reading, not a recommended step. The pack's headline for wissensdatenbank (wb): coding-agent memory kept as plain Markdown, retrieved by section with a token price shown before the agent pays. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; the pack suggests no trial. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a search tool is not a gate and the pack plants no such case, but a question that shares no word, stem or part-word with the note that answers it, which per the README misses it, and one that writes a word of that note with its diacritics folded, which per the README's example still matches, would be the matching cases for its word-matching limit. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Indexing the shared notes vault or any copy of it, letting its briefing or section reads stand in for summary-first recall, writing notes or journal lines through it, changing the vault's layout, headings or frontmatter to fit it, accepting its local-time and path handling on the Mac, installing it in any seat, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it has 1 star and 0 open issues, as the pack's metadata read gives them, and was created on the pack's own day, an hour before the pack was written, and last pushed less than a quarter of an hour before it. Its benchmark, 28 of 28 against 26 of 28 and 7 of 28, 1,016 tokens against 1,896 and 2,737, about 45% fewer, and 20 to 40 ms a call, is the author's, from a single vault of the author's, and was not reproduced here, and per the README the text-search tool ties on a rare identifier you already know. Per the pack's unconfirmed list, its 28-question benchmark and latency are author-reported, and the manager bot should require a run receipt before any adoption wording. It matches words, not meaning. Its help texts and messages are German for now, and its note command writes German headings. Its index is a derived copy of the notes on each machine, rebuilt from the Markdown, so the notes stay the only source of truth.
