entries.title: hstack: a frontier model directs and approves; small models write, test and review
entries.why: Split of coding work between a frontier model and small models for one coding CLI, packaged as three skills and seven shell scripts (72 KB; 0 open issues and no tagged release yet in the pack's metadata read), as the pack reads its full README, its repository tree (39 blobs), its benchmark results and raw results files, its three skill files and its start and wait scripts; it currently runs on the coding CLI one of our seats runs, with that vendor's frontier model directing and its small model doing the work. The small-model lead writes the spec, the plan, the tests and the code, fans out to 1 to N sub-agents, runs an independent reviewer sub-agent that adds breaking tests and posts checkpoints; the frontier writes an intake of at most 20 lines (why, numbered acceptance criteria, constraints and risks), approves or revises the plan, answers checkpoints with terse directives, runs the definition-of-done commands once, reviews only the files on its risk line and approves or rejects, and it never writes product code. Its start script snapshots the repository into an isolated worktree and launches the lead headless; its wait script blocks until a checkpoint event file exists or the lead exits, then prints the event or the exit code; a direct script writes an approve, revise or answer directive with why, what and how; and a collect and a merge script turn the worktree into a patch and apply it only after the frontier approves. In the author's one measured task, a benchmark of six TypeScript modules, the frontier alone cost $2.46 and hstack $1.59, 35% less, the small model's whole share being $0.10; both sides passed 82/82 hidden acceptance tests and the type check, while wall time rose from 4.3 to 12.4 minutes. The small model made 215 calls (4.6M tokens, 88% cached) and the frontier 39, and 83% of the frontier's $1.49 was uncached input, reading, not writing. The author's proposed next levers, not yet measured, are one frontier session kept across checkpoints (cache at $0.20/M instead of $4/M) and a smaller checkpoint context. Per the pack's own limits line, it is one task and one benchmark, author-run; the hidden suite is in the repository and was written by the same project, so neither side sees it during the run, but it is not an independent benchmark; it runs on that one coding CLI today, and its roadmap says other coding CLIs come later; its wait script itself checks the event directory every 5 s, so never poll means the frontier does not poll, not that the script is driven by file-system events; the frontier's reading cost is the dominant term until the proposed session and context changes are tested; and it is MIT, so no license concern, but has no release or version pin. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it is the clearest public cost decomposition of the seat pattern we already run, a frontier that drafts and approves while small models do bounded work, and our usage dashboard already shows frontier reading as the expensive part; the transferable mechanics, per the pack, are the intake of at most 20 lines with testable acceptance criteria, plan and done as the only mandatory checkpoints, a hidden acceptance suite neither side sees, an isolated worktree and one approval before any merge, which it maps directly onto our intent, spec and plan files and our code-decides-done rule. Per the playbook, the usage dashboard shows per-CLI quota and health cards, an overall activity share from local transcripts that is not plan dollars, and a routine fire proxy labelled PROXY, not dollars or tokens (#usage), so that it shows frontier reading as the expensive part is the pack's reading, not a playbook figure. Per the pack, its division in which the small model writes the code conflicts with our standing rule that small models are advisory only and never write real code, so that part must not be copied into the lanes it names; the safe trial would be on a seat it calls an allowed implementer, or the pattern used for frontier-approved checkpoints only, with a Haiyuan rule change if anyone wants more. Per the playbook, that rule binds the default small models in their small-job roles, where they never implement real code, never write the Field Brief and never count as a reviewer, on a two-week trial from 2026-10-28 (#roster), while the seat whose coding CLI hstack runs on is an optional implementer, and its small model may implement when Haiyuan asks (#roster, #coding); the pack places the rule in our always-on bots' lanes. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the usage dashboard, routines and the EM loop; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the EM loop, in which intent, spec and plan are committed before any slice bigger than a one-line fix, the spec holding the acceptance criteria the reviewers check and the plan the ordered slices, test plan and done definition, the implementer building from the accepted plan and opening the PR without waiting for reviewers, and the agent that wrote the code never approving it (#em-loop); entries.title: AHE-Beta: simulated users file issues; merge only on a verified requirement and review
entries.why: Research preprint by Jiahang Lin, Jiahao Chen, Yiding Wang, Shichun Liu, Chengjun Pan, Shihan Dou, Honglin Guo, Yuyang Hu, Changhao Jiang, Zhenhua Han, Hang Yan, Qi Zhang, Tao Gui and Xuanjing Huang (Fudan University et al.), submitted to arXiv as 2611.24924v1 in its software engineering category, 47 pages including appendices, on requirement-centered harness evolution, as the pack reads its arXiv record and its full text; the paper describes the method and does not release it, the pack finding no code or artifact link. It is a six-round loop that changes the harness while the base model stays fixed. First, user-driven evaluation: 50 personas, differing in acceptance bar, expected autonomy and ability to check results, among other traits, drive a simulated user through multi-turn work on an evolution task; the simulator sees only the user-facing interface, the replies and progress, never the harness implementation, keeps a goal ledger, files issues for gaps and gives a user rating from 1 to 4, so the interaction exposes implicit requirements that a single final review misses. Second, team-based modification: a triage role filters out issues about the user's task rather than the harness, rejects stale or already satisfied ones and rewrites the rest as project-agnostic requirements with session evidence; an architect merges requirements that share a root cause into structural requirements; a product manager mines unstated requirements from all sessions into at most three product requirement documents per round; and developers write an RFC (objective, constraints, non-goals, candidate designs and 2 to 6 file-disjoint tasks with acceptance criteria), implement in dependency order, run lint and tests and open a pull request. Third, requirement-driven selection: admission passes only requirements and requirement documents backed by session evidence, with an evidence package of runtime logs, public task descriptions and execution conditions that excludes user conversations, hidden tests and graders; design review checks that the RFC specifies a test that could falsify it; code review returns PASS or REWORK against the RFC's acceptance criteria with the full test suite; and a pull request merges only when its approval is bound to the current head and the RFC still matches the reviewed design, the merge closing the requirement. Benchmark scores are not consulted during selection. The paper reports that on 38 held-out Harbor tasks (14 coding, 12 optimization, 7 analysis and 5 tool use), with one vendor model executing and a second model of the same family as the engineering team, pass@1 rose from 21.9% to 33.3%, against 27.2% for a named coding CLI's harness and 23.7% and 21.1% for two other named harness baselines, the user rating rose from 2.59 to 3.04 and execution tokens fell 40.8%, from 2.40M to 1.42M per task; real users preferred AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid blind A/B pairs; and, applied unchanged to two other base models, pass@1 rose 15.8 and 5.3 points over the base harness. Its sharp secondary finding: 34 of 137 passed sessions delivered no completed reply and got the minimum user rating of 1, because the verifier read the final workspace while the user saw only what the harness reported, so pass@1 alone can hide non-delivery. All of these figures are the paper's. Per the pack's own limits line, it uses one simulator model and a selected persona set, up to 32 scenarios over six rounds, with broader coverage and more simulator models untested; the paper warns that biased personas may favour some groups and that an over-proactive harness may act beyond what users allow when requirements are unclear; no public code or artifact was found, so adopting it means building the loop ourselves; and its license, Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0, is a paper license, not a code license. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our skill and routine changes are often selected by benchmark score, a single anecdote or a reviewer's preference, and this gives a written loop from observed user friction to an issue, a requirement, an RFC and a reviewed merge that closes the requirement; per the pack, it maps almost one to one onto our intent, spec and plan files, the rule that a review's VERDICT line names the head SHA and the code-decides-done rule, while adding the piece we usually skip: the requirement must be verified and closed, and the change must be general rather than task-specific. Per the pack, the non-delivery result is a direct warning for Field Brief and EM runs: a passing check does not prove the user saw the result. How our skill and routine changes are selected is the pack's reading, not a count; per the playbook, a new routine passes Three-Run Proof, Observe, Correct and Release, before it goes active, a manual control (#three-run-proof, #controls-inventory), a skill or prompt change gets a replay check first, proposed in the inventory because its replay set is not built (#replay-check, #controls-inventory), and, under a rule adopted 2026-11-15, a change to how a routine behaves goes into its versioned skill as a reviewed diff (#versioned-routine-skills). Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to routines, the EM loop and the vault; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the EM loop's chain of intent, spec and plan, the intent written by research or product with its problem, constraints, non-goals and success signal, the spec holding the acceptance criteria the reviewers check, accepted by Haiyuan before plan mode, and the implementer building from the accepted plan and never approving its own work (#em-loop); two blind reviews, each attempting disproof against two or three rejection criteria named before reading the diff and each ending in a VERDICT line on the current head SHA, a review with no parseable line or an older SHA being UNPARSED, never an LGTM, manual in the inventory (#disproof-review, #review-verdict-line, #controls-inventory), and regista, a report-only verdict binder installed on the Mac on 2026-11-09 that ties a verdict to the exact diff it read, its pull request not merged, called by an EM rule written 2026-11-10 and not yet run on a real pull request (#lab-adopted-tools); done only when a deterministic check passes, with self-reports advisory only, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory), and the rule that a passing check says what it examined and what it does not show, a status message not being the content it reports on and a preview not being the delivered file, policy text only (#check-can-fail); a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record); the ask restated before a non-trivial task and checked against Haiyuan's words verbatim, policy text only (#intake-restatement, #verbatim-ask); a repeat lesson turned into a proposed skill diff where the rule is applied, not another paragraph in the never-again list, a manual control (#repeat-lesson, #controls-inventory); the rule that three clean runs only catch large regressions, policy text only (#detection-floor); and the harness evaluation design, 28 cases in four arms, a proposal not approved and not run as of 2026-10-24, scored by a sealed check written before the first run, in which zero failures is inconclusive, not a pass (#harness-eval). So an intent, spec and plan chain with acceptance criteria, blind disproof reviews pinned to the head SHA, done decided by a deterministic check that says what it examined, restated asks, repeat lessons turned into skill diffs and staged promotion of routines are ours already, as manual controls, policy text and one report-only tool, and an evaluation design that calls zero failures inconclusive is a proposal that has not run; the delta is a loop driven by what simulated users of the harness run into: personas that see only the user-facing interface and file issues, requirements filtered, merged and admitted only with session evidence that leaves out hidden tests and graders, an RFC that must name a test that could falsify it, a merge that closes its requirement and selection that never reads benchmark scores; its non-delivery result, that a passed session may still have given the user no completed reply, is a secondary finding, not a step of the method. The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names harness-wrangler (2026-10-14), repeated graded runs per task and variant with a confidence interval on the difference, set aside in the 10-18 Lab triage, and pstack (2026-10-20), blind A/B tests of a skill change in which old and new versions run the same task and one judge scores both, parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review because our unrun eval design comes first, as the evaluation neighbours, and prove-it-done (2026-10-13), receipt-gated completion whose one-line checks a bundled script re-runs, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage, as the receipt neighbour; per the pack, AHE-Beta changes what gets proposed and what is allowed to merge, a process card, not another eval tool. The Lab also holds agent-harness-eval (2026-10-29), the same tasks on two harness versions with pass rates and an interval per task, inconclusive never a pass, a Lab proposal; overclaim (2026-10-14), done claims scored against a hidden check the agent never saw, set aside in the 10-18 Lab triage as reference evidence; plan-validation (2026-10-18), which checks that each requirement has a task and a test and each task an approved requirement, set aside in the 10-18 Lab triage; phase-barrier (2026-10-03), a stage gate from requirement and spec through tests, implementation and delivery, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage; and the verification-loops post (2026-11-16), partly in the harness as four policy-text rules adopted that day. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for requirement, personas, simulated user, simulator, user rating, non-delivery and pass@1 finds no match; per the pack the paper's method is described, not released, and nothing from it is built here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no trial, install or adoption step for this KEEP, and per its limits line adopting it means building the loop ourselves; its why line, that the loop maps onto our artifacts and adds requirements that are verified, closed and general, is the pack's reading, not a recommended step. The pack's headline for AHE-Beta: requirement-centered harness evolution: user-simulator issues, triage/architect/PM/developer roles, and merge only on a verified requirement plus review. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and the pack suggests no trial; the paper's comparisons, against its base harness and three other harness baselines, are the paper's own, not a negative control for a trial of ours. The playbook asks that a gate be seen failing on a planted broken copy, beside a healthy control and an empty input, before it is trusted, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); the paper's admission, design review, code review and head-bound merge approval are gates by the playbook's definition, checks whose result something acts on or a record cites, and the pack supplies no planted broken copy, healthy control or empty input for any of them. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Building the loop, simulating users against any seat, bot or routine, writing personas, letting simulated users file issues, changing how skill or routine changes are proposed, reviewed or merged, adding a delivered-reply check to done receipts, spending on model runs for it, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it is a preprint that describes a method, not a tool, and no code or artifact was found. Its results, the 21.9% and 33.3% pass@1, the 27.2%, 23.7% and 21.1% baselines, the 2.59 and 3.04 ratings, the 40.8% fewer tokens, the 31 of 48 pairs, the 15.8 and 5.3 points and the 34 of 137 passed sessions with no completed reply, are paper-reported and were not reproduced here; per the pack's unconfirmed list, the non-delivery number is a paper finding, not a measurement of our pipeline. It rests on one simulator model, the same one that executes the tasks, and a selected persona set, with up to 32 scenarios over six rounds. It was submitted within the pack's window, about an hour and forty minutes after it opened. The window is the pack's own: a catch-up covering 2026-11-18 09:12 PT to 2026-11-19 09:05 PT, which pays the remainder of 2026-11-18, the date it names as missed. No local measurement backs this row; the pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. Harness statuses above are read from the staged playbook, whose inventory is dated 2026-10-20, not from a live audit. Per the pack, the collector read its arXiv record through the export API and its full HTML and PDF text in the foreground; nothing was run, and the collection spent $0. entries.plainTitle: AHE-Beta: improve an agent harness from what simulated users run into
entries.whatItIs: A research paper on improving an agent harness in rounds: simulated users who see only its replies and progress updates file issues, agent roles turn them into requirements and designs, and a change merges only with review approval on its latest version, the merge closing its requirement.
entries.whyItMatters: It is a written way to pick harness changes from problems simulated users hit rather than from scores, and it warns that a passed check can hide that the user got no answer. Only a Lab proposal, not built here: the paper's figures are its own, no code was released, and any change needs Haiyuan.

entries.title: git-porter: Git handoff through a receiver with branch-prefix rules and a split key
entries.why: Transport layer in Rust (87 blobs, a tests tree among them; 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read; the pack names a package-manager tap for it) for exactly the pattern of an agent on its own machine or account with no push access, as the pack reads its full README, its repository tree, its 0.1.0 release and its access and trust design note. The sender runs a send command against the receiver's account over ordinary SSH; the receiver matches the repository by its remotes, so no path sync is needed, applies its policy and forwards the branch to origin, and a receive command fetches back and only ever fast-forwards. Tags, deletions, symbolic branches and branches checked out in a receiver worktree are refused; history rewrites need force-with-lease or force, and force-with-lease rechecks origin at the last known commit. The policy lives on the receiver: authorized keys, which can be repeated; allowed push prefixes, literal branch-prefix namespaces, an empty list meaning read-only; a search root and a strict mode, canonicalized under the receiver's home directory, so that symlinks and linked-worktree metadata cannot escape; the forge hostnames it may publish to; default-branch pushes, off by default; and the skipWrappedKey opt-in, explicitly dangerous, which removes per-push sender approval. The receiver parses commands and never evaluates them as shell, and it fails closed if its policy is removed while a forced-command SSH entry remains. The forwarding private key is encrypted at rest on the receiver and unlocked for one push only after the sender signs an unlock request, so neither side can use it alone. A send reports the receiver update and the origin update separately, as published, not published, moved, unknown or not attempted, and if origin rejects, the receiver update is rejected too. Per the pack's own limits line, it is version 0.1.0 with 1 star; its trust model explicitly trusts the receiver account, root, repository administrators and the local filesystem, so it is not a sandbox against them; it requires SSH setup and a receiver account, and no path for another desktop operating system is claimed; it protects branch scope and publication, not the content of the diff, so review still has to happen; and the skipWrappedKey opt-in is explicitly dangerous and should stay off. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our box-to-Mac staging and any future dedicated agent account lack a safe, typed handoff: either the agent has push credentials, which is too much, or a human copies diffs, which is slow and error-prone; per the pack, git-porter gives the agent a one-way, prefix-limited, default-branch-protected path back to the repo, with a machine-readable publication outcome that could go straight into a done receipt, VERIFIED only on published and inspected on moved or unknown. Per the pack, its receiver-side policy is the enforcement half of our no-push-unless-asked rule, and its refusal of branches checked out in a worktree fits our parallel-worktree discipline. Per the playbook, the box-to-Mac staging it names is for vault files, with the Mac vault as the source of truth and a file staged on the box not backed up until its Mac copy exists and the hashes match (§12, #staged-on-box-not-backup); the implementer commits, pushes and opens the PR without waiting for reviewers, and a merge happens only on Haiyuan's ask or a standing order for that repo (#em-loop); the auto-review intent list asks first for send, publish, push, delete and pay (§12); an always-on play keeps no push to main among the must-hold rules meant for hooks (#em-loop); and standing publish approvals cover the Field Brief and the Lab and playbook pushes to the hub (#promotion-ladder); so a push is asked first, done inside a lane or covered by a standing approval, and the playbook states no single no-push-unless-asked rule. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the vault, the Mac CLIs and the manager bot's chief-of-staff role; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the Mac vault as the source of truth for the box, a file staged on the box not backed up until its Mac copy exists and the hashes match, adopted 2026-11-15 (§12, #staged-on-box-not-backup), and, adopted the same day, a current copy of anything we would have to rebuild after a box wipe, kept in the Mac vault or a private git repo, refreshed at least daily and checked by hash, never copied into the public hub, with secrets never leaving the box in the clear (#shared-box-not-permanent); the ownership guard, enforced since 2026-10-20, under which each launch gets an attempt ID and a workspace and only the current attempt can publish, a stale attempt's publish being refused (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory); a claim that work was pushed counting only when the record backs it, the commit existing and the push landed with nothing ahead of upstream, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), done receipts whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that ran and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted (#done-receipt), and done itself decided by a deterministic check, a commit pushed to the remote among them, a manual control (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory); an approval that covers the item as approved, a PR head SHA included, re-checked right before the RED action runs, policy text only (#approval-recheck), merges, permissions and publishing being RED actions that always go to Haiyuan (#gyr-authority); the rules adopted 2026-11-15 that a credential a run needs is injected from outside the agent, so its environment and readable files hold no live secret (#secrets-not-visible), that an unattended run gets hard bounds held in trusted code, a network allowlist, writes only in its work directory, process isolation and no unrestricted full-access mode (#trusted-control-plane), and that each persistent agent has its own identity, distinct from the user's (#agent-identity), all three installing nothing; the agent-CLI contract's dry run, which shows what a harness script that deletes, moves or pushes would change and changes nothing, adopted 2026-10-31, policy text only until a lint exists (#agent-cli-contract, #agent-cli-contract-5-6); the vault's own rule that it never posts, pays, deploys, merges or sends, its scripts holding no post, push or send call, a manual control (#controls-inventory); and the pause and resume note format, which names the branch or worktree and never itself commits, pushes or authorizes a relaunch, a reference format with no status given (#launch). entries.title: switchboard: terminal picker, sidebar and status bar for agents that need you or are done
entries.why: Keyboard-only terminal-multiplexer layer in Python (3.11 or newer; 56 blobs, 21 of them test files; 0 open issues in the pack's metadata read) for people running coding agents in panes, as the pack reads its full README (529 lines), its repository tree, its 1.3.0 release and its project file. It has five pieces: a popup picker, repository, then worktree, then agents, with state dots and a preview of the pane Enter will land on; a persistent sidebar, 32 columns wide, that redraws live; a status-bar segment for sessions that need you or are done; a multiplexer alert on every client, plus a sound, when an unwatched session needs you or finishes; and a hook command, with an optional agent name and an event, that updates state. Enter lands on the most urgent agent's pane, needs-you before done, done before working and working before idle, then the lead before a teammate, then the lowest window and pane. State lives in the multiplexer's pane options on each agent's pane, with no daemon, no polling and no state file. Hooks for two coding CLIs and a third coding agent turn their events into needs, with a key and a reason, working, with a task, done, idle, start, teammate and end; the second CLI is tracked from its version 0.170 on and only when started with its no-daemon option. An event from the second or third agent counts only if it runs inside the pane, as a descendant of the pane's process, so a daemon reporting another terminal's pane is dropped, and a state command exists for tools with no adapter. A permission prompt or a question sets needs-you, which stays until it is answered; finishing a turn while you are in another session sets done and alerts; visiting the pane turns done into idle. A slow approved command keeps needs-you until it finishes, because the first CLI sends no event when an approval ends. Git status is read for every worktree at once with a one-second limit, so a slow or broken repository shows no status rather than blocking the list, and a multiplexer session-restore plugin restores the sidebar. Per the pack's own limits line, it requires version 3.8 or newer of the terminal multiplexer, while our seat had 3.7c at collect time, so a trial needs an upgrade first, plus a fuzzy finder 0.59 or newer, a patched icon font and Python 3.11 or newer; only the three agents' adapters ship, so our other seats would need state-command wrappers, not written or tested here; the second CLI's tracking needs its no-daemon option, and a session of it inside a session of the first CLI is not tracked; a failed turn of the second CLI shows working until the next prompt, and its tool-server input never shows needs-you; and it has 0 stars and was hours old at collect time, not installed. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our Mac seats live in the terminal multiplexer under our multiplexer launcher, and our watchdog only knows quiet: it cannot tell a seat waiting on a permission prompt from one that finished a turn or one still working; per the pack, switchboard adds exactly that attention routing across all sessions, who needs Haiyuan, who is done, which worktree and branch, and what the pane is asking, without a new daemon or state file, its state command is the hook for our other seats' wrappers, and its pane-option model fits our multiplexer isolation rules, with no shared state file and no server-wide polling. Per the playbook, the watchdog acts on a log silent for about 540 s, counts a stated background wait as alive for at most 30 minutes after its line, parks a run whose attempt carries a stop marker and holds a run whose wait deadline it cannot read (#launch, #background-wait, #intentional-stop, #unreadable-deadline), so it reads a little more than quiet, though nothing in it tells a run waiting on a person from one that is done or working; the multiplexer isolation rule asks that a test or script put every multiplexer call on its own private socket and that no seat kill the shared multiplexer server or another agent's sessions (#max-throughput), and whether a layer that writes options on every agent's pane of the shared server fits it is not settled here; and an earlier terminal board of sessions waiting on you was set aside because Haiyuan works from chat and the decision queue, not from a terminal board (below). Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the terminal multiplexer, the Mac CLIs and routines; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: long Mac runs launched through the multiplexer launcher with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s that resumes the same session, a manual convention, since nothing blocks a bare or unwatched launch (#launch, #controls-inventory); the ownership guard, enforced since 2026-10-20 (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), and, installed in the launcher and the watchdog on 2026-11-01, a stop marker that the watchdog and every automatic resume respect (#intentional-stop) and the background-wait allowance above (#background-wait); the EM's 15-minute heartbeat over live agent tasks, which reads the kick ledger first and does not replace the watchdog (#em-loop), with a no-progress flag in a report-only shadow trial that is logged and not sent (#no-progress-flag); two report-only Mac checks, installed with no schedule, one reporting the freshness of run logs, packs and receipt lines (#report-only-checks); one daily decision queue for every item waiting on Haiyuan, re-raised once after three days, emergencies still going to chat, a rule with no tooling adopted (#decision-queue, #decision-queue-kill-receipts); the rule adopted 2026-11-15 that a new routine, or a new kind of message from one, starts quiet: a message that asks Haiyuan for a decision or an acceptance, reports a failure, a gap or an owed run, delivers a result someone asked for, is required by another rule or is of a kind Haiyuan has agreed to is sent as today, and any other is logged as a would-send line until Haiyuan, shown those lines, agrees, its Monday room-noise check report-only (#earn-attention); one receipt line per routine run, with chat kept quiet on success (#receipt-line); P0 urgency kept keyword-only, with no standing 5-minute poller (§16); and the run lesson that one plugin's tool-use hooks hung 1.5 to 6 or more minutes per tool call and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons). entries.title: retrymemo: memory lifted retrieval scores but showed no clear effect in 125 agent runs
entries.why: Independent research, not a product, made of six experiments, v1 to v5 plus a final replay, asking whether memory stops coding agents repeating mistakes (1,867 KB in the pack's metadata read), as the pack reads its full README (144 lines) and its 177-line case study, which is also published as a web page, with the results files not independently recomputed. The offline retrieval tests, v1 to v4: v1 found a session hit@5 of 64.2%, but a query-blind ranking scored about the same, a metric confound; v2, a fair file-level held-out comparison, found +3.0 points over a no-session control (95% CI -2.7 to +8.0, no clear gain); v3 found sessions worse than a fix index (-4.7, CI -8.8 to -1.2); and v4 found that a failed attempt's memory could point the next attempt at the right file, hit@1 69.0% against 60.0% (+9.0, CI +4.8 to +14.3, pre-registered), which measures file identification, not task completion. The real-agent tests: v5 ran 144 tasks and 576 runs with one vendor model and a minimal coding-agent scaffold, where steps went from 19.73 to 19.19 (-2.7%, an interval that includes 0) and 86.1% against 87.5% of tasks were solved, no clear effect; the final replay was 5 tasks by 5 memory conditions by 5 seeds, 125 runs, all 125 of which passed their task, and none of its three pre-registered comparisons showed a clear effect, a hand-picked lesson against none at 0.00 [-0.15, 0.15], retrieved memory against none at +0.10 [-0.20, 0.45] and a hand-picked lesson against a random one at 0.00 [-0.15, 0.15]; the replay spent $4.53 of a $10 cap. Its method controls: memory is cut by time, at the task's creation date for v1 to v4 and at the review record's time for the replay; every experiment from v2 on was pre-registered and frozen with a git tag before held-out scoring; and the replay runs in a container with no network, a fail-closed privacy check and a hash-chained spend ledger checked before each model request, and is scored in a fresh container with withheld tests. The case study's practical lessons: measure behavior, not retrieval; memory competes with the repository; raw history is a poor memory format; keyword retrieval over review prose misses, the useful lesson reaching the memory text for one task of five; and leaks are everywhere, in git history, dependency caches and branch names, so check the full request, not only the prompt. All of these figures are the author's. Per the pack's own limits line, the replay has four primary tasks, so the smallest possible p-value is 0.125 and nothing could be significant; two of the four sit at the ceiling and three of the four already show the lesson in the repository; v5 and the replay use one agent and one model family; the memory is raw review records cut to 18,000 characters, not distilled lessons; the replay cannot be rerun from the repository, its private task inputs and memory texts being withheld; the frozen analysis has two known reporting gaps, secondary comparisons without bootstrap intervals and token counts that miss 32 format-error responses; v1 to v4 measure file overlap, a proxy; and it has 0 stars. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our harness invests heavily in vault recall, one-line lessons and saying which recalled lesson changed the work, and this is a rare pre-registered negative result showing that a better retrieval metric can coexist with no behavioral change; per the pack, the transferable method is the discipline: freeze the experiment before scoring, cut memory by time to prevent leakage, report a paired interval, count the full request, not just the prompt, for leaks, and judge the agent's behavior rather than hit@5, and it should temper any plan to add more retrieval or bigger memory dumps without a behavioral test. Per the playbook, recall is a grep over the one-line summary line that opens each new note, written in the exact names a later search would use, and a read of each older note's title, the full note opened only when it applies, and the post-task note, and the done receipt where one is written, name the recalled lessons applied, or none applied, policy text only (#memory-loop); its write-to-be-found rule comes from a paper that did not measure it, and the recalled-lessons line is the agent's own report, so whether recall changes what our agents do is not measured here. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the vault, routines and the EM loop; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the shared notes vault as long-term memory, a context repository rather than a chat log, read before every task (#vault); the memory loop above, write only what is new, a summary line first, deletions only after Haiyuan approves the specific items, and say what recall applied, policy text only (#memory-loop), the post-task note a manual control (#controls-inventory); entries.title: Vercel Board: schema-checked messages and task state kept on the board with each task, adapted as a weekly report-only check for nightly runs with no kick-ledger row and for handoff packets
entries.why: Vercel launched Board on 2026-11-18 (X post at 17:59 PT; blog post "Introducing Vercel Board" the same day) as an experimental hosted message board for people and agents, in the blog's words "a headless communication primitive and message store for your agents across tools and environments". Two of its ideas are behind this card. Messages can carry structured data under a named, versioned schema (the blog's example is security-finding@1, "where @1 is the version"), and "Board validates the data when posted". And work handed out through the board starts from a task kept on the board: "Once a task is on Board, an agent can claim it, post updates, and record the result", so, as the Lab decision reads it, board-dispatched work and its record do not come apart. Read with @luosky0314's article (2026-11-19 16:59 PT), a secondary write-up; the Lab decision checked it against Vercel's pages and found that it describes the features correctly but overstates four points. For example, it repeats the blog's over-50% merge figure, Vercel's own unaudited number, while citing only the X post, whose text does not contain it; the post's 48-second video was not checked. Lab decision (memo r1, 2026-11-19, after two blind reviews): skip the hosted board, because our command-line seats would write with the owner's Vercel login under display names, data would sit in Vercel's US storage, readable by default across the team, the product is an experimental beta, and it would be a second task store beside the kick ledger. It recommended adapting three of Board's ideas into the ledger we already run, each report-only at first; this card covers two: Gap E, runs that never get a ledger row, and Gap B, handoff packets never checked against their schema. Gap A, recording a run's end on its row, is a separate proposal. Why the ledger went quiet (read-only check, 2026-11-19 ~23:45 PT; its box reads were not repeated from the Mac): the file is alive (it parses, 486 rows, last update 2026-11-18 03:12 PT, no lock or path change) but it is no longer the live record of coding work. Its status writer, the engineering-manager bot's 15-minute heartbeat that moved rows from posted to launched, pr_open and done, was paused by that bot on 2026-11-05 after it launched reviews below the 15 GB disk floor, a floor removed harness-wide on 2026-11-07; the 11-16 weekly receipts also found no heartbeat receipt line after 11-05. From 2026-11-08 a 30-minute pull-request watch over three repositories replaced it, and the watch writes its own state and receipts files, not the ledger. Rows from that bot stop at 2026-11-06. From 11-07 to 11-19 the check found only nightly-audit rows added (11-08 to 11-16 and 11-18; the audit's slot is 02:59 PT): the 11-17 slot was skipped with the Mac offline and its 09:38 PT catch-up ran with no row; on 11-19 the seat was not kicked, so no row was due. No automatic close was recorded after 11-06: the only closes were a one-off reconcile on request on 11-16, and the 11-18 row still reads launched although its run exited 0 at 03:37 PT. The missing 11-17 row already misled one run: the 11-18 audit prompt expected the seat that had run on 11-17 "from the ledger alone", and the 11-17 kick note caught it. The heartbeat, which opened the ledger before checking sessions and pull requests (#em-loop), is paused, and so is the manager bot's 08:06 pickup check, which compared the ledger with live runs and pull requests; Haiyuan approved that pause on 2026-10-23 (#coding-em-kicks). No November decision note mentions the watch, the kick ledger or its file (a full vault search was not done). The playbook still describes the ledger and the 15-minute heartbeat as live (#coding-em-kicks; #overview-day), and the vault copy of the review skill and, per the check, two box skills still describe the ledger as live. What the report reads instead. Expected nights come from the schedule, not from whatever records exist: one due window per night for the nightly audit (02:59 PT in the playbook's schedule, read on a stated date, #overview-day), built with the window rules of #claim-vs-receipts, which also list a paused routine as paused and leave an unclosed window unjudged. For each judged window it reads the nightly-audit lines in the routine receipts log (box /home/box/agent-data/receipts/routine-receipts.log, #receipt-line), from a copy whose sha256 and as-of time are recorded; the vault's kick note for that night (Ship/builds/YYYY-MM-DD-bqaa-nightly-kick-*.md); and, in the run directory that note names, the run prompt, launch record or log that carries the kick id or launch attempt ID, and the exit record or result file. The ledger (box /home/box/agent-data/handoffs/coding-em-kicks.json) is read only for its rows and packets. Pull-request work since 11-08 lives in the watch's files (box /home/box/agent-data/handoffs/three-repo-watch-state.json and its receipts file). Their format was not read here, so whether they identify individual reviews since 11-08 is not verified; until a read-only copy shows stable per-review ids across those dates, the report shows only the watch's passes for that span, with no per-review count and no missing-row flags. Check 1, nights with no row, in two layers. Each judged window first gets the routine's outcome as #claim-vs-receipts defines it: ran (an ok line), did not run (only skip, fail or parked lines; owed under the payback rule when the Mac was down, #kill-condition), missed (no receipt line, whether or not a kick note exists: owed, never dropped) or unreadable, a gap; a receipts copy that is empty, unreadable or has no line in the span is nothing measured, never a pass. A payback counts only with its own later ok line whose note names the owed window, and a failed payback leaves the window owed. Then every distinct kick in the window is listed with its row status, whatever the routine's outcome: row present (a row with the kick's id); ran with no row (a run prompt, launch record or log carrying the kick id or launch attempt ID, a result or exit file from that attempt in the run directory the kick note names, and a readable ledger with no row of that id); run not shown (a kick note or ok line without that evidence, or evidence whose id matches no note, since a receipt line is written even when nothing happened and a note can be written for a kick that never launched); or not kicked, only when a record says so, as 11-19's receipt does. A result or exit file counts if it names the kick's attempt ID. A file with no ID counts only with a confirmed launch of that attempt and proof that its output folder was fresh or used only by that attempt. A file that is only newer than a prepared prompt does not count; it leaves the kick as run not shown. A kick that covers several windows, such as one catch-up for a whole outage, is counted once. Kicks are matched to notes and rows by kick id or launch attempt ID, never by nearby timestamps: the 11-17 catch-up ran 6 h 39 min after its 02:59 slot. Check 2, packets against the dated rules: each row is dated by its own posted_at, else created_at, converted to PT. Before 2026-09-25: legacy, skipped, never backfilled. From 2026-09-25: a packet with from, to, job_type (exactly one of feature, bug, docs, review or audit), objective, artifacts, decisions, constraints, open_questions (an empty list is fine, a missing key is not) and next_gate; v is optional and, if present, must be 1. A missing, empty or non-text next_gate is flagged; any other value outside the six the schema note lists (hermetic_ci, dual_lgtm, fact_check, repro, haiyuan_merge, haiyuan_approval), such as the memo's planted "merge", is reported for review, not failed, because the 09-25 decision and the playbook give next_gate values only as examples. On a bug job, repro may be missing or null until the repro step runs but must be a path once the implementer has launched; when a row cannot show which launch happened, that part is reported as not verified. From 2026-10-31: packet.source is also required, holding Haiyuan's words as written or, for a long ask or one containing a secret, a message link with its opening lines and any secret left out, or routine:<name> for a routine kick. A missing, empty or non-text source, or a routine source with no name, is flagged; whether other text is his exact words is not checked, because the original message is not in the ledger. Older rows are not backfilled. A row with no date is listed as undated, never passed. For each failing row it also says whether the row carries the packet_incomplete note the rule calls for; the inventory counts a missing field with no note as a fail (#coding-em-kicks; #handoff-packet; #controls-inventory). Today the packet's only check is a shadow completeness check by our decision layer that never blocks and, per the schema note, does not read source until the manager bot updates it. Output and exit codes: one report per run with counts per outcome and per rule, giving row ids and field names, never field values; exit 0 clean, 1 findings, 2 unreadable or empty input, which is a gap, never a pass (#check-can-fail; #negative-claim-check). Proof before it counts (#gate-broken-copy), on copies only, with expected results written first. Nights: a copied ledger without the 11-17 row, plus its receipt line, kick note, run prompt and exit record, with the launch record and fresh-folder proof that a file with no ID needs, must list that kick as ran with no row; the healthy control, the same copy with a matching row, row present; a kick note and an ok line with no execution evidence, run not shown; a parked line saying the seat was not kicked, like 11-19's, did not run and not kicked; a fail line beside a confirmed kick, the kick still listed; two kicks for one owed window, each with its own row status; a scheduled night with no receipt line, with or without a kick note, missed, the noted kick still given its own row status; an exit file with no ID that is only newer than a prepared prompt, and an old exit file left by an earlier attempt, each run not shown; a payback line that names no window, not counted. Packets: no packet at 2026-09-24 23:59 PT skipped, at 2026-09-25 00:00 PT flagged; no source at 2026-10-30 23:59 PT passes (a UTC stamp of 2026-10-31T06:59Z is that minute), at 2026-10-31 00:00 PT flagged; a valid packet with no v passes; planted faults job_type "bugfix", a missing open_questions key, a missing or blank next_gate, an empty source on a 10-31 row and a launched bug job with a null repro, each flagged; next_gate "merge", reported for review; an empty or unreadable ledger or receipts copy, exit 2. Fail = a planted case not flagged, the control flagged, a scheduled night dropped, a pass on empty input, or any write to the ledger. What it never does: block or delay a kick; launch, resume or close anything; or write the ledger (no status changes, no packet_incomplete notes, no backfill). Any message beyond its own report follows the start-quiet rule (#earn-attention). Who reads it in the next 7 days, and what happens while it is parked. While the card is parked, nothing runs and nobody reads a report: no routine calls it, the Lab wiring ledger, which holds rows for adopted items only, has no row for it, and the Monday Lab promotion check on 11-23 (11:30 PT), which asks each adopted card to name what uses it within 7 days, has nothing here to promote; promotion would also need three clean runs, a tested rollback and complete receipts (#promotion-gate). Meanwhile the quiet ledger is still read as it is: the nightly audit picks its seat from it, and the 11-16 weekly receipts listed it as a source; on 11-18 the manager used the previous kick note to correct the seat the ledger suggested. If Haiyuan decides the ledger's future and OKs a build, the first reader would be the manager bot when it compiles the Monday weekly receipts (next 2026-11-23, 10:47 PT, Hunt/agent-manage/YYYY-MM-DD-weekly-receipts.md). The 11-16 edition read the receipts log and the ledger and listed due runs with no receipt line; the next one would add the report's nights that ran with no row (11-17 so far), its missed nights and its packet counts. Haiyuan, who spot-checks one artifact there, would use them to follow up missing runs and packet gaps under the record he chose, and any row repair would still need his OK. The keep-or-retire decision itself comes first and can draw on what exists now: the census, the receipts, the kick notes and the 11-19 ledger check. The first report would be a one-time history pass: the 169 rows posted since 2026-09-25 (a census snapshot at ~21:30 PT on 11-19 found 63 packets and no packet_incomplete note, so at least 106 lack one; the run recounts rather than reusing the snapshot, and the census has no count for the source rule) and the nightly windows of 11-08 to 11-19, which must list the 11-17 kick as ran with no row and give 11-19 as did not run, with no kick. If the writers stay as observed, that week's new rows will be nightly-audit rows for 11-20 to 11-26, catch-ups included (the 11-12 catch-up got a row), and the report checks every row added in the week. A weekly report would not serve the nightly seat pick: it arrives too late for the next night, so that pick still needs the previous kick note, as on 11-18. Three clean runs on new rows (#three-run-proof) need rows to be written again. Decision: Haiyuan approved this card on 2026-11-19 (ask at 23:37 PT). Nothing is installed. What has to happen first: Haiyuan decides whether the kick ledger stays the record of coding work, in which case row writing has to resume, or is retired, in which case the row check moves to whatever record replaces it and the packet check to wherever packets then live; either way the skills and playbook text that still describe the ledger get updated. Building the report, wiring it into any routine, any ledger write, and retiring or reviving the ledger each need his separate OK. Caveats: the census counts are a snapshot relayed from the box; the Lab decision notes that receipts were incomplete in an earlier receipts trial, which is why kick notes and run directories are further inputs; the heartbeat pause, the watch files, the receipt lines and the run exit times come from the 2026-11-19 check and the bots' own messages and were not re-read from the Mac; the watch files' format is unread. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.source: Haiyuan-approved Lab card · 2026-11-19 23:37 PT · Lab decision memo r1, Vercel Board: adopt or skip for our harness (2026-11-19, Gaps E and B, after two blind reviews), with the same night's read-only ledger check · Vercel launch post on X, 2026-11-18 17:59 PT: https://x.com/vercel/status/2123234769236619673 · Vercel blog, Introducing Vercel Board, 2026-11-18: https://vercel.com/blog/introducing-vercel-board · @luosky0314 article on X, 2026-11-19 16:59 PT: https://x.com/luosky0314/status/2123581866901110922
keeps: Gap E, adapted from the memo's daily check to a weekly read-only report: the nightly audit's due windows from the schedule, checked against receipt lines, kick notes, each run's prompt and exit record, and kick-ledger rows, matched by kick id or attempt ID, never by timestamp.

Gap B, adapted: a read-only check of each row's handoff packet against the dated rules: a packet from 2026-09-25, packet.source from 2026-10-31, repro before an implementer launches on a bug job, older rows never backfilled.
From Board's schema idea, only the check against a named, versioned format; here it runs as a weekly report, not when a row is written.
skippedAsCovered: The hosted board itself: command-line seats would write with the owner's login, data would sit in Vercel's US storage, it is an experimental beta, and it would be a second task store beside the ledger.
Leases that expire and hand a task to another worker (Gap C): one owner per run is already enforced by the ownership guard (#watchdog-resume-safety).
Task dependencies (Gap D): each lane already expresses its own join, and the memo found no incident in its sources caused by steps running out of order.
Recording a run's end on its row (Gap A): a separate proposal, not approved with this card.
Blocking a kick on a bad packet, or one locked write path for the ledger: either would change an adopted rule and needs Haiyuan.
entries.plainTitle: A weekly read-only report: nightly audits with no ledger row, and handoff packets that break the rules
entries.whatItIs: A weekly report that only reads. It lists nightly audit runs that left no row in the kick ledger, the file meant to hold one row per coding job; pull-request work, now logged elsewhere, is reported separately. It also checks each row's handoff packet, a short job record, against the rules of the day it was posted. It never stops a job, starts anything or edits the ledger. The idea comes from Vercel Board.
entries.whyItMatters: The ledger went quiet: after 11-06 only the nightly audit added rows, none was closed automatically, and pull-request work moved elsewhere. The 11-17 catch-up audit got no row, so the next night's audit expected the wrong seat. At least 106 of 169 rows since 9-25 lack the required packet. Haiyuan approved this card on 2026-11-19, but nothing is built or read. Once he decides the ledger's future and OKs a build, its findings would reach him in the Monday weekly receipts. Wiring and ledger writes need his OK too.
entries.statusNote: Card approved 2026-11-19 for a weekly read-only report, but nothing is built or installed, so nothing runs and no one reads it; it waits on Haiyuan's decision whether the kick ledger stays the record of coding work or is retired, and building or wiring it and any ledger write each need his separate OK (#coding-em-kicks; #handoff-packet; #claim-vs-receipts).

entries.title: GoldenBrain: a local control desk over a Markdown note queue, with resumable CLI sessions
entries.why: Local control desk for tasks handed to coding CLIs, built on a Python web framework behind a plain browser UI and needing Python 3.12 or newer, as the pack reads its README, its French README, its repository tree and its metadata. It works with any plain folder of Markdown notes, compatible with a common notes app, and keeps each task as a note in a cascade tree that shows its status, its live activity and an engine indicator. It connects to command-line harnesses through their own CLI commands, three coding CLIs in the pack's heading and the commands of four in its why and how lines, and their sessions can be monitored live or resumed at any time. The agent works on the task note through structured card templates: when an execution phase finishes, it appends a done card with artifacts, changes and verification evidence, keeping the note, per the pack, as the single source of truth. A side-by-side view shows the person's own notes beside the agent's live conversation. Its row in the pack has no limits line, no delta-versus-Lab line and no recommended step. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, GoldenBrain directly implements our team's core pattern, the notes vault as the task ledger and the Mac CLI agents as the workers: each task is a Markdown note in a vault folder, GoldenBrain places, queues, supervises and links ordinary CLI harness sessions, and when the agent finishes, it writes a structured summary card back into the note for a person to review; per the pack, that makes it an off-the-shelf reference for a vault-driven supervisor UI and for session resumption. Per the playbook, the vault is the team's long-term memory on the Mac, treated as a context repository and not a chat log, and proof of done is a vault note path or a live URL (#vault); the always-on bots orchestrate and the Mac CLIs execute, with the vault as the memory both layers share (§12); and coding work is tracked as rows in a box-side kick ledger, posted, launched, pull request open or done, or blocked with a note, with no status given (#coding-em-kicks), a ledger that the Lab's Haiyuan-approved decision card of 2026-11-19, parked, records as no longer the live record of coding work. So the vault as our task ledger is the pack's reading, not the playbook's. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the vault, the manager bot's chief-of-staff role, the Mac CLIs and handoffs; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: the vault lifecycle, in which every agent reads the shared contract file, the never-again list, its recent notes and the Decisions that touch the work before a task, and files a dated note after it that opens with a one-line summary and names the recalled lessons applied, manual in the inventory, the memory loop itself policy text only (#vault, #memory-loop, #controls-inventory); memory rules under which every fact routes to one of five buckets, task state a bucket apart from shared memory, and fast-clock facts such as a pull request's tip SHA, quota or CI state are re-fetched live before any action or claim, with no status given (#memory-rules); done receipts whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that actually ran, each with its evidence, and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted (#done-receipt), done itself decided only by a deterministic check, agent self-reports advisory, a manual control in the inventory (#code-decides-done, #controls-inventory); long Mac runs launched through the launcher in a terminal session with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog at about 540 s that resumes the same session, a manual convention, since nothing blocks a bare or unwatched launch (#launch, #controls-inventory), a resume allowed only once the old agent is proven gone, enforced by the ownership guard since 2026-10-20 (#watchdog-resume-safety, #controls-inventory), a stop marker that keeps a run stopped on purpose from being resumed, installed 2026-11-01 (#intentional-stop), resumes that first check the live state behind each step that writes, with no status given (#idempotent-resume), and a pause and resume note reference format naming the branch or worktree, the session and attempt and the remaining work, which never itself authorizes a relaunch (#launch); a handoff packet carrying the ask verbatim on manager handoffs and new coding kicks, report-only in the inventory (#handoff-packet, #controls-inventory), which a census snapshot relayed from the box for that 2026-11-19 decision card found missing from most kick-ledger rows posted since 2026-09-25; the source-event dedupe rule adopted 2026-11-15, policy text only on the Lab card for that adoption, under which each new kick-ledger row records the key of the event that prompted it and a new kick counts as a duplicate, which starts no run, only if a row already carries its key and the EM, comparing their packets, finds that row asks for the same job type and the same objective, while two kicks that word the same work differently may both run and a kick whose source gives no identifier is launched normally, with a note that it has no source key, a rule for new kick-ledger rows only (#source-event-dedupe); and the requirement, adopted the same day, that live ledgers and other box state we would have to rebuild after a wipe keep a copy in the Mac vault, committed to the vault's private git as Haiyuan chose at adoption, while throwaway work can stay on the box, each such keeper allowed to stay DUE until the first full pass over the keeper list ends, at most seven days after adoption, and the copy job counting as done only once one file has been test-restored, the copy to be refreshed at least daily and checked by hash, with no status given beyond its adoption (#shared-box-not-permanent). So a vault that holds the record and the proof, done held to checks that ran, supervised runs that survive a dead window and resume only once the old agent is gone, a typed handoff rule, a dedupe rule for new ledger rows and a rule for daily hash-checked copies of box ledgers are ours already, as manual controls, policy text, a report-only check and the enforced ownership guard; the delta is one local app that keeps each task as a note in a notes folder, links the coding session behind it for live watching or a later resume, shows the person's notes beside the live conversation, and has the agent append its own done card to the note; the pack does not say whether it refuses a task queued twice or keeps a checked copy of its notes. The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names relevo (2026-10-03), plan and report handoffs between an architect agent and builder agents in their own copies of the repository, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage as a supervisor install while manager-bot handoffs and the kick ledger already cover it, and sets GoldenBrain apart as vault notes integrated as the durable task queue and supervisor for CLI sessions. The Lab also holds starlane (2026-10-12), a personal harness around a Markdown notes vault with read-only specialist agents and capped routines, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage; sctxx (2026-09-23), a model-free handoff written from finished transcripts, set aside in the 09-27 triage because vault notes and the kick ledger already carry handoff state; Agent Host Protocol (2026-11-18), agent sessions whose state a host keeps so that they outlive the window they started in, a Lab proposal; session-sentinel (2026-11-14), a list of the agent sessions a reboot or crash cut off mid-task, a Lab proposal; switchboard (2026-11-19), a terminal add-on that shows which coding agent needs you, a Lab proposal; and the pause-and-resume card of 2026-10-20, partly in the harness as the reference format above, with no routine writing one. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for control desk, task queue, task ledger, supervisor, done card, side by side and web UI finds no match; per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no trial, install or adoption step for this KEEP; its why line, an off-the-shelf reference for a vault-driven supervisor UI and session resumption, is the pack's reading, not a recommended step. The pack's headline for GoldenBrain: local control desk for tasks handed to AI coding agents (three named coding CLIs) backed by a Markdown vault note queue & resume loop. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and no negative control is named; the pack suggests no trial. Its done card is the agent's own report on its work, so under our rules it would be a claim to check against the record, never the check that decides done (#code-decides-done, #claim-vs-record). The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Installing it or its web UI on the Mac, pointing it at the vault or at any vault folder, letting it start, supervise or resume any seat's sessions, moving task state into vault notes, letting an agent's done card stand in for a done receipt's VERIFIED line, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it has 3 stars, as the pack's metadata read gives them; it was created at 06:47 PT on the pack's own day, about two and a half hours before the pack was written, and last pushed at 08:42 PT, both within the window, and its head commit a6c741c is stamped 08:42 PT, as the pack gives them. Its Python 3.12 requirement and its local web UI were not exercised here, and how its done card, its cascade tree and its resume behave was read from its READMEs, not seen. The window is the pack's own: a catch-up covering 2026-11-19 09:05 PT to 2026-11-20 09:15 PT, which pays back the 2026-11-20 collect skipped while the Mac was offline. The pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. Harness statuses above are read from the staged playbook, whose inventory is dated 2026-10-20, not from a live audit. Per the pack, the collector read its two READMEs, its tree and its repository metadata through the code host's API; nothing was installed or run, and the collection spent $0. Both stamps carry a time and are converted to PT. Apache-2.0, 3 stars, created 2026-11-20 06:47 PT, pushed 2026-11-20 08:42 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
entries.plainTitle: GoldenBrain: hand tasks to coding agents as notes, then watch or resume them
entries.whatItIs: A local app that keeps each task for a coding agent as a note in a plain folder of Markdown notes, links it to the agent's session, which can be watched live or resumed later, and has the agent add a done note with its changes and evidence.
entries.whyItMatters: Per the collection notes it mirrors how we work, but here the notes vault is our memory and proof of done, not the task list. Only a Lab proposal, not installed: the agent's done note is its own report, not a check that passed, and any change needs Haiyuan.
entries.statusNote: A Lab proposal only: nothing of it is installed, and done is still decided by the manual rule that a deterministic check must pass, not by an agent's own report (#code-decides-done; #controls-inventory).

entries.title: delivery-workflows: per-change spec, plan and state files, with guards on unproven done
entries.why: Spec-driven delivery workflows for coding agents, written in Markdown, shell and JSON, as the pack reads its README, its file tree, its plugin definitions and its standards documentation. One shared phase engine has two front doors: one starts from an issue-tracker card, and the other starts from a requirement document, a code-host issue or a spec-framework folder and needs no external tracker. Every task keeps a strict three-file working folder for its change: a spec with numbered acceptance criteria, the architectural design, a rubric and the evidence required, frozen once the planning gate passes; a plan that is the task ledger, each task a checkbox line with a task id, a parallel tag and an acceptance-criterion tag, with explicit dependencies, plus a chronological log of one line per event; and a machine-readable state file of the current phase, depth, human and reviewer approvals and scope boundaries, which the pack's why line gives as phase, approvals and evidence logs. Dedicated critic and verifier briefs carry negative disproof framing, and guard hooks reject completion if tests or acceptance proofs are missing; per the pack, it enforces engineering standards as automated blocking gates. Its row in the pack has no limits line, no delta-versus-Lab line and no recommended step. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it maps directly onto our EM loop artifacts, the intent, spec and plan files, the dual LGTM and the done receipt, and formalizes an automated delivery engine in which a change folder holds the spec, frozen after the plan gate, the plan with its parallel and acceptance-criterion tags, and the state file, with engineering standards enforced as automated blocking gates. entries.title: agent-copy-sort: lists abandoned agent worktrees and removes only checked, confirmed ones
entries.why: Skill for auditing and cleaning up the worktrees and clones coding agents leave behind, with a script in Python 3.10 or newer, tests and a CI workflow, packaged in the skill-file format the pack says three coding CLIs share, as the pack reads its README, its skill file, its script, its tests and its CI workflow. entries.title: MODEC-CE: stable-first prompt order for cache hits, measured with a sealed evidence chain
entries.why: Measurement harness for cache-aware prompt ordering in multi-agent model calls, in Python 3.10 or newer with the standard library only, as the pack reads its Spanish README with its English summary, its source tree, its tests, its price file and its sealed pilot evidence through the code host's API; the verifier was not run. It reorders each prompt's segments from most stable to most variable (foundation, context, history, role, task, volatile) so that the shared prefix is the part the provider can cache, keeps the content identical between arms and checks it with a SHA-256 fingerprint. A second lever, which the author calls Super-Tokens, replaces each earlier output with a content-hash reference, a truncation of at most 350 characters and its anchors, so history shrinks without a semantic summary. Each measurement is sealed in a SHA-256 hash chain, with an optional HMAC, and a usage field the provider does not report is marked absent and stops the run rather than recording zero cache hits (fail-closed). Per the pack, the author's real pilot on 2026-11-21 used one provider and one model, 3 runs of 16 calls (48 in all, 24 measured calls per arm), arms alternated, three agents, one orchestrator and a generated corpus, and its summary file reports a cache-hit rate of 38.96% for the naive role-first arm against 82.46% for its own order, a cost of $0.034746 against $0.012054 at the declared peak tariff, a 65.3% total-cost saving per run derived from that tariff with an assumed 300 output tokens per request, not from an invoice, total latency of 37.07 s against 38.30 s, about 3% slower, 2 of 3 runs slower, not significant and not the claim, and 50 evidence records; its independent verifier recomputes each digest, each link to the previous hash and each run's saving from the recorded call costs, but not cost from tokens and tariff, and the log has no HMAC and no external anchor, so integrity is checkable but authorship is not. Its delta line in the pack sets it apart from cache-live-control, which decides the cache lifetime per chat, effortless, which shows a cache countdown, and token-weather, which paces usage against the clock, as the missing ordering and measurement layer for multi-agent calls, reporting a real provider pilot rather than a simulation. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our alternate seat runs one provider's model through a model router, and our prompts carry a very large stable prefix (the shared contract file, vault rules, the pack template and skill text) before a small volatile task, so moving the stable block first is, per the pack, a zero-code change with a measurable cost effect, and the measurement design (the same content, a SHA-256 fingerprint, alternating arms, absent is not zero) is reusable for any seat; it would also give our usage dashboard a causal test rather than a display: hold content fixed, change the order, compare cache-read tokens and cost. Per the playbook, that seat's default model runs through a model router on pay-as-you-go credits, at per-token prices the playbook lists (#roster, #providers); the size of our stable prefix and any cache effect are the pack's reading, not a measurement. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to usage and routines; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: a usage dashboard refreshed three times a day, enforced by box crons the Mac cannot read, with per-seat quota and health cards, an activity share read from local transcripts rather than plan dollars and a routine-fire count labelled as a proxy, not dollars or tokens (#usage, #controls-inventory), and the official per-bot usage page read before each Monday kill review, adopted 2026-11-15, with a usage-page gap written when it cannot be read (#official-per-bot-usage), and the playbook describes no cache-read figure on either (see the search below); lookups that error, are rate-limited or come back unexpectedly empty reported as a gap, never as zero, manual in the inventory (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory), and a paged or capped read counted only when it reached the end, policy text only (#paged-reads), the nearest rules to the author's absent-is-not-zero stop; a new check counted only after it is seen failing on a deliberately broken input, a check that examined nothing reported as nothing measured, policy text only (#check-can-fail); the performance-comparison evidence fields, the note that follows the rule that a change is judged by rules it cannot edit, which ask, among seven fields, for the limiter, production-equivalent settings and the alternating-run count with its median and range, call a comparison without a limiter or comparable settings inconclusive and keep external numbers external until reproduced here, with no status given on the page (#check-out-of-reach); run limits whose defaults include $0 spend without Haiyuan's approval, manual (#run-limits, #controls-inventory); and a harness evaluation design whose arms are scored by a sealed check written before the first run with a negative control, in which zero failures is inconclusive, a proposal not approved and not run (#harness-eval). So refusing to read a missing figure as zero, counting only checks that ran, keeping outside numbers outside until reproduced and a dashboard that shows usage are ours already, as manual rules, policy text and box routines; the delta is a way to put the stable part of each prompt first and to measure the cache effect with fixed content, alternating arms and a sealed log. The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names cache-live-control (2026-10-05), set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage as cache lifetime tuning for interactive chats while our runs are one-shot, effortless (2026-10-06), set aside in the same triage because a per-prompt effort judge conflicts with our maximum-effort defaults, and token-weather (2026-10-05), set aside in that triage with its usage-pacing idea sent to a coding handoff proposal. The Lab also holds, unnamed by the pack, a plugin card of 2026-10-01 that puts question-independent context first so more of the prompt is cached on the coding-agent harness our alternate seat runs, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage as an unpublished local plugin whose cache numbers do not transfer to our routed setup, so the ordering idea itself is not new to the Lab and the delta is the measurement design and the pilot; and contextscope (2026-10-02), which shows which part of a request broke the prompt cache, set aside in the same triage with no traced cache problem in our one-shot runs. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): MODEC-CE second, as a measurement, not a rewrite: on a scratch call set through our alternate seat's route, hold content fixed (a SHA-256 of each segment), alternate stable-first against role-first, and read the provider's cache usage fields; claim a saving only if the provider reports cache reads, and otherwise record a no-cache-usage gap. entries.title: agentia-harness: an improvement loop judged by a gate outside its write scope
entries.why: Engineering base around an agent runtime, not another agent framework, in TypeScript on a JavaScript runtime at version 20 or newer, with a CI workflow and 8 test groups plus an offline end-to-end group, as the pack reads its 465-line README in Chinese, its shared contract file, an architecture review dated 2026-11-21, its source tree, its starter example, a fake model endpoint and offline end-to-end scripts, and its CI workflow through the code host's API. It adds three things the runtime deliberately leaves out. Agents and skills are versioned Markdown files with frontmatter, pinned by a lock file whose check fails CI on drift; a skill runs as a sub-run whose system prompt is its body and does not see the main conversation, so it can be evaluated on its own. An eval bench uses rule-based assertions only (text that is or is not contained, matches, tool subsequences and exact tool counts, tool arguments, skills used, a clean finish, token and iteration ceilings) with no model judge; a train split feeds attribution and proposals, a holdout split is run once, only after a single candidate is chosen, timeouts count as failures, and retries happen only on an error stop, never after a failed assertion. Its improvement loop collects failures from the eval report, clusters them by rules, proposes a change (the only model step), verifies it on an in-memory copy with zero side effects, then accepts or reverts it (the only source write, atomic and journaled); the regression gate is lexicographic and a hard veto: a case that passed at baseline and fails on the candidate blocks, a lower pass rate blocks, a flat pass rate with cost or tokens up more than 10% blocks, and a higher pass rate allows, with token growth recorded. One proposal is made per round, the holdout is never reused to try a second candidate, a decision ledger records each proposal's prediction before verification and reconciles it as realized, not realized or unverified, a regress command re-runs the full suite after adoption and exits 1 on a regression, and a revert is explicit and fingerprint-checked. Its delta line in the pack sets it apart from harness-wrangler, which measures harness patterns with repeated runs and confidence intervals, pstack, which runs blind A/B skill evals, tenex, eval-driven development with k-run bars, and prove-it-done, which checks receipts, as the governed improvement loop: train and holdout separation, a gate outside the write scope, single-variable adoption, a lexicographic regression gate, rollback and an evidence ledger in one system. Per the pack, it also surfaced a bug we care about: when an endpoint does not report usage, its cost estimate was set to zero instead of being left undefined, so unknown spend and zero spend collapsed and the budget gate silently failed, the same class of error our usage dashboard must avoid; that bug is the pack's reading of the repository. entries.title: Agent Memory OS: one-shot task tickets and a rule arena that replays past cases
