Its layers are raw transcripts, read-only and parsed in place; salient lessons with positive and negative cases; a structured wiki with one project handover page of at most 80 lines, single-owner pages and an immutable section of verbatim user quotes; and a top index hard-capped at 200 lines or 25 KB. One search goes through all four layers and returns line numbers, headings and backlink clues. A two-pass dreaming step has a cheap model find contradictions in its first pass, then double-verifies both the target sentence and the evidence verbatim before appending them to a to-check section, never editing human prose; its second pass is a zero-model, zero-cost health check of the index budget, page bloat, broken links and orphans, stale checks and hub candidates. entries.title: agent-orchestration (osnoser1): quota-aware routing with reset-time parsing
entries.why: A skill in the shared skill-file format that turns a coding-agent conversation into a quota-aware orchestrator, with an optional helper script in Python 3.9 or newer on the standard library, as the pack reads its README, its skill file, its references on selection, quota errors, harnesses, supervision and verification, its catalog, an example assets file, the helper script and its tests and fixtures through the code host's API. It discovers providers and models, classifies each task by complexity and risk into a tier floor (T1 to T4), and picks a model by preferred strength or family, quota health, policy, soonest reset, cost and effort. The helper probes live quotas through three vendors' own interfaces (one tool's zero-token usage command, one vendor's usage endpoint read with local OAuth credentials that are never logged, and token-count events in another tool's session files for today and yesterday); marks a quota low at 85% or more and exhausted at 98% or more, both configurable, with grouped quota pools so that an exhausted model group does not lock other model families on the same provider; parses mid-run quota errors into an exhausted-until time from absolute dates, time-zone names or relative wording such as a reset in 4h29m, scoped to the model or group that hit the limit; and, when no model meets the tier, by default stages the work: a first phase runs low-risk preparation on the best below-tier model, records a resume follow-up at the target's earliest reset plus 2 minutes, then switches the same child in place to the tier-meeting model for the second phase, the risky change or review, with wait and proceed as explicit alternatives. It also chooses a reviewer at step start by tier, with a fallback order (a different family, then the same family, then below tier, then the same model fresh), a delta re-review rule and a shared evidence pack for cross-family reviews; writes a decision ledger per delegation (timestamp, repository base name, surface, task class, model and effort, reviewer, an outcome of ok, failed, quota, stall or rework, and a findings count) with no prompts, code, secrets, full paths or personal data; and reads an orchestration section of a repository's shared contract file for high-risk paths, model preferences, evidence, checkpoints and known failure remedies. Its delta line in the pack sets it apart from agent-quota-tracker, which keeps rolling-window state and pokes, agent-runway, which checks quota before dispatch, CAPO, which checkpoints at a quota wall and relaunches on another CLI, and downshift, which routes by a deterministic per-subagent policy, as adding live per-provider probes, grouped pools, mid-run error parsing, a staged below-tier plan with an in-place switch and a delegation ledger: selection and recovery, not just a gate or a display. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this is the same shape of problem as the pack itself: the seat scheduled for this slot is quota-limited until 2026-11-22 16:00 PT, and a usable alternate exists; per the pack, the skill's rule that work never waits for a reset while a usable tier-meeting candidate exists matches our keep-going rule, its staged plan is a disciplined version of what we do ad hoc (prepare on the alternate, then switch back for the risky step), its reset-time parser is directly reusable for 429 messages, and its decision ledger would give our three-way capacity split an outcome record instead of a guess. Per the playbook, the hourly collect rotates across three seats by hour (#pipeline), each seat has its fallbacks in the roster, and a fallback seat swaps in immediately when a seat is out (#roster, #max-throughput); the playbook names no keep-going rule, so that comparison is the pack's (see the search below). entries.title: Canopy: live notices of agent collisions and signed, rule-checked landings
entries.why: Coordination and landing layer above git for many agents working in separate worktrees, on a JavaScript runtime at version 22.13 or newer and git 2.38 or newer, with no package-manager dependencies, as the pack reads its full README, its 411-line test report (an in-repo independent tester's report plus builder addenda), its security note, its roadmap, its root tree, its CI workflow and its release metadata through the code host's API. It watches hooks and git to keep a live record of what each agent read and wrote; when one agent changes a function another agent has read or is calling, the second is told on its next tool call, before either commits. Its land command judges a branch by what it really changed, what that affects, how much of the affected code the agent read, whether outside content entered the session and whether the section's rules pass, then lands it, asks a person or refuses; each landing is one signed merge commit with a signed record, and a pre-receive hook on the canonical repository refuses any other route into the main branch. Its rules live in a rules file read from the main branch, never from the branch being judged, so a branch cannot lower the bar it is judged against; they include checks on the exact merge commit, performance budgets, a minimum coverage, a maximum number of changed lines, protected paths, rules against tainted and unwitnessed changes, and a revalidation setting of always or disjoint. It also lists users, owners and model tiers, a second-opinion feature, vulnerability advisories from an open database, environments and promotions, chat and webhook notifications, a live map and a command that shows what changed on the main branch since a worktree last saw it. Per the pack, the repository's own measured table, the builder's, says 93/93 tests pass, a hook round trip takes 0.46 ms at p50 and 1.54 ms at p95 over 2,400 hooks, a semantic conflict is first reported 22 ms after the edit, indexing takes 0.3 s and 1.6 s for 1,000 and 10,000 files, landing adds about 0.6 s, and eight unrelated branches landing at once take 12.2 s with always, 5.9 s with disjoint and 9.2 s for a plain serial queue; the in-repo independent tester ran 83 tests (79 pass, 4 fail in its second snapshot), found defects D1 to D10 and did not count 10 regression tests that failed with 'fetch failed', and the builder's addendum says the open defects were fixed and the final suite is 93/93, a builder claim the pack did not reproduce. entries.title: BriefCheck: checks a review's file-and-line citations against the real diff

It has three deterministic checks plus a skill in the shared skill-file format. Its check command reads any free-form Markdown pull-request review, from standard input, a diff, a local git range, staged changes or a pull request, and verifies every file-and-line citation and every base-side citation against the real diff, flagging deleted lines cited as new-side, lines outside the visible hunks, unknown files and missing citations. Its verify command validates a review table in its own Markdown format against the diff and an optional test log: the table's structure, its canonical judgments (Supported, Contradicted and Insufficient evidence), every file-and-line citation or range on both the new and the base side, and a test-log commit that must match the reviewed diff, with a JSON output and gates that can fail a CI job on contradicted, insufficient or unresolved items. Its pack command assembles an issue, a unified diff and optional test logs from local files, a local git range or a pull-request link inside a boundary framed against prompt injection, and an annotate command prints explicit base and new line numbers for every hunk line; the skill produces a requirement-by-requirement audit table that keeps implementation evidence, test definitions and commit-matched test runs apart, and a CI action publishes one verified comment and fails the job on a chosen gate. Per the pack, its CI matrix runs Python 3.10 to 3.13 plus 3.13 on another desktop operating system, installs the package without dependencies, and runs its unit tests, an offline demo and checks of three fixtures; none of that was run here. Its delta line in the pack sets it apart from claimtrace, which checks claims in a report against the session log, the citation claim-support card, which checks citations claim by claim, prove-it-done, which re-runs one-line checks, treeproof, which signs tree-bound test receipts, and a prior push-gate Lab card, which gates a push on a fresh review at the exact commit, as a diff-line citation verifier that knows the base and new sides, deleted lines, out-of-hunk lines and a test-log commit: narrower and more deterministic than a review agent, and broader than a receipt. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our review and receipt rules say evidence must be explicit, and our packs and pull requests often carry file-and-line citations a model produced; this is the cheapest deterministic check it found for whether a cited line actually existed in the diff, and it also catches a stale test log by its commit, the same class of failure, per the pack, as a review verdict that outlives the head commit. entries.title: Realm: two gates over typed facts; a trivial check is citable only by its author
entries.why: Shared task-and-fact substrate for agents: one embedded-database file with typed nodes (task, fact, decision, artifact and attempt) and two hard gates, in Python 3.9 or newer on the standard library plus a Rust port, as the pack reads its 205-line README, its shared contract file, its briefing, its schema, its 12 test files, its Python command-line tool, its Rust port and its interface code through the code host's API. Its done gate refuses, with exit 2, unless every fact the task reaches through its requires and depends-on links is verified and untainted and the task's lease is still valid, and it also refuses on an expired lease even if no one else has taken the task. Its cite gate refuses unverified, refuted, contested and uncheckable facts, and its sharp rule is that a fact that passed only a trivial check, such as true, or exit 0 in under 50 ms with no output, is citable by its author but refused for everyone else: 'An agent can fool itself; it cannot fool the others.' Citing a fact as an assumption marks a hypothesis and transitively taints everything downstream of it, the done gate refuses any task that depends on a tainted fact, and the taint clears on its own once the root fact is verified. Tasks are leased with a compare-and-swap and a fencing token, 15 minutes by default; a query returns only what changed since a given point; an orchestrate command runs a goal across five coding CLIs it names, a dispatch command hands an existing task to a worker, a run command records the arguments, the exit status and the git revision, and a state command shows the frontier, the leases and the taint; its exit codes tell a refusal (2), a failed verify (5) and an uncheckable fact (8) apart. Per the pack, it ships 12 test files, a Python implementation, a Rust port with a byte-for-byte compatible schema and an interface with snapshot tests, and it has no CI workflow; none of it was run here. Its delta line in the pack sets it apart from prove-it-done, which re-runs one-line checks but records self-reports, agent-orchestra, which needs an independent verifier's witnessed PASS, agent-role-contracts, an offline preflight on declarations, and treeproof, which signs tree-bound test receipts, as making tasks and facts first-class, gating both done and citation, propagating taint and adding the explicit trivial-check authorship rule: a substrate, not another review tool. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our done reports and handoffs are only as good as the facts they cite, and today verified can mean the agent said so; this makes a task's completion depend on typed, checkable facts and makes a fact citable by others only after a real check, though its author may cite one that passed only a trivial check, and its authorship rule catches the cheapest self-serving check. Per the pack, it maps to our done-receipt contract, the prove-it-done card and the handoff packet, and its query for what changed since a given point is a clean way to re-learn only what changed after a handoff. That reading of our receipts is the pack's: per the playbook, self-reports are advisory and done needs a deterministic check that passed (#code-decides-done). Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to the EM loop and routines; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: done decided only by a concrete, deterministic check, such as green tests, an expected file, a commit pushed to the remote or a live page returning 200, with agent self-reports advisory only (#code-decides-done), a completion claim counted only when the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), and a new check counted only after it is seen failing on a deliberately broken input, a check that examined nothing reporting nothing measured and a passing check saying what it examined and what it does not show (#check-can-fail), all manual in the inventory (#controls-inventory), the nearest rules to the trivial-check rule; a gate trusted only after it is seen failing on a planted broken copy beside a healthy control, adopted 2026-11-02 as standard practice, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy); a done receipt whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that actually ran, each with its evidence, and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted (#done-receipt), and a report-only claim checker installed 2026-11-10 that marks each claim in a done report verified, unverified, contradicted or unparsed against the run's own transcript, wired by a closeout rule with no run record yet (#lab-adopted-tools); a zero, none or quiet claim made only after a lookup that worked, manual in the inventory (#negative-claim-check, #controls-inventory); fast-clock facts such as the Mac connection, the pull-request tip commit, quota, access status and CI state re-fetched live before any action or claim, with no status given (#memory-rules); cited vault paths checked before a pointer is written, a manual rule whose lint tool is not installed (#pointer-check); for handoffs, a structured packet on every manager handoff and every new coding kick that passes ownership, not transcripts, with a shadow completeness check that never blocks (#handoff-packet), report-only in the inventory (#controls-inventory); So deterministic done, claims checked against the record, seen-to-fail checks, receipts that name what was not verified and an ownership guard with its own tokens are ours already, as manual rules, policy text, a report-only tool and an enforced guard; the delta is typed facts that a task's done and any citation must pass through, taint that follows an assumption downstream, and the rule that a trivially checked fact counts only for its author. entries.title: eval-hygiene: a measured run-to-run noise floor and two-arm power arithmetic
entries.why: Short measurement note with runnable arithmetic for coding-agent comparisons, two standard-library Python scripts, one for power and one for spread, as the pack reads its 113-line README, both scripts and its license file through the code host's API. Its floor comes from one identical brief, one pristine folder per run, serial runs on the same model with a 1,200 s cap, six runs and none censored: 94,528, 108,047, 147,073, 107,761, 118,354 and 110,013 tokens, a mean of 114,296, a standard deviation of 17,786, a coefficient of variation of 15.6% (13% on output tokens) and a max-to-min ratio of 1.56; the most expensive run produced the shortest implementation, cost and quality were not correlated in six runs, and with n=6 the floor is rough, its own interval for the coefficient running from about 5.9% to 25.2%. Its loudest term was the harness, not the model: a first batch with a broken grader had a 31.9% token coefficient and 373k mean tokens per job, and a second batch with the grader fixed had 15.6% and 114k, with the same brief, model and folder hygiene, so fixing the measurement code made runs 3.3× cheaper and halved the spread. On sample size, the old rule n = (2*cv/effect)**2 sizes one mean against a fixed constant, while comparing two arms needs about 3.5× more, n per arm = 2 (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 (cv / effect)^2: at a 15.6% coefficient and a real 15% difference, two-sided alpha 0.05, 5 runs per arm give 0.33 power, 6 give 0.38, 10 give 0.58, 15 give 0.75 and 20 give 0.86, 17 per arm reach 80% and 23 reach 90%, and five per arm resolve only about a 28% difference at 80%. Its judge floor: where a judge runs something that can vary, run the reference implementation repeatedly and report its failure rate as the floor under every claim; one suite put a spurious failure on one run in five against an unchanged reference, while deterministic compile or byte-compare judges need no repeats. A second harness agreed: a decomp fleet's 15 runs on one finished task at its cheapest rung gave a cost coefficient of 14.5% (a 95% interval of roughly 9 to 20%) against 15.6% here; in that sample cache reads were 81% of tokens and the noisiest component (a 27% coefficient), output was 46% of spend, cache writes 37% and cache reads 17%, total tokens varied by 23.8% against 14.5% for cost, load correlated +0.55 with wall-clock time and +0.23 with cost (n=15, not significant), and all 15 runs passed a gate that different code also passed, so a saturated gate flatters every arm. Per the pack, its evidence is the two scripts with their formulas and a worked example, plus the exact run values and intervals in the README, with no CI, no tests and no independent audit; the author is an agent, and the note itself says a correction is a new claim and needs the same check. Its delta line in the pack sets it apart from the detection-floor card, which states the principle, Harness Wrangler, repeated graded runs with a confidence interval, pstack's blind A/B evals and harness-diff, which prints the detectable effect first, as adding a measured spread floor, the two-arm power formula, the judge-reference floor and the saturated-gate check, and names its most useful line for us: 'five per arm resolves only about a 28% difference at 80% power.' Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our Three-Run Proof is a standing rule and the Lab already has the detection-floor card, under which three runs only catch large regressions; this note supplies a measured floor and the arithmetic, which the pack works out as roughly 20 to 30% power for three runs per arm against a 15% effect, a real comparison needing about 17 runs per arm, and it warns that comparing agents by token count reads the noisiest line on the invoice and that a gate which passes everything is not a comparison. Per the pack, that changes how we should design any skill, prompt or harness A/B and how we read vendor savings claims, and it maps to the Harness Wrangler and pstack blind A/B cards; that is the pack's reading, and the three-runs figure is the pack's arithmetic, not the author's. Per its suggested tags in the pack, it maps to routines and usage; that mapping is the pack's reading, not a decision. We already have: Three-Run Proof before a new routine goes active, observing, correcting on a second input and releasing after a third consecutive clean run, never automating the first success (#three-run-proof), and promotion only after three clean runs, a tested rollback and complete receipts (#promotion-gate), both manual in the inventory (#controls-inventory); a promotion note that says three runs catch only large regressions and lists every case that got worse even when all three passed, policy text only (#detection-floor); a replay of saved runs before promoting a skill or prompt change, proposed, from a replay set of 20 to 50 of our own failures judged on the worst of three runs, one with a reworded instruction, a set that is not built (#replay-check, #replay-set, #controls-inventory); a harness evaluation design of 28 of our own cases, 21 dev and 7 held out, scored by a sealed check written before the first run with a negative control, in which zero failures is inconclusive, a proposal not approved and not run (#harness-eval); the performance-comparison evidence fields, the note that follows the rule that a change is judged by rules it cannot edit, which ask, among seven fields, for the limiter, production-equivalent settings and the alternating-run count with its median and range, call a comparison without a limiter or comparable settings inconclusive and keep external numbers external until reproduced here, with no status given on the page (#check-out-of-reach); a flaky test reported under NOT VERIFIED with its hit rate, failures out of runs, never retried until green, policy text only (#flaky-tests), the nearest rule to the judge-reference floor; a check counted only after it is seen failing on a deliberately broken input, policy text only (#check-can-fail), and a gate trusted only after it is seen failing on a planted broken copy beside a healthy control, adopted 2026-11-02 as standard practice, policy text only (#gate-broken-copy), the nearest rules to the saturated-gate check; a gate of our decision layer whose verdicts one answer dominates allowed to go active only if it beats that constant majority answer, manual in the inventory (#constant-baseline, #controls-inventory); and for cost, a usage dashboard refreshed three times a day, enforced by box crons the Mac cannot read, with an activity share read from local transcripts rather than plan dollars and a routine-fire count labelled as a proxy, not dollars or tokens (#usage, #controls-inventory), the official per-bot usage page read before each Monday kill review, adopted 2026-11-15 (#official-per-bot-usage), and run limits with $0 spend without Haiyuan's approval, manual in the inventory (#run-limits, #controls-inventory). So three clean runs with a stated detection floor, an unbuilt replay set judged on the worst of three, an unrun design in which zero failures is inconclusive, alternating runs with a median and range, flaky-test hit rates and gates seen failing are ours already, as manual rules, policy text and proposals; the delta is a measured spread floor, the two-arm power arithmetic that says how many runs a comparison needs, a judge floor measured on an unchanged reference, and the warning, per the pack, that comparing agents by token count reads the noisiest line on the invoice. The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names the detection-floor card (2026-10-04), in the harness as the promotion-note rule above, Harness Wrangler (2026-10-14), set aside in the 10-18 Lab triage as a pattern only with no license file, each comparison costing model spend while our replay set is not built, pstack's blind A/B skill evals (2026-10-20), parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review because our existing unrun eval design comes first, and harness-diff (2026-11-04), paired A/B runs that print the smallest detectable effect first, a Lab proposal. The Lab also holds, unnamed by the pack, agent-harness-eval (2026-10-29), the same tasks on two harness versions where inconclusive is not a pass, a Lab proposal; Beyond Leaderboard Ranks (2026-11-17), where most steps along the best cost-for-accuracy lines were too close to call, a Lab proposal; retrymemo (2026-11-19), whose comparisons planned in advance showed no clear effect, a Lab proposal; Driftproof (2026-10-15), with-and-without-skill evals that issue model-bound receipts, set aside in the 10-18 Lab triage; and Archestra (2026-09-21), in the harness as the constant-baseline rule above. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for A/B, per arm, statistical power, coefficient of variation, reference implementation and saturated finds no match; per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): eval-hygiene fifth, as a correction to our Three-Run Proof: use its power script before the next A/B, since at a 15.6% coefficient a 15% effect needs 17 runs per arm for 80% power while five per arm give about 33% power and resolve only about a 28% difference; for a cheap comparison, at about $0.014 a run by the pack's figure, 17 per arm would cost about 50 cents, which the pack calls no reason to skip; and check that the gate can fail the differences the runs actually produce, since a 100% against 100% gate is not a comparison. The pack's headline for eval-hygiene: a measured ~15.6% cost-noise floor, the two-arm power arithmetic, and judge floors for coding-agent comparisons. The pack's stop/kill condition: no explicit trial rejection criterion is supplied for this KEEP, and the pack leaves the trial's stopping threshold unspecified; it does name a control, the note's judge floor: repeated runs of an unchanged reference implementation, which put a spurious judge failure on one run in five; its own check is that the gate must be able to fail the differences the runs actually produce, since a gate that passes both sides 100% of the time cannot tell them apart; and it does not say which harness change to make. The playbook asks each routine prompt for a pre-written kill condition, rules with no tooling adopted, checked in the manual Monday kill review (#kill-condition, #decision-queue-kill-receipts, #kill-review, #controls-inventory). Changing our three-run rule or the promotion gate, adding a runs-per-arm or power requirement to any comparison, spending on comparison runs, even at the pack's cheap 17-per-arm estimate, which the $0 default reserves for Haiyuan (#run-limits), running its scripts on our usage data, adding a spread figure to the usage dashboard, or defining a kill criterion would each be a separate Haiyuan decision; changing our three-run rule needs Haiyuan, and no new seat is added. A hook, wrapper, routine or shared-state change is Tier 3 work, policy text only (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: it has 0 stars, is 7 KB and has no release; it was created at 16:25 PT on 2026-11-21 and last pushed at 06:11 PT on 2026-11-22, both within the window. Its evidence is n=6, one brief, one model and one machine; the second harness's 15-run sample is a separate measurement on someone else's harness, with a fourth block interrupted at 2 of 5 runs, and the design it would have wanted, 4 blocks of 5 runs at least 3 hours apart, was not run. The 15.6% coefficient (13% on output tokens) with its own interval of about 5.9% to 25.2%, the broken-grader batch (31.9%, 373k mean tokens, 3.3× cheaper after the grader fix), the power figures, the one-in-five spurious judge failure and the second harness's figures, among them its 14.5% cost coefficient, are the author's, not ours; the formulas assume approximate normality while cost is right-skewed, and its interval for the coefficient is explicitly optimistic. It is a note plus two scripts, not a harness or a test runner, with no CI, no tests and no independent audit, and its author is an agent. It does not say which harness change to make, only how much evidence a claim needs. The three-runs-per-arm power figure is the pack's arithmetic, and the cost estimate for 17 runs per arm is the pack's, not the author's. The window is the pack's own: one continuous window from 2026-11-21 10:50 PT to 2026-11-22 08:58 PT, 22 h 08 m, collected by the seat scheduled for that day, and the pack says no catch-up was needed. The pack's own Mac readings were collection-time measurements, not a fresh health check. Harness statuses above are read from the staged playbook, whose inventory is dated 2026-10-20, not from a live audit. entries.plainTitle: eval-hygiene: how many runs it takes to tell two agent setups apart
entries.whatItIs: A short note with two small scripts that measures how much token use varies between identical agent runs and works out how many runs each side of a comparison needs before a difference can be trusted.
entries.whyItMatters: Per the collection notes, by the author's figures from six runs on one model, five runs a side resolve only about a 28% difference at 80% power. Only a Lab proposal and not installed; any change needs Haiyuan, including to our three-run rule.

entries.title: dsh-ai-team: an independent read-only reviewer's pass needs graded evidence
entries.why: Plugin for the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs that adds, as the pack reads its README, a separation of powers in three parts: workers implement, an independent read-only reviewer verifies, and a person arbitrates when the reviewer escalates, with a DAG orchestration engine on top of that harness. It does not rebuild the harness's own teammate rosters, task boards or message boards, which it leaves to the harness's official experimental agent-team feature; instead it enforces that no worker can issue its own completion certificate. The reviewer gives strictly one of three verdicts: pass, rework with minimal fix instructions, or escalate, packaged as a single decision for a person; a pass mechanically needs evidence graded E0 to E3 (an assertion, a log snippet, reproducible output, or a deterministic test or hash), and its parser gates force any pass that lacks evidence into rework. Its delta line in the pack sets it apart from a prior seat-worker Lab card, workers in worktrees with review-gated merges, a prior message-bus Lab card, a main-to-line message bus, corralai, whose critic must differ from the writer, and prove-it-done, done receipts in which a self-report never counts, as adding an independent acceptance officer with the E0 to E3 evidence hierarchy and three-state verdicts, mechanically preventing self-certification of completion. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, agent self-reports of completion are notoriously unreliable, which is why our harness has code-decides-done, disproof reviews and done receipts; the seat harness's official agent teams manage message dispatch but lack an independent verification gate, and this plugin supplies the missing mechanical verification layer, so that a task cannot exit until an independent inspector verifies real evidence. The pack says our harness enforces those three rules; per the playbook they are manual, and the claim checker beside them is report-only (see below). We already have: for done, done decided only by a deterministic check, with self-reports and our decision layer's completion check advisory only (#code-decides-done), a completion claim counted only when the session record backs it, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record), and a new check counted only after it is seen failing on a deliberately broken input (#check-can-fail), all manual in the inventory (#controls-inventory), a done receipt whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that actually ran, each with its evidence, and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted (#done-receipt), and a report-only claim checker installed 2026-11-10 that gives each claim in a done report VERIFIED, UNVERIFIED, CONTRADICTED or UNPARSED against the run's own transcript, wired by a closeout rule with no run record yet (#lab-adopted-tools); for review, two blind reviews by the reviewer seats on docs, drafts, Lab cards, full-team tests and code pull requests, each reviewer seeing the pull request with intent, spec and plan, plus failing catch tests on analytics SDK pull requests and, on design tasks, the chosen sketch with the rejected options and their evidence, never the other's review, the implementer never reviewing the same artifact, manual in the inventory (#reviewer-rule, #em-loop, #catch-tests, #plan-in-code, #controls-inventory), each review ending in one verdict line on the head commit, APPROVE, REQUEST_CHANGES or ESCALATE, where ESCALATE means only Haiyuan can call it and a review with no parseable line is UNPARSED and never an approval (#review-verdict-line), reviewers who name 2 to 3 rejection criteria before reading and return a FAIL with evidence: file and line, command + output or a failing input (#disproof-review), and a blocking P0 or P1 that cites file and line, command + output or a failing input, or is downgraded to P2 or re-asked once (#review-convergence); for the seat, the seat this plugin targets doing advisory source collection on its hour and, in its small-model role, advisory triage and lint only, never real code, Field Brief writing or review (#coding, #roster), its harness pinned to the 0.2.1 line, enforced in the inventory by the daily update skipping it (#roster, #controls-inventory), and its model run on pay-as-you-go credits (#providers); and for installs, an optional pre-install scan of one third-party skill folder before it is added, a report-only trial, never a gate, with three known gaps (#preinstall-skill-scan), beside a run lesson in which one plugin's tool-use hooks hung and stalled two runs and the relaunch turned the plugin off for that run only (#mac-run-lessons). So deterministic done, advisory self-reports, a report-only claim checker, two blind reviews with an escalate verdict that only Haiyuan decides, and evidence rules for blockers are ours already, as manual rules and a report-only check; the delta is one plugin inside that seat in which an independent read-only reviewer must issue every pass, a parser gate turns a pass without graded evidence into rework, and a DAG engine runs the work. The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names a prior seat-worker Lab card (2026-11-11), worker agents in isolated worktrees with logged takeovers and review-gated merges, a Lab proposal; a prior message-bus Lab card (2026-10-19), parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review because a desktop-only bus does not serve our headless runs; corralai (2026-10-04), whose critic must differ from the writer, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage as already covered by implementer-is-not-reviewer, disproof review and the check-can-fail rule; and prove-it-done (2026-10-13), receipt-gated completion in which self-reports are recorded but never counted, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage because our done receipt already lists each check with its evidence and it is a skill, not a gate. The Lab also holds, unnamed by the pack, claimtrace (2026-11-07), partly in the harness as the report-only claim checker above; agent-role-contracts (2026-10-19), an offline preflight that rejects self-review and stale handoffs, parked in the 10-25 weekly Lab review in favor of a narrower handoff pilot first; and mstar-harness (2026-11-13), three independent review seats by default and then a separate acceptance step mapped to evidence, a Lab proposal. A text search of the playbook, on the raw page and on its visible text, for acceptance officer, evidence grade, rework, DAG and self-certification finds no match; per the pack this project is not installed and not run here. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pack names no step, scope or trial for this KEEP; its verdict is candidate proposal only (not-adopted), and its draft lines would make the plugin the missing mechanical verification layer for that seat's agent teams, so that no task exits until an independent inspector verifies real evidence. entries.title: dual-brain-guard: blocks commit, push and turn end until a second model audits the diff
entries.why: Zero-dependency, harness-agnostic guard, as the pack reads its README: a command-line tool, a tool server and a native hook adapter for three coding CLIs it names, two of which our seats run (#roster), that mechanically blocks a git commit, a git push, evasive git commands (the pack's examples are git --no-pager commit, git -C repo push and a pull-request merge through the code host's command-line tool) and the end of a turn, by exit code 2, until an independent second model audits the uncommitted git diff produced after the worker's last edit. Edits delegated to that second model advance a mutation counter rather than the audit counter; anti-spoofing logic rejects backgrounded commands and false-green error strings; and opt-outs are not sticky, lasting one turn. Its delta line in the pack sets it apart from regista, a commit blocked without a reviewer verdict fingerprinted to the exact diff, a prior push-gate Lab card, a fresh-session review at the exact commit, treeproof, tree-bound signed test receipts, and ai-jury, a cross-vendor review jury, as a zero-dependency mechanical hook runner across those three CLIs that intercepts their before-tool, after-tool and stop events to catch evasive git calls and blocks completion (exit 2) until an out-of-band second brain reviews the exact diff after the final edit. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it directly addresses a standing team rule that drafts must receive blind review before completion; prompt-only rules that ask an agent to wait for review are frequently bypassed by eager model loops, and this guard enforces that boundary at the shell and stop-hook level, so that no code is committed without an out-of-band audit of the final diff, a claim the guard's own one-turn opt-outs qualify. That reading of our rule is the pack's: per the playbook, the two blind reviews cover docs, drafts, Lab cards, full-team tests and code pull requests, and in the code lane they run on the pull request after the implementer has committed and pushed (see below), not before a commit. We already have: for review, two blind reviews by the reviewer seats on docs, drafts, Lab cards, full-team tests and code pull requests, each reviewer seeing the pull request with intent, spec and plan, plus failing catch tests on analytics SDK pull requests and, on design tasks, the chosen sketch with the rejected options and their evidence, never the other's review, the implementer never reviewing the same artifact, manual in the inventory (#reviewer-rule, #em-loop, #catch-tests, #plan-in-code, #controls-inventory), with the gate two APPROVE verdict lines on the current head commit, and a verdict that names an older commit UNPARSED and never an approval (#review-verdict-line); in the play-by-play, the implementer builds, runs the repository's one-command tests, commits, pushes and opens the pull request without waiting for reviewers, a local CLI review is an optional extra, never a gate, and a merge happens only when Haiyuan asks or under a standing order for that repository (#em-loop); a report-only verdict binder installed 2026-11-09, which adds the sha256 of the diff from the merge base to the head to the verdict line so that a push after the review makes the verdict STALE, blocks and changes nothing by itself, and is wired by a rule in the dual-approval step with no run on a real pull request yet, its card's commit hook not installed (#lab-adopted-tools); the rule that a completion claim must match the session record, with a test-tamper scan of the diff by the EM and each reviewer, a prose rule with no hook installed, under which an enforcing stop hook would be a separate drafted, blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record), the scan also looking for commits made with --no-verify, which skips a repository's hooks, policy text only (#check-can-fail); and a run lesson in which one plugin's tool-use hooks hung and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons). So review on the exact head, a diff-bound verdict check, a tamper scan and the merge gate are ours already, as manual rules and a report-only check; the delta is a block inside the coding CLI itself, on commit, push and the end of a turn, and on some evasive git commands, a pull-request merge among them, until a second model has audited the diff after the last edit, with delegated edits counted as edits and opt-outs that last one turn. The Lab already holds nearby cards: the pack names regista (2026-11-02), a commit hook that needs a reviewer's verdict fingerprinted to the exact diff, partly in the harness as the verdict binder above, with no commit hook installed; a prior push-gate Lab card (2026-10-15), a push gate that needs a fresh-session review at the exact commit, set aside in the 10-18 Lab triage because its review-at-this-commit rule already holds as prose and a live push gate was left to Haiyuan; treeproof (2026-11-17), signed test receipts bound to the working tree with a stop gate that yields after three blocks in a row on the same tree, a Lab proposal; and ai-jury (2026-10-04), a cross-vendor review jury, set aside in the 10-13 Lab triage because a review fan-out costs tokens and a third review seat needs Haiyuan. The Lab also holds, unnamed by the pack, DiffQuorum (2026-11-16), a joint verdict that needs separate files from at least two authors, a Lab proposal, and mstar-harness (2026-11-13), three review seats by default and then an acceptance step mapped to evidence, a Lab proposal.
